They do not accept, do not wish to hear, do not listen to, and do not apply their minds for the sake of knowledge to the brief words, detailed words, illustrative words, and repeated instructions of the Buddhas and their disciples. They are disobedient, do not follow the words, act in opposition, and turn their faces away. Thus, because they do not accept the words, the detailed speech, the teaching, and the instruction of the Buddhas and their disciples, they are called 'avadāniya'. ## 'Settled in the uneven' (te visame niviṭṭhā) means they are established in uneven (unwholesome) bodily action, established in uneven verbal action, established in uneven mental action, established in the uneven taking of life, established in the uneven taking of what is not given, established in the uneven misconduct in sensual pleasures, established in the uneven false speech, established in the uneven malicious speech, established in the uneven harsh speech... established in the uneven frivolous speech... established in the uneven greed, established in the uneven ill-will... established in the uneven wrong view, established in the uneven volitional formations, established in the five uneven cords of sensual pleasure, established in the five uneven hindrances.
29: Those who are attached, established, reached, entered into, obsessed, resolved on, stuck, clinging, and obstructed are settled in the impure, uneven states (visama-dhamma). ## 'Brought to suffering, they lament' means: 'brought to suffering' refers to those who have reached suffering, have fully reached suffering, have approached suffering; those who have reached the hands of Māra, have fully reached the hands of Māra, have approached the hands of Māra; those who have reached death, have fully reached death, have approached death. 'They lament' means they talk, they wail, they sorrow, they grow weary, they weep, they weep beating their breasts, and they fall into confusion. Thus, brought to suffering, they lament. ## 'What will we become after passing away from here?' means: after passing away from this human life, what will we become? Will we become denizens of hell, will we become animals, will we become hungry ghosts, will we become humans, will we become devas, will we become beings with form, will we become formless beings, will we become beings with perception, will we become beings without perception, or will we become beings with neither-perception-nor-non-perception? 'Will we exist in the future, or will we not exist? What will we be? In what way will we be? Having been what, what will we become in the future?' Thus, rushing into doubt, entering into uncertainty, and being of two minds, they talk, they wail, they sorrow, they grow weary, they weep, they weep beating their breasts, and they fall into confusion. Thus, 'What will we become after passing away from here?' ## Therefore, the Blessed One said: ## 'Greedy for sensual pleasures, intent on them, and deluded, those impure ones are settled in uneven states. Brought to suffering, they lament: "What will we become after passing away from here?"' ## Therefore, a being should train right here in this Dispensation; whatever in the world one knows as an uneven state, For the sake of that uneven state, one should not practice unevenly; for the wise say this life is short. ## 'Therefore, a being should train right here in this Dispensation' means: 'therefore' means for that reason, for that cause, due to that condition, because of that origin, seeing such danger in sensual pleasures. 'Should train' refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). ## What is the training in higher virtue? Here, in this Dispensation, a monk is virtuous...
30:
(The monk) dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults, and having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. The small group of virtue, the large group of virtue; for the attainment of wholesome states, virtue is the foundation, the beginning, the basis of conduct, the restraint, the closure, the gate, and the chief—this is the training in higher virtue.

What is the training in higher mind? Here, in this teaching, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of initial and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity—this is the training in higher mind.

What is the training in higher wisdom? Here, in this teaching, a monk is wise; he is possessed of wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' He understands as it really is: 'These are the taints (āsavas)'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of the taints'; he understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints'—this is the training in higher wisdom.

One should train while contemplating these three trainings, train while knowing, train while seeing, train while reflecting repeatedly, train while resolving the mind, train while being convinced through faith, train while exerting energy, train while establishing mindfulness, train while concentrating the mind, train while understanding with wisdom, train while knowing with direct knowledge what should be directly known, train while fully understanding what should be fully understood, train while abandoning what should be abandoned, train while developing what should be developed...
31:
One should train while realizing the Dhamma that should be realized, one should practice the conduct, practice well, and proceed by undertaking it.

"In this teaching" (idha) means: in this view, in this patience, in this preference, in this undertaking, in this Dhamma, in this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this word of the Buddha, in this holy life, in this teaching of the Teacher, in this individual existence, in this world of humans—therefore it is said "in this teaching."
"Being" (jantu) means: a being, a person ...pe... a man—therefore, "therefore, a being should train right here in this teaching."

In the phrase "Whatever uneven things one may know in the world": "Whatever" is a term encompassing everything in every way, without exception, entirely. "One may know uneven things" means: one should know uneven bodily action as an uneven thing, one should know uneven verbal action as an uneven thing, one should know uneven mental action as an uneven thing, one should know uneven killing of living beings as an uneven thing, one should know uneven taking of what is not given as an uneven thing, one should know uneven sexual misconduct as an uneven thing, one should know uneven false speech as an uneven thing, one should know uneven malicious speech as an uneven thing, one should know uneven harsh speech as an uneven thing, one should know uneven frivolous chatter as an uneven thing, one should know uneven covetousness as an uneven thing, one should know uneven ill-will as an uneven thing, one should know uneven wrong view as an uneven thing, one should know uneven volitional formations as uneven things, one should know the five uneven cords of sensual pleasure as uneven things, one should know the five uneven hindrances as uneven things; one should cognize them, specially know them, repeatedly know them, and penetrate them. "In the world" means: in the world of misery ...pe... in the world of sense bases. Thus, "Whatever uneven things one may know in the world."

"One should not practice unevenly because of that uneven thing" means: one should not practice unevenly because of uneven bodily action, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven verbal action, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven mental action, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven killing of living beings, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven taking of what is not given, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven sexual misconduct, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven false speech, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven malicious speech, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven harsh speech, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven frivolous chatter, one should not practice unevenly because of uneven...
32:
One should not practice unrighteous conduct because of covetousness (abhijjhā); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of unrighteous ill-will (byāpāda); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of unrighteous wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of unrighteous formations (saṅkhāra); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of the five unrighteous cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of the five unrighteous hindrances (nīvaraṇa); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of unrighteous volition (cetanā); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of unrighteous longing (patthanā); one should not practice unrighteous conduct because of unrighteous determination (paṇidhi); one should not follow it, should not indulge in it, should not undertake it. This means: for that reason, one should not practice unrighteous conduct.

The wise say that this life (jīvita) is very brief. Life means life-span, duration, subsistence, maintenance, movement, occurrence, preservation, living, and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). Furthermore, life is brief for two reasons: it is brief because of the shortness of its duration, or it is brief because of the shortness of its own nature (sarasa). How is life brief because of the shortness of its duration? In the past mind-moment (cittakkhaṇa), one lived, but does not live now and will not live in the future. In the future mind-moment, one will live, but does not live now and did not live in the past. In the present mind-moment, one lives, but did not live in the past and will not live in the future.

"Life, the physical body, and all pleasure and pain,
Are joined with a single mind; the moment passes very quickly.

Even the deities who remain for eighty-four thousand eons,
Do not live joined with two mind-moments.

Whatever aggregates (khandhā) cease for one who is dying or for one who is staying here,
All are similar, having passed away without reconnection.

Between the aggregates that have just broken up and those that will break up in the future,
There is no difference in the characteristic of those that have ceased in the interval.

One is not born with what has not yet arisen; one lives only with the present.
When the mind breaks, the world is dead; this is a designation in terms of ultimate reality.

Just as waters flow to the lowlands, being inclined by desire,
So the uninterrupted streams flow, conditioned by the six sense bases (saḷāyatana).

The broken aggregates do not go to a storehouse; there is no heap in the future.
Those that have arisen stand like a mustard seed on the point of a needle."
34:
Bhikkhus, this life of humans is very short. One must go to the hereafter; one should understand the truth through wisdom, one should perform meritorious deeds, and one should lead the holy life. For those who are born, there is no such thing as not dying. Bhikkhus, even if one is said to live long, he lives only for a hundred years, or slightly more or less than that.

Human life is short; a good person should despise it.
One should practice with urgency, like one whose head is on fire, for there is no place where Death does not come.
Days and nights pass, life ceases.
The life of mortals comes to an end like the water in small streams.

"The wise say this life is very short." In this context, "Dhīrā" refers to those who are wise, steadfast, endowed with fortitude, and who have abandoned evil. "Dhī" refers to wisdom (paññā). That wisdom consists of: knowing in various ways, knowing the nature of things, investigating and examining impermanence etc., choosing the Four Noble Truths, marking, closely marking, repeatedly marking, the state of being wise, skillfulness, the state of being a good person, clear manifestation, reflection, close observation, wisdom like the earth, wisdom that crushes defilements, wisdom that leads to welfare, insight-wisdom (vipassanā), clear comprehension, wisdom like a goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the weapon of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). Because they are endowed with such wisdom, they are called "Dhīrā" (the wise).

Alternatively, "Dhīrā" refers to those who possess knowledge regarding the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, dependent origination, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the twenty-two faculties, the nine powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold path, the four fruits, and Nibbāna. These wise ones say, teach, speak, show, and designate thus: "The life of humans is short, it is limited, it is little, it lasts but a moment, it is fleeting, it is temporary, it does not last long, it cannot endure for a long time."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, a creature in this world should practice having known [evil]; for no reason in the world should one lead an uneven life. The wise say this life is very short."

I see this multitude of beings in the world trembling, overcome by craving in existences; lowly men lament in the mouth of Death, not being free from craving for repeated existences.
35:
I see this multitude of beings in the world trembling. "Passāmi" means I see with the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu), I see with the divine eye (dibbacakkhu), I see with the wisdom eye (paññācakkhu), I see with the Buddha eye (buddhacakkhu), and I see with the universal eye (samantacakkhu); I see, I look, I gaze, I investigate. "Loke" refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of bases.

"Paripphandamānaṃ" means trembling with the trembling of craving, trembling with the trembling of views, trembling with the trembling of defilements, trembling with the trembling of effort, trembling with the trembling of karmic result, trembling with the trembling of misconduct. Trembling being lustful with lust, trembling being hateful with hatred, trembling being deluded with delusion, trembling being bound by pride, trembling being touched by views, trembling being distracted by restlessness, trembling being unable to reach a decision due to doubt, trembling being under the influence of underlying tendencies. Trembling due to gain, trembling due to loss, trembling due to fame, trembling due to obscurity, trembling due to praise, trembling due to blame, trembling due to pleasure, trembling due to pain. Trembling due to birth, trembling due to aging, trembling due to sickness, trembling due to death, trembling due to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Trembling due to the suffering in hell, trembling due to the suffering in the animal kingdom, trembling due to the suffering in the realm of hungry ghosts, trembling due to the suffering among humans. Trembling due to the suffering rooted in entering the womb, trembling due to the suffering rooted in staying in the womb, trembling due to the suffering rooted in emerging from the womb, trembling due to the suffering attached to one who is born, trembling due to the suffering connected with others for one who is born, trembling due to the suffering caused by one's own effort, trembling due to the suffering caused by the effort of others. Trembling due to the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkha), trembling due to the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), trembling due to the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). Trembling due to the suffering of eye disease, trembling due to the suffering of ear disease, trembling due to the suffering of nose disease... [pe] ... tongue disease... body disease... head disease... ear disease... mouth disease... tooth disease... cough... asthma... catarrh... internal heat... fever... stomach disease... fainting... diarrhea... piercing pain... cholera... leprosy... boils... eczema... consumption... epilepsy... ringworm... itch... scabies... pustules... smallpox... disease caused by blood... disease caused by bile... diabetes... hemorrhoids... tumors... fistula... disease originating from bile... disease originating from phlegm... disease originating from wind... disease originating from the conflict of the humors... disease produced by change of season... disease produced by improper care... disease produced by an attack...
36:
Through disease, through disease born of the ripening of kamma, through cold, through heat, through hunger, through thirst, through defecation, through urination, through the painful suffering caused by the contact of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; through the suffering of a mother's death, the suffering of a father's death, the suffering of a brother's death, the suffering of a sister's death, the suffering of a son's death, the suffering of a daughter's death; through the suffering of the ruin of relatives, the ruin of wealth, the affliction of disease, the ruin of virtue, and the ruin of view—I, the Buddha, see (with the fleshly eye), know (with the divine eye), behold (with the wisdom eye), observe (with the Buddha eye), and investigate (with the universal eye) beings trembling, quivering, shaking, vibrating, swaying, and rocking. This is the meaning of the phrase: "I see the world trembling."

In the phrase "this generation gone to craving in existences," "pajā" is a designation for beings. Craving (taṇhā) consists of craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental objects. "Taṇhāgataṃ" means one who is produced by craving, followed by craving, permeated by craving, approached by craving, cast down by craving, oppressed by craving, and whose mind is overwhelmed by craving. "Bhavesu" refers to the sense-existence (kāma-bhava), the fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava), and the immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava). This is the meaning of the phrase: "this generation gone to craving in existences."

In the phrase "lowly men lament in the mouth of Death," "lowly men" (hīnā narā) are called lowly because they are endowed with lowly bodily actions, lowly verbal actions, and lowly mental actions. They are called lowly men because they are endowed with lowly killing of living beings, lowly taking what is not given, lowly sexual misconduct, lowly false speech, lowly malicious speech, lowly harsh speech, lowly frivolous chatter, lowly covetousness, lowly ill-will, and lowly wrong view. They are also called lowly men because they are endowed with lowly formations (saṅkhāra), the five lowly cords of sensual pleasure, the five hindrances, lowly intention, and lowly aspiration (patthanā, paṇidhi). They are lowly (hīna), degraded (nihīna), deficient (ohīna), inferior (omaka), vile (lāmaka), insignificant (chatukka), and trifling (paritta). This is the meaning of "lowly men."

"Lament in the mouth of Death" means: in the mouth of Death, which is the mouth of Māra, those who have reached death, arrived at death, or approached death; those who have reached Māra, arrived at Māra, or approached Māra; those who have reached mortality, arrived at mortality, or approached mortality—they lament, wail, sorrow, grow weary, weep, beat their breasts and cry, and fall into delusion. This is the meaning of: "lowly men lament in the mouth of Death."

In the phrase "with craving not yet gone in various existences," craving refers to craving for forms up to craving for mental objects. "Bhavābhavesu" means in various existences: in kamma-existence, in renewed existence, in sense-existence; in kamma-existence, in sense-existence, in renewed existence, in fine-material existence; in kamma-existence, in fine-material existence, in renewed existence, in immaterial existence...
37:
...in kamma-existence, in immaterial existence, in renewed existence, in repeated existence; in repeated destiny, in repeated rebirth, in repeated conception, in the repeated manifestation of individual existence; those with craving not gone, craving not departed, craving not given up, craving not vomited, craving not released, craving not abandoned, and craving not relinquished—these are those with craving not yet gone in various existences.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"I see the world trembling, this generation gone to craving in existences;
Lowly men lament in the mouth of Death, with craving not yet gone in various existences."

Behold those trembling in what is called 'mine', like fish in a stream with little water where the flow has dried up; seeing this state, one should live without 'mine-ness', not forming attachment to existences.

In the phrase "Behold those trembling in what is called 'mine'," "mine-ness" (mamatā) is of two kinds: craving-mine-ness (taṇhā-mamatā) and view-mine-ness (diṭṭhi-mamatā). What is craving-mine-ness? It is that which is delimited, bounded, restricted, defined, possessed, and cherished as "mine" by means of craving. It is the grasping: "This is mine, that is mine, this much is mine, to this extent is mine"; my forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles; rugs, clothes, female and male slaves, goats, sheep, poultry, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, mares, fields, sites, silver, gold, villages, towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, countries, treasuries, and granaries; one even regards the entire earth as "mine" by the power of craving. Whatever the one hundred and eight modes of craving are, this is craving-mine-ness.

What is view-mine-ness? It is personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) with twenty bases, wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) with ten bases, extremist view (antaggāhika-diṭṭhi) with ten bases; such views, the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the contortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views, grasping, secondary grasping, adherence, misinterpretation, the wrong path, the false way, falsity, the sectarian sphere, distorted grasping, perverted grasping, erroneous grasping, wrong grasping, the grasping of "truth" in what is not truth. Whatever the sixty-two types of views are, this is view-mine-ness.

In the compound phrase "Behold those trembling in what is called 'mine'," those who suspect that the object they regard as "mine" will be snatched away or destroyed, they tremble; while it is being snatched away, they tremble; after it has been snatched away, they tremble. Those who suspect that the object they regard as "mine" will change and perish, they tremble; while it is changing, they tremble; after it has changed and perished, they tremble, they quiver, they shake, they vibrate, they sway, they rock, they tremble violently. Behold those who are trembling, quivering, shaking, vibrating, swaying, rocking, and trembling violently with their hair standing on end.
38:
Look, behold, contemplate, and investigate. See those trembling in what is cherished as 'mine' (mamāyita). They are just like fish in a place with little water where the stream has dried up. Just as fish in shallow water, in a place where water is exhausted, tremble, quiver, shake, and shudder when they are oppressed, pulled out of the mud, or pecked at by crows, hawks, or herons; even so, beings tremble when they fear their cherished possessions will be snatched away, while they are being snatched away, and after they have been snatched away. They tremble, quiver, shake, and shudder in various ways when they fear those possessions will change and perish, while they are changing, and after they have changed and perished.

Seeing this danger (ādīnava), one should practice without the attachment of 'mine'. Seeing this danger, having compared and investigated it, and having clearly understood it, one should abandon craving-attachment (taṇhā-mamatta) and relinquish view-attachment (diṭṭhi-mamatta). One should live and practice without cherishing as 'mine', without grasping, without misapprehending, and without being obsessed with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; with forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; with family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites; with the sensual realm (kāmadhātu), the fine-material realm (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial realm (arūpadhātu); with sensual becoming (kāmabhava), fine-material becoming (rūpabhava), immaterial becoming (arūpabhava), becoming with perception (saññābhava), becoming without perception (asaññābhava), becoming with neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññābhava), one-constituent becoming (ekavokārabhava), four-constituent becoming (catuvokārabhava), and five-constituent becoming (pañcavokārabhava); and with things past, future, and present that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.

One should practice without forming attachment (āsatti) in existences. One should live without forming attachment—that is, craving (taṇhā), lust (rāga), greed (lobha), and the unwholesome roots—in the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial existences, and without giving rise to desire, affection, and passion.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
39:
“See those trembling in what is cherished, like fish in a place with little water where the stream has dried up. Seeing this, one should practice without 'mine', not forming attachment in existences.”

Having removed desire for both ends, having fully understood contact (phassa) through comprehension (pariññā) and being without greed, not doing what is self-reproachable, the steadfast wise one is not smeared by what is seen and heard.

“Having removed desire for both ends” means: Regarding 'ends' (anta), contact is one end, the origin of contact (samudaya) is the second end. The past is one end, the future is the second end. Pleasant feeling is one end, painful feeling is the second end. Name (nāma) is one end, form (rūpa) is the second end. The six internal bases are one end, the six external bases are the second end. Self-identity (sakkāya) is one end, the origin of self-identity is the second end.

Desire (chanda) refers to: sensual desire (kāmacchanda), sensual lust (kāmarāga), sensual delight (kāmanandī), sensual craving (kāmataṇhā), sensual affection (kāmasneha), sensual fever (kāmapariḷāha), sensual infatuation (kāmamucchā), sensual immersion (kāmajjhosāna), the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the yoke of sensuality (kāmayoga), clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna), and the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchandanīvaraṇa). “Having removed desire for both ends” means one should remove, thoroughly remove, abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to non-existence the desire for both ends.

“Having fully understood contact and being without greed” means: Contact (phassa) refers to eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, mind-contact; designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa), resistance-contact (paṭighasamphassa); contact to be felt as pleasant, contact to be felt as painful, contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant; wholesome contact, unwholesome contact, indeterminate contact; sense-sphere contact, fine-material-sphere contact, immaterial-sphere contact; empty contact, signless contact, undirected contact; mundane contact, supramundane contact; past contact, future contact (present contact, etc.). Such a nature of contact, the act of touching, the state of being touched, is called contact.
40:
Present contact, such contact as this, the mode of touching, the act of touching, the state of being well-touched—this is called contact (phassa).

'Having fully understood contact' means having fully understood contact through the three types of full understanding: full understanding as the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding as investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). What is full understanding as the known? One knows contact: one knows and sees, 'This is eye-contact (cakkhusamphassa), this is ear-contact (sotasamphassa), this is nose-contact (ghānasamphassa), this is tongue-contact (jivhāsamphassa), this is body-contact (kāyasamphassa), this is mind-contact (manosamphassa), this is designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa), this is impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa), this is contact to be felt as pleasant, this is contact to be felt as painful, this is contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, this is wholesome contact, this is unwholesome contact, this is indeterminate contact, this is sense-sphere contact, this is fine-material-sphere contact, this is immaterial-sphere contact, this is contact characterized by voidness (suññata), this is signless contact (animitta), this is undirected contact (appaṇihita), this is mundane contact, this is supramundane contact, this is past contact, this is future contact, this is present contact'—this is full understanding as the known.

What is full understanding as investigation? Having known it thus, one investigates contact as impermanent (anicca), as suffering (dukkha), as a disease (roga), as a boil (gaṇḍa), as a dart (salla), as a calamity (agha), as an affliction (ābādha), as an alien (para), as disintegrating (paloka), as a plague (īti), as a disaster (upaddava), as a fear (bhaya), as a menace (upasagga), as unstable (cala), as fragile (pabhaṅgu), as non-permanent (adhuva), as no protection (atāṇa), as no shelter (aleṇa), as no refuge (asaraṇa), as empty (ritta), as vain (tuccha), as void (suñña), as non-self (anatta), as a danger (ādīnava), as subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma), as coreless (asāraka), as the root of calamity (aghamūla), as murderous (vadhaka), as non-existence (vibhava), as with taints (sāsava), as conditioned (saṅkhata), as Māra's bait (mārāmisa), as subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death, as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as subject to defilement (saṅkilesadhamma), as origin (samudaya), as disappearance (atthaṅgama), as gratification (assāda), as danger (ādīnava), and as escape (nissaraṇa)—this is full understanding as investigation.

What is full understanding as abandoning? Having investigated it thus, one abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to an end the desire and lust (chandarāga) for contact. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, whatever desire and lust there is for contacts, abandon it. Thus that contact will be abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, done away with...'
41:
"...having the nature of not arising in the future'—this is full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). 'Having fully understood contact' means having fully understood contact through these three types of full understanding. 'Unattached' (anānugiddha): greed (gedha) is called craving (taṇhā). Whatever lust, intense lust... covetousness, greed, unwholesome root there is. For whomsoever this greed is abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge—he is called 'unattached' (agiddha). He is unattached to sights, unattached to sounds, unattached to smells, unattached to tastes, unattached to tangibles, unattached to family... group... dwelling... gain... fame... praise... happiness... robes... alms-food... lodging... medicinal requisites for the sick, unattached to the sense-sphere... fine-material-sphere... immaterial-sphere... sense-sphere existence... fine-material-sphere existence... immaterial-sphere existence... existence with perception... existence without perception... existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception... one-constituent existence... four-constituent existence... five-constituent existence... past... future... present... unattached to things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; not greedy, not infatuated, not obsessed, greed-less, greed-gone, greed-relinquished, greed-vomited, greed-freed, greed-abandoned, greed-renounced, lust-less, lust-gone, lust-relinquished, lust-vomited, lust-freed, lust-abandoned, lust-renounced, without hunger (craving), quenched, cooled, experiencing happiness, he dwells with a self that has become sublime—this is the meaning of 'having fully understood contact, he is unattached.'

In the phrase 'not doing that which is self-reproaching,' 'yada' means 'that which.' 'Self-reproaching' (attagarahī) means one reproaches oneself for two reasons: because of what was done and because of what was not done. How does one reproach oneself because of what was done and what was not done? 'I have committed bodily misconduct, I have not performed bodily good conduct'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed verbal misconduct, I have not performed verbal good conduct'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed mental misconduct, I have not performed mental good conduct'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed the taking of life, I have not practiced the restraint from taking life'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed the taking of what is not given, I have not practiced the restraint from taking what is not given'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed sexual misconduct, I have not practiced the restraint from sexual misconduct'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed false speech, I have not practiced the restraint from false speech'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed slanderous speech, I have not practiced the restraint from slanderous speech'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed harsh speech, I have not practiced the restraint from harsh speech'—thus one reproaches oneself. 'I have committed frivolous chatter, I have not practiced the restraint from frivolous chatter'—thus one reproaches oneself.
42: He reproaches himself. 'I have committed covetousness (abhijjhā); I have not practiced non-covetousness (anabhijjhā),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have committed ill-will (byāpāda); I have not practiced non-ill-will (abyāpāda),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have held wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi); I have not held right view (sammādiṭṭhi),' thus he reproaches himself. In this way, he reproaches himself for what has been done (unwholesome) and for what has not been done (wholesome). Alternatively, 'I am one who does not fulfill the virtues (sīla),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I am one who does not guard the doors of the sense faculties (indriya),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I am one who is immoderate in eating (bhojane amattaññū),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I am one who is not devoted to wakefulness (jāgariya),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I am one who is not endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the four right efforts (sammappadhāna),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the five faculties (indriya),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the five powers (bala),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the Noble Eightfold Path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not fully understood the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not abandoned the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not developed the truth of the path (magga-sacca),' thus he reproaches himself. 'I have not realized the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca),' thus he reproaches himself. In this way, he reproaches himself for what has been done and for what has not been done. One who does not perform, does not produce, does not generate, does not bring about through the power of craving, and does not manifest in any way such deeds for which one reproaches oneself, is called 'one who does not do what is self-reproachable.' In the phrase 'The wise one is not smeared by what is seen or heard,' smearing (lepa) is of two kinds: the smearing of craving (taṇhā-lepa) and the smearing of views (diṭṭhi-lepa). This is the smearing of craving; this is the smearing of views. 'Dhīra' means the wise, the intelligent, the one possessed of understanding, the one possessed of knowledge, the one with brilliant wisdom, the one with firm wisdom. The wise one (dhīra), having abandoned the smearing of craving and having relinquished the smearing of views, is not smeared by what is seen, is not smeared by what is heard, is not smeared by what is sensed, is not smeared by what is cognized; he is not particularly smeared, not attached through fetters. He is unsmeared, not particularly defiled, not stained; he is one who has emerged, escaped, and is well-liberated (from defilements), unyoked, and dwells with a mind that has made no boundaries. Thus: 'The wise one is not smeared by what is seen or heard.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Having removed desire for both ends, having fully understood contact (phassa) and being without greed, not doing what is self-reproachable, the wise one (dhīra) is not smeared by what is seen or heard.'
43: By fully understanding perception (saññā) through the three types of full understanding (pariññā), one should cross over the four floods (ogha); the sage (muni), the Arahant, is unsmeared by possessions (pariggaha). Having pulled out the dart of defilements and dwelling with diligent mindfulness, that Arahant has no longing for this world or the next. 'By fully understanding perception through the three types of full understanding, one should cross over the four floods' means: Perception (saññā) includes perception of sensual desire (kāma-saññā), perception of ill-will (byāpāda-saññā), perception of cruelty (vihiṃsā-saññā), perception of renunciation (nekkhamma-saññā), perception of non-ill-will (abyāpāda-saññā), perception of non-cruelty (avihiṃsā-saññā), perception of forms (rūpa-saññā), perception of sounds (sadda-saññā), perception of smells (gandha-saññā), perception of tastes (rasa-saññā), perception of touches (phoṭṭhabba-saññā), and perception of mental objects (dhamma-saññā). Such noting, the mode of noting, and the state of noting is called perception. 'Fully understanding perception' means fully understanding it through the three types of full understanding: full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). What is full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā)? It is knowing perception. One knows and sees: 'This is perception of sensual desire... this is perception of mental objects.' This is called full understanding of the known. What is full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā)? Having thus known it, one investigates perception as impermanent (anicca), as suffering (dukkha), as a disease (roga), as a boil (gaṇḍa) [associated with the root of suffering and the oozing of defilements], as a dart (salla) [hard to extract], as a calamity (agha), as an affliction (ābādha), as an alien (para), as disintegrating (paloka), as a plague (īti), as a disaster (upaddava), as a fear (bhaya), as an adversity (upasagga), as unstable (cala), as fragile (pabhaṅgu)... as the origin (samudaya), as the passing away (atthangama), as the gratification (assāda), as the danger (ādīnava), and as the escape (nissaraṇa). This is called full understanding by investigation. What is full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā)? Having thus investigated, one abandons the desire and lust (chandarāga) for perception. As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, abandon the desire and lust for perception... it will be like a palm-tree stump, not to arise again.' This is full understanding by abandoning. 'One should cross over the flood' means crossing the floods of sensual desire (kāmogha), existence (bhavogha), views (diṭṭhogha), and ignorance (avijjogha). 'The sage is unsmeared by possessions' means: Possession (pariggaha) is of two kinds: craving-possession (taṇhā-pariggaha) and view-possession (diṭṭhi-pariggaha). 'Muni' (sage) refers to knowledge (ñāṇa), wisdom, non-delusion (amoha).
44:
Investigation of states is Right View; one endowed with that wisdom is called a sage (muni), one who has attained sagehood (mona). There are three types of sagehood (moneyya): bodily sagehood, verbal sagehood, and mental sagehood.

What is bodily sagehood? The abandoning of the three types of bodily misconduct is bodily sagehood. The three types of bodily good conduct are bodily sagehood. Knowledge having the body as its object is bodily sagehood. Full understanding of the body is bodily sagehood. The Path associated with full understanding is bodily sagehood. The abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily sagehood. The attainment of the fourth jhāna, which is the cessation of bodily formations (in-and-out breaths), is bodily sagehood. This is bodily sagehood.

What is verbal sagehood? The abandoning of the four types of verbal misconduct is verbal sagehood. The four types of verbal good conduct are verbal sagehood. Knowledge having speech as its object is verbal sagehood. Full understanding of speech is verbal sagehood. The Path associated with full understanding is verbal sagehood. The abandoning of desire and lust for speech is verbal sagehood. The attainment of the second jhāna, which is the cessation of verbal formations (thought and examination), is verbal sagehood. This is verbal sagehood.

What is mental sagehood? The abandoning of the three types of mental misconduct is mental sagehood. The three types of mental good conduct are mental sagehood. Knowledge having the mind as its object is mental sagehood. Full understanding of the mind is mental sagehood. The Path associated with full understanding is mental sagehood. The abandoning of desire and lust for the mind is mental sagehood. The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, which is the cessation of mental formations, is mental sagehood. This is mental sagehood.

"The bodily sage, the verbal sage, the mental sage who is without taints; the sage endowed with sagehood, they call one who has abandoned everything."

"The bodily sage, the verbal sage, the mental sage who is without taints; the sage endowed with sagehood, they call one who has washed away evil."

There are six types of sages endowed with these three qualities of sagehood: the lay sage, the homeless sage, the sage in training, the sage beyond training, the solitary sage, and the sage of sages. Who are the lay sages? Those laypeople who have seen the state (attained the fruit) and understood the Teaching—these are lay sages. Who are the homeless sages? Those renunciants who have seen the state and understood the Teaching—these are homeless sages. The seven types of trainees are sages in training. Arahants are sages beyond training. Paccekabuddhas are solitary sages. The Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas are called sages of sages.
45:
"One does not become a sage by silence alone if one is foolish and ignorant. But the wise man, as if holding a pair of scales, takes up what is noble and avoids evil. Because he avoids evil, he is a sage; for that reason, he is a sage. He who understands both worlds is called a sage for that reason."

"Knowing the Dhamma of the good and the bad in the whole world, internally and externally, having crossed over the net of attachment, worshipped by gods and humans—he is a sage."

Staining (lepa) is of two kinds: the staining of craving and the staining of views. ... This is the staining of craving, this is the staining of views. A sage, having abandoned the staining of craving and relinquished the staining of views, is not stained, not smeared, not defiled in regard to possessions (pariggaha). Being unstained, unsmeared, undefiled, departed, released, liberated, dissociated, he dwells with a mind that has made an end of boundaries. This is the meaning of 'the sage is not stained in regard to possessions.'

In the phrase 'with the dart removed, he practices heedfully,' there are seven darts (salla): the dart of lust, the dart of hatred, the dart of delusion, the dart of pride, the dart of views, the dart of sorrow, and the dart of doubt (kathaṃkathā). For whom these darts are abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, burnt by the fire of knowledge—he is called one with the dart removed, one with the dart extracted, one with the dart pulled out, one with the dart well-removed, one with the dart drawn out, one with the dart very well-drawn out, one who has relinquished the dart, one who has vomited the dart, one who is freed from the dart, one who has abandoned the dart, one who has relinquished the dart once more. He is one without hunger, quenched, cooled, experiencing happiness, and he dwells with himself become sublime. This is the meaning of the term 'abbhūḷhasallo.'

'Practices (caraṃ)' means practicing, dwelling, moving, proceeding, protecting, maintaining. 'Heedful (appamatto)' means one who acts with care, acts constantly, acts firmly, one whose conduct is not sluggish, whose desire is not discarded, whose burden of effort is not laid down in regard to wholesome states. Thinking, 'How shall I fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is not yet fulfilled, or how shall I support with wisdom the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled in various wholesome states?'—the desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, non-regression, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, determination, devotion, and heedfulness in those states. Thinking, 'How shall I fulfill the aggregate of concentration that is not yet fulfilled, or how shall I [support] the aggregate of concentration that is already fulfilled in various wholesome states...'
46:
In the words, “I shall investigate with wisdom”... (similarly with virtue and concentration), one should exert effort in wholesome states. In the thought, “How shall I fulfill the incomplete aggregate of wisdom... the aggregate of liberation... the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation? Or how shall I investigate with wisdom the already fulfilled aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation in those various wholesome states?”—therein, the desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardency, striving, resolve, application, and heedfulness in wholesome states are present.

In the thought, “How shall I fully understand the suffering that has not yet been fully understood? How shall I abandon the defilements that have not yet been abandoned? How shall I develop the path that has not yet been developed? How shall I realize the cessation (Nibbāna) that has not yet been realized?”—therein, the desire, effort, exertion, endeavor, persistence, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardency, striving, resolve, application, and heedfulness in wholesome states are present. Thus, he is one who has pulled out the thorn and lives heedfully.

“He does not long for this world or the next” means he does not long for this world, which is his own individual existence (attabhāva), nor does he long for the next world, which is another’s individual existence. He does not long for this world, which is his own form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; nor does he long for the next world, which is another’s form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. He does not long for this world, which is the six internal sense bases; nor does he long for the next world, which is the six external sense bases. He does not long for this world, which is the human world; nor does he long for the next world, which is the deva world. He does not long for this world, which is the sense sphere; nor does he long for the next world, which is the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere. He does not long for this world, which is the sense sphere and the fine-material sphere; nor does he long for the next world, which is the immaterial sphere. Furthermore, he does not long for, desire, enjoy, wish for, crave, or yearn for destiny (gati), rebirth (upapatti), conception (paṭisandhi), existence (bhava), saṃsāra, or the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). Therefore, it is said, “He does not long for this world or the next.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Having fully understood perception, one should cross the flood; the sage is not smeared by possessions. With the thorn pulled out, living heedfully, he does not long for this world or the next.”

## The Exposition of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta, the Second, is finished.
47:
## 3. Exposition of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta

Now, I shall explain the exposition (niddesa) of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta:

Some indeed speak with a corrupted mind and truly criticize. Furthermore, others speak, considering that criticism to be the truth. The Sage (Muni) does not enter into a dispute that has arisen; therefore, there is no mental barrenness (khila) in the Sage anywhere.

“Some indeed speak with a corrupted mind” means those sectarians (titthiyas) speak with a corrupted mind, an opposing mind, a hostile mind, a struck mind, a repeatedly struck mind, a hateful mind, and a repeatedly hateful mind; they criticize and accuse the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with what is untrue.

“Furthermore, others speak, considering it the truth” means those who believe, accept, and are convinced by the words of those sectarians, perceiving them as true, real, factual, certain, unwavering, and unerring, also criticize and accuse the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with what is untrue.

“The Sage does not enter into a dispute that has arisen” means that dispute has arisen, been produced, generated, manifested, and appeared through the voices of others, insults, and false accusations against the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Regarding “The Sage does not enter,” “Sage” (Muni) refers to the knowledge called “mona”—that wisdom, full understanding, non-delusion, investigation of states, and right view. One endowed with that knowledge is called a Sage, one who has attained sagacity... (pe)... having transcended the net of craving and views, that Sage stands. One who enters into a dispute does so for two reasons: either he enters into a dispute because he has committed a fault, or when he is criticized and accused, he becomes angry, resentful, and dissatisfied, manifesting anger, hate, and discontent. The Sage does not enter into a dispute for two reasons: he does not enter into a dispute because he has committed no fault, or even when criticized and accused, he does not become angry, resentful, or dissatisfied, and does not manifest anger, hate, or discontent. He does not enter, take up, or cling to a dispute for these two reasons.

“Therefore, there is no mental barrenness in the Sage anywhere” means for that reason, there is no state of a corrupted mind or mental barrenness (khila) in the Sage. The five mental barrennesses do not exist, nor do the three barrennesses of greed, hatred, and delusion. Those barrennesses have been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge. “Anywhere” (kuhiñci) means they do not exist at any time, within oneself, externally, or both internally and externally. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Some indeed speak with a corrupted mind; furthermore, others speak, considering it the truth. The Sage does not enter into a dispute that has arisen.”
48:
Because he does not approach, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not settle into dogmatic views, it is said: 'The sage does not enter into the dispute that has arisen.'

Therefore, for that reason, on that account, due to that cause, for the sage, there is no state of a corrupted mind or a mind like a barren wasteland (khila). There are no five mental barrennesses (cetokhila), nor are there the three barrennesses. The barrenness of lust, the barrenness of hatred, and the barrenness of delusion do not exist, are not manifest, are not found, and are not present. They have been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, and made incapable of arising again, burnt by the fire of knowledge. 'Kuhinci' means at any time, in anything, at any place, whether internally, externally, or both. Therefore, it means 'For the sage, there is no barrenness anywhere.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Some indeed speak with a corrupt mind, and some also speak with a truthful mind;
The sage does not enter into the dispute that has arisen, therefore there is no barrenness for the sage anywhere.'

'How could one overcome his own view? Led by desire and settled in his preference,
Making himself complete, he would speak according to how he knows.'

'How could one overcome his own view?' means: Those ascetics of other sects, having killed the female wanderer Sundarī and by publicizing the dispraise of the Sakyan ascetics, thought: 'In this way, we shall regain gain, fame, honor, offerings, and respect.' They held such views, such patience, such preference, such beliefs, such inclinations, and such intentions. They were unable to overcome their own views, patience, preference, beliefs, inclinations, and intentions. Instead, only infamy (ayasa) returned to them. Thus, it means 'How could one overcome his own view?'

Alternatively: 'The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is false'—one who holds such a view, how could he overcome, transcend, or go beyond his own view, patience, preference, belief, inclination, and intention? Why is that? Because for him, that view is thus completed, taken up, grasped, misapprehended, dogmatically settled into, obsessed over, and resolved upon. Thus, it means 'How could one overcome his own view?' 'The world is not eternal... (and so on) ...the world is finite... the world is infinite... the soul is the same as the body...'
49:
'The soul is one thing, the body is another; the Tathāgata exists after death; the Tathāgata does not exist after death; the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, everything else is false'—one who holds such a view, how could he overcome, transcend, or go beyond his own view, patience, preference, belief, inclination, and intention? Why is that? Because for him, that view is thus completed, taken up, grasped, misapprehended, dogmatically settled into, obsessed over, and resolved upon. Thus is the meaning of the phrase 'How could one overcome his own view?'

In the phrase 'Led by desire, settled in preference' (chandānunīto ruciyā niviṭṭho): 'Led by desire' means one is led, carried away, swept along, and brought by one's own view, patience, preference, and belief. Just as one is led, carried away, swept along, and brought by an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, a chariot-vehicle, an ox-vehicle, a goat-vehicle, a sheep-vehicle, a camel-vehicle, or a donkey-vehicle; in the same way, one is led, carried away, swept along, and brought by one's own view, patience, preference, and belief. This is the meaning of 'Led by desire'. 'Settled in preference' means one is settled, established, attached, approached, obsessed over, and resolved upon by one's own view, preference, and belief. This is the meaning of 'Led by desire, settled in preference'.

'Making himself complete' (sayaṃ samattāni pakubbamāno) means: He makes himself well, makes himself full, makes himself non-deficient; he makes himself the foremost, the best, the chief, the supreme, the excellent, and the most eminent. Thinking, 'This teacher is all-knowing (omniscient),' he makes himself well, full, non-deficient, the foremost, the best, the chief, the supreme, the excellent, and the most eminent. Thinking, 'This Dhamma is well-expounded... this group (Saṅgha) is well-practiced... this view is auspicious... this practice is well-prescribed... this path is leading to liberation,' he makes himself well, full, non-deficient, the foremost, the best, the chief, the supreme, the excellent, and the most eminent; he produces, generates, brings forth, and manifests it. This is the meaning of 'Making himself complete'.

'He would speak according to how he knows' (yathā hi jāneyya tathā vadeyya) means: In whatever way he knows, in that way he would speak, tell, say, explain, and express. Thinking, 'The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is false,' in whatever way he knows, in that way he would speak, tell, say, explain, and express. Thinking, 'The world is not eternal... (and so on) ...neither exists nor does not exist,' in that way...
50:
“The Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist after death; only this is true, all else is vain”—as one knows, so one would say, preach, tell, clarify, and explain in various ways. As one knows, so one would speak.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“How could one overcome one's own view? Led by desire, settled in preference, making oneself complete, as one knows, so one would speak.”

The person who, unasked by others, speaks of their own virtue and practices—the skilled call that an ignoble quality, that one who speaks of oneself.

Regarding the phrase 'Yo attano sīlavatāni jantū': 'Yo' refers to a being of such nature, such association, such disposition, such state, such attainment, such quality—whether a king (khattiya), a brahmin, a merchant (vessa), a worker (sudda), a householder, a renunciant, a deva, or a human. 'Sīlavatāni' means there is both virtue (sīla) and practice (vata), and there is practice that is not virtue. What is both virtue and practice? Here, a monk is virtuous, living restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, undertaking and training in the training rules. The restraint, guarding, and non-transgression therein is virtue. The undertaking is practice. It is virtue in the sense of restraint; it is practice in the sense of undertaking. This is called both virtue and practice. What is practice but not virtue? The eight ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)—the forest-dweller's practice, the alms-food eater's practice, the rag-robe wearer's practice, the three-robe wearer's practice, the house-to-house seeker's practice, the one-session eater's practice, the sitter-up's practice, and the any-bed user's practice—these are called practice, not virtue. The undertaking of energy is also called practice, not virtue. “Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in the body dry up. Until I have attained what is to be reached by human strength, human power, human energy, and human effort, there shall be no relaxing of energy”—thus one uplifts the mind and strives. Such an undertaking of energy is called practice, not virtue.
51:
“I will not speak, I will not drink, I will not leave the monastery; as long as the thorn of craving is not pulled out, I will not lie down (sleep).” One uplifts the mind and strives. Such an undertaking of energy is also called practice, not virtue. “I will not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging.” One uplifts the mind and strives. Such an undertaking of energy is also called practice, not virtue. “I will not rise from this seat, descend from the walkway, leave the monastery, leave the lean-to, the mansion, the attic, the cave, the grotto, the hut, the gabled house, the gate-tower, the hall, the pavilion, the meeting hall, the shed, or the foot of the tree until my mind is liberated from the taints without clinging.” One uplifts the mind and strives. Such an undertaking of energy is also called practice, not virtue. “In this very morning, I will bring, fully bring, reach, touch, and realize the Noble Dhamma.” One uplifts the mind and strives. Such an undertaking of energy is also called practice, not virtue. “In this very midday, in the evening, in the morning, in the afternoon, in the first watch, in the middle watch, in the last watch, in the dark fortnight, in the bright fortnight, in the rainy season, in the winter, in the summer, in the first stage of life, in the middle stage of life, in the last stage of life, I will bring, fully bring, reach, touch, and realize the Noble Dhamma.” One uplifts the mind and strives. Such an undertaking of energy is also called practice, not virtue. 'Jantu' means a being, a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a life, a creature, a being, a being, a man. It refers to a being who speaks of their own virtue and practices. 

Regarding 'Anānupuṭṭhova paresaṃ pāvā': 'Paresaṃ' refers to others—kings, brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, renunciants, devas, or humans. 'Anānupuṭṭho' means unasked, unquestioned, unrequested, uninvited, without being inspired. 'Pāvā' means speaking of one's own virtue, or practice, or both virtue and practice. It is saying, “I am accomplished in virtue,” or “accomplished in practice,” or “accomplished in virtue and practice,” by way of birth, lineage, noble status, beauty, wealth, study, or occupation.
52:
Whether by means of an art, or by means of the eighteen branches of science, or by learning, or by ready wit, or by any other ground; or saying, 'I am one who has gone forth from a high family,' or 'I am one who has gone forth from a great family,' or 'I am one who has gone forth from a family of great wealth,' or 'I am one who has gone forth from a family of magnificent possessions'; or saying, 'I am famous and renowned among laypeople and those who have gone forth,' or 'I am a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites'; or saying, 'I am a bearer of the Suttas (Suttantika),' or 'I am a bearer of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara),' or 'I am a Dhamma-preacher (Dhammakathika),' or 'I am a forest-dweller (Āraññika),' or 'I am an alms-food eater (Piṇḍapātika),' or 'I am a rag-robe wearer (Paṃsukūlika),' or 'I am a three-robe wearer (Tecīvarika),' or 'I am an uninterrupted alms-goer (Sapadānacārika),' or 'I am one who refuses later food (Khalupacchābhattika),' or 'I am a sitter (Nesajjika),' or 'I am one who uses whatever seat is offered (Yathāsanthatika)'; or saying, 'I am an attainer of the first jhāna,' or 'I am an attainer of the second jhāna,' or 'I am an attainer of the third jhāna,' or 'I am an attainer of the fourth jhāna,' or 'I am an attainer of the sphere of infinite space,' or 'I am an attainer of the sphere of infinite consciousness,' or 'I am an attainer of the sphere of nothingness,' or 'I am an attainer of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception'—thus, unasked by others, one speaks of oneself, declares, talks, explains, and expresses.

The skilled ones say that such an act is a non-noble practice (anariya-dhamma). 'The skilled ones' refers to those who are skilled in the aggregates (khandha), skilled in the elements (dhātu), skilled in the sense-bases (āyatana), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), skilled in the right efforts (sammap-padhāna), skilled in the bases of power (iddhipāda), skilled in the faculties (indriya), skilled in the powers (bala), skilled in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), skilled in the path (magga), skilled in the fruit (phala), and skilled in Nibbāna. These skilled ones say: 'This nature is the practice of non-nobles; it is not the practice of the Nobles. This nature is the practice of fools; it is not the practice of the wise. This nature is the practice of the unworthy; it is not the practice of the worthy.' Thus they say, declare, talk, explain, and express. Therefore, it is said: 'The skilled ones say that such an act is a non-noble practice.'

'He who praises himself by himself.' 'Atumā' refers to oneself. 'Praises himself by himself' means that he, by himself, speaks of himself: 'I am one possessed of virtue,' or 'I am one possessed of vows,' or 'I am one possessed of virtue and vows'; or by means of birth, or by lineage, or by being a son of a good family, or by beauty of complexion, or by wealth, or by study of the Vedas, or by occupation, or by art, or by science, or by learning, or by wisdom, or by any other ground; or from a high family...
53:
...saying that he has gone forth from a noble family of warriors or brahmins, or from a family with a large retinue, or from a family of great wealth, or from a family of magnificent possessions such as a householder; or that he is famous and renowned with a large following among laypeople and those who have gone forth; or that he is a recipient of the four requisites, namely robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines suitable for the sick; or that he is a bearer of the Suttas, or a bearer of the Vinaya, or a Dhamma-preacher who teaches the Abhidhamma; or that he is one who dwells in the forest, or one who goes for alms, or one who wears rag-robes, or one who possesses only three robes, or one who goes on an uninterrupted alms-round, or one who does not eat after time, or one who has abandoned lying down and only sits, or one who uses whatever seat is provided, or one who has attained the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna, the sphere of infinite space, or the sphere of infinite consciousness.

'Having abandoned both non-existence and existence, having completed the task of the path, with rebirth exhausted—that person is called a Bhikkhu.'

Or he says, teaches, speaks, shows, and declares that he is an attainer of the sphere of nothingness, or an attainer of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the meaning of the phrase 'He who praises himself by himself.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'The person who, unasked by others, speaks of his own virtues and vows to others,
the wise say that he who thus praises himself by himself is practicing a non-noble doctrine.'

A peaceful monk, with a mind quenched from defilements, does not thus boast of himself regarding his virtues. For that Arahant in whom the prominences (ussada) such as lust do not exist anywhere in the world, the wise say that he is one possessed of the noble doctrine.

'A peaceful monk with a mind quenched from defilements.' 'Santo' (peaceful) means one who is peaceful because of the calming of lust, peaceful because of the calming of hatred, peaceful because of the calming of delusion, anger, malice, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, treachery, obstinacy, impetuosity, pride, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence. He is peaceful because of the calming, quieting, allaying, extinguishing, quenching, departure, and subsiding of all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all burning, and all unwholesome formations.
54:
One is called peaceful because of being calmed, especially calmed, extinguished, and fully stilled.

A bhikkhu is so called because he has broken seven things. He has broken self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), he has broken doubt (vicikicchā), he has broken attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa), he has broken lust (rāga), he has broken hatred (dosa), he has broken delusion (moha), and he has broken conceit (māna). He has broken the evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death.

By the path developed by oneself,
Having reached Nibbāna where defilements are extinguished, and being free from doubt,
Having abandoned both the state of non-existence and existence,
Having lived the holy life and ended renewed existence, he is truly a bhikkhu.
(Thus the Blessed One said to Sabhiya.)

"A peaceful monk with a cooled mind" (Santo ca bhikkhu abhinibbutatto) means one whose mind is cooled because lust has been extinguished, cooled because hatred has been extinguished, cooled because delusion has been extinguished, and cooled because anger... ill-will... denigration... domineering... envy... stinginess... deceit... fraud... stubbornness... impetuosity... conceit... arrogance... intoxication... heedlessness... all defilements... all misconduct... all distress... all fever... all burning... and all unwholesome formations (saṅkhāra) have been extinguished. This is the meaning of "Santo ca bhikkhu abhinibbutatto."

In the phrase "Itihanti sīlesu akatthamāno," the word "itihanti" refers to the connection of words, the combination of words, the completion of words, the assembly of letters, the euphony of consonants, and the sequence of words. "Not boasting about virtues" (sīlesu akatthamāno) means: in this Dispensation, some people are boasters and braggarts. They boast and brag, saying, "I am accomplished in virtue," or "accomplished in vows," or "accomplished in virtue and vows," or by birth, or by lineage, or by being a son of a good family, or by beauty of complexion... or "I am an attainer of the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception." He does not boast or brag in this way. He is detached, withdrawn, and abstinent from boasting; he has emerged, is released, and is liberated from it, dwelling with a mind that has broken through boundaries and is dissociated from defilements. This is the meaning of "Itihanti sīlesu akatthamāno."
55:
“The wise call that practice the Noble Dhamma” means: the wise are those skilled in the aggregates (khandha), skilled in the elements (dhātu), skilled in the sense bases (āyatana), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), skilled in the right efforts (sammappadhāna), skilled in the bases of power (iddhipāda), skilled in the faculties (indriya), skilled in the powers (bala), skilled in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), skilled in the path (magga), skilled in the fruits (phala), and skilled in Nibbāna. These wise ones say: “This is the Dhamma of the Nobles, it is not the Dhamma of the non-nobles; this is the Dhamma of the wise, it is not the Dhamma of fools; this is the Dhamma of the virtuous, it is not the Dhamma of the non-virtuous.” Thus they speak, thus they teach the Nobles, thus they declare, thus they show, thus they express. Therefore, it is said, “The wise call that practice the Noble Dhamma.”

“For whom there are no protuberances (ussada) anywhere in the world” means: “For whom” refers to the Arahant whose taints are exhausted. “Protuberances” (ussada) are the seven protuberances: the protuberance of lust, the protuberance of hatred, the protuberance of delusion, the protuberance of conceit, the protuberance of views, the protuberance of defilements, and the protuberance of kamma. For that Arahant, these protuberances do not exist, are not present, are not found; they are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. “Anywhere” means in any place, whether internal, external, or both. “In the world” means in the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, or the world of sense bases. Therefore, it is said, “For whom there are no protuberances anywhere in the world.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“A monk who is peaceful with a cooled mind, not boasting about such virtues,
For whom there are no protuberances anywhere in the world,
Him the wise call one of Noble Dhamma.”

For whom there are conceived, constructed, and put forward views that are not pure; seeing an advantage for himself in his own view, he relies on that shaky peace (view) based on it.

“For whom there are conceived and constructed dhammas” means: “Conception” (pakappanā) is of two kinds: conception through craving (taṇhā-pakappanā) and conception through views (diṭṭhi-pakappanā). ... [omitted] ... This is conception through craving. ... [omitted] ... This is conception through views. “Constructed” (saṅkhatā) means highly constructed, firmly established; or it means impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of the nature of decay, of the nature of passing away, of the nature of fading away, and of the nature of cessation.
56:
Conditioned (saṅkhatā). For one who holds views (diṭṭhigatika), the sixty-two views are called 'dhammas'. The things conceived and conditioned by that person are called 'saṅkhata'.

Placed in front, existing, and not pure (purakkhatā santi avīvadātā). 'Purakkhatā' means there are two ways of placing in front: placing craving in front (taṇhāpurakkhāra) and placing views in front (diṭṭhipurakkhāra). Because craving has not been abandoned and views have not been relinquished, that person lives and moves placing craving or views in front. They have craving as their banner, craving as their standard, craving as their authority. They have views as their banner, views as their standard, views as their authority. They move about surrounded by craving or views. This is called 'purakkhatā'. 'Santi' means they exist, they are found. 'Avīvadātā' means they are not pure, they are defiled, they are conducive to defilement. This is 'purakkhatā santi avīvadātā'.

Whatever benefit one sees in one's own view (yadattani passati ānisamsaṃ). 'Atta' refers to views (diṭṭhi). One sees two kinds of benefits in one's own view: benefits in the present life and benefits in the future life. What is the benefit of a view in the present life? Whatever view the teacher has, the disciples also have that view. The disciples respect, revere, honor, venerate, and pay homage to the teacher who holds such a view. Because of that veneration, the teacher receives the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines for the sick. This is the benefit of a view in the present life. What is the benefit of a view in the future life? This view is sufficient for becoming a nāga, a garuḍa, a yakkha, an asura, a gandhabba, a Great King (Cātumahārājika), Sakka (Indra), a Brahmā, or a deity. This view is capable of purification and liberation. Through this view, beings are purified and liberated. 'I too shall be purified and liberated through this view'—thus one expects future results. This is the benefit of a view in the future life. One sees, looks at, investigates, and contemplates these two kinds of benefits in one's own view.
57:
Depending on that view, he resorts to an unstable peace dependent on conditions (diṭṭhisanti). There are three kinds of peace (santi): absolute peace (accantasanti), peace of the factors (tadangasanti), and conventional peace (sammutisanti).

What is absolute peace? The deathless Nibbāna is called absolute peace. That Nibbāna is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. This is called absolute peace.

What is peace of the factors? For one who has attained the first jhāna, the hindrances are stilled. For one who has attained the second jhāna, initial and sustained thought are stilled. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture is stilled. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, pleasure and pain are stilled. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form, the perception of sensory impact, and the perception of diversity are stilled. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space is stilled. For one who has attained the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness is stilled. For one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness is stilled. This is called peace of the factors.

What is conventional peace? The sixty-two views, which are the peace of views (diṭṭhisanti), are called conventional peace. Indeed, in this context, only conventional peace is intended. 'Taṃ nissito kuppapaṭiccasantiṃ' means one who especially resorts to, depends on, is associated with, approaches, is deeply attached to, and is convinced of the peace (view) that is unstable, highly unstable, trembling, greatly trembling, moving, afflicted, conceived, specially conceived, impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, and subject to destruction, decay, fading away, and cessation.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"For whom there are specially conceived and conditioned dhammas,
Placed in front, existing, and not pure;
Whatever benefit he sees in his own view,
Depending on that, he resorts to an unstable peace dependent on conditions."

"Adherence to views is indeed not easily overcome,
Having reached a conclusion among doctrines, they are firmly grasped.
Therefore, a person, regarding those adherences,
Both rejects and takes up a doctrine."

In the phrase "diṭṭhīnivesā na hi svātivattā", "diṭṭhīnivesā" refers to the adherence and misapprehension that "The world is eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile." This is called adherence to views. "The world is not eternal... the world is finite... the world is infinite..."
58:
The world is eternal, the world is not eternal; the world is finite, the world is infinite; the soul is the same as the body, the soul is one thing and the body another; the Tathāgata exists after death, the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. To think, to misapprehend, and to be inclined towards the view that 'This alone is the truth, all else is falsehood' is called 'adherence to views' (diṭṭhinivesana). Adherences to views are not easily transcended. They are difficult to transcend, difficult to cross over, extremely difficult to cross over, difficult to go beyond, and difficult to abandon. Therefore, adherences to views are not easily transcended.

'Having decided and well-grasped among dhammas' means: 'Among dhammas' refers to the sixty-two types of views. 'Having decided' means having decided, having judged, having investigated, having thoroughly investigated, having weighed, having examined, having clarified, and having made clear.
