'Well-grasped' means grasping by limit, grasping in a heap, grasping as the best, grasping by parts, grasping by accumulation, and grasping by thorough accumulation. To have grasped, misapprehended, adhered to, entered into, and decided that 'This view alone is true, real, factual, existent, as it is, and not otherwise' is what is meant by 'having decided and well-grasped among dhammas.'

'Therefore, a man in those adherences' means: 'Therefore' means for that reason, because of that cause, because of that condition, because of that origin. 'Man' means a being, a man, a youth, a person, an individual, a life-force, a creature, a human, a descendant of Manu. 'In those adherences' means in those adherences to views.

'Discards and takes up a dhamma' means: 'Discards' means discarding for two reasons—discarding because of others' criticism or discarding because of one's own inability. How does one discard because of others' criticism? Another person criticizes: 'That teacher is not omniscient, the Dhamma is not well-expounded, the group is not well-practicing, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path is not leading out (to liberation); in this teacher and so on, there is no purity, no special purity, no complete purity, no liberation, no special liberation, no complete liberation; in this teacher and so on, they are not purified, they are not liberated; they are low, base, inferior, insignificant, of little strength.' Thus another criticizes. When thus criticized, one discards the teacher, discards the teaching of the Dhamma, discards the group, discards the view, discards the practice, and discards the path. In this way, one discards because of others' criticism. How does one discard because of inability? Being unable to fulfill virtue, one discards virtue; being unable to fulfill a vow, one discards the vow.
59:
One who is unable to fulfill virtue and vows discards virtue and vows. Thus one discards because of inability. 'Takes up a dhamma' means one takes up a teacher, takes up the teaching of the Dhamma, takes up a group, takes up a view, takes up a practice, takes up a path, misapprehends it, and adheres to it. In this way, one discards and takes up a dhamma.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Adherences to views are indeed not easily transcended, having decided and well-grasped among dhammas;
Therefore, a man in those adherences discards and takes up a dhamma.'

For the Cleansed One (Dhona), there is no specially conceived view in this world in various states of existence;
Having abandoned deception and conceit, by what [path] would that Cleansed One go, being one who does not rely [on anything]?

'For the Cleansed One, there is no specially conceived view in this world in various states of existence' means: 'Dhona' refers to wisdom (paññā). That wisdom which is understanding, searching, investigating, thoroughly investigating, investigation of dhammas, marking, noting, observing, erudition, skill, cleverness, discernment, reflection, examination, breadth, sagacity, guidance, insight, clear comprehension, a goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the illumination of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of dhammas, right view. Why is wisdom called 'Dhona'? Because by that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Verbal misconduct... mental misconduct is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Lust is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, domineering are shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Envy is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Stinginess is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Deception is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Guile is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Obstinacy is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence are shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. All defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments...
60:
All unwholesome formations are shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely cleansed. For that reason, wisdom is called 'dhonā'.

Alternatively, by Right View, wrong view is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely cleansed. By Right Resolve, wrong resolve is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely cleansed. By Right Speech, wrong speech is shaken off, washed... [and so on]... By Right Action, wrong action is shaken off... By Right Livelihood, wrong livelihood is shaken off... By Right Effort, wrong effort is shaken off... By Right Mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is shaken off... By Right Concentration, wrong concentration is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely cleansed. By Right Knowledge, wrong knowledge is shaken off... By Right Liberation, wrong liberation is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely cleansed.

Alternatively, by the Noble Eightfold Path, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome formations are shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely cleansed. The Arahant is endowed with, fully endowed with, attained to, fully attained to, possessed of, fully possessed of, and accomplished in these cleansing qualities. Therefore, the Arahant is called 'Dhona'. He is a 'Dhona' because he has shaken off lust, shaken off evil, shaken off defilements, and shaken off fevers. 'Kuhinci' means in any place, whether internally, externally, or both internally and externally. 'Loke' means from the world of suffering up to the world of the sense bases.

'Pakappitā' refers to the two kinds of constructions: construction through craving and construction through views... this is construction through craving... this is construction through views. 'Bhavābhave' means in various states of existence: in the kamma-process and the rebirth-process; in the sense-sphere existence, the kamma-process and the rebirth-process in the sense-sphere; in the fine-material existence, the kamma-process and the rebirth-process in the fine-material sphere; in the immaterial existence, the kamma-process and the rebirth-process in the immaterial sphere; in repeated existence, repeated destiny, repeated rebirth, repeated conception, and the manifestation of repeated individualities. For the Dhona (the Purified One), there is no view constructed, specially constructed, specially conditioned, or firmly established anywhere in the world or in various states of existence; such views do not exist, are not found, and are not available. Those views have been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. This is the meaning of 'For the Dhona, there is no constructed view anywhere in the world in various states of existence.'

In the phrase 'Having abandoned deceit and conceit, he is a Dhona', 'māyā' (deceit) refers to a deceptive practice. Here, someone, having committed misconduct by body, having committed misconduct by speech, having committed misconduct by mind...
61:
...having committed misconduct, for the purpose of concealing that evil, he harbors an evil wish: 'May others not know me,' he wishes; 'May others not know me,' he resolves; 'May others not know me,' he speaks; 'May others not know me,' he strives with his body. Such deceit, being deceitful, overstepping, trickery, fraud, craftiness, evasion, hiding, thorough hiding, veiling, complete veiling, not making open, not making manifest, concealment, and evil action—this is called deceit (māyā).

Conceit (māna) is, in one way, the loftiness of mind. In two ways, it is the conceit of self-exaltation and the conceit of disparaging others. In three ways, it is the conceit 'I am superior,' the conceit 'I am equal,' and the conceit 'I am inferior.' In four ways, one generates conceit because of gain, one generates conceit because of fame, one generates conceit because of praise, and one generates conceit because of happiness. In five ways, one generates conceit thinking, 'I am a recipient of pleasant sights,' one generates conceit thinking, 'I am a recipient of pleasant sounds... smells... tastes... touches.' In six ways, one generates conceit because of the perfection of the eye, one generates conceit because of the perfection of the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind. In seven ways, it is conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), pride-over-pride (mānātimāna), inferiority-conceit (omāna), over-estimation (adhimāna), 'I am' conceit (asmimāna), and wrong conceit (micchāmāna). In eight ways, one generates conceit by receiving gain and generates inferiority-conceit by not receiving gain; one generates conceit by having fame and generates inferiority-conceit by not having fame; one generates conceit by being praised and generates inferiority-conceit by being blamed; one generates conceit by being happy and generates inferiority-conceit by being in pain. In nine ways, it is the conceit 'I am superior to the superior,' 'I am equal to the superior,' 'I am inferior to the superior,' 'I am superior to the equal,' 'I am equal to the equal,' 'I am inferior to the equal,' 'I am superior to the inferior,' 'I am equal to the inferior,' and 'I am inferior to the inferior.' In ten ways, someone in this world generates conceit because of birth, or lineage, or noble family, or beauty, or wealth, or study, or occupation, or craft, or science, or learning, or wit, or any other grounds. Such conceit, conceiving, the state of conceiving, loftiness, haughtiness, flaunting like a banner...
62:
The uplifting of the mind, the state of one desiring a banner—this is called conceit (māna). "The Dhona who has abandoned deceit and conceit" means: The Dhona, having abandoned deceit and conceit, having dispelled them, having made an end of them, and having brought them to a state of non-existence, is called "the Dhona who has abandoned deceit and conceit."

In the phrase "By what means would that one without attachments go?": There are two kinds of attachments (upaya)—the attachment of craving (taṇhā-upaya) and the attachment of views (diṭṭhi-upaya). ... This is the attachment of craving. ... This is the attachment of views. For him, the attachment of craving has been abandoned, and the attachment of views has been relinquished. Because the attachment of craving is abandoned and the attachment of views is relinquished, by what lust would that person without attachments go? By what hatred would he go? By what delusion would he go? By what conceit would he go? By what view would he go? By what restlessness (uddhacca) would he go? By what doubt (vicikicchā) would he go? By what underlying tendencies (anusaya) would he go? (Would he go) as "one who is lustful," or "one who is hateful," or "one who is deluded," or "one who is bound," or "one who is misapprehending," or "one who is distracted," or "one who is undecided," or "one who has reached a firm stance"? Those volitional formations (saṅkhāra) that perform special conditioning have been abandoned. Because the volitional formations have been abandoned, by what means would he go to a destination (gati)? (Would he go) as "one born in hell," or "one born in the animal realm," or "one born in the realm of hungry ghosts," or "a human," or "a deva," or "one with form," or "one without form," or "one with perception," or "one without perception," or "one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception"? There is no cause (hetu), no condition (paccaya) arising from an effect, no reason (kāraṇa) residing in its own result for such a state. This is the meaning of "By what means would that one without attachments go?"

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"For the Dhona (the cleansed one), there is no preconceived view anywhere in the world, regarding various states of existence;
Having abandoned deceit and conceit, by what means would that Dhona, being without attachments, go?"
"Indeed, only one with attachments enters into disputes regarding various things. By what means and how could one speak of the one without attachments?
For him, there is no view of 'self' (atta) or 'non-self' (niratta); he has shaken off every view right here."

In the phrase "Indeed, only one with attachments enters into disputes regarding various things": There are two kinds of attachments—the attachment of craving and the attachment of views. ... This is the attachment of craving. ... This is the attachment of views. For him, the attachment of craving is not yet abandoned, and the attachment of views is not yet relinquished. Because the attachment of craving is not abandoned and the attachment of views is not relinquished, he enters into disputes regarding various things. He is spoken of as "one who is lustful," "one who is hateful," "one who is deluded," "one who is bound," "one who is misapprehending," or "one who is distracted."
63:
Because craving has not been abandoned and the support of views has not been relinquished, he comes to be spoken of in various ways as "one who is lustful," "one who is malicious," "one who is deluded," "one who is bound," "one who is misapprehending," "one who is distracted," "one who is unable to decide," or "one who is obsessed." Those volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) have not been abandoned. Because they have not been abandoned, he enters into speech regarding a destination (gati) among the five destinations, as "a hell-being," "an animal," "a hungry ghost," "a human," "a deva," "one with form," "one without form," "one with perception," "one without perception," or "one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception." He enters into, approaches, grasps, misapprehends, and adheres to such speech. Truly, one who has the supports of craving and views enters into disputes regarding various things.

"By what means and how could one speak of the one without attachments?" means: Attachments (upaya) are twofold: the attachment of craving and the attachment of views. For that Arahant, the attachment of craving has been abandoned and the attachment of views has been relinquished. Because craving is abandoned and views are relinquished, by what lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, view, restlessness, doubt, or underlying tendencies could one speak of that person without attachments as "one who is lustful," "one who is malicious," "one who is deluded," "one who is bound," "one who is misapprehending," "one who is distracted," "one who is unable to decide," or "one who is obsessed"? Those volitional formations have been abandoned. Because they are abandoned, by what means could one speak of him as "a hell-being" ... or "one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception"? There is no cause (hetu), no condition (paccaya), no reason (kāraṇa) by which one could speak, preach, declare, illustrate, or designate him. Thus, by what means and how could one speak of the one without attachments?

"For him, there is no 'self' (atta) or 'non-self' (niratta)" means: There is no view of self (attadiṭṭhi) as "self," and no view of annihilation (ucchedadiṭṭhi) as "non-self." There is no "self" to be grasped as "I," and no "non-self" to be relinquished as "not-I." If there is grasping for someone, there is also relinquishing; if there is relinquishing, there is also grasping. The Arahant has completely transcended grasping and relinquishing; he has gone beyond growth and decline. That Arahant is one who has lived the ten abodes (ariyavāsa), practiced the path of conduct, completed the journey, reached the destination (Nibbāna), and for him, the saṃsāra of birth and death no longer exists, and there is no further renewed existence (punabbhava). Thus, for that Arahant, there is no "self" or "non-self."

"He has shaken off every view right here" means: For that Arahant, the sixty-two views have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt up by the fire of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. That Arahant has shaken off, removed, thoroughly discarded, relinquished, and dispelled every view in this very existence.
64:
That Arahant has brought all views to an end, has brought them to non-existence. That Arahant has shaken off all doctrines in this very existence.

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
“Only one who is attached (to craving and views) enters into disputes regarding various teachings. But how and by what means could one speak of an Arahant who is unattached? For that Arahant, there is no notion of 'self' (atta) nor 'non-self' (niratta). That Arahant has shaken off all doctrines in this very existence.”

## The Exposition of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta, Part Three, is finished.

## 4. Exposition of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta

Now, the exposition of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta will be presented—

I see the pure, the supreme, the healthy,
Purity of a person comes through what is seen;
Knowing thus, “This is supreme,”
The observer of purity believes that [seeing] to be knowledge.

In the phrase “I see the pure, the supreme, the healthy”— “I see the pure” means I see purity, I look at purity, I contemplate purity, I focus on purity, I investigate purity. “The supreme health” refers to the attainment of supreme health, the attainment of protection, the attainment of shelter, the attainment of refuge, the attainment of fearlessness, the attainment of the unshakeable, the attainment of the deathless, the attainment of Nibbāna. Thus, it means “I see the pure, the supreme, the healthy.”

In the phrase “Purity of a person comes through what is seen”— it means that through the eye-consciousness seeing forms, there is purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation for a person. It means the person is pure, specially pure, completely pure, liberated, specially liberated, and completely liberated. Thus, it means “Purity of a person comes through what is seen.”

In the phrase “Knowing thus, ‘This is supreme’”— it means one who knows thus, knows repeatedly, knows distinctly, knows by penetrating. Knowing, having known, having weighed, having judged, having clarified, having made clear that “This vision is supreme, the best, the foremost, the most excellent, the chief, the highest, the most sublime.” Thus, it means “Knowing thus, ‘This is supreme’.”
65:
“The observer of purity believes that [seeing] to be knowledge” means: he who sees purity is an “observer of purity” (suddhānupassī). “Believes it to be knowledge” means he believes that the eye-consciousness seeing forms is knowledge, is the path, is the way, is the exit from Saṃsāra. Thus, the observer of purity believes it to be knowledge.

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
“I see the pure, the supreme, the healthy; purity of a person comes through what is seen. Knowing thus, ‘This is supreme,’ the observer of purity believes that [seeing] to be knowledge.”

“If purity comes to a person through what is seen” means: if through the eye-consciousness seeing forms, there were to be purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, liberation from danger, and special liberation for a person; then the person would be pure, specially pure, completely pure, liberated, liberated from danger, and specially liberated. Thus, it means “If purity comes to a person through what is seen.”

“Or if he abandons suffering through knowledge” means: if through the eye-consciousness seeing forms, a person were to abandon the suffering of birth, abandon the suffering of aging, abandon the suffering of sickness, abandon the suffering of death, and abandon the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, physical pain, grief, and despair. Thus, it means “Or if he abandons suffering through knowledge.”

“He is purified by another while still having acquisitions” means: a person is [supposedly] purified, specially purified, completely purified, liberated, liberated from the states of woe, and specially liberated by another impure path, by a wrong practice, by a way that does not lead out of Saṃsāra, excluding the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), excluding the right efforts (sammappadhāna), excluding the bases of power (iddhipāda), excluding the faculties (indriya), excluding the powers (bala), excluding the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and excluding the Noble Eightfold Path. “With acquisitions” (sopadhīko) refers to one who is possessed of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, craving, views, defilements, and grasping. Thus, it means “He is purified by another while still having acquisitions.”

“For his view itself speaks of him as one who says so” means: that very view speaks of that person, saying, “This person is one of wrong view, one of perverted vision.” “As one who says so” refers to one who says, teaches, speaks, explains, and designates in such a manner. “The world is eternal...”
66:
"The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain"—to one who speaks, teaches, says, illustrates, or expresses thus; or "The world is not eternal... the world is finite... the world is infinite... the soul is the same as the body... the soul is different from the body... the Tathāgata exists after death... the Tathāgata does not exist after death... the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain"—to one who speaks, teaches, says, illustrates, or expresses thus, the view itself says, "This person has wrong view, a perverted vision."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"If a man's purity comes by seeing alone,
Or if he abandons suffering through knowledge,
Then he who still has acquisitions (upadhi) is purified by something else;
The view itself speaks of the one who says so."

A Brahmana (an Arahant) does not speak of purity through other means—through what is seen, heard, virtue and vows, or what is sensed. He is unsullied by both merit and evil, has abandoned the view of self, and does not perform volitional formations in this life.

In the phrase "Na brāhmaṇo aññato suddhimāha diṭṭhe sute sīlavate mute vā," the word "na" expresses negation. One is called a "Brahmana" because seven things have been discarded: sakkāya-diṭṭhi (identity view), vicikicchā (doubt), sīlabbata-parāmāsa (clinging to rules and observances), rāga (lust), dosa (hatred), moha (delusion), and māna (conceit). Evil unwholesome states that are defiling, productive of new existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death have been discarded.

The Blessed One said:
"Having expelled all evil unwholesome states,
Free from the stains of defilements, with a well-concentrated mind,
Having crossed over the cycle of rebirth and reached perfection,
Not resorting to craving and views, and unperturbed by worldly conditions—such a one is called a Brahma (Brahmana)."
67:
The Brahmin (Arahant) who has put away evil does not speak of, teach, say, explain, or express purity, supreme purity, or total purity, nor liberation, supreme liberation, or total liberation, through an impure path other than the Noble Path, through wrong practice, or through a path that does not lead to liberation—excluding the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), excluding the right efforts (sammappadhāna), excluding the bases of power (iddhipāda), excluding the faculties (indriya), excluding the powers (bala), excluding the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and excluding the Noble Eightfold Path. Therefore, it is said, "A Brahmin does not say he is purified by another means."

Regarding (the belief in purity) in what is seen, heard, virtue and vows, or what is sensed: some recluses and brahmins believe in purity through sight (diṭṭhi-suddhi). They believe that seeing certain forms is auspicious (maṅgala) and seeing certain forms is inauspicious (amaṅgala). What kind of forms do they believe are auspicious to see? Having risen early, they look for auspicious forms—seeing a blue jay, seeing a young bamboo shoot during the Phussa constellation, seeing a pregnant woman, seeing a boy being carried on shoulders, seeing a full pot, seeing a red fish, seeing a thoroughbred horse, seeing a thoroughbred carriage, seeing a bull, or seeing a tawny cow. They believe seeing such forms is auspicious. What kind of forms do they believe are inauspicious to see? Seeing a pile of straw, seeing a pot of curd, seeing an empty pot, seeing a dancer, seeing a naked ascetic, seeing a donkey, seeing a donkey carriage, seeing a single-yoke vehicle, seeing a blind person, seeing a person with crooked hands, seeing a lame person, seeing a paralyzed person, seeing an old person, or seeing a sick person. They believe seeing such forms is inauspicious. These are the recluses and brahmins who believe in purity through sight. They believe that through seeing, they attain purity, supreme purity, total purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and total liberation.

Some recluses and brahmins believe in purity through hearing (suta-suddhi). They believe that hearing certain sounds is auspicious and hearing certain sounds is inauspicious. What kind of sounds do they believe are auspicious to hear? Having risen early, they listen for auspicious sounds—hearing "May you prosper," or "It is increasing," or "It is full," or "Phussa (constellation)," or "Sorrowless," or "Joyful," or "Good constellation," or "Good omen," or "Glory," or "Increasing glory." They believe hearing such sounds is auspicious. What kind of sounds do they believe are inauspicious to hear? Hearing "Blind," or "Crooked," or "Lame," or "Paralyzed," or "Old," or "Sick," or "Dead," or "Cut," or "Break," or "Burn," or "Destroyed," or "None." They believe hearing such sounds is inauspicious. Such sounds...
68:
They believe that hearing sounds such as "blind," "crippled," "lame," "paralyzed," "aged," "sick," "dead," "cut," "split," "burn," "destroyed," or "no longer exists" is inauspicious. These recluses and brahmins are those who hold the view of purification through hearing (suta-suddhi). They believe that only through hearing do they attain purity, great purity, total purity, liberation, great liberation, and total liberation.

Some recluses and brahmins hold the view of purification through virtue (sīla-suddhi). They believe that merely through virtue, merely through restraint, merely through self-control, and merely through non-transgression do they attain purity, great purity, total purity, liberation, great liberation, and total liberation. The recluse Muṇḍikāputta said this: "Householder, I designate a person who is endowed with four qualities as one who is accomplished in wholesome states, possessed of the highest wholesome states, one who has attained the supreme attainment, an invincible recluse. What are the four? Here, householder, he does not perform any evil deed with the body, he does not speak any evil word, he does not think any evil thought, and he does not lead an evil livelihood. Householder, I designate a person who is endowed with these four qualities as one who is accomplished in wholesome states, possessed of the highest wholesome states, one who has attained the supreme attainment, an invincible recluse." In the same way, some recluses and brahmins hold the view of purification through virtue. They believe that merely through virtue, merely through restraint, merely through self-control, and merely through non-transgression do they attain purity, great purity, total purity, liberation, great liberation, and total liberation.

Some recluses and brahmins hold the view of purification through vows (vata-suddhi). They are those who practice the elephant-vow, the horse-vow, the cow-vow, the dog-vow, the crow-vow, the Vāsudeva-vow, the Baladeva-vow, the Puṇṇabhadda-vow, the Maṇibhadda-vow, the fire-worship-vow, the Naga-vow, the Supaṇṇa-vow, the Yakkha-vow, the Asura-vow, the Gandhabba-vow, the Mahārāja-vow, the Moon-god-vow, the Sun-god-vow, the Indra-vow, the Brahma-vow, the Deva-vow, or the vow of worshipping the directions. These recluses and brahmins are those who hold the view of purification through vows. They believe that only through vows do they attain purity, great purity, total purity, liberation, great liberation, and total liberation.

Some recluses and brahmins hold the view of purification through touch (muta-suddhi). At the appropriate time, they rise and perform acts such as touching the earth, touching green grass, touching cow dung, touching a tortoise, treading on a ploughshare, touching a sesame cart, or eating auspicious sesame.
69:
They apply auspicious sesame oil, eat auspicious tooth-sticks, bathe with fine clay, wear auspicious garments, and wind auspicious turbans. These recluses and brahmins are those who hold the view of purification through touch (muta-suddhi). They believe that only through touch do they attain purity, great purity, total purity, liberation, great liberation, and total liberation. The Brahmin (the Arahant) does not say that purity comes from any other cause.

Regarding "diṭṭhe sute sīlavate mute vā": The Brahmin does not say that purity is attained through purification by sight, nor through purification by hearing, nor through purification by virtue, nor through purification by vows, nor through purification by touch; he does not speak of it, declare it, show it, or designate it. Therefore, it is said: "The Brahmin does not say that purity comes from any other cause, whether from sight, hearing, virtue, vows, or touch."

Regarding "puññe ca pāpe ca anūpalitto": "Merit" (puñya) refers to the wholesome volitional formations (kusalābhisaṅkhāra) occurring in the three realms of existence, and "evil" (apuñya) refers to all unwholesome states. When wholesome volitional formations, unwholesome volitional formations, and imperturbable volitional formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm-tree stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and made such that they are not liable to arise in the future—by this much, one is not smeared, not specially smeared, not smeared in association with fetters, by either merit or evil. One is not defiled, not specially defiled, but like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, one is not wetted; like one who has left his house, one has gone out; like one liberated from the hands of an enemy, one is freed, well-liberated, and dwells with a mind that is detached from defilements and free from boundaries. Therefore, it is said: "Untainted by both merit and evil."

Regarding "attañjaho nayidha pakubbamāno": "Attañjaho" means one who has abandoned self-view (attadiṭṭhi). "Attañjaho" means one who has abandoned grasping (gāha). "Attañjaho" means that all taking, handling, adhering, entering into, and firm entering into by the power of craving and the power of views have been relinquished, vomited, freed, abandoned, and repeatedly renounced. "Nayidha pakubbamāno" means that in this Dispensation, one does not perform, does not generate, does not specially generate, does not produce, and does not produce in every way any wholesome volitional formations, unwholesome volitional formations, or imperturbable volitional formations. Therefore, it is said: "Having abandoned self-view, he no longer constructs (new existence) in this world."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The Brahmin does not say that purity comes from any other cause, whether from sight, hearing, virtue, vows, or touch. Untainted by both merit and evil, having abandoned self-view, he no longer constructs (new existence) in this world."
70:
Abandoning what was before, they rely on another; following the stream of craving, they do not cross over attachment. They seize and they relinquish, like a monkey letting go of a branch to seize another.

'Abandoning what was before, they rely on another' means: Abandoning the former teacher, they rely on another teacher. Abandoning the former teaching, they rely on another teaching. Abandoning the former group, they rely on another group. Abandoning the former view, they rely on another view. Abandoning the former practice, they rely on another practice. Abandoning the former path, they rely on another path, becoming attached, entering into, excessively clinging to, and focusing upon it. This is the meaning of 'Abandoning what was before, they rely on another.'

'Following the stream of craving, they do not cross over attachment' means: 'Ejā' is said to be craving (taṇhā). Whatever lust, passion... [and so on]... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome roots exist. 'Ejānugā' refers to those who follow craving, who have reached craving, who are spread over by craving, who are immersed in, fallen into, oppressed by, and whose minds are possessed by craving. They cannot cross over, cannot emerge from, cannot transcend, cannot completely surpass the attachment of lust, the attachment of hatred, the attachment of delusion, the attachment of conceit, the attachment of views, the attachment of defilements, and the attachment of misconduct. This is the meaning of 'Following the stream of craving, they do not cross over attachment.'

'They seize and they relinquish' means: They seize a teacher, then letting go of that teacher, they seize another. They seize a teaching, then letting go of that teaching, they seize another. They seize a group, then letting go of that group, they seize another. They seize a view, then letting go of that view, they seize another. They seize a practice, then letting go of that practice, they seize another. They seize a path, then letting go of that path, they seize another. They both seize and let go, they take up and they relinquish. This is the meaning of 'They seize and they relinquish.'

'Like a monkey letting go of a branch to seize another' means: For example, just as a monkey wandering in a great forest seizes a branch, then letting go of that branch, seizes another branch. In the same way, many recluses and brahmins seize and let go, take up and relinquish many various views. This is the meaning of 'Like a monkey letting go of a branch to seize another.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Abandoning what was before, they rely on another; following the stream of craving, they do not cross over attachment. They seize and they relinquish, like a monkey letting go of a branch to seize another.'
71:
A being, having personally undertaken vows, goes from high to low, being attached to perceptions. But the one of broad wisdom, a sage who has realized the Truth through the knowledges, does not go from high to low.

'Sayaṃ samādāya vatāni jantu' means undertaking by oneself. 'Vatāni' refers to the elephant-vow, the horse-vow, the cow-vow, the dog-vow, the crow-vow, the Vāsudeva-vow, the Baladeva-vow, the Puṇṇabhadda-vow, the Maṇibhadda-vow, the fire-vow, the naga-vow, the garuda-vow, the yakkha-vow, the asura-vow... [and so on]... taking up, undertaking, being preoccupied with, accepting, handling, and clinging to the practice of worshipping the directions. 'Jantu' means a being or a person.

'Uccāvacaṃ gacchati saññasatto' means going from one teacher to another, from one preacher to another, from one group to another, from one view to another, from one practice to another, from one path to another. 'Saññasatto' refers to one who is attached, intensely attached, attached by perceiving as beautiful or pleasant, clinging, and bound by lust to the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill-will, the perception of cruelty, and the perception of views. Just as a bundle hanging on a peg or an ivory hook in a wall is attached, stuck, and bound, even so is one who is attached, stuck, and bound to the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill-will, the perception of cruelty, and the perception of views.

In the phrase 'Vidvā ca vedehi samecca dhammaṃ', 'Vidvā' means one who is wise, specially knowledgeable, possessed of wisdom, investigative, and reflective. 'Vedehi': the knowledge, wisdom, faculty of wisdom, power of wisdom, investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya) enlightenment factor, examination, insight, and right view present in the four paths are called 'Veda'. It refers to the Arahant who, through those path-knowledges, has reached the end of birth, aging, and death; who has reached the end through fruition; who has reached the end of the world; who has reached Nibbāna. He is called 'Vedagū' because he has reached the end of what should be known, or because he has reached the end of the round of suffering through path-knowledges, or because he knows the seven things. He has already realized self-identity view, doubt, wrong grasp of rules and observances, lust, hatred, delusion, and conceit. That Arahant has already realized the evil unwholesome states that are defiling, productive of new existence, distressing, and resulting in suffering, which lead to future birth, aging, and death.
72:
...is known, lust is known, hatred is known, delusion is known, conceit is known. For that Arahant, the evil unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering when they ripen, and leading to future birth, aging, and death, are known.

Sabhiya, in this world, one should distinguish with wisdom all the known things belonging to recluses and brahmins.
Being free from lust in all feelings, and because of having transcended all enmity, such a person is called a 'Vedagū' (one who has reached the end of all that is to be known).

'Widwā ca vedehi samecca dhammaṃ' means thoroughly approaching and penetrating the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'All conditioned things are impermanent'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'All conditioned things are suffering'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'All things are non-self'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'With ignorance as condition, formations arise'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'With formations as condition, consciousness arises'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'With consciousness as condition, mind-and-matter arises'... 'With mind-and-matter as condition, the six sense bases arise'... 'With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises'... 'With contact as condition, feeling arises'... 'With feeling as condition, craving arises'... 'With craving as condition, clinging arises'... 'With clinging as condition, existence arises'... 'With existence as condition, birth arises'... 'With birth as condition, aging and death arise'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'This is suffering'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'This is the origin of suffering'... 'This is the cessation of suffering'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'These are the taints (āsavas)'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'This is the origin of the taints'... 'This is the cessation of the taints'... 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'These things are to be known with higher knowledge'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. 'These things are to be fully understood'... 'These things are to be abandoned'... 'These things are...'
73:
...to be developed,' and 'These things are to be realized'—thus one thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom. One thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom regarding the origin, disappearance, gratification, danger, and escape of the six bases of contact, such as the eye. One thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom regarding the origin, disappearance, gratification, danger, and escape of the five aggregates of clinging, which are grasped through craving and views. One thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom regarding the origin, disappearance, gratification, danger, and escape of the four great elements. One thoroughly approaches and penetrates the Four Noble Truths with wisdom, knowing that 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' In this way, a person who knows the Truths through the Path-knowledge is called 'Widwā' (the Wise).

A person of broad wisdom (Bhūripañño), whose wisdom is like the earth, does not go to the high or the low; in other words, he does not move from one teacher to another, from one Dhamma-preacher to another, from one group to another, from one view to another, from one practice to another, or from one path to another. 'Bhūripañño' refers to one who possesses great wisdom, extensive wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. The earth is called 'Bhūri'. Because he is endowed with wisdom that is vast and expansive like the earth, it is said that the one with earth-like wisdom does not go to the high or the low.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'A being attached to perceptions and such, having personally undertaken various practices, reaches high and low states.
An Arahant who knows the ultimate, having seen the Truths through the Path-knowledge, no longer reaches high or low, superior or inferior states.'

That Arahant stands having destroyed Mara's army in all things; in objects seen, heard, or sensed,
Who can propose any view in this world to that Arahant, who lives having opened the veil of defilements?

'Army' (senā) refers to the army of Mara. Bodily misconduct is Mara's army, verbal misconduct is Mara's army, mental misconduct is Mara's army. Lust, hatred, delusion, anger (kodha), grudge (upanāha), and all unwholesome formations are called Mara's army.

This was spoken by the Blessed One:
'Sensual lust is your first army,
Discontent (arati) is called the second,
Hunger and thirst are your third,
Craving is called the fourth.'
74:
The fifth army is called sloth and torpor (thina-middha); the sixth is called fear (bhīru). The seventh is called doubt (vicikicchā); the eighth is called contempt (makkha) and obstinacy (thambha).

Gain, renown, honor, and whatever fame is falsely obtained, as well as exalting oneself and disparaging others (these are your armies).

These armies of Namuci (Mara) strike down (recluses and brahmins); a coward cannot conquer them, but only one who conquers them attains the happiness (of the path and fruit).

When all the armies of Mara and all opposing defilements are conquered, subdued, crushed, destroyed, and turned away by the four noble paths, such a person is called 'visenibhūta' (one who has disbanded the army). That Arahant is one who has disbanded the army regarding the seen, the heard, the sensed, and the cognized. He is one who has disbanded the army in all things, whether seen, heard, or sensed.

'Tam eva dassiṃ vivaṭaṃ carantaṃ' means: it refers to that very person who habitually sees purity, especially one who sees supreme purity, absolute purity, radiant purity, and complete radiant purity. Alternatively, it refers to one who has the vision of purity. 'Vivaṭaṃ' means the coverings of craving, views, defilements, misconduct, and ignorance have been opened. These coverings have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, destroyed, opened, removed, utterly cut off, calmed, and stilled, so that they are no longer liable to arise. 'Carantaṃ' means one who practices, lives, maintains the postures, proceeds, protects, and makes a living in a balanced way.

In the phrase 'kenīdha lokasmi vikappayeyya', 'kappa' (construction/conceptualization) is of two kinds: craving-construction (taṇhā-kappa) and view-construction (diṭṭhi-kappa). That Arahant has abandoned craving-construction and relinquished view-construction. Having abandoned craving and views, by what lust, hate, delusion, conceit, view, restlessness, doubt, or underlying tendencies could he be categorized? How could he be conceptualized as 'one who is lustful', 'one who is hateful', 'one who is deluded', 'one who is fettered', 'one who is misapprehending', 'one who is distracted', 'one who is doubting', or 'one who is obsessed'? Since the volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) that produce such states have been abandoned, by what formations could he be designated as 'a denizen of hell', 'an animal', 'a ghost', 'a human', 'a deva', 'one with form', 'one without form', 'percipient', 'non-percipient', or 'neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient'? The cause by which he would reach such a specific designation no longer exists. 'In this world' refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates (khandha), the world of elements (dhātu), and the world of sense bases (āyatana).
75:
Since the volitional formations (saṅkhāra) that produce rebirth have been abandoned, and because those formations are gone, by what formation could he be conceptualized in a destination of rebirth as a denizen of hell, an animal, a ghost, a human, a deva, one with form, one with only mental aggregates, one who is percipient, one who is non-percipient, or one who is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient? The cause by which he would be conceptualized, by which he would reach a specific state, or by which he would fall into conceptualization does not exist; the supporting condition does not exist; the proximate cause does not exist. 'In the world' means in the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases—by what thing could he be specifically conceptualized in this world?

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'That Arahant has disbanded the army in all things; whatever is seen, heard, or sensed,
He sees only that, and wanders with the covering of defilements opened;
By what could he be specifically conceptualized in this world?'

'They do not construct, they do not place in front' means: constructions (kappa) are of two kinds—craving-construction and view-construction. ... [as before] ... This is craving-construction. ... [as before] ... This is view-construction. For those Arahants, craving-construction is abandoned and view-construction is relinquished. Because craving-construction is abandoned and view-construction is relinquished, they do not construct, do not generate, do not produce, do not bring into being, and do not manifest either craving-construction or view-construction. Thus, 'they do not construct'. 'They do not place in front' means: 'placing in front' (purekkhāra) is of two kinds—craving-preference and view-preference. ... [as before] ... This is craving-preference. ... [as before] ... This is view-preference. For those Arahants, craving-preference is abandoned and view-preference is relinquished. Because craving-preference is abandoned and view-preference is relinquished, they do not wander placing craving or views in front. They have no banner of craving, no signal of craving, no predominance of craving. They have no banner of views, no signal of views, no predominance of views. They do not wander surrounded by craving or views. Thus, 'they do not construct, they do not place in front'.

'They do not say "ultimate purity"' means: they do not speak of, do not preach, do not recite, do not show, and do not express 'ultimate purity' (accanta-suddhi) in the sense of purity through the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-suddhi), the view of non-action (akiriya-diṭṭhi), or the doctrine of eternalism (sassata-vāda). Thus, 'they do not say "ultimate purity"'.
76:
He abandons the tied bond which is the bond of grasping (ādāna-gantha). There are four bonds (gantha): the bodily bond of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha), the bodily bond of ill-will (vyāpāda-kāyagantha), the bodily bond of clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbata-parāmāsa-kāyagantha), and the bodily bond of dogmatic attachment to "this is the truth" (idaṃsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha). Attachment to one's own view is the bodily bond of covetousness. Resentment and dissatisfaction towards the doctrines of others is the bodily bond of ill-will. Over-apprehending one's own virtue, or vows, or both virtue and vows, thinking "purity comes through this practice," is the bodily bond of clinging to rules and observances. Grasping one's own view as "this alone is the truth" is the bodily bond of dogmatic attachment. Why is it called the bond of grasping? Because through these bonds, they grasp, cling to, seize, misapprehend, and repeatedly focus on form... feeling, perception, formations, consciousness, destination, rebirth, conception, existence, and the round of saṃsāra. For that reason, it is called the bond of grasping. "Visajja" means completely relinquishing and abandoning the bonds. Alternatively, it means shaking off and abandoning the knots, ties, bonds, specific bindings, various bindings, attachments, clingings, and obstructions—the bonds of craving, conceit, and views. Just as one prepares or dismantles a beast of burden, a chariot, a cart, or a palanquin, so too, completely relinquishing and abandoning the bonds, or shaking off and abandoning the knots and bonds, is called "ādāna-ganthaṃ gathitaṃ visajja."

They do not form expectations (āsā) for anything in the world. "Āsā" refers to craving, lust, intense passion, covetousness, greed, and the root of the unwholesome. "They do not form expectations" means they do not create, generate, produce, or bring them into existence. "For anything" means internally, externally, or both internally and externally. "In the world" means in the world of the states of deprivation, the human world, the deva world, the world of the aggregates (khandha), the world of the elements (dhātu), and the world of the sense bases (āyatana).

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
They do not plan (through craving and views), they do not place anything at the forefront,
Nor do they speak of "ultimate purity."
Having abandoned the tied bond which is the bond of grasping,
They do not form expectations for anything in the world.

For the Brahmana who has gone beyond the boundary, there is nothing to be grasped through knowing or seeing.
He is not one who lusts for sensual passion, nor is he attached to the absence of passion (dispassion);
For him here, there is nothing grasped as supreme.

"Boundary" (sīmā) refers to the four boundaries: sakkāya-diṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbata-parāmāsa, diṭṭhānusaya, vicikicchānusaya, and the defilements associated with them. This is the first boundary.
77:
The Brahmin who has expelled evil has crossed the four boundaries of defilements. For that Arahant, there is nothing grasped as 'this is supreme' after knowing with the knowledge of others' minds or seeing with the divine eye.

There are four boundaries (sīmā). Personality belief, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, the underlying tendency of views, the underlying tendency of doubt, and the defilements that reside together with these states constitute the first boundary.

The coarse fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the coarse underlying tendency of sensual lust, the underlying tendency of aversion, and the defilements that reside together with these states constitute the second boundary.

The subtle fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the subtle underlying tendency of sensual lust, the underlying tendency of aversion, and the defilements that reside together with these states constitute the third boundary.

Lust for fine-material existence, lust for immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of lust for existence, the underlying tendency of ignorance, and the defilements that reside together with these states constitute the fourth boundary.

When one has crossed, fully crossed, and transcended these four boundaries by means of the four noble paths, he is called 'one who has crossed the boundaries' (sīmātigo).

He is called a 'Brahmin' because he has expelled seven things. Personality belief has been expelled, doubt has been expelled, attachment to rites and rituals has been expelled... (etc.). He who is independent and stable is called a Brahma (Brahmin). 'Tassa' (for him) refers to the Arahant who is free from defilements and whose taints are exhausted.

'Ñatvā' (knowing) means knowing with the knowledge of others' minds or knowing with the knowledge of recollecting past lives. 'Disvā' (seeing) means seeing with the physical eye or seeing with the divine eye. 'For the Brahmin who has crossed the boundary, there is nothing grasped after knowing and seeing' means that for that Arahant, there is no taking, misapprehending, insisting upon, adhering to, or resolving that 'this knowing and seeing is supreme, the peak, the best, the most excellent, the foremost, the highest, or the most noble.' These things have been abandoned, cut off, calmed, fully stilled, are incapable of arising again, and have been burnt by the fire of knowledge.

'He is not passionate with passion, nor attached to dispassion' means: those who are attached, greedy, tied, infatuated, engrossed, stuck, adhering, and obstructed in the five cords of sensual pleasure are called 'rāgaratta' (passionate with passion). Those who are attached, greedy, tied, infatuated, engrossed, stuck, adhering, and obstructed in the fine-material and immaterial attainments are called 'virāgaratta' (attached to dispassion). 'He is not passionate with passion, nor attached to dispassion' means when sensual lust, lust for fine-material existence, and lust for immaterial existence have been abandoned, their roots cut, made like a palm-tree stump, rendered non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. For these reasons, he is said to be not passionate with passion, nor attached to dispassion.
78:
For that Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is no clinging, grasping, misapprehending, adhering, or resolving in this world that 'This view is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, pre-eminent, highest, or excellent.' Such things do not exist, are not present, are not found, and are not obtainable. They have been abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, and are incapable of arising again, having been burned by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, it is said: "For that Arahant, there is no clinging to anything as supreme in this world."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"For the Brāhmaṇa (Arahant) who has crossed the boundary, there is no view grasped through knowing or seeing.
He is neither attached to passion nor delighted in dispassion (attainments). For him, there is no clinging to anything as supreme in this world."

## The Exposition of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta, the Fourth, is finished.

## 5. Exposition of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta

Next, I shall speak the exposition of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta:
"A being who dwells clinging to his own views as 'supreme' makes that (his teacher, etc.) the most excellent in the world.
He says all others besides that view are 'inferior.'
Therefore, he is one who has not overcome disputes."

"Dwelling clinging to his own views as 'supreme'" means: There are some recluses and brahmins who hold views. Among the sixty-two views, they take up one view or another, grasping it, clinging to it, misapprehending it, and adhering to it as "This is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, pre-eminent, highest, and excellent." They dwell, reside, inhabit, and live within their respective views. Just as householders dwell in houses, or those with offenses dwell in offenses, or those with defilements dwell in defilements; in the same way, some recluses and brahmins who hold views take up one of the sixty-two views, grasping it, clinging to it, misapprehending it, and adhering to it as "This is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, pre-eminent, highest, and excellent." They dwell, reside, inhabit, and live within their respective views. This is the meaning of "dwelling clinging to his own views as supreme."
79:
"Yaduttariṃ kurute jantu loke" means: "Yaṃ" refers to that (teacher, etc.). "Uttariṃ kurute" means making it superior, making it foremost, best, distinguished, pre-eminent, highest, or excellent. He makes it superior by thinking, "This teacher is omniscient"; he makes it foremost, best, distinguished, pre-eminent, highest, and excellent. He makes it superior by thinking, "This Dhamma is well-expounded, this group (Saṅgha) is well-practiced, this view is auspicious, this practice is well-prescribed, this path is leading out (of Saṃsāra)"; he makes it superior, foremost, best, distinguished, pre-eminent, highest, and excellent; he produces it, he specifically produces it. "Jantu" means a being, a person, a man. "Loke" means from the world of woe to the world of sense bases. Thus, it means "a being makes that (his own view) superior in the world."

"Hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāha" means: Setting aside his own teacher, the expounded Dhamma, the group, the view, the practice, and the path, he rejects, casts out, and disregards all other doctrines. He says, "That teacher is not omniscient, the Dhamma is not well-expounded, the group is not well-practiced, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path is not leading out. In these (other) teachers and groups, there is no purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, or complete liberation. In these, they are not purified, not specially purified, not completely purified, not liberated, not specially liberated, not completely liberated. They are inferior, low, base, vile, contemptible, and insignificant." Thus he speaks, thus he relates, thus he says, thus he points out, thus he designates. Therefore, it means "he says all others besides that (his own view) are inferior."

"Tasmā vivādāni avītivatto" means: For that reason, for that cause, due to that condition, because of that origin. "Vivādāni" means disputes over views, quarrels over views, contentions over views, altercations over views, and strife over views. "Avītivatto" means one who has not crossed over, not fully crossed over, not overcome. Therefore, it means "Therefore, he has not overcome disputes."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
## "A being who dwells clinging to his own views as 'supreme' makes that (his own view) superior in the world. He says all others besides that view are 'inferior.' Therefore, he is one who has not overcome disputes."

Whatever benefit one sees for oneself in what is seen, heard, in virtue and vows, or in what is sensed (muta), grasping firmly to that very thing, he sees all others as inferior.
80:
He sees a benefit for himself in what is seen, heard, or in virtue and vows, or in what is sensed. 'Yadattanī' means 'that which is in oneself.' A view (diṭṭhi) is called 'atta' (self). In one's own view, one sees two kinds of benefits: the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life. What is the benefit in the present life regarding a view? There is a teacher who holds such a view, and the disciples also hold the same view as that teacher. The disciples respect, revere, honor, and worship that teacher who holds such a view. Because of such worship, he receives the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick. This is the benefit in the present life regarding a view.

What is the benefit in the future life regarding a view? This view is sufficient for becoming a Naga, a Supaṇṇa (Garuda), a Yakkha, an Asura, a Gandhabba, a Mahārāja, an Indra, a Brahma, or a Deva. This view is sufficient for purity, special purity, complete purity, liberation, special liberation, and complete liberation. Through this view, beings are purified and liberated. One becomes an expectant of future results, thinking, 'In the future, I shall be purified and liberated by this view.' This is the benefit in the future life regarding a view.

He sees these two benefits in his own view. He also sees two benefits in the purity of what is seen (diṭṭhasuddhi). He also sees two benefits in the purity of what is heard (sutasuddhi). He also sees two benefits in the purity of virtue (sīlasuddhi). He also sees two benefits in the purity of vows (vatasuddhi). He also sees two benefits in the purity of what is sensed (mutasuddhi), namely, the benefit in the present life and the benefit in the future life. What is the benefit in the present life regarding the purity of what is sensed? There is a teacher who holds such a view, and the disciples also hold the same view as that teacher... (pe)... This is the benefit in the present life regarding the purity of what is sensed. What is the benefit in the future life regarding the purity of what is sensed? This view is sufficient for becoming a Naga... (pe)... This is the benefit in the future life regarding the purity of what is sensed. In the purity of what is sensed, he sees these two benefits with the fleshly eye, looks with the divine eye, regards with the wisdom eye, contemplates with the Buddha eye, and investigates with the all-seeing eye. This is the meaning of the words: 'He sees a benefit for himself in what is seen, heard, or in virtue and vows, or in what is sensed.'

'Tadeva so tattha samuggahāya' means that very view. 'Tattha' means in one's own view, in one's own preference, and in one's own doctrine. 'Samuggahāya' means taking, specially taking, grasping, misapprehending, and being convinced that 'This view alone is the highest, the foremost, the most excellent, the chief, the most sublime, and the most noble.' This is the meaning of the words: 'Tadeva so tattha samuggahāya.'
81:
He sees, looks at, contemplates, and investigates other teachers, teachings, groups, views, practices, and paths as inferior, very inferior, low, bad, vile, and insignificant. This seeing is meant by 'nihīnato passati sabbam-aññaṃ' (he sees all others as inferior).

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever benefit he sees for himself in what is seen, heard, or in virtue and vows, or in what is sensed; grasping that very thing firmly therein, he sees all else as inferior."

Whatever one relies upon and sees another as inferior, the wise call that a bond. Therefore, a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, sensed, or on virtue and vows.

In the phrase "Taṃ vāpi ganthaṃ kusalā vadanti," the wise (kusalā) are those who are skilled in the aggregates (khandha), skilled in the elements (dhātu), skilled in the sense bases (āyatana), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), skilled in the right efforts (sammappadhāna), skilled in the bases of power (iddhipāda), skilled in the faculties (indriya), skilled in the powers (bala), skilled in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), skilled in the path (magga), skilled in the fruit (phala), and skilled in Nibbāna. These wise ones say, "This is a bond, this is an attachment, this is a fetter, this is an impediment (palibodha) that prevents escape from Saṃsāra." Thus they say, thus they teach, thus they recite, thus they show, and thus they designate. This is the meaning of the phrase "Taṃ vāpi ganthaṃ kusalā vadanti."

In the phrase "Yaṃ nissito passati hīnam-aññaṃ," "yaṃ nissito" refers to one who relies on, repeatedly relies on, clings to, resorts to, enters into, and attends to a certain teacher, teaching, group, view, practice, or path. "Passati hīnam-aññaṃ" means he sees, looks at, contemplates, and investigates other teachers, teachings, groups, views, practices, and paths as inferior, very inferior, low, bad, vile, and insignificant. This is the meaning of the phrase "Yaṃ nissito passati hīnam-aññaṃ."

In the phrase "Tasmā hi diṭṭhaṃ va sutaṃ mutaṃ vā, sīlabbataṃ bhikkhu na nissayeyya," "tasmā" means for that reason, because of that cause, because of that condition, because of that origin, [he should not rely on] what is seen, or purity through what is seen, or what is heard, or purity through what is heard, or what is sensed, or purity through what is sensed, or virtue...
82:
Or one should not rely on, take up, grasp, or be obsessed with the purity of virtue or the purity of vows. Therefore, a monk should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, or on virtue and vows.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'The wise call that a bond, depending on which one sees another as inferior; therefore, a monk should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, or on virtue and vows.'

One should not form a view in the world through knowledge, virtue, or vows. One should not present oneself as 'equal', nor think of oneself as 'inferior' or 'superior'.

'One should not form a view in the world through knowledge, virtue, or vows' means: One should not form, produce, generate, manifest, or bring into existence a view through the knowledge of the eight attainments, the five superknowledges, or wrong knowledge, or through virtue, vows, or virtue and vows. 'In the world' means in the world of the states of deprivation, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases; in such a world, one should not form a view through knowledge, virtue, or vows.

'One should not present oneself as equal' means: One should not present oneself as 'I am equal' based on birth, lineage, family status, beauty, wealth, study, occupation, craft, science, learning, wit, or any other grounds.

'One should not think of oneself as inferior or superior' means: One should not present oneself as 'I am inferior' based on birth, lineage, and so forth, or any other grounds. One should not present oneself as 'I am superior' based on birth, lineage, and so forth, or any other grounds.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
83:
## 
“One should not construct views in the world, nor by knowledge, nor by virtue and vows. One should not consider oneself equal, nor think of oneself as inferior or superior.

Having abandoned the view of self and not clinging, that person does not make a dependency even with knowledge. He truly does not take sides among those who are divided; he does not return to any view.”

'Attāṃ pahāya anupādiyāno' means—'Attāṃ pahāya' means abandoning the view of self (attadiṭṭhi), abandoning the grasping of self. It means abandoning, discarding, removing, making an end of, and leading to non-existence that which is grasped, handled, reflected upon, entered into, and clung to by the power of craving and views—this is 'attāṃ pahāya'. 'Anupādiyāno' means not clinging, not grasping, not handling, and not reflecting upon by way of the four types of clinging (upādāna). Thus, it is said 'attāṃ pahāya anupādiyāno'.

'Ñāṇenapi so nissayaṃ no karoti' means he does not make, produce, generate, bring into existence, or manifest a dependency on craving or a dependency on views through the knowledge of the eight attainments (samāpatti), the five superknowledges (abhiññā), or wrong knowledge.

'Sa ve viyattesu na vaggasārī' means that person does not follow by way of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear among those who are divided, fallen into duality, split, holding various views, various tolerances, various preferences, various doctrines, depending on various view-dependencies, and following the four biased courses (agati) of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear. He does not go by the power of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, restlessness, doubt, or underlying tendencies (anusaya). He is not carried away, led, swept away, or bound and taken by partisan things.
84:
That person does not go to any view. For him, the sixty-two views have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. He does not go to any view, he does not return to them—therefore, it is said: "He does not go to any view."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Having abandoned the self and not clinging, he does not rely even on knowledge;
He does not take sides among those who are divided, he does not go to any view."

For the Arahant, there is no craving for both extremes in this world or the next, for the sake of existence and non-existence. For that Arahant, there are no fixations whatsoever in the teachings, having decided and grasped them.

In the phrase "Yassūbhayante paṇidhīdha natthi bhavābhavāya idha vā huraṃ vā": "Yassa" refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed. "Anta" (extreme): contact is one extreme, the origin of contact is the second extreme. The past is one extreme, the future is the second extreme. Pleasant feeling is one extreme, painful feeling is the second extreme. Name is one extreme, form is the second extreme. The six internal bases are one extreme, the six external bases are the second extreme. Identity (sakkāya) is one extreme, the origin of identity is the second extreme. "Paṇidhi" refers to craving. Whatever lust, passion... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome roots there are, these are called "paṇidhi".

"Bhavābhavāya" means for the sake of the existence of kamma, for the sake of renewed existence, for the sake of sense-sphere existence, for the sake of the existence of kamma and sense-sphere existence, for the sake of renewed existence and fine-material existence, for the sake of the existence of kamma and fine-material existence, for the sake of renewed existence and immaterial existence, for the sake of the existence of kamma and immaterial existence, for the sake of renewed existence, for the sake of repeated existence, for the sake of repeated destiny, for the sake of repeated rebirth, for the sake of repeated relinking, for the sake of the repeated production of individual existence. "Idha" means one's own individual existence; "hura" means another's individual existence. "Idha" means one's own form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; "hura" means another's form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Idha" means the six internal bases; "hura" means the six external bases. "Idha" means the human world; "hura" means...
85:
...the heavenly world (devaloka) is called "hura". "Idha" is the sense element (kāmadhātu), and "hura" is the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu). Or, "idha" is the sense element and the fine-material element, and "hura" is the immaterial element. "Yassūbhayante paṇidhīdha natthi bhavābhavāya idha vā huraṃ vā" means: for that Arahant, craving (paṇidhi) for both extremes, for the sake of existence and non-existence, in this world or the next, does not exist, is not found, is not available; it is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge.

"Nivesanā tassa na santi keci" means: "Nivesanā" refers to the two kinds of fixations—craving-fixation (taṇhā-nivesanā) and view-fixation (diṭṭhi-nivesanā)... this is craving-fixation... this is view-fixation. For that Arahant whose taints are destroyed, there are no fixations whatsoever; they do not exist, are not found, are not available; they are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge.

"Dhammesu niccheyya samuggahītaṃ" means: "Dhammesu" refers to the sixty-two views. "Niccheyya" means having decided, having judged, having investigated, having thoroughly investigated, having weighed, having scrutinized, and having made clear. "Samuggahītaṃ" means grasping by way of limits, grasping by way of groups, grasping by way of excellence, grasping by way of parts, grasping by way of accumulation, grasping by way of collection, thinking "This alone is the truth, the reality, the suchness, the fact, the exact, the non-distorted"; such grasping, misapprehending, adhering, being engrossed in, and being resolved upon do not exist, are not found, are not available; they are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"For whom there is no craving for both extremes in this world or the next, for the sake of existence and non-existence;
For him, there are no fixations whatsoever, having decided among the teachings and grasped them."

For that Arahant, there is not even the slightest perception fashioned regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed. By what could one in this world categorize that Brahmin who does not take up any view?
86:
In this world, for that Arahant, there is not even the slightest specially fashioned perception regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed. "Tassa" refers to that Arahant who is far from defilements and whose taints (āsavas) are exhausted. For that Arahant, whether in seeing, hearing, or sensing, or in the belief in purity through seeing, purity through hearing, or purity through sensing, there are no views (diṭṭhi) that are preceded by perception, specially fashioned by perception, seized by perception, originated, well-originated, conceived, specially conceived, conditioned, specially conditioned, or well-established; they do not exist, they are not found, they are not obtained. Those views have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, tranquilized, are incapable of arising again, and have been burnt by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, it is said: "In this world, for that Arahant, there is not even the slightest specially fashioned perception regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed."

Regarding the phrase "That Brahmin who does not cling to views," a Brahmin is so called because he has discarded seven things. He has discarded the view of self (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)... (and so on). One who is not dependent on craving and views and who is unshaken by the worldly conditions is called a Brahmin. "That Brahmin who does not cling to views" refers to that Arahant who does not take up, does not cling to, does not misapprehend, and does not enter into views with attachment.

Regarding the phrase "By what would one specially conceive in this world?", there are two kinds of conceptions (kappa): craving-conception (taṇhākappa) and view-conception (diṭṭhikappa)... (and so on). This is craving-conception... this is view-conception. For that Arahant, craving-conception has been abandoned, and view-conception has been relinquished. Because craving-conception is abandoned and view-conception is relinquished, by what lust would he conceive? By what hatred would he conceive? By what delusion would he conceive? By what conceit would he conceive? By what view would he conceive? By what restlessness would he conceive? By what doubt would he conceive? By what underlying tendencies would he conceive? How could he be conceived as "one who is lustful," "one who is hateful," "one who is deluded," "one who is fettered," "one who is misapprehending," "one who is distracted," "one who has reached doubt," or "one who has reached strength [in views]"?

Those volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) have been abandoned. Because volitional formations have been abandoned, by what could he conceive the destinations (gati)? How could he be conceived as "a denizen of hell," "an animal," "a peta," "a human," "a deva," "one with form," "one without form," "one with perception," "one without perception," or "one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception"? That cause (hetu) does not exist, that condition (paccaya) does not exist, that reason (kāraṇa) does not exist by which he would conceive, specially conceive, or fall into special conception. "In this world" means in the world of the planes of misery... up to the world of the sense bases. Therefore, it is said: "By what would one specially conceive in this world?"

## Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"In this world, for that Arahant, there is not even the slightest specially fashioned perception regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed;
By what would one specially conceive in this world that Brahmin who does not cling to views?"
87:
They do not conceive, nor do they place [anything] in front; even doctrines are not accepted by them.
The Brahmin (Arahant) is not to be led by precepts and vows; such a one, having gone to the far shore, does not return.

"Na kappayanti na purekkharonti" means—there are two kinds of "kappa" (conception): craving-conception (taṇhākappa) and view-conception (diṭṭhikappa). What is craving-conception? It is the marking out, delimiting, defining, circumscribing, possessing, and cherishing through the formation called craving. Thinking, "This is mine, that is mine, this much is mine, to this extent is mine," one cherishes through the power of craving one's own forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; rugs, clothing, female slaves, male slaves, goats, sheep, poultry, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, donkeys, fields, lands, silver, gold, villages, towns, royal capitals, countries, provinces, treasuries, and storehouses; one even cherishes the entire great earth through the power of craving. Whatever is the range of the one hundred and eight types of craving—this is called craving-conception.

What is view-conception? The twenty types of the view of self (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), the ten types of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), the ten types of views of extreme (antaggāhikadiṭṭhi), and such views, the resort of views, the thicket of views, the wilderness of views, the distortion of views, the vacillation of views, the fetter of views, grasping, secondary grasping, adherence, misapprehension, the wrong path, the false way, falsity, the sectarian landing-place, the grasp of perversion, the grasp of the contrary, the grasp of inversion, the false grasp, the grasping of what is not true as true, and the sixty-two types of views—this is called view-conception. Those Arahants have abandoned craving-conception and relinquished view-conception. Because craving-conception is abandoned and view-conception is relinquished, they do not conceive, do not produce, do not well-produce, do not manifest, and do not manifest intensely either craving-conception or view-conception. Therefore, it is said: "Na kappayanti."

"Na purekkharonti" means—there are two kinds of "purekkhāra" (placing in front/preference): craving-preference (taṇhāpurekkhāra) and view-preference (diṭṭhipurekkhāra). ... This is craving-preference... this is view-preference. Those Arahants have abandoned craving-preference and relinquished view-preference. Because craving-preference is abandoned and view-preference is relinquished, they do not walk placing craving or views in front. They do not have craving as their banner, they do not have craving as their leader or entourage, they are not under the mastery of craving. They do not have views as their banner, they do not have views as their leader or entourage, they are not under the mastery of views. They do not walk surrounded by craving or views. Therefore, it is said: "Na kappayanti na purekkharonti."
88:
