In the phrase “dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitāse,” the word “dhamma” refers to the sixty-two [wrong] views. “Tesaṃ” refers to those Arahants whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). “Na paṭicchitāse” means they do not accept or adhere to the view that “The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is falsehood.” They do not accept: “The world is not eternal... the world is finite... the world is infinite... the soul and the body are the same... the soul is one thing and the body is another... the Tathāgata exists after death... the Tathāgata does not exist after death... the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is falsehood.” Thus, they do not accept those views.

In the phrase “na brāhmaṇo sīlavatena neyyo,” the word “na” expresses negation. He is called a “Brahmin” because he has cast out (bāhita) the seven things, starting with identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). Identity view has been cast out by him... [and so on]. That Arahant who is poised (tādī) and does not depend on craving or views is called a Brahmin. A Brahmin (Arahant) is not led, not conducted, not carried away, and not swept away by virtue, or by vows, or by both virtue and vows; he is not taken hold of by defilements. Thus, a Brahmin is not led by virtue and vows.

In the phrase “pāraṅgato na pacceti tādī,” the word “pāra” (the far shore) refers to the deathless Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and liberation. That Arahant is called “pāraṅgato” because he has reached the far shore of Nibbāna. He has reached the end of the world of formations. For that Arahant, the extensive saṃsāra of birth and death no longer exists, and there is no more renewed existence. “Na pacceti” means he does not return to or come back to the defilements that have been abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). He does not return to or come back to the defilements abandoned by the path of once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga). He does not return to or come back to the defilements abandoned by the path of non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). He does not return to or come back to the defilements abandoned by the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). Thus, the Arahant who has reached the far shore does not return. “Tādī” means the Arahant is called “poised” (tādī) in five ways: he is poised regarding the agreeable and disagreeable; he is poised because of abandoning [defilements]; he is poised because of having crossed over [the flood]; he is poised because of being liberated; and he is poised because he is designated by such qualities.

How is the Arahant poised regarding the agreeable and disagreeable? The Arahant is poised in gain and in loss, in fame and in obscurity, in praise and in blame, and in pleasure and in pain. Some people might anoint one of his arms with sandalwood perfume.
89:
Some people might anoint one of his arms with sandalwood perfume; some might cut the other arm with an axe. There is no lust or attachment towards the arm anointed with perfume, and no anger or aversion towards the arm being cut with an axe. He dwells having abandoned both affection and repulsion; he has transcended being uplifted by affection and being oppressed by repulsion; he has completely transcended both affection and repulsion. In this way, the Arahant is poised (tādī) regarding agreeable and disagreeable objects.

How is the Arahant called poised (tādī) because of abandoning? The Arahant has abandoned lust, vomited it out, been freed from it, eliminated it, and relinquished it. He has abandoned, vomited out, been freed from, eliminated, and relinquished: hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, disparaging, malice, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all anxieties, and all unwholesome volitional formations. In this way, the Arahant is called poised because of abandoning.

How is the Arahant called poised (tādī) because of having crossed over? The Arahant has crossed the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. He has crossed, gone beyond, got across, transcended, and completely surpassed the entire path of saṃsāra. He has lived the life, practiced the conduct, and for him, the saṃsāra of birth and death and renewed existence no longer exist. In this way, the Arahant is called poised because of having crossed over.

How is the Arahant called poised (tādī) because of being liberated? The Arahant’s mind is liberated, specially liberated, and well-liberated from lust. His mind is liberated, specially liberated, and well-liberated from hatred, from delusion, from anger, enmity, disparaging, malice, envy, stinginess, deceit, craftiness, obstinacy, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, negligence, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all anxieties, and all unwholesome volitional formations. In this way, the Arahant is called poised because of being liberated.

How is the Arahant called poised (tādī) because he is designated by such qualities? The Arahant is designated as “virtuous” because of his virtue; as “faithful” because of his faith; as “energetic” because of his energy; as “mindful” because of his mindfulness; as “concentrated” because of his concentration; as “wise” because of his wisdom; as “one with threefold knowledge” because of his threefold knowledge; and as “one with six higher powers” because of his six higher powers. Since he is designated by such qualities, he is called poised. In this way, the Arahant is called poised because he is designated by such qualities. This is the meaning of the phrase: “One who has gone to the far shore does not return; such a one is poised.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
90:
The Arahants do not construct (defilements); they do not place (craving and views) at the forefront. Those Arahants do not accept (cling to) any phenomena. The Arahant, known as a Brahmin, is not to be led by virtue and vows; having reached the further shore, such a one of such nature does not return.

## 5. Exposition of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta

## 6. Exposition of the Jarā Sutta

Furthermore, I shall speak the exposition of the Jarā Sutta—

Short indeed is this life; one dies even within a hundred years. Even if one lives beyond a hundred years, then one dies indeed of old age.

Regarding the phrase "Short indeed is this life" (Appaṃ vata jīvitaṃ idaṃ): Life (jīvita) means life-span, duration, subsistence, maintenance, proceeding, revolving, guarding, the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). Furthermore, life is short or brief for two reasons: either because of the brevity of its duration (ṭhitiparitittatā) or because of the brevity of its inherent nature (sarasaparittatā). How is life short because of the brevity of its duration? In the past thought-moment, one lived; one does not live now, nor will one live. In the future thought-moment, one will live; one does not live now, nor has one lived. In the present thought-moment, one lives; one cannot be said to have lived, nor to be about to live.

Individual existence (attabhāva) together with life,
And all pleasures and pains,
Are associated with only a single thought;
The moment passes quickly.

There are devas who remain,
For eighty-four thousand aeons;
Yet even they do not live,
Associated with two thoughts.

For one who remains here or for one who dies,
Those aggregates (khandhas) which have ceased,
Go to their end without rebirth;
All aggregates are similar.

Those aggregates that perish in the immediate past,
And those that will perish in the future,
There is no difference in the characteristics,
Of the present aggregates that cease in between.

One is not born by the unarisen future aggregate,
One lives only by the present moment;
With the destruction of thought, the world is dead;
In the ultimate sense, it is merely a designation (paññatti).
91:
Just as they proceed according to the inclination when directed by desire,
So phenomena having the six sense-bases (saḷāyatana) as their cause,
Proceed in an uninterrupted stream.

The aggregates that perish do not reach a store,
There is no heap of them in the future;
Those phenomena that arise and remain,
Are like a mustard seed on the point of an awl.

The destruction of arisen phenomena,
Is placed before those phenomena;
They remain with the nature of perishing,
Unmixed with previous aggregates.

They come from the unseen;
Having perished, they go to the unseen;
Like a flash of lightning in the sky,
They arise and pass away.

Thus, life is short because of the brevity of its duration.

How is life short because of the brevity of its inherent nature (sarasaparittatā)? Life is connected with the in-breath, connected with the out-breath, connected with both in-breath and out-breath, connected with the four great elements, connected with the nutriment that is eaten, connected with the heat of kamma-born fire (usmā), and connected with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-viññāṇa). The root cause of these things, ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā), is weak. The previous causes, clinging (upādāna) and existence (bhava), are also weak. Whatever causal conditions there are, they are also weak. Whatever predominant factors there are, they are also weak. Co-existent factors are weak. Associated factors are weak. Conascent factors are weak. Whatever factors that perform the function are also weak. These things are always mutually weak; they are mutually unstable. These things cast each other down; they have no protection for each other, nor can they make each other stand. There is no factor that causes them to arise (independently).

One thing does not diminish by another,
These things are entirely to be known by the mind;
Previous things cause these things to arise,
Those that cause them to arise have already died in the past.

Previous causes and subsequent effects,
Never see each other.

Thus, life is short because of the brevity of its inherent nature.

Furthermore, in comparison with the life of the devas of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā), the life of humans is short, brief, small, momentary, fleeting, and insignificant; it does not last long, it does not endure for a long time. In comparison with the life of the Tāvatiṃsa devas... Yāma devas, Tusita devas, Nimmānarati devas, Paranimmitavasavatti devas, and the devas of the Brahma realm (Brahmakāyika), the life of humans is short, brief, small, momentary, fleeting, and insignificant; it does not last long, it does not endure for a long time.
92:
Life cannot endure for a long time; life cannot last long. Compared to the life of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, Yāma devas, Tusita devas, Nimmānarati devas, Paranimmitavasavatti devas, and Brahmakāyika devas, the life of humans is very little; life is but a small amount; life is meager; life lasts but a moment; life is fleeting; life is very little; life cannot endure for a long time; life cannot last long.

The Blessed One has spoken thus: "Bhikkhus, this life of humans is short; one must go to the next world. It should be understood with wisdom; merit should be performed; the holy life should be lived. For one who is born, there is no such thing as not dying. Bhikkhus, he who lives long, lives for a hundred years, or a little less or a little more."

"Short is the life of humans; a good man should despise it.
One should act as if his head were on fire; there is no escape from the arrival of death.
Days and nights pass by; life is cut short.
The life of mortals is exhausted like the water in small streams."

Indeed, this life is very short.

"One dies even within a hundred years" means: one passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes even at the stage of the kalala (embryo). One passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes even at the stage of the abbuda (foetal swelling). One passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes even at the stage of the pesi (piece of flesh). One passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes even at the stage of the ghana (solid mass). One passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes even at the stage of the pasākha (the five branches/limbs). One passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes just after being born. One passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes in the delivery room. One who is half a month old also passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes. One who is one month old... two months old... three months old... four months old... five months old also passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes. One who is six months old... seven months old... eight months old... nine months old... ten months old... one year old also passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes. One who is two years old... three years old... four years old... five years old... six years old... seven years old... eight years old... nine years old... ten years old... twenty years old... thirty years old... forty years old... fifty years old... sixty years old... seventy years old... eighty years old... ninety years old also passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes. Thus, one dies even within a hundred years.
93:
"Even if one lives beyond a hundred years" means if someone lives past a hundred years, they might live for one year, two years, three years, four years, five years... ten years, twenty years, thirty years, or even forty years. This is what is meant by "even if one lives beyond a hundred years."

"But indeed, he dies of old age" means when he becomes old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, reached the end of life, with broken teeth, grey hair, a bald head like it was shaven, wrinkled skin, dark spots on the body, a bent and crooked frame, leaning on a staff. He passes away, dies, disappears, and perishes through old age; there is no escape from death.

"As ripe fruits have a fear of falling in the morning, so for mortals who are born, there is always the fear of death."

"Just as all clay vessels made by a potter end in breaking, so is the life of mortals."

"Whether young or old, whether foolish or wise, all go under the power of death; all have death as their end."

"When they are overcome by death and going to the next world, a father cannot save his son, nor can relatives save their kinsmen."

"Look! While relatives are watching and wailing much, mortals are led away one by one, like cattle to the slaughter. Thus the world is afflicted by death and old age."

But indeed, he dies of old age.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Indeed, this life is very short; one dies even before reaching a hundred years. Even if one lives beyond a hundred years, indeed, he dies of old age."
94:
People grieve over the things they cherish; for indeed, possessions are not permanent. Seeing that this state of separation is evident, one should leave the household life and dwell as a monk.

'People grieve over the things they cherish' means: 'People' refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans. There are two kinds of cherishing (mamatte): cherishing through craving and cherishing through views. They grieve when they fear their cherished objects will be snatched away, they grieve while they are being snatched away, and they grieve after they have been snatched away. Furthermore, they grieve when they fear their cherished objects will change and perish, they grieve while they are changing, and they grieve when they have changed and perished; they become exhausted, they lament, they beat their breasts and wail, and they fall into confusion. This is the meaning of 'People grieve over the things they cherish.'

'For indeed, possessions are not permanent' means: There are two kinds of possessions (pariggaha): possession through craving and possession through views. Possession through craving is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to change. Possession through views is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to change.

For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, do you see any possession that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that will remain the same forever like the eternal?' 'No, Bhante.' 'Good, bhikkhus! I too, bhikkhus, do not see any possession that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that will remain the same forever like the eternal.' Possessions that are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change do not exist, are not found, are not present, and cannot be obtained. This is the meaning of 'For indeed, possessions are not permanent.'

'Seeing that this state of separation is evident' means: In the presence of, in the existence of, and in the occurrence of variation (nānābhāva), separation (vinābhāva), and changeability (aññathābhāva). For this was said by the Blessed One to the Venerable Ānanda: 'Enough, Ānanda! Do not grieve, do not lament. Have I not told you before, Ānanda, that there is variation, separation, and changeability from all that is dear and appealing? How, Ānanda, can it be obtained here—that which...'
95:
...is born, come-to-be, conditioned, and subject to disintegration, should not disintegrate? That is not possible. Due to the change and variation of preceding aggregates, elements, and sense bases, succeeding aggregates, elements, and sense bases arise.' Thus, the state of separation is evident.

In the phrase 'Seeing this, one should not live in a house,' 'iti' (thus) serves as a word-junction, a word-combination, a word-filler, a collection of letters, a smoothness of consonants, and a sequence of words. 'Seeing this' means seeing (the faults), weighing, investigating, discerning, and making clear, while being free from the state of cherishing (mamatte) things as 'mine.' 'One should not live in a house' means cutting off all impediments of the household life, cutting off the impediments of wife and children, cutting off the impediments of relatives, cutting off the impediments of friends and colleagues, cutting off the impediments of hoarding wealth; shaving off hair and beard, donning the saffron robes, and having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, reaching the state of having nothing, one should wander alone, dwell, move about, behave, protect, maintain, and sustain oneself. Thus, seeing this, one should not live in a house.

## Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"People grieve over the things they cherish as 'mine'; for indeed, possessions are not permanent.
Seeing that the state of separation is evident, one should not live in a house."

"A man thinks of a certain thing as 'this is mine,' yet he must leave that thing even through death.
Knowing this, the wise man, being a devotee of the Buddha and others, should not incline towards cherishing (through craving and views)."

In the phrase 'he must leave that thing even through death,' 'death (maraṇa)' refers to the passing away, the falling away, the breaking up, the disappearance, the mortality, the making of an end (kālaṅkiriyā), the breaking up of the aggregates, the laying down of the carcass, and the cutting off of the life-faculty of various beings from their respective orders of beings. 'That thing (taṃ)' refers to the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. 'He must leave (pahīyati)' means it is abandoned, he leaves it, he renounces it, it disappears, it perishes. For it was also said: ...
96:
Wealth abandons a mortal first, or the mortal abandons that wealth first. Those who possess wealth and crave sensual pleasures are not eternal; therefore, I do not grieve in the time of grief.

The moon rises, waxes, and wanes. The sun, having destroyed the darkness and honored the great world-system, sets in the evening and becomes invisible. I have understood the worldly conditions (lokadhamma); therefore, I do not grieve in the time of grief.

Even by death, that is abandoned. In the phrase "a man thinks 'this is mine'," "that thing" refers to the aggregate of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Man" is a mere designation, a name, a concept, a common usage, a worldly convention, a name-making, a naming, a nomenclature, an expression, a syllable, and an utterance. "Thinks 'this is mine'" means thinking through the obsession of craving (taṇhā), the obsession of views (diṭṭhi), the obsession of conceit (māna), the obsession of defilements (kilesa), the obsession of misconduct (duccarita), the obsession of effort (payoga), and the obsession of result (vipāka).

In the phrase "knowing this fault, the wise one," it means knowing, weighing, investigating, and making clear this fault, and making it manifest in the midst of cherishing; thus he is called "the wise one who knows thus." A "wise one" (paṇḍita) is one who is steadfast, who knows the way to happiness, who gathers both kinds of benefits, who is unshaken in the welfare of himself and others, who knows the profound meaning, who illuminates cause and effect, and who is free from defilements.

In the phrase "the devotee should not incline towards cherishing," cherishing (mamatta) is of two kinds: craving-cherishing and view-cherishing. ...pe... This is craving-cherishing. ...pe... This is view-cherishing. "Devotee" (māmaka) means a devotee of the Buddha, a devotee of the Dhamma, and a devotee of the Saṅgha. He cherishes the Blessed One, and the Blessed One favors that person. For the Blessed One said: "Monks, those monks who are hypocritical, stubborn, talkative, arrogant, haughty, and uncomposed; monks, those monks are not my devotees. Monks, those monks have departed from this Dhamma-Vinaya. They do not attain growth, increase, and fullness in this Dhamma-Vinaya. Monks, those monks who are not hypocritical, not talkative, who are wise and steadfast, not stubborn, and well-composed; monks, those monks are my devotees. Monks, those monks have not departed from this Dhamma-Vinaya. They attain growth, increase, and fullness in this Dhamma-Vinaya."
97:
“Those who are hypocritical, stubborn like a stake, talkative for the sake of the four requisites, arrogant, haughty, and uncomposed, they do not flourish in the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One.

“Those who are not hypocritical, not talkative for the sake of the four requisites, who are wise and steadfast, not stubborn, and well-composed, they indeed flourish in the Dhamma taught by the Fully Enlightened One.”

A devotee (māmaka) of the Buddha and so forth should not incline towards cherishing as “this is mine.” A devotee, having abandoned craving-cherishing and relinquished view-cherishing, should not incline, should not bend down towards cherishing (mamatta). He should not be one who leans towards, slopes towards, tends towards, is intent on, or is dominated by that craving and those views; thus it is said, “the devotee should not incline towards cherishing as this is mine.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
“Even by death, a man must abandon that which he thinks is mine. Knowing this, the wise one, a devotee, should not incline towards cherishing.”

Just as a man who has woken up does not see what was encountered in a dream, so too, one does not see a loved person who has passed away and gone to another world.

“What was encountered in a dream” means that which was associated with, united with, or gathered together. “A man who has woken up does not see” means that a man while dreaming sees the moon, sees the sun, sees the great ocean, sees Sineru the king of mountains, sees an elephant, sees a horse, sees a chariot, sees infantry, sees a battle array, sees the delight of a park, sees the delight of a forest, ...pe... sees the delight of the ground, ... sees the delight of a lotus pond. However, upon waking, he sees nothing at all; thus it is said, “a man who has woken up does not see.”

In the phrase “so too a loved person,” “so too” completes the simile. “Loved person” refers to a person who is cherished, such as a mother, a father, a brother, a sister, a son, a daughter, a friend, a minister, a relative, or a kinsman from the mother’s or father’s side.
98:
One who has passed away is called 'peta'. The phrase 'petaṃ kālaṅkataṃ na passati' means that one who has died and passed away cannot be seen (with the physical eye), cannot be seen by looking, cannot be met or seen, is not known, and cannot be obtained anymore.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Just as a man, when awakened, does not see what he met in a dream, even so, one does not see the beloved person who has died and passed away."

Those people whose names are spoken were once seen and heard. Only the name will remain to be told of the deceased being.

In the phrase 'those people who were seen and heard', 'seen' (diṭṭha) refers to those who have visible forms that are perceived by eye-consciousness. 'Heard' (suta) refers to those who have sounds that are perceived by ear-consciousness. 'Those people' refers to the collective of kings, brahmins, merchants, laborers, householders, monastics, devas, and humans.

In the phrase 'those whose names are spoken', 'those' refers to those kings, brahmins, merchants, laborers, householders, monastics, devas, and humans. 'Name' (nāma) refers to enumeration, designation, concept, convention, naming, name-making, name-giving, terminology, linguistics, and expression. 'Is spoken' (pavuccati) means is said, is told, is recited, is shown, or is called.

'Only the name will remain' means that the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are abandoned, relinquished, discarded, disappeared, and perished. Only the name remains. 'To be told' (akkheyyaṃ) means to be told, to be spoken, to be said, to be shown, or to be called. In the phrase 'of the deceased being', 'deceased' (petassa) refers to one who is dead and has passed away. 'Being' (jantuno) refers to a creature, a human, a youth, a person, an individual, a life, a soul, a being, a person, or a man.

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
99:
“Those people who were seen and heard, whose names are spoken; only the name will remain to be told of the deceased being.”

Those greedy for beloved objects do not abandon sorrow, lamentation, and avarice. Therefore, the sages, seeing safety (Nibbāna), wander having abandoned possessions (pariggaha).

In the sentence 'Those greedy for beloved objects do not abandon sorrow, lamentation, and avarice'—

Sorrow (soka) refers to the sorrow, the act of sorrowing, the state of sorrowing, internal parching, internal over-parching, internal burning, internal over-burning, mental distress, unhappiness, and the dart of sorrow of one affected by the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, the loss of health, the loss of virtue, the loss of right view, or any other kind of loss, or one touched by any kind of painful state.

Lamentation (parideva) refers to the wailing, the great wailing, the act of wailing, the state of wailing, the act of lamenting, the state of lamenting, verbal outburst, empty talk, distorted talk, repetitive talk, the act of repetitive talking, and the state of repetitive talking of one affected by the loss of relatives... the loss of right view, or any other kind of loss, or one touched by any kind of painful state.

Avarice (macchariya) refers to the five types of avarice: avarice regarding dwellings, avarice regarding families, avarice regarding gains, avarice regarding status (beauty/fame), and avarice regarding the Dhamma. Such avarice, the act of being avaricious, the state of being avaricious, selfishness, stinginess, being tight-fisted, and the lack of generosity of the mind is called avarice. Furthermore, avarice regarding the aggregates, avarice regarding the elements, avarice regarding the sense bases, and grasping are also called avarice.

Greed (gedha) is called craving (taṇhā). Whatever passion, intense passion... covetousness, greed, and unwholesome roots are called greed.

Possessiveness (mamatta) is of two kinds: craving-possessiveness and view-possessiveness. ... This is craving-possessiveness ... This is view-possessiveness.

They sorrow because they fear their beloved objects will be snatched away; they sorrow while they are being snatched away; and they sorrow after they have been snatched away. They sorrow because they fear their beloved objects will change and perish; they sorrow while they are changing; and they sorrow after they have changed and perished. They also lament because they fear their beloved objects will be snatched away.
100:
They lament even while a cherished object is being snatched away, and they lament after it has been snatched away. Those who are anxious about the change and destruction of a cherished object also lament; they lament while it is changing, and they lament after it has changed. They guard, keep, cherish, and are possessive and stingy over a cherished object. They do not abandon sorrow, they do not abandon lamentation, they do not abandon stinginess, they do not abandon greed; they do not completely abandon, do not dispel, do not bring to an end, and do not cause to not arise again. Therefore, those who are greedy for cherished objects cannot abandon sorrow, lamentation, and stinginess. Therefore, the sages, seeing Nibbāna which is safety, live having abandoned possession (attachment).

'Therefore' means for that reason, because of that cause, because of seeing that fault. 'Muni' (sage) refers to wisdom. Whatever wisdom, full understanding... non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. Those endowed with that knowledge are called sages; they have attained the state of a sage. There are three states of a sage (moneyya): bodily sagehood, verbal sagehood, and mental sagehood... one who has transcended the net of craving and views is called a sage. 

'Possession' (pariggaha) is of two kinds: possession through craving and possession through views... this is possession through craving... this is possession through views. Sages, having relinquished possession through craving and having renounced, abandoned, given up, dispelled, destroyed, and caused to not arise again possession through views, live, dwell, move, proceed, protect, maintain, and sustain themselves. 

'One who sees safety' (khemadassino) means one who sees the deathless Nibbāna, which is safety. That state which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. 'One who sees safety' means one who habitually sees safety, one who habitually sees a shelter, one who habitually sees a refuge, one who habitually sees the deathless Nibbāna, which is free from falling away. Therefore, the sages, seeing Nibbāna which is safety, live having abandoned possession.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Greedy for cherished objects, they do not abandon sorrow, lamentation, and stinginess;
Therefore, the sages, seeing safety, live having abandoned possession.'

For a monk who lives withdrawn, frequenting a secluded seat,
They call that his completeness, who would not show himself in existence.

In the phrase 'a monk who lives withdrawn,' it refers to the seven types of noble learners (sekha) and the Arahants. Why are the seven types of noble learners called so? Because they live... withdrawing the mind from various objects, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, calming, crushing, forbidding, guarding, and securing it with the wall of the mind. Withdrawing the mind at the eye-door... they live guarding it. At the ear-door, nose-door, tongue-door, body-door, and mind-door, they also live withdrawing the mind, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, calming, crushing, forbidding, guarding, and securing it with the wall of the mind.
101:
In the phrase 'for a monk who lives withdrawn' (patilīnacarassa bhikkhuno): the seven types of noble learners (sekha) are called 'living withdrawn.' The Arahant is also 'withdrawn.' Why are the seven types of noble learners called 'living withdrawn'? Because those noble learners live, move, dwell, proceed, act, protect, maintain, and sustain themselves while withdrawing the mind from various objects, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, restraining, forbidding, guarding, and securing it. They live... withdrawing the mind at the eye-door, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, restraining, forbidding, guarding, and securing it. At the ear-door... (pe)... at the nose-door... at the tongue-door... at the body-door... at the mind-door, they live... withdrawing the mind, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, restraining, forbidding, guarding, and securing it.

For example, just as a chicken feather or a piece of sinew, when thrown into a fire, shrinks, shrivels, and recoils, and does not stretch out; even so, those noble learners live... withdrawing the mind from various objects, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, restraining, forbidding, guarding, and securing it. At the eye-door... (pe)... at the ear-door... at the nose-door... at the tongue-door... at the body-door... at the mind-door, they live... withdrawing the mind, shrinking back, recoiling, contracting, restraining, forbidding, guarding, and securing it. For that reason, the seven types of noble learners are called 'living withdrawn.' 'For a monk' (bhikkhuno) refers to either a virtuous worldling monk or a noble learner monk; thus is the meaning of the phrase 'for a monk who lives withdrawn.'

In the phrase 'frequenting a secluded seat' (bhajamanassa vivittamasanaṃ): the place where they sit is called a 'seat' (āsana). These are: a couch, a chair, a rug, a mat, a piece of hide, a grass mat, a leaf mat, or a straw mat. That seat is empty, secluded, and deeply secluded from seeing unsuitable visible objects; it is empty, secluded, and deeply secluded from hearing unsuitable sounds; from smelling unsuitable odors... from tasting unsuitable flavors... from touching unsuitable tangibles... it is empty, secluded, and deeply secluded from the five unsuitable cords of sensual pleasure. One who frequents, thoroughly frequents, associates with, resorts to, thoroughly associates with, and repeatedly associates with such a secluded seat is meant by 'frequenting a secluded seat.'
102:
That state of one who does not show oneself in existence is called sāmaggiya (concord). There are three kinds of sāmaggiya: gaṇasāmaggī (concord of the group), dhammasāmaggī (concord of the Dhamma), and anabhinibbattisāmaggī (concord of non-rebirth).

What is gaṇasāmaggī? If many monks live in concord, in agreement, without dispute, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection—this is called gaṇasāmaggī.

What is dhammasāmaggī? They are the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the noble eightfold path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga). These qualities converge into a single object, they are clear, well-established, and liberated. In these qualities, there is no dispute or contention. This is called dhammasāmaggī.

What is anabhinibbattisāmaggī? If many monks attain final Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu). In the Nibbāna element of those Arahants, no deficiency or fullness is perceived. This is called anabhinibbattisāmaggī.

Regarding 'in existence' (bhavane): for hell-beings, hell is the abode; for animals, the animal realm is the abode; for hungry ghosts, the realm of hungry ghosts is the abode; for humans, the human world is the abode; for devas, the deva world is the abode. That state of one who does not show oneself in existence is called sāmaggiya. If a person does not show oneself in hell which is thus concealed, does not show oneself in the animal realm, does not show oneself in the realm of hungry ghosts, does not show oneself in the human world, and does not show oneself in the deva world—this concord of his is fitting, suitable, worthy, and appropriate. Thus they say, preach, recite, show, and designate. Therefore, it is said: 'That state of one who does not show oneself in existence is called sāmaggiya.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'For a monk who lives withdrawn, who frequents a secluded seat, that state of one who does not show oneself in existence is called sāmaggiya (concord).'

The sage (muni) who is independent in all spheres (āyatana) does not create what is dear, nor what is undear. In that sage, lamentation and selfishness do not cling, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf.
103:
It is said that the sage is independent in all spheres. 'All' (sabba) refers to the twelve spheres (āyatana): eye and forms, ear and sounds, nose and odors, tongue and tastes, body and tangibles, mind and mental objects. The 'sage' (muni) refers to wisdom... That monk who lives having transcended the net of craving and views, who is without suffering, and who is worthy of offerings, is called a sage. The 'independent one' (anissita) refers to one who has abandoned the two dependencies: the dependency of craving (taṇhā-nissaya) and the dependency of views (diṭṭhi-nissaya)... This is the dependency of craving... This is the dependency of views. The sage, having abandoned the dependency of craving and relinquished the dependency of views, is independent of the eye, independent of the ear, independent of the nose, independent of the tongue, independent of the body, independent of the mind; independent of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, mental objects; independent of family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicinal requisites for the sick; independent of the sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, the immaterial element; independent of sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, five-constituent existence; independent of the past, the future, the present; independent of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. He is independent of all things, unattached, not approaching, not clinging, not adhering, having gone out, having departed, being liberated, being detached, living with a mind that has made no boundaries. Thus, 'the sage is independent in all spheres'.

'Does not create what is dear, nor what is undear' means that there are two kinds of dear things (piya): beings or formations (saṅkhāra). What are dear beings? Here, they are those who desire one's welfare, benefit, comfort, and security—mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, relatives, or kinsmen. These are dear beings. What are dear formations? Pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. These are dear formations. There are also two kinds of undear things (appiya): beings or formations. What are undear beings? Here, they are those who desire one's harm, lack of benefit, discomfort, and lack of security, or who wish to take one's life. These are undear beings. What are undear formations? Unpleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. These are undear formations. 'Does not create what is dear, nor what is undear' means he does not create what is dear through the power of lust, thinking, 'This being is dear to me, and these formations are pleasant.' He does not create what is undear through the power of hatred, thinking, 'This being is undear to me, and these formations are unpleasant.' He does not produce, does not bring about, does not manifest, and especially does not make them appear.
104:
Through the power of anger, he does not do, produce, generate, manifest, or especially manifest what is unpleasant. Therefore, it is said: "He does not create what is dear, nor what is undear."

"Just as water does not smear a lotus leaf, so lamentation and stinginess do not smear him" means: "In him" refers to that Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). "Lamentation" (parideva) is the wailing, lamenting, repeated lamenting, idle talk, and intense wailing of one affected by the loss of relatives, wealth, health, virtue, or view, or any other misfortune or painful state. "Stinginess" (macchariya) consists of the five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, families, gains, praise, and the Dhamma. Such stinginess, the act of being stingy, the state of being stingy, the shrinking of the mind, meanness, harshness, and the mind's grasping—this is called stinginess. Furthermore, stinginess regarding the aggregates (khandha), the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), and attachment are also called stinginess.

"Just as water does not smear a lotus leaf" means: "Paṇṇa" refers to a lotus leaf. "Vāri" refers to water. Just as water does not smear, stick to, or wet a lotus leaf, so too, in that Arahant whose taints are destroyed, lamentation and stinginess do not smear, stick to, or wet him. That Arahant is not smeared, stuck to, or wetted by those defilements; he has emerged, escaped, and is liberated from them, dwelling with a boundless mind. Therefore, it is said: "Just as water does not smear a lotus leaf, so lamentation and stinginess do not smear him."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The sage (muni) is independent in all things; he does not create what is dear, nor what is undear. Just as water does not smear a lotus leaf, so lamentation and stinginess do not smear that sage."

Just as a water drop does not smear a lotus leaf, and as water does not smear a lotus flower, so the sage is not smeared by what is seen, heard, or sensed (diṭṭha-suta-muta).

"Just as a water drop does not smear a lotus leaf" means: "Udabindu" refers to a drop of water. "Pokkhara" refers to a lotus leaf. Just as a water drop does not smear, stick to, or...
105:
In the explanation of "Just as a water drop does not smear a lotus leaf, and as water does not smear a lotus flower": "Udabindu" refers to a drop of water. "Pokkhara" refers to a lotus leaf. Just as a water drop does not smear, especially not smear, does not smear in connection with fetters, does not smear in connection with delusion, especially not smear in connection with delusion, and does not wet the lotus leaf even though it reaches it—this is the meaning of the phrase "udabindu yathāpi pokkhare." "Paduma" refers to a lotus flower. "Vāri" refers to water. Just as water does not smear, especially not smear, does not smear in connection with fetters, does not smear in connection with delusion, especially not smear in connection with delusion, and does not wet the lotus flower like water resting on a lotus petal—this is the meaning of the phrase "padume vāri yathā na limpati."

In the explanation of "So the sage is not smeared by what is seen, heard, or sensed": "So" (evaṃ) indicates the completion of the simile. Regarding the word "sage" (muni): Knowledge is called muni... because he has transcended the seven types of attachment such as lust and the sevenfold net of craving and views, he is called a sage. There are two types of smearing (lepa): the smearing of craving (taṇhā-lepa) and the smearing of views (diṭṭhi-lepa). ... This is the smearing of craving. ... This is the smearing of views. The sage, having abandoned the smearing of craving and relinquished the smearing of views, is not smeared by the seen, is not smeared by the heard, is not smeared by the sensed, is not smeared by the cognized; he is not especially smeared, not smeared in connection with the net of fetters, not smeared in connection with delusion, especially not smeared in connection with delusion. Just as water does not stay on a lotus leaf, he is not wetted; like one who has left home, he has emerged; like one who has discarded snake venom, he has abandoned it and does not take it back; like one freed from bonds, he is liberated from defilements and dwells with a boundless mind. This is the meaning of "So the sage is not smeared by what is seen, heard, or sensed."

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Just as a water drop does not smear a lotus leaf, and as water does not smear a lotus flower, so the sage is not smeared by what is seen, heard, or sensed."

The wise sage does not conceive of himself by means of what is seen, heard, or sensed; he does not desire any other purity; he is neither attached nor detached.

In the explanation of "The pure one (dhona) does not conceive by means of that, whether it be the seen, heard, or sensed": "Dhona" refers to wisdom (paññā). That wisdom which knows through impermanence and so on, the wisdom that knows phenomena according to their nature... non-delusion (amoha), investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). Why is wisdom called "dhona"? By that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off (dhuta) by the first path, washed (dhota) by the second path, well-washed (sandhota) by the third path, and specially washed (niddhota) by the fourth path. Verbal misconduct... mental misconduct is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and specially washed. Lust is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and specially washed. Hatred, delusion, anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), hypocrisy (makkha), spite (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), all defilements, all misconduct, all distress (daratha), all fever (pariḷāha), all anguish (santāpa), and all unwholesome formations are shaken off, washed, well-washed, and specially washed. Therefore, wisdom is called "dhona".
106:
Alternatively, by Right View, wrong view is shaken off (by the first path), washed (by the second path), thoroughly washed (by the third path), and completely purged (by the fourth path). By Right Resolve, wrong resolve is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely purged. By Right Speech, wrong speech is shaken off... By Right Action, wrong action is shaken off... By Right Livelihood, wrong livelihood is shaken off... By Right Effort, wrong effort is shaken off... By Right Mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is shaken off... By Right Concentration, wrong concentration is shaken off... By Right Knowledge, wrong knowledge is shaken off... By Right Liberation, wrong liberation is shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely purged.

Alternatively, by the Noble Eightfold Path, all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome formations are shaken off, washed, thoroughly washed, and completely purged. An Arahant is endowed with, fully endowed with, attained to, fully attained to, possessed of, fully possessed of, and accomplished in these purifying qualities. Therefore, an Arahant is called 'Dhona' (the Purified One). That Arahant has shaken off lust, shaken off evil, shaken off defilements, and shaken off fevers; therefore, he is called 'Dhona'.

The Arahant called 'Dhona' does not conceive or imagine himself (through craving, conceit, or views) by means of what is seen, heard, or sensed. The Dhona does not conceive the seen, does not conceive in the seen, does not conceive from the seen, and does not conceive 'I have seen'. He does not conceive the heard, does not conceive in the heard, does not conceive from the heard, and does not conceive 'I have heard'. He does not conceive the sensed, does not conceive in the sensed, does not conceive from the sensed, and does not conceive 'I have sensed'. He does not conceive the cognized, does not conceive in the cognized, does not conceive from the cognized, and does not conceive 'I have cognized'.

This was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, to think "I am" is a conceiving (the proliferation of craving, conceit, and views). To think "This is I" is a conceiving. To think "I shall be" is a conceiving. To think "I shall not be" is a conceiving. To think "I shall be possessed of form" is a conceiving. To think "I shall be formless" is a conceiving. To think "I shall be percipient" is a conceiving. To think "I shall be non-percipient" is a conceiving. To think "I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" is a conceiving. Monks, conceiving is a disease, conceiving is a boil, conceiving is a dart, conceiving is a calamity. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: "We will dwell with a mind that does not conceive."' Thus, the Arahant called Dhona does not conceive or imagine by means of what is seen, heard, or sensed.
107:
The phrase 'He does not desire purity through another' means that the Dhona (the Arahant who has washed away defilements) does not desire, delight in, long for, or aspire to purity, supreme purity, total purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or total liberation through any other impure path, wrong practice, or path that does not lead out of Saṃsāra, other than the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path.

'He neither lusts nor is he lustless' means that all foolish worldlings lust. Starting from noble worldlings, the seven types of trainees (sekkhas) are becoming lustless (detaching from lust). An Arahant, however, neither lusts nor is he lustless. He does not lust because of the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, being one whose lust, hatred, and delusion are already gone. That Arahant has lived the holy life, has fulfilled the required conduct... the round of birth, aging, and death no longer exists for him; there is no further becoming.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'The Dhona does not conceive himself by means of what is seen, heard, or sensed; he does not desire purity through another; he neither lusts nor is he lustless.'

## The Exposition of the Jarā Sutta is Finished.

## 7. Exposition of the Tissa Metteyya Sutta

Now, I shall speak the exposition of the Tissa Metteyya Sutta:

'O Venerable One who is free from suffering, please tell me the distress (suffering) that arises for one devoted to sexual intercourse. Having heard your teaching, we shall train in seclusion (viveka),' thus requested the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.

In the phrase 'of one devoted to sexual intercourse' (methunamanuyuttassa): sexual intercourse is called 'non-dhamma' (asaddhamma), 'village practice' (gāmadhamma), 'lowly practice' (vasaladhamma), 'coarse practice' (duṭṭhulla), 'ending in washing with water' (odakantika), 'secret practice' (rahassa), and 'the union of a couple' (dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti). Why is it called sexual intercourse (methuna dhamma)? Because it is the nature of two people—a woman and a man—who are alike in being affected by lust, intensely lustful, oozing with defilements, overwhelmed by defilements, whose wholesome minds are exhausted, and who are similar in their oozing defilements. For example, just as two people quarreling are called 'methunaka' (a pair), or two people fighting, speaking, arguing, elaborating, showing, or informing are called 'methunaka', so too it is called sexual intercourse because it is the nature of two people who are alike in being affected by lust and defilements. 'Devoted to sexual intercourse' means one who is well-devoted or intensely devoted to sexual intercourse.
108:
Two persons who engage in quarreling are also called 'methunaka' (partners). Two persons who engage in talking are also called 'methunaka'. Two persons who engage in disputing are also called 'methunaka'. Two persons who engage in legal affairs are also called 'methunaka'. Two persons who engage in arguing are also called 'methunaka'. Two persons who engage in conversation are also called 'methunaka'. In the same way, the nature of a man and a woman who are both lustful, intensely passionate, oozing with defilements, overwhelmed by defilements, whose minds are exhausted of merit, and who are similar in their oozing defilements, is called 'methunadhamma' (sexual practice).

'Methunamanuyuttassa' means one who is well-engaged in sexual practice, one who strives in it, one who is joined to it, one who is together joined to it, one who is habituated to it, one who frequently practices it, one who prioritizes it, one whose mind inclines towards it, one whose body leans towards it, one whose body tends towards it, one who is deeply immersed in it, and one who makes it primary.

In the phrase 'Iccāyasmā Tisso Metteyyo', 'Iccā' is a word-connection, a sequence of words, a completion of a word, a combination of letters, a smoothness of consonants, and the order of words. 'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a term of reverence, and a term of deference. 'Tisso' is the name of that elder, a designation, a concept, an appellation, a naming, a naming-act, a manifestation, a syllable (consonant), and an utterance. 'Metteyyo' is the clan name (gotra) of that elder, a designation, a concept, and an appellation. Thus it is said, 'Iccāyasmā Tisso Metteyyo'.

In the phrase 'Vighātaṃ brūhi mārisa', 'Vighātaṃ' means oppression, destruction through oppression, affliction, friction, danger, and affliction (upassagga). 'Brūhi' means speak, show, make known, establish, open up, analyze, clarify, and reveal. 'Mārisa' is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a term of reverence, and a term of deference. Thus it is said, 'Vighātaṃ brūhi mārisa'.

'Sutvāna tava sāsanaṃ' means having heard your words, teaching, instruction, and repeated instruction with the ear, having received them with the ear-sensitivity, having learned them well, having borne them in mind without forgetting, and noting them.

In the phrase 'Viveke sikkhiṣṣāmase', 'Viveka' (seclusion) is of three kinds: kāyaviveka (physical seclusion), cittaviveka (mental seclusion), and upadhiviveka (seclusion from acquisitions). What is kāyaviveka? Here, a bhikkhu frequents a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a mountain cave, a cemetery, a woodland, the open air, or a heap of straw; he dwells physically secluded. That bhikkhu goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, sleeps alone, enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, and in a secluded place alone...
109:
...sits, alone he undertakes walking meditation, alone he wanders, alone he dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, maintains, and sustains his life. This is called kāyaviveka (physical seclusion).

What is cittaviveka? For one who has attained the first jhāna, the mind is secluded from the hindrances. For one who has attained the second jhāna, the mind is secluded from initial and sustained thought. For one who has attained the third jhāna, the mind is secluded from rapture. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, the mind is secluded from pleasure and pain. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite space, the mind is secluded from the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity. For one who has attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, the mind is secluded from the perception of the sphere of infinite space. For one who has attained the sphere of nothingness, the mind is secluded from the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness. For one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the mind is secluded from the perception of the sphere of nothingness. For a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), the mind is secluded from self-identity view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, the underlying tendency to view, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the defilements associated with them. For a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi), the mind is secluded from gross sensual lust, gross ill-will, the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust, the gross underlying tendency to ill-will, and the defilements associated with them. For a Non-returner (Anāgāmi), the mind is secluded from subtle sensual lust, subtle ill-will, the subtle underlying tendency to sensual lust, the subtle underlying tendency to ill-will, and the defilements associated with them. For an Arahant, the mind is secluded from lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance, and the defilements associated with them, and externally from all signs (nimitta). This is called cittaviveka (mental seclusion).

What is upadhiviveka? Defilements, aggregates (khandha), and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are called 'upadhi' (acquisitions). The deathless Nibbāna is called upadhiviveka. That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—this is upadhiviveka.

Kāyaviveka occurs for those who have secluded bodies, being free from company and delighting in renunciation. Cittaviveka occurs for those with pure minds who have reached supreme purification. Upadhiviveka occurs for those persons free from acquisitions who have reached the unconditioned Nibbāna. Regarding the phrase "We shall train in seclusion," that elder has by nature already trained in the trainings. Nevertheless, based on the Dhamma teaching and wishing to hear the Dhamma, he said, "We shall train in seclusion."

Therefore, the Venerable Tissa Metteyya said this:
110: Venerable Tissa Metteyya addressed the Buddha thus: 'O Noble One, please tell the ruin of one devoted to sexual intercourse. Having heard your teaching, we shall train in seclusion (viveka).' The Blessed One, addressing him as 'Metteyya', said: 'For one devoted to sexual intercourse, the teaching is lost. He practices wrongly; this is ignoble in him.' 'Methunamanuyuttassa' means: Sexual intercourse (methunadhamma) is the unworthy practice (asaddhamma), the village practice (gāmadhamma), the vile practice (vasaladhamma), the coarse practice (duṭṭhulla), that which ends in washing with water (odakantika), the secret practice (rahassa), and the union of a pair (dvayaṃdvayasamāpatti). Why is it called 'methunadhamma'? Because it is the common practice of two people who are lustful, intensely impassioned, oozing with defilements, overwhelmed, and whose minds are possessed. Just as two people who quarrel are called 'methunaka' (a pair), or two who fight, or two who argue, or two who debate, or two who engage in a legal case, or two who dispute, or two who converse; in the same way, because it is the common practice of two people who are lustful, intensely impassioned, oozing with defilements, overwhelmed, and whose minds are possessed, it is called 'methunadhamma'. 'Methunamanuyuttassa' refers to one who is well-devoted, respectfully devoted, intensely striving, joined with, practicing, frequently engaging in, valuing, leaning towards, inclining towards, tending towards, entering into, and prioritizing that sexual intercourse. 'Metteyya' is how the Blessed One addressed the Elder by his lineage. 'Bhagavā' (Blessed One) is an epithet of respect. Furthermore, He is 'Bhagavā' because He has destroyed lust (bhaggarāga), destroyed hatred (bhaggadosa), destroyed delusion (bhaggamoha), destroyed conceit (bhaggamāna), destroyed wrong view (bhaggadiṭṭhi), destroyed the thorns of defilements (bhaggakaṇṭaka), and destroyed all defilements (bhaggakilesa). He is 'Bhagavā' because He has associated with, analyzed, and categorized the Jewel of Dhamma. He is 'Bhagavā' because He has made an end to existences. He is 'Bhagavā' because He has a developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, and developed wisdom. Or, He is 'Bhagavā' because He frequents remote forest lodgings that are quiet, free from noise,
111: free from the breath of people, suitable for human seclusion, and appropriate for meditation. Or, He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses (bhāgī) the four requisites: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions. He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses the flavor of meaning (attharasa), the flavor of Dhamma (dhammarasa), the flavor of liberation (vimuttirasa), higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā). He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses the four jhānas, the four immeasurables (appamaññā), and the four formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti). He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses the eight deliverances (vimokkha), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhāyatana), and the nine successive attainments (anupubbavihārasamāpatti). He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses the ten perceptions (saññābhāvanā), the ten kasina attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassatisamādhi), and the attainment of foulness (asubhasamāpatti). He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path. He is 'Bhagavā' because He possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the six higher powers (abhiññā), and the six Buddha-qualities (buddhadhamma). This name 'Bhagavā' was not given by His mother, nor by His father, nor by His brother, nor by His sister, nor by His friends and colleagues, nor by His relatives, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities. This name 'Bhagavā' is a realized designation of the Blessed Buddhas, which arose at the end of the Path of Arahatship along with the attainment of omniscience at the root of the Bodhi tree. 'Metteyya' refers to the Blessed One [addressing him]. 'The teaching is lost' means the teaching is lost through two causes: the teaching of scriptures (pariyatti sāsana) is lost, and the teaching of practice (paṭipatti sāsana) is lost. What is the teaching of scriptures? It is the Tipiṭaka that he has learned: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. This is the teaching of scriptures. This too is lost, disappears, is forgotten, is utterly forgotten, and becomes obscured. Thus, the teaching is lost. What is the teaching of practice? It is the right practice, the practice in accordance with the supramundane, the practice not contrary to the supramundane, the practice in accordance with the meaning, the practice in accordance with the Dhamma, fulfilling the virtues, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. This is the teaching of practice. This too is lost, disappears, is forgotten, is utterly forgotten, and becomes obscured. Thus, the teaching is lost.
112:
## 
'Practices wrongly' means—he kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, commits robbery by breaking into treasuries, commits gang robbery, waits on the path to rob, goes to another's wife, and speaks falsehood. Thus, he practices wrongly.

'This practice in him is not noble' means—this wrong practice in that person is the nature of the ignoble, the nature of fools, the nature of the deluded, the nature of the ignorant, and the nature of the eel-wrigglers (amarāvikkhepa). Thus, this practice in him is not noble.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Metteyya, for one devoted to sexual intercourse,
The teaching of the Buddha declines;
He practices wrongly, and that practice in him is not noble."

Having formerly lived alone, he who indulges in sexual intercourse, they call that commoner in the world low, like a swaying vehicle.

'Having formerly lived alone' means—living alone formerly occurs through two reasons: by way of reaching the state of a monk (pabbajjā) or by way of abandoning the group to live alone. How does one live alone formerly by way of reaching the state of a monk? Having cut off all concerns of household life, concerns of children and wife, concerns of relatives, concerns of friends and associates, and concerns of hoarding; having shaved hair and beard, donning saffron-dyed robes, and having gone forth from the home life to homelessness, reaching the state of having nothing, he lives, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, and maintains himself alone. Thus, one lives alone formerly by way of reaching the state of a monk.

How does one live alone formerly by way of abandoning the group to live alone? That person, having thus gone forth, frequents solitary forest dwellings and remote lodgings that are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, suitable for retreat. He goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone, returns alone, sits in private alone, practices walking meditation alone, lives, dwells, moves, proceeds, protects, and maintains himself alone. Thus, one lives alone formerly by way of abandoning the group to live alone.

'He who indulges in sexual intercourse' means—what is called sexual intercourse (methunadhamma) is the practice of those who are not virtuous... for that reason it is called sexual intercourse. He who—
113: —indulges means: he who at a later time, having discarded the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, and having returned to the lower life, indulges in, associates with, frequents, and practices sexual intercourse. Thus, "he who indulges in sexual intercourse." "In the world, like a swaying vehicle" means: it is like a swaying vehicle in the world. "Vehicle" refers to an elephant-vehicle, a horse-vehicle, an ox-vehicle, a goat-vehicle, a sheep-vehicle, a camel-vehicle, or a donkey-vehicle. That vehicle, being swaying, untamed, poorly prepared, and undisciplined, takes the wrong path, climbs over uneven stumps and stones, breaks the vehicle and the rider's footrest, and falls down a cliff. Just as that swaying vehicle, being untamed, poorly prepared, and undisciplined, takes the wrong path; even so, that one who has gone astray, being like a swaying vehicle, takes the wrong path, takes up wrong view... takes up wrong concentration. Just as that swaying vehicle, being untamed, poorly prepared, and undisciplined, climbs over uneven stumps and stones; even so, that one who has gone astray, being like a swaying vehicle, climbs onto uneven bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions. He climbs onto uneven killing of living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, gossip, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. He climbs onto uneven formations, onto the five cords of sensual pleasure, and onto the hindrances. Just as that swaying vehicle, being untamed, poorly prepared, and undisciplined, breaks the vehicle and the rider's footrest; even so, that one who has gone astray, being like a swaying vehicle, breaks himself in hell, in the animal realm, in the realm of hungry ghosts, in the human world, and in the deva world. Just as that swaying vehicle, being untamed, poorly prepared, and undisciplined, falls down a cliff; even so, that one who has gone astray, being like a swaying vehicle, falls into the cliff of birth, falls into the cliff of aging, falls into the cliff of sickness, falls into the cliff of death, and falls into the cliff of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. "In the world" means in the world of suffering and the human world. This is the meaning of "like a swaying vehicle in the world." "They call the worldling low" means: they say the worldling is inferior. For what reason are they called "worldlings" (puthujjana)? They are worldlings because they generate many (puthu) defilements; they are worldlings because their self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is many and undestroyed; they are worldlings because they look at the faces of many teachers; they are worldlings because they have not emerged from all destinations (gati).
114:
Worldlings (puthujjanas) are so called because they process various and diverse volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). They are called worldlings because they are swept away by various and diverse floods (ogha). They are called worldlings because they are tormented by various and diverse torments (santāpa). They are called worldlings because they are burned by various and diverse fevers (pariḷāha). They are called worldlings because they are attached to, greedy for, bound to, infatuated with, deeply obsessed with, fastened to, entangled in, and obstructed by the five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa). They are called worldlings because they are covered, hindered, obstructed, closed off, concealed, and overturned by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

"They call a worldling low" means that they speak of, describe, tell of, show, and designate a worldling as low, base, inferior, mean, of low disposition, and insignificant.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One who, having previously lived alone, indulges in sexual intercourse, is called a low worldling in the world, like a swaying vehicle.
Whatever fame and reputation he had before, that also diminishes for him. Having seen this disadvantage, one should train to abandon sexual intercourse."

"Whatever fame and reputation he had before, that also diminishes for him"—what does this mean? What is fame (yasa)? Here, someone was previously respected, honored, revered, venerated, and esteemed in his state as a monk. He was a recipient of the four requisites: robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal offerings. This is called fame (yasa). What is reputation (kitti)? Here, someone previously had a renowned reputation in his state as a monk, being wise, competent, sagacious, learned, a brilliant speaker, and of fine wit. Or he was known as an expert in the Suttas (suttantika), an expert in the Vinaya (vinayadhara), a Dhamma teacher (dhammakathika), a forest dweller (āraññika), an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika), a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), a three-robe wearer (tecīvarika), an uninterrupted alms-goer (sapadānacārika), one who refuses later food (khalupacchābhattika), a sitter (nesajjika), or one who uses whatever bed is provided (yathāsanthatika). Or he was known as an attainer of the first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, or the fourth jhāna. Or he was known as an attainer of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called reputation (kitti). Thus: "Whatever fame and reputation he had before."
115:
"That also diminishes for him" means that at a later time, for that person who has abandoned the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training and returned to the low life (of a layman), that fame and that reputation and good report diminish, decline, decay, fall away, disappear, and vanish. This is the meaning of the words: "Whatever fame and reputation he had before, that also diminishes for him."

"Having seen this disadvantage, one should train to abandon sexual intercourse"—here, "this disadvantage" refers to the fame and reputation one had in the previous state as a monk, and the lack of fame and lack of reputation that arise when one later abandons the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, and training to return to lay life; it refers to this success and failure. "Having seen" means having looked at, weighed, investigated, and made clear those advantages and disadvantages. "One should train" refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā).

What is the training in higher virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort (ācāra-gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. There are small groups of virtue and large groups of virtue. Virtue is the foundation, the beginning, the base, the restraint, the closure, the forefront, and the precursor for the attainment of wholesome states. This is the training in higher virtue.

What is the training in higher mind? Here, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. ... (omitted text) ... He enters and dwells in the second jhāna, the third jhāna, and the fourth jhāna. This is the training in higher mind.

What is the training in higher wisdom? Here, a monk is wise; he possesses wisdom regarding the arising and passing away (of phenomena), which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is: "This is suffering." He understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering." He understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering." He understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering." He understands as it really is: "These are the taints (āsavas)." He understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints." He understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints." He understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints." This is the training in higher wisdom.

Sexual intercourse (methunadhamma) is that which is the practice of those who are not good (asaddhamma). ... (omitted text) ... For that reason, it is called sexual intercourse.
116:
Seeing this danger as well, one should train to completely abandon sexual intercourse. For the sake of abandoning, stilling, relinquishing, and subsiding sexual intercourse, one should train in the training of higher virtue (adhisīla), the training of higher mind (adhicitta), and the training of higher wisdom (adhipaññā). One should train in these three trainings while contemplating the danger, while knowing, while seeing, while reflecting repeatedly, while steadying the mind, while resolving with faith, while exerting effort, while establishing mindfulness, while concentrating the mind, while understanding with wisdom, while knowing with direct knowledge what should be known with direct knowledge, while fully understanding what should be fully understood, while abandoning what should be abandoned, while developing what should be developed, and while realizing what should be realized. One should practice, conduct oneself well, and proceed by undertaking them. Thus, seeing this danger as well, one should train to completely abandon sexual intercourse.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever fame and reputation there was before, that of his diminishes. Seeing this danger as well, one should train to completely abandon sexual intercourse."

Overwhelmed by thoughts, he broods like a wretched person. Hearing the sound of others' [reproach], such a person becomes dejected.

"Overwhelmed by thoughts, he broods like a wretched person" means: being touched, overwhelmed, permeated, possessed, and covered by sensual thoughts (kāmasankappa), thoughts of ill-will (byāpādasankappa), thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsāsankappa), and thoughts of wrong view (diṭṭhisankappa), he broods like a wretched person, like a fool, like one utterly confused; he broods, he broods intensely, he broods closely, he broods dejectedly. Just as an owl on a tree branch broods, broods intensely, broods closely, and broods dejectedly while seeking a mouse; just as a fox on a riverbank broods, broods intensely, broods closely, and broods dejectedly while seeking fish; just as a cat in a rubbish heap between two houses broods, broods intensely, broods closely, and broods dejectedly while seeking a mouse; just as a donkey with a broken back broods, broods intensely, broods closely, and broods dejectedly in a rubbish heap between two houses; even so, that person who has fallen from the holy life, being touched, overwhelmed, permeated, possessed, and covered by sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of cruelty, and thoughts of wrong view, broods like a wretched person, like a fool, like one utterly confused; he broods, he broods intensely, he broods closely, and he broods dejectedly. Thus, overwhelmed by thoughts, he broods like a wretched person.
117:
Hearing the sound of others' [reproach], such a person becomes dejected. "Others" refers to preceptors (upajjhāya), teachers (ācariya), fellow students of the same preceptor, fellow students of the same teacher, friends, acquaintances, or companions. They rebuke him, saying: "Friend, it is a loss for you, it is poorly gained by you, that having obtained such a noble Teacher, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, and having obtained such a community of Noble Ones (ariyagaṇa), you have abandoned the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training for the sake of the low practice of sexual intercourse and returned to the low life. You had no faith in wholesome states, no shame (hiri) in wholesome states, no fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) in wholesome states, no energy (vīriya) in wholesome states, no mindfulness (sati) in wholesome states, and no wisdom (paññā) in wholesome states." Upon hearing, listening to, grasping, considering, and perceiving their words, elaborations, explanations, instructions, and admonitions, he becomes dejected; he is oppressed, struck, pained, and displeased. "Such a person" (tathāvidho) means one of such a nature, of such a state, of such a kind, of such a sort—referring to the one who has fallen from the holy life. Thus, hearing the sound of others' [reproach], such a person becomes dejected.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Overwhelmed by thoughts, he broods like a wretched person. Hearing the sound of others' [reproach], such a person becomes dejected."

Furthermore, when rebuked by the words of others, he prepares weapons. For him, this false speech is indeed a great attachment.

In the phrase "Furthermore, when rebuked by the words of others, he prepares weapons," the word "atha" (furthermore) signifies the connection of words, the combination of words, the completion of words, the union of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequence of words. "Weapons" (satthāni) are of three kinds: the bodily weapon, the verbal weapon, and the mental weapon. The three types of bodily misconduct are the bodily weapon; the four types of verbal misconduct are the verbal weapon; the three types of mental misconduct are the mental weapon. "Rebuked by the words of others" means when rebuked by preceptors, teachers, fellow students of the same preceptor, fellow students of the same teacher, friends, acquaintances, or companions, he speaks a deliberate lie. He says, "Venerable sir, I was very delighted in the monkhood. However, I had to support my mother, and for that reason, I have returned to the lay life."
118:
“I must support my father; for that reason, I have departed from the Dispensation (disrobed),” he says. “I must support my brother... I must support my sister... I must support my son... I must support my daughter... I must support my friends... I must support my servants... I must support my relatives... I must support my kinsmen; for that reason, I have departed from the Dispensation,” he says.
