He creates a weapon of speech, elaborates it, produces it, generates it, brings it into being, and manifests it. Thus, when urged and prompted by others, he creates weapons of speech.

“This is his great attachment (mahāgedha)” means—this deliberate lying is his great attachment, a great forest, an impenetrable thicket, a great wilderness, a great uneven path, a great crookedness, a great mire, a great swamp, a great anxiety, and a great bond. This is what is meant by “This is his great attachment.”

“He engages in falsehood” means—speaking untruth is called mosavajja (falsehood). In this world, a certain person, being in an assembly, or in a gathering, or among relatives, or in a guild, or in a royal court, when summoned as a witness and questioned, “O man, tell what you know,” says “I know” when he does not know, or “I do not know” when he knows, or “I see” when he does not see, or “I do not see” when he sees. Thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of others, or for the sake of some small material gain (āmisa), he deliberately speaks untruth; this is called mosavajja.

Furthermore, falsehood (musāvāda) occurs through three factors: having the intention before speaking, “I will speak a lie”; knowing while speaking, “I am speaking a lie”; and knowing after speaking, “I have spoken a lie.” Through these three factors, falsehood occurs. Furthermore, falsehood occurs through four factors: knowing before speaking, “I will speak a lie”; knowing while speaking, “I am speaking a lie”; knowing after speaking, “I have spoken a lie”; and concealing one’s own view (diṭṭhi). Through these four factors, falsehood occurs. Furthermore, falsehood occurs through five, six, seven, or eight factors: knowing before, during, and after speaking, along with concealing one’s view (diṭṭhi), concealing one’s preference (khanti), concealing one’s liking (ruci), concealing one’s perception (saññā), and concealing one’s nature (bhāva). Through these eight factors, falsehood occurs. This is what is meant by “He engages in falsehood.”
119:
“He engages in falsehood” means he takes up, enters into, plunges into, and penetrates falsehood. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “When urged by the arguments of others, he creates weapons; this is his great attachment, he engages in falsehood.”

“Known as a wise man, committed to the solitary life, yet if he indulges in sexual intercourse, he will suffer like a fool.”

“Known as a wise man” means—in this case, a certain person was previously famous and renowned in his state as a monk, as being “wise, clever, sagacious, learned, an eloquent speaker, of ready wit, a master of the Suttas, a master of the Vinaya, a Dhamma-teacher... a winner of the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.” Being thus known, recognized, and renowned is what is meant by “Known as a wise man.”

“Committed to the solitary life (ekaccariyaṃ adhiṭṭhito)” means—he is committed to the higher life through two reasons: either by way of renunciation (pabbajjā) or by way of abandoning the group (gaṇāvavassagga). How is he committed to the higher life by way of renunciation? Having cut off all the impediments of household life... thus he is committed to the higher life by way of renunciation. How is he committed to the higher life by way of abandoning the group? Having thus renounced, he dwells alone in remote forest dwellings... thus, by abandoning the group and its attendants, he is committed to the higher life; this is what is meant by “Committed to the solitary life.”

“Yet if he indulges in sexual intercourse” means—sexual intercourse is that which is the un-dhamma (assadhamma), the practice of villagers (gāmadhamma)... for that reason it is called sexual intercourse. “Yet if he indulges in sexual intercourse” means—at a later time, having discarded the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, and having returned to the low life of a layman, he indulges in, is devoted to, is occupied with, and is fully engaged in sexual intercourse.

“He will suffer like a fool” means—like a wretched person, like a fool, like a deluded person, he suffers, he is afflicted, he is tormented. He kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, carries away plunder, commits robbery, waylays travelers, goes to the wives of others, and speaks falsehood. In this way, he suffers, is afflicted, and is tormented. The kings, having captured him, subject him to various punishments (royal penalties). They flog him with whips, beat him with sticks, cut off his hands, cut off his feet, cut off both hands and feet, cut off his ears, cut off his nose. They also subject him to the boiling gruel-pot, the shell-shave (shaving the head as smooth as a shell), the mouth-lamp (opening the mouth and lighting a lamp inside), the fire-garland (wrapping the body in oil-soaked cloth and setting it on fire), the hand-torch, the hay-weave (flaying the skin from the neck down), the bark-dress, the antelope-stand (pinning to the ground and burning), and the flesh-hooking (pulling flesh with hooks).
120:
The kings arrest [him] and cause various tortures to be inflicted. They beat [him] with whips, with canes, and with half-staffs. They cut off the hands, the feet, and both hands and feet. They cut off the ears, the nose, and both ears and nose. They perform the 'gruel-pot' [torture], the 'shell-shave', the 'Rāhu's mouth', the 'fire-garland', the 'hand-torch', the 'grass-sheath', the 'bark-dress', the 'antelope-stand', the 'flesh-hooking', the 'coin-cut', the 'alkali-wash', the 'pivot-turn', and the 'straw-seat'. They also pour hot oil, have him bitten by dogs, impale him alive on a stake, and cut off his head with a sword. In this way, he undergoes pain, suffering, and intense affliction.

Furthermore, one overcome by sensual craving (kāmatanhā), with a mind obsessed, seeking wealth, plunges into the great ocean by boat. Facing cold and facing heat, tormented by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, nearly dying of hunger and thirst, he goes to the country of Tigumba, to Takkola, to Takkasila, to Kālamukha, to Purapura, to Vesunga, to Verāpatha, to Java, to Tāmali, to Vaṅga, to Eḷabandhana, to Suvaṇṇakūṭa, to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, to Tambapaṇṇi, to Suppādaka, to Bharukaccha, to Suraṭṭha, to Baṅgaloka, to Baṅgaṇa, to Saramatagaṇa, to Yona, to Paramayona, to Vinaka, to Mūlapada, and to the Maru desert. He travels by the knee-path, the goat-path, the sheep-path, the spike-path, the umbrella-path, the bamboo-path, the bird-path, the mouse-path, the cliff-path, and the cane-path. In this way, he undergoes pain, suffering, and intense affliction.

If, while seeking wealth, he does not obtain it, he experiences the pain and grief rooted in non-acquisition. In this way, he undergoes pain, suffering, and intense affliction.

If, while seeking wealth, he obtains it, he experiences the pain and grief rooted in guarding the acquired wealth: 'How may kings not take my wealth? How may thieves not take it? How may fire not burn it? How may water not wash it away? How may unwanted heirs not take it?' Even as he guards and protects it, that wealth perishes. He...
121:
...experiences the pain and grief rooted in separation [from wealth]. In this way, he undergoes pain, suffering, and intense affliction. 'And even he, if entangled in sexual intercourse, suffers like a fool.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'He who is known as a wise man, who is established in solitary practice, even he, if entangled in sexual intercourse, suffers like a fool.'

Knowing this danger, the sage, in the former and the latter [states] here, should firmly practice solitary wandering and should not indulge in sexual intercourse.

In the phrase 'Knowing this danger, the sage, in the former and the latter [states] here,' 'this' (etaṃ) refers to the praise and fame in the former state of being a monk, and the lack of praise and fame for one who, in the latter state, renounces the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, and the training to return to the low life [of a layman]; it refers to such success and failure. 'Knowing' (ñatvā) means having known, having weighed, having investigated, and having made clear. 'Sage' (muni): knowledge is called mona. That wisdom which knows... (etc.) he who has transcended the web of attachment is called a sage. 'Here' (idha) means in this view, in this patience, in this preference, in this view, in this Dhamma, in this Vinaya, in this Dhamma-Vinaya, in this well-spoken word, in this holy life, in this teaching of the Teacher, in this existence, in this human world. Thus, knowing this danger, the sage, in the former and the latter [states] here, should firmly practice solitary wandering.

'Should firmly practice solitary wandering' (ekaccariyaṃ daḷhaṃ kayirā) means one should firmly practice solitary wandering through two reasons: either by the reason called renunciation (pabbajjā) or by the reason called abandoning the company (gaṇāvavassagga). How does one firmly practice solitary wandering by renunciation? Having cut off all anxieties of household life, having cut off anxieties regarding children and wife, having cut off anxieties regarding relatives, having cut off anxieties regarding friends and colleagues, having cut off anxieties regarding accumulation, having shaved off hair and beard, having donned the saffron robes, having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, having reached the state of having no possessions, one should wander alone, dwell alone, move alone, behave alone, protect [oneself] alone, and maintain [oneself] alone. Thus, one firmly practices solitary wandering by renunciation.

How does one firmly practice solitary wandering by abandoning the company? That monk, having thus gone forth, should resort to remote forest-lodgings that are quiet, free from noise, with a breeze away from people, suitable for human secrecy, and appropriate for seclusion. He should walk alone, stand alone, sit alone, lie down alone, and enter the village for alms alone.
122:
One should withdraw alone, one should sit in solitude, one should resolve upon walking meditation alone, one should practice alone, stay alone, maintain one's posture alone, proceed alone, protect oneself alone, sustain oneself alone, and keep oneself going alone. Thus, by relinquishing the company of a group, one should firmly practice the solitary life—this means one should firmly practice the solitary life, one should make it stable, one should be firm in undertaking it, one should be steadfast in undertaking wholesome states. For this reason, it is said: "One should firmly practice the solitary life."

"One should not engage in sexual intercourse" means: sexual intercourse is that which is the ignoble practice, the practice of villagers... [pe]... for that reason, it is called sexual intercourse. One should not associate with, should not engage in, should not consort with, should not indulge in, should not practice, should not perform in any way, and should not proceed by undertaking sexual intercourse. For this reason, it is said: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Having known this danger, the sage, in this world, both before and after,
Should firmly practice the solitary life, and should not engage in sexual intercourse."

"One should train in seclusion itself; this is the highest of the Noble Ones.
One should not think oneself superior because of that; he is indeed near to Nibbāna."

"One should train in seclusion itself" means: regarding seclusion (*viveka*), there are three kinds of seclusion—physical seclusion (*kāya-viveka*), mental seclusion (*citta-viveka*), and seclusion from acquisitions (*upadhi-viveka*). What is physical seclusion? ... [pe] ... this is seclusion from acquisitions. Physical seclusion is for those whose bodies are secluded and who delight in renunciation. Mental seclusion is for those with purified minds who have attained supreme purity. Seclusion from acquisitions is for those persons who are free from acquisitions and have reached the unconditioned. Regarding training (*sikkhā*), there are three trainings—the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom... [pe]... this is the training in higher wisdom. "One should train in seclusion itself" means one should train in, should practice, should perform, and should proceed by undertaking seclusion itself. For this reason, it is said: "One should train in seclusion itself."

"This is the highest of the Noble Ones" means: the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddhas, and the Paccekabuddhas are called Noble Ones (*Ariyas*). For these Noble Ones, this practice of seclusion is the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent. For this reason, it is said: "This is the highest of the Noble Ones."

"One should not think oneself superior because of that" means: one should not practice elation, should not practice arrogance, should not practice pride, should not practice stubbornness, and should not practice obstinacy because of the practice of physical seclusion. One should not generate pride because of it; one should not be stiff, particularly stiff, or hold one's head high because of that seclusion. For this reason, it is said: "One should not think oneself superior because of that."
123:
"He is indeed near to Nibbāna" means that person is in the vicinity of, close to, nearby, and not far from Nibbāna. For this reason, it is said: "He is indeed near to Nibbāna."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One should train in seclusion itself; this is the highest of the Noble Ones.
One should not think oneself superior because of that; he is indeed near to Nibbāna."

Beings who are attached to sensual pleasures envy the sage who wanders empty [of defilements], who is without regard for sensual pleasures, and who has crossed the flood.

"Of the sage who wanders empty" (*rittassa munino carato*) means: one who is empty, secluded, and profoundly secluded from all defilements. One who is empty, secluded, and profoundly secluded from bodily misconduct, from verbal misconduct... [pe]... from mental misconduct, from lust, from hatred, from delusion, from anger (*kodha*), from malice (*upanāha*), from contempt (*makkha*), from domineering (*paḷāsa*), from envy (*issā*), from avarice (*macchariya*), from deceit (*māyā*), from fraud (*sāṭheyya*), from obstinacy (*thambha*), from impetuosity (*sārambha*), from pride (*māna*), from arrogance (*atimāna*), from intoxication (*mada*), from negligence (*pamāda*), from all defilements, from all misconduct, from all distress (*daratha*), from all fever (*pariḷāha*), from all burning (*santāpa*), and from all unwholesome volitional formations. "Sage" (*muni*) means one who possesses the knowledge called *mona*... [pe]... because he has transcended the net of attachment, he is called a sage. "Wandering" (*carato*) means one who is practicing, living, maintaining his posture, proceeding, protecting, sustaining, and keeping himself going. This is the meaning of "of the sage who wanders empty."

"Without regard for sensual pleasures" (*kāmesu anapekkhino*) means one who has no longing for sensual pleasures. Sensual pleasures (*kāma*) are twofold in brief: objective sensuality (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilement sensuality (*kilesa-kāma*)... [pe]... these things are called objective sensuality... [pe]... these things are called defilement sensuality. Having fully understood objective sensuality, and having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and made non-existent the defilement sensuality, one is without regard for sensual pleasures. Such a person has given up sensual pleasures, vomited them, is freed from them, has abandoned them, and has relinquished them. He is free from lust, has given up lust, vomited it, is freed from it, has abandoned it, and has relinquished it. He is without craving, extinguished, cooled, experiences happiness, and dwells with a mind that has become sublime. This is what is meant by "without regard for sensual pleasures."

"Beings who are attached to sensual pleasures envy the one who has crossed the flood" means: "beings" (*pajā*) is a term for living beings. Beings are enamored with, greedy for, attached to, infatuated with, engrossed in, clinging to, and fettered by sensual pleasures. Those beings envy the one who has crossed the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance; the one who has crossed the path of all formations; the one who has crossed over, gone beyond, transcended, fully transcended, and surpassed; the one who has reached the other shore, which is Nibbāna; the one who has [reached] the other shore...
124:
One who has reached the end, one who stands having reached the end; one who has reached the limit, one who stands having reached the limit; one who has reached the boundary, one who stands having reached the boundary; one who has reached the goal, one who stands having reached the goal; one who has reached the refuge, one who stands having reached the refuge; one who has reached the shelter, one who stands having reached the shelter; one who has reached the protection, one who stands having reached the protection; one who has reached the fearless state, one who stands having reached the fearless state; one who has reached the unchanging Nibbāna, one who stands having reached the unchanging Nibbāna; one who has reached the immortal Nibbāna, one who stands having reached the immortal Nibbāna; one who has reached Nibbāna, one who stands having reached Nibbāna—they desire, they delight in, they long for, they aspire to, they yearn for such a person.

Just as debtors long for and aspire to the state of being debt-free; just as the sick long for and aspire to health; just as those bound by fetters long for and aspire to release from fetters; just as slaves long for and aspire to the state of liberty; just as those who have entered upon a desert journey long for and aspire to a safe ground; in the same way, beings who are attached, greedy, clinging, infatuated, absorbed, stuck, fastened, and obstructed by sensual pleasures—they desire, they delight in, they long for, they aspire to, they yearn for one who has crossed the flood of sensual pleasures, one who has crossed the flood of existence... (pe)... one who has reached Nibbāna, one who stands having reached Nibbāna. Beings clinging to sensual pleasures long for the one who has crossed the flood.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'For the sage who is empty (of defilements) and wanders without expectation of sensual pleasures,
For the one who has crossed the flood, the beings clinging to sensual pleasures long for him.'

## The Exposition of the Tissa Metteyya Sutta, the Seventh, is finished.

## 8. Exposition of the Pasūra Sutta

Now, the exposition of the Pasūra Sutta will be stated:

They claim, "Purity is only here," and do not say there is purity in other teachings.
Saying that what they rely on is good, many are established in their individual truths.

"They claim, 'Purity is only here'" means they speak of, tell of, recite, manifest, and declare purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and complete liberation only in this view. They speak of, tell of, recite, manifest, and declare purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and complete liberation, saying, "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is vain." "The world is non-eternal..."
125:
...the world. The world is finite. The world is infinite. The soul is the same as the body. The soul is different from the body. The Tathāgata exists after death. The Tathāgata does not exist after death. The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death. The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. "This alone is the truth, everything else is vain"—thus they speak of, tell of, recite, manifest, and declare purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and complete liberation. Thus, they claim purity is only here.

"They do not say there is purity in other teachings" means that except for their own teacher, the Dhamma taught, the group, the view, the practice, and the path, they discard, reject, and cast aside all other doctrines. They say, "That teacher is not all-knowing, the Dhamma is not well-expounded, the group has not practiced well, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path is not leading to liberation. In that view, there is no purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or complete liberation. In that view, they are not purified, not supremely purified, not completely purified, not liberated, not supremely liberated, not completely liberated. They are inferior, very inferior, low, base, wretched, and insignificant." Thus they speak, say, tell, recite, manifest, and declare. Thus, they do not say there is purity in other teachings.

"Saying that what they rely on is good" means whatever teacher, Dhamma taught, group, view, practice, and path they rely on, depend on, are attached to, have approached, are absorbed in, and are devoted to. "In that view" means in their own view, in their own patience, in their own preference, in their own doctrine (they are established). "Saying it is good" means they say it is good, they say it is beautiful, they say it is wise, they say it is firm, they say it is logical, they say it is reasoned, they say it is characterized, they say it is causal, they say it is grounded; they say this according to their own doctrine. Thus, they say that what they rely on is good.

"Many are established in their individual truths" means many recluses and brahmins are established, settled, attached, approached, absorbed, and devoted to many individual truths. They are established, settled, attached, approached, absorbed, and devoted, saying, "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is vain." They are established... (pe)... saying, "The world is non-eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, everything else is vain." Thus, many are established in their individual truths.

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
126:
“They say, ‘Purity is only here’; they do not say there is purity in other teachings. Saying that what they rely on is good, they are individually entrenched in their various truths.”

Desiring debate, they enter an assembly and mutually regard each other as fools. Desiring praise and claiming to be skilled, they rely on others and engage in contentious talk.

“Te vādakāmā parisaṃ vigayha” means: “Te vādakāmā” refers to those who desire debate, intend for debate, prioritize debate, and practice while seeking debate. “Parisaṃ vigayha” means approaching, entering, and going into an assembly of nobles (khattiya), an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics. Thus, it is said: “Te vādakāmā parisaṃ vigayha.”

“Bālaṃ dahantī mithu aññamaññaṃ” means: “Mithu” refers to two persons who are quarreling, disputing, engaging in verbal strife, creating a legal case, competing in debate, or conversing. They regard, see, observe, contemplate, and examine each other as a fool, as low, as inferior, as insignificant, as wretched, as base, or as trifling. Thus, it is said: “Bālaṃ dahantī mithu aññamaññaṃ.”

“Vadanti te aññasitā kathojjaṃ” means: “Aññasitā” refers to those who rely on, are attached to, or have entered into another teacher, another doctrine, another group, another view, another practice, or another path. “Kathojjaṃ” refers to quarreling, strife, wrong views, disputes, or verbal conflict. Alternatively, “kathojjaṃ” refers to talk that is without essence and is inferior. They speak, utter, demonstrate, and call out words of quarreling, strife, and dispute. Thus, it is said: “Vadanti te aññasitā kathojjaṃ.”

“Pasaṃsākāmā kusalāvadānā” means: “Pasaṃsākāmā” refers to those who desire praise, intend for praise, prioritize praise, and wander about seeking praise. “Kusalāvadānā” refers to those who are accustomed to saying, regarding their own views: “We are clever, we are wise, our speech is firm, our speech is appropriate, our speech is reasoned, our speech is characterized by logic, our speech is supported by evidence, and our speech is timely.” Thus, it is said: “Pasaṃsākāmā kusalāvadānā.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
127:
“Desiring debate, they enter an assembly and mutually regard each other as fools. Desiring praise and claiming to be skilled, they rely on others and engage in contentious talk.”

“One who is engaged in debate in the midst of an assembly becomes distressed, desiring praise. When his view is refuted, he becomes dejected; seeking faults in others, he is shaken by criticism.”

“Engaged in debate in the midst of an assembly” means exerting oneself and approaching to speak one's own view in the midst of an assembly of nobles, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics.

“He becomes distressed, desiring praise” means that one who desires, craves, and is attached to praise, commendation, fame, and reputation becomes distressed even before the conversation begins. He is filled with doubt: “Will I be victorious? Will I be defeated? How shall I refute him? How shall I make my view pure? How shall I make it distinctive? How shall I make it repeatedly distinctive? How shall I entwine him? How shall I unravel the argument? How shall I cut down his view? How shall I form a collection of arguments?” Thus, even before the conversation, he is distressed by doubt. This is what is meant by “He becomes distressed, desiring praise.”

“When his view is refuted, he becomes dejected” means that the assembly of investigators, attendants, and experts refutes him. They refute him on the grounds of meaning, saying, “You have spoken words devoid of meaning.” They refute him on the grounds of phrasing, saying, “You have spoken words devoid of phrasing.” They refute him on both grounds, saying, “You have spoken words devoid of both meaning and phrasing.” They refute him by saying, “Your meaning is poorly presented; your phrasing is poorly established. Your meaning and phrasing are poorly presented and poorly established. Your refutation was not achieved; your establishment of your own view was poorly done. You did not achieve anything distinctive; you performed your repeated distinctions poorly. You did not achieve an entwining; you performed your unraveling poorly. You did not achieve a cutting of the view; you performed your collection of arguments poorly. Your speech is inconsistent, poorly spoken, poorly uttered, poorly expressed, spoken in a different manner, and is a bad utterance.” When his view is thus refuted, he becomes dejected...
128:
When one's doctrine is refuted, one becomes dejected (dispirited) means: when one's doctrine is refuted, one is oppressed, struck, afflicted, and reaches sorrow, thus becoming dejected.

He gets angry because of blame and seeks faults means: he gets angry, is resentful, and becomes stubborn due to blame, censure, ill-repute, and the bringing of discredit; he manifests anger, malice, and dissatisfaction. "Fault-seeker" means one who seeks faults, seeks holes, discards virtues and seeks only flaws, seeks slips, seeks failures, and seeks defects. Therefore, it is said, "He gets angry because of blame and seeks faults."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Engaged in talk in the midst of an assembly, desiring praise, one becomes frustrated [when it is not received].
When his doctrine is refuted, he becomes dejected; he gets angry because of blame and seeks faults."

Those who examine questions say that his doctrine is defeated and diminished.
That one with a defeated doctrine sorrows, laments, and moans, "He has surpassed me."

They say his doctrine is diminished means: they say his doctrine is low, very low, diminished, wasted, not developed, and not fulfilled; thus they speak, tell, show, and declare.

Refuted by those who examine questions means: there are those assemblies, attendants, and onlookers who examine questions. They reject [his doctrine]. They reject it in terms of meaning, saying, "He speaks words devoid of meaning." They reject it in terms of phrasing, saying, "He speaks words devoid of phrasing." They reject it in terms of both meaning and phrasing, saying, "He speaks words devoid of both meaning and phrasing." They reject it saying, "Your meaning is poorly conveyed, your phrasing is poorly established, your meaning and phrasing are poorly conveyed and poorly established; your refutation is not achieved, your counter-argument is poorly done, your distinction is not made, your counter-distinction is poorly done, your entanglement is not resolved, your disentanglement is poorly done, your cutting off [of the argument] is not achieved, your circle [of logic] is poorly done; it is inconsistent talk, poorly spoken, poorly told, poorly uttered, and poorly articulated."
129:
He laments, he sorrows, he is one with a defeated doctrine. 'He laments' (paridevati) means: "I considered one thing, I thought another, I attended to one thing, I noted another. That person has a great faction, a great following, a great retinue. This assembly is also divided, not united. In a united assembly, conversation is not the cause; I will destroy it next time." Such speech, idle talk, confused talk, bewailing, the manner of bewailing, the state of one who bewails—this is 'he laments'. 'He sorrows' (socati) means: "He has victory, I have defeat. He has gain, I have loss. He has fame, I have infamy. He has praise, I have blame. He has happiness, I have suffering. He is respected, revered, esteemed, honored, and venerated, and he receives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. I am not respected, not revered, not esteemed, not honored, not venerated, and I do not receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites." Thus he sorrows, is weary, laments, beats his breast and cries, and falls into great confusion—this is 'he laments, he sorrows'. 'One with a defeated doctrine' (hīnavādo) means one with an inferior doctrine, a very inferior doctrine, a deficient doctrine, a declining doctrine, an incomplete doctrine—this is 'he laments, he sorrows, one with a defeated doctrine'.

'He has surpassed me' (upaccagā maṃ) means: "That person has surpassed my doctrine with his doctrine, has closely surpassed, has especially surpassed, has well surpassed, has transcended." This is 'he has surpassed me'. Alternatively, it means he wanders, dwells, behaves, proceeds, maintains, lives, and makes a living by subduing, overwhelming, exhausting, and crushing my doctrine with his doctrine. This is also 'he has surpassed me'. Idle talk, confused talk, bewailing, the manner of bewailing, the state of one who bewails is called 'anutthunā' (bewailing). Therefore, the Blessed One said—

## "When they say one's doctrine is defeated, and it is rejected in the presence of those investigating questions, that person with a defeated doctrine laments, sorrows, and bewails, saying 'He has surpassed me'."

(Conclusion of the Nissaya—The great hermit named Khanti, residing at Mandalay Hill in the Royal City of Mandalay, with the intention of making the Buddha's Sāsana prosper and flourish so that all people may enjoy the three types of happiness—human, celestial, and Nibbāna—caused the Tipiṭaka and Aṭṭhakathā texts, which are the foundation of the Sāsana, to be printed in books to prevent them from disappearing. This Sokappame Nissaya of the Magadha Pali was composed at the Bhāvanārāma Medhāvivāsa Monastery near Mandalay Hill.)
130:
These disputes arise among ascetics; in these [disputes], there is elation and depression. Seeing this disadvantage, one should refrain from contentious talk; there is no other benefit besides obtaining praise.

'These disputes arise among ascetics' means: 'Ascetics' refers to any who have gone forth and entered the ascetic life outside this Dispensation. These quarrels of views, contentions of views, conflicts of views, disputes of views, and strifes of views arise, are born, are produced, are generated, and appear among ascetics—thus, 'these disputes arise among ascetics.'

'In these [disputes], there is elation and depression' means: There is victory and defeat, gain and loss, fame and obscurity, blame and praise, happiness and pain, joy and grief, the pleasant and the unpleasant, attraction and repulsion, elation and depression, compliance and opposition. Through victory, the mind is elated (opened up); through defeat, the mind is depressed (closed off). Through gain, the mind is elated; through loss, the mind is depressed. Through fame, the mind is elated; through obscurity, the mind is depressed. Through praise, the mind is elated; through blame, the mind is depressed. Through happiness, the mind is elated; through pain, the mind is depressed. Through joy, the mind is elated; through grief, the mind is depressed. Through promotion, the mind is elated; through demotion, the mind is depressed—thus, 'in these [disputes], there is elation and depression.'

'Seeing this disadvantage, one should refrain from contentious talk' means: Seeing, observing, weighing, investigating, and making clear this disadvantage, one should refrain from quarrels of views. 'Contentious talk' (kathojja) refers to quarrels, contentions, conflicts, and disputes. Alternatively, 'contentious talk' is speech that is essence-less and lusterless. One should not engage in contentious talk, should not quarrel, should not contend, should not conflict, and should not dispute. One should abandon, dispel, eliminate, and bring to an end [such things], so that they do not arise again. One should be one who abstains, refrains, and stays away from quarrels, contentions, conflicts, and disputes.
131:
Seeing [the disadvantage of disputes] in this way, one should refrain from contentious talk. [Such a person] is one who has departed, escaped, detached, and disassociated from disputes, and should dwell with a mind free from boundaries—thus, 'seeing this, one should refrain from contentious talk.'

'There is no other benefit besides obtaining praise' means: Apart from obtaining praise, there is no other benefit—neither one's own benefit, nor the benefit of others, nor the benefit of both, nor the benefit in the present life, nor the benefit in the future life, nor the shallow (obvious) benefit, nor the deep benefit, nor the hidden benefit, nor the obscure benefit, nor the benefit to be inferred (neyya), nor the explicit benefit (nīta), nor the blameless benefit, nor the benefit free from defilements, nor the pure benefit, nor the ultimate benefit. These do not exist, are not found, and are not obtained—thus, 'there is no other benefit besides obtaining praise.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"These disputes arise among ascetics; in these [disputes], there is defeat and victory.
Seeing this disadvantage, one should refrain from contentious talk; there is no other benefit besides obtaining praise."

Or he is praised there, having declared his view in the midst of the assembly; he laughs and is elated by that, having achieved that goal as he intended.

'Or he is praised there' means: He is praised, lauded, celebrated, and extolled in that view of his, in his patience, in his preference, and in his doctrine—thus, 'or he is praised there.'

'Having declared his view in the midst of the assembly' means: In the midst of an assembly of nobles (khattiyas), an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics, he declares his own view, explains his tradition, strengthens it, expands it, clarifies it, illuminates it, speaks it, and presents it—thus, 'having declared his view in the midst of the assembly.'

'He laughs and is elated by that' means: He is pleased, glad, overjoyed, delighted, and has his intentions fulfilled because of that victory. Or, he laughs showing his teeth. He is elated because of that victory.
132:
Due to the benefit of victory, the mind becomes elated, uplifted like a banner, exalted, and possesses the desire for the mind to be like a pinnacle. Because of that victory, that person experiences joy, laughter, and mental exaltation.

This refers to reaching, attaining, and especially gaining the benefit of victory. It means things happening according to one's mind, intention, and consciousness.

Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

"Or he is praised there, having declared his doctrine in the midst of the assembly; he laughs and becomes elated because of that, having attained that goal just as he intended."

"Whatever elation there is, that is for him a ground for destruction. He speaks with conceit and overbearing pride. Seeing this danger, one should not engage in disputes. For the skilled say that purity is not attained through that [dispute]."

Whatever elation, hoisting of the banner, exaltation, and desire for the mind to be like a pinnacle exists—that elation is for him a ground for affliction, oppression, assault, calamity, and misfortune.

That person speaks with conceit (māna) and also with overbearing pride (atimāna).

Seeing this danger, having weighed it, investigated it, and made it clear, one sees the fault in quarrels, brawls, contentions, disputes, and strife caused by views. One should not engage in quarrels, brawls, contentions, disputes, or strife; one should abandon them, dispel them, end them, and ensure they do not arise again. One should dwell far removed from those disputes, completely abstaining, liberated, and with a mind that has transcended boundaries.
133:
"For the skilled do not say that purity is attained through that" means: There are those skilled in the aggregates (khandha), skilled in the elements (dhātu), skilled in the sense bases (āyatana), skilled in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), skilled in the right efforts (sammappadhāna), skilled in the bases of power (iddhipāda), skilled in the faculties (indriya), skilled in the powers (bala), skilled in the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), skilled in the path (magga), skilled in the fruits (phala), and skilled in Nibbāna. These skilled wise ones do not say, speak, utter, show, or declare that purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or total liberation is attained through quarrels, brawls, contentions, disputes, or strife caused by views. Thus, "the skilled do not say that purity is attained through that dispute."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Whatever elation there is, that is for him a ground for destruction; yet this one speaks with conceit and overbearing pride. Seeing this danger, one should not engage in disputes; for the skilled do not say that purity is attained through that."

Just as a hero nourished by royal food goes forward roaring, desiring a rival hero; O hero, go to where that [wrong-viewer] is; for that which is for the sake of combat (dispute) no longer exists [for me] since before, at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

"Just as a hero nourished by royal food" means: A hero is one who is steady, energetic, brave, fearless, unshakable, undaunted, and does not flee from the battlefield. "Nourished by royal food" means one who is fed, nurtured, provided for, and made to prosper with the king's food, clothing, and wealth.

"Goes forward roaring, desiring a rival hero" means: That person approaches, seeking, longing for, and searching for a rival man, a rival soldier, or an opponent who will fight him, while roaring with a brave voice, shouting, and making a fearless sound.

"O hero, go to where that one is" means: Go to wherever that person of wrong views is; approach only him, go beyond only him. He alone is the rival hero, rival man, rival soldier, or opponent for you.

"For that which is for the sake of combat no longer exists since before" means: Even before, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the defilements (kilesa) that act as enemies, that cause disharmony, that act as thorns, and that act as opponents no longer exist, are not manifest, and are not found. Those defilements have been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, and extinguished. Being unfit to arise again, they have been burnt by the fire of the knowledge of the Path (magga-ñāṇa). "Yadidaṃ yudhāya" means that this exhaustion of the body called combat, dispute, quarrel, opposition by view, or strife (should exist, but such a thing no longer exists for me).

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
Just as a hero nourished by royal food goes forward roaring, desiring a rival hero; O hero, go to where that one is; for that which is for the sake of combat no longer exists since before, at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

Those who, taking up a view, engage in disputes, saying "Only this my view is true..."
134:
(Those defilements) do not exist, they are not found, they are not obtained; they have been abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). "Yadidaṃ yudhāya" means: for the purpose of battle, for the purpose of strife, for the purpose of quarreling, for the purpose of dispute, for the purpose of contention, for the purpose of verbal conflict—this bodily exhaustion for such purposes no longer exists at the foot of the Bodhi tree.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Just as a warrior nourished by the food provided by a king, desiring a rival warrior, goes forth roaring;
O warrior, go only to where that rival is; for me, this bodily exhaustion for the purpose of fighting no longer exists at the foot of the Bodhi tree."

Those who, having grasped a view, dispute, and also say, "Only this is the truth."
Speak to them; when a dispute has arisen, those who act as opponents do not exist in this Dispensation.

"Ye diṭṭhimuggayha vivādayanti" means: those who, having taken, grasped, seized, misapprehended, and adhered to one or another of the sixty-two views, engage in dispute, strife, quarreling, contention, and verbal conflict, saying: "You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya; I understand this Dhamma-Vinaya. How could you understand this Dhamma-Vinaya? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. My words are consistent; yours are inconsistent. What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. Your long-practiced habit is overturned. Your argument is refuted; you are defeated. Go and seek release from your argument, or resolve it if you can!"—thus, those who, having grasped a view, dispute.

"Idameva saccanti ca vādayanti" means: they say, speak, recite, explain, and declare, "The world is eternal; only this is the truth, everything else is false." They say, speak, recite, explain, and declare, "The world is not eternal... (pe)... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; only this is the truth, everything else is false." Thus, they say, "Only this is the truth."

"Te tvaṃ vadassū na hi tedha atthi, vādamhi jāte paṭisenikattā" means: you should speak to those who hold such views with argument against argument, with suppression against suppression, with counter-action against counter-action, with distinction against distinction, with further distinction against further distinction, with entangling...
135:
They say, recite, explain, and declare, "Only this is the truth, everything else is false." They say, "The world is eternal," or "The world is not eternal," or "The being neither exists nor does not exist after death." This is the meaning of the phrase "Idameva saccanti ca vādayanti."

"Te tvaṃ vadassu na hi tedha atthi" means: you should speak to those who hold such views with argument, with suppression, with establishing them in your own view, with various superiorities, with repeated distinctions, with entangling and disentangling, with cutting off the argument, and with a collection of arguments. For you, there are no fearless enemies, no rival persons, no rival enemies standing before you, and no rival wrestlers who strike back. This is the meaning of that phrase.

"Vādamhi jāte paṭisenikattā" means: when a doctrine has well arisen, has clearly arisen, has become manifest, those who act as opponents, those who act inconsistently, those who act as rivals, and those who act as enemies would engage in dispute, strife, contention, debate, and verbal conflict. Such persons do not exist, are not found, are not obtained; they have been abandoned... (pe)... and burnt by the fire of the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. This is the meaning of the phrase "Te tvaṃ vadassū na hi tedha atthi vādamhi jāte paṭisenikatā."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Those who, having grasped a view, dispute, and also say, 'Only this is the truth.'
Speak to them; when a battle of doctrines arises, there is no one in this Dispensation to act as an opponent against you."

"O Pasūra, those Arahants (khīṇāsava) who wander having disbanded the army of defilements, do not oppose view with view. In those Arahants who have no grasping of 'this view is supreme' in this Dispensation, what retaliation could you find?"

"Visenikatvā pana ye caranti" means: the army of Māra is called 'the army' (senā). Bodily misconduct is Māra's army, verbal misconduct is Māra's army, mental misconduct is Māra's army, greed is Māra's army, hatred is Māra's army, delusion is Māra's army, anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), hypocrisy (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fevers, all torments, and all unwholesome formations (akusala-saṅkhāra) are called Māra's army.

This was said by the Blessed One:
"Sensual pleasures are your first army, the second is called discontent... (pe)... the Asura cannot defeat him; having conquered, he alone obtains happiness."

When all Māra's armies and all opposing defilements have been conquered, defeated, broken, crushed, and turned away by the four Noble Paths, it is therefore said "visenikatvā" (having disbanded the army). Those Arahants who are khīṇāsava wander, dwell, and move about.
136:
They live, they maintain their postures, they carry on, they protect, they subsist, they sustain their lives. Those who wander having disbanded the army (of defilements) do not conflict with views through views. For those Arahants, the sixty-two views have been abandoned, uprooted, calmed, stilled through non-arising, are incapable of arising, and have been burnt by the fire of knowledge. Those Arahants do not conflict with views through views, they do not deviate, they are not oppressed, they are not affected, and they are not obstructed.

Among those Arahants whose taints are exhausted, what kind of opponent, enemy, adversary, or rival combatant could you find? For those Arahants whose taints are exhausted, there is no view that is grasped, misapprehended, adhered to, or insisted upon as "This view is supreme, foremost, best, distinguished, chief, highest, or excellent"; such views do not exist, are not present, are not found, and have been abandoned.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
## Those who wander having disbanded the army, do not conflict with views through views.
## What would you gain among them, Pasūra, for whom nothing is grasped as supreme here?

Then you came with thoughts, thinking about views in your mind. You will not be able to compete with the Buddha, who has shaken off defilements.

"Atha" (Then) is a conjunction of words, a combination of words, a completion of a word, a union of syllables, a smoothness of consonants, and a sequence of words. "Pavitakkamagama" (came with thoughts) means coming while thinking, reflecting, and resolving: "Will I be victorious or will I be defeated? How shall I suppress him? How shall I establish my own view? How shall I distinguish myself? How shall I entangle him? How shall I speak to escape blame? How shall I cut his doctrine? How shall I create a circle of doctrine?" and so on.
137:
"How shall I act? How shall I cut his doctrine? How shall I create a circle of doctrine?" Thinking thus, reflecting deeply, thinking about victory and defeat, you have arrived, approached, reached, and come to compete with me. This is the meaning of "Then you came with thoughts."

In the phrase "thinking about views in your mind"—"Mind" (mano) refers to that which is consciousness, mind, mentality, heart, the pure (paṇḍara), the mind-base, the mind-faculty, consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, and the corresponding mind-consciousness element. Thinking about views with the mind, reflecting deeply: "The world is eternal" or "The world is not eternal" ... "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—this is called "thinking about views in your mind."

In the phrase "You have come to compete with the Buddha who has shaken off defilements, you will not be able to compete with that Buddha"—Wisdom is called "Dhona." It is the wisdom that knows through impermanence, etc., the wisdom that knows the nature of things ... non-delusion, investigation of states (dhammavicaya), and right view. Why is wisdom called "Dhona"? Because by that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Verbal misconduct ... all unwholesome formations are shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Alternatively, by right view, wrong view is shaken off ... by right intention, wrong intention ... by right liberation, wrong liberation is shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. Alternatively, by the Noble Eightfold Path, all defilements, misconduct, distress, fevers, torments, and unwholesome formations are shaken off, washed, well-washed, and thoroughly washed. The Blessed One is endowed with, possessed of, approached by, and attained to these "dhoneyya" qualities; therefore, the Blessed One is called "Dhona." He has shaken off lust, shaken off evil, shaken off defilements, and shaken off fevers; thus he is "Dhona."

"You have come to compete with the Buddha who has shaken off defilements, you will not be able to compete with that Buddha" means: Pasūra the wanderer is not capable of coming to compete, taking up a rivalry, and discussing or conversing with the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has shaken off defilements and knows all things. Why is he not capable? Because Pasūra the wanderer is low, inferior, base, contemptible, lowly, and insignificant. But the Blessed One is the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the chief, the highest, the most excellent, and the supreme Lord. Just as a rabbit is not capable of coming to compete and taking up a rivalry with a rutting bull elephant; just as a jackal is not capable of coming to compete and taking up a rivalry with a lion, the king of beasts; just as a young calf...
138:
Just as a cow is unable to take up the yoke and compete with a bull of great strength; just as a crow is unable to take up the yoke and compete with the king of eagles named Venateyya; just as an outcaste is unable to take up the yoke and compete with a Universal Monarch; just as a dust-demon is unable to take up the yoke and compete with Sakka, the king of gods; in the same way, the wanderer named Pasūra is unable to take up the yoke and compete with the Buddha, the Blessed One, who has shaken off all defilements, to discuss, to converse, or to engage in debate.

For what reason is he unable? Pasūra the wanderer has low wisdom, inferior wisdom, base wisdom, contemptible wisdom, degraded wisdom, and limited wisdom. The Blessed One, however, possesses great wisdom, wide wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom; He is skilled in the classification of wisdom, possesses analytical knowledge that has reached its divisions, has attained the four analytical insights, has reached the four intrepidities, and bears the ten powers. He is a bull among men, a lion among men, an elephant among men, a noble thoroughbred among men, a burden-bearer among men. He possesses infinite knowledge, infinite power, and infinite fame. He is rich, possessing great wealth, endowed with the wealth of wisdom. He is the leader, the trainer, the guide; He is the one who makes others understand, who makes them contemplate, who watches over them, and who inspires faith.

The Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path. He is the knower of the path, the one who understands the path, the one who is skilled in the path. And now, His disciples live following the path, having attained it afterwards.

The Blessed One knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen. He has become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the one who brings out the meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. There is nothing that is unknown, unseen, unperceived, unrealized, or untouched by the wisdom of the Blessed One. With regard to the past, future, and present, all things in every aspect come into the range of the Blessed One's knowledge. If there is anything that is a knowable thing (neyya-dhamma) to be known—whether it be one's own benefit, the benefit of others, the benefit of both, the benefit in this life, the benefit in the life to come, the plain meaning, the deep meaning, the secret meaning, the concealed meaning, the meaning to be known, the inferred meaning, the faultless meaning, the stainless meaning, the pure meaning, or the ultimate meaning—all such meanings revolve only within the knowledge of the Buddha.
139:
All bodily actions of the Blessed One follow after knowledge; all verbal actions follow after knowledge; all mental actions follow after knowledge (they are never without knowledge). The Blessed One possesses unobstructed knowledge regarding the past, unobstructed knowledge regarding the future, and unobstructed knowledge regarding the present. As far as there are knowable things (neyya), so far does His knowledge extend; as far as His knowledge extends, so far are there knowable things. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and there is no path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These two things, the knowable and knowledge, stand within each other's limits. Just as between two well-fitted halves of a casket, the lower half does not exceed the upper, and the upper half does not exceed the lower, but they stand within each other's limits; in the same way, the knowable things and the knowledge of the Blessed One stand within each other's limits. As far as there are knowable things, so far is there knowledge; as far as there is knowledge, so far are there knowable things. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and there is no path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These things stand within each other's limits, and the knowledge of the Blessed One proceeds in all things.

All things are connected to the Blessed One's reflection (āvajjana), His wish, His attention, and the arising of His thought. The knowledge of the Blessed One proceeds among all beings. The Blessed One knows the inclinations (āsaya) of all beings, knows their latent tendencies (anusaya), knows their conduct (carita), and knows their dispositions (adhimutti). He discerns beings who have little dust in their eyes or much dust in their eyes, those with keen faculties or dull faculties, those with good qualities or bad qualities, those easy to teach or difficult to teach, and those capable of attaining the path and fruit or those incapable. The world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, revolves only within the knowledge of the Buddha.

Just as all fish and turtles, including even the great Timi-timingala fish, revolve only within the great ocean; in the same way, the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, revolves only within the knowledge of the Buddha. Just as all birds, including even the king of eagles named Venateyya, revolve only in a portion of the sky; in the same way, even those who are equal to Sāriputta in wisdom revolve only in a portion of the Buddha's knowledge. The knowledge of the Buddha stands pervading and surpassing the wisdom of devas and humans.

Those wise kshatriyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics—who are subtle, who have mastered the doctrines of others, and who are like archers capable of splitting a hair—wander about as if they could destroy the doctrines of others with their wisdom.
140:
Those wise men speak as if they are destroying the views of others with their own wisdom. Having prepared and formulated their questions, they approach the Tathāgatas and ask questions that are deep in meaning and those that are conclusive. Those questions are indeed preached by the Blessed One, answered, and pointed out along with their reasons. They come to a state of complete failure in the presence of the Blessed One. In that matter, the wisdom of the Blessed One shines exceedingly. For this reason, they ask. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "You have come with premeditated thoughts, thinking of speculative views in your mind. You have come to compete with the Pure One (Dhona), but you will not be able to proceed."

## The Exposition of Pasūra Sutta is finished (Eighth).

## 9. Māgaṇḍiya Sutta Niddesa

Now, I shall speak the commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta—

Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga, no desire even for sexual intercourse arose in me. Seeing this body full of urine and excrement, how could there be any desire for love? I would not even wish to touch it with my foot.

Having seen the daughters of Māra—Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga—with the fleshly eye, no desire, lust, or affection for sexual intercourse arose. Therefore, it is said: "Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga, there was no desire even for sexual intercourse."

What is this body, full of urine, full of excrement, full of phlegm, full of blood, a heap of bones connected by sinews, smeared with blood and flesh, wrapped in skin, covered by the outer skin, oozing and trickling from various openings, inhabited by a host of worms, and filled with various kinds of impurities? I would not even wish to step on it with my foot, let alone have sexual intercourse or union. Therefore, it is said: "What is this body full of urine and excrement? I would not even wish to touch it with my foot." And it is not surprising that a person who yearns for celestial sensual pleasures would not desire human ones, or if one yearns for human sensual pleasures...
141:
...one who yearns for celestial sensual pleasures would not desire [this woman]. If you do not desire, take pleasure in, yearn for, long for, or crave for both kinds of sensual pleasures (celestial and human), what is your vision? With what view are you endowed? thus he asks.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga, no desire even for sexual intercourse arose in me. What is this body full of urine and excrement? I would not even wish to touch it with my foot."

If you do not desire such a 'woman-treasure' (itthi-ratana) who is yearned for by many kings, what do you say of your view, your practice of virtue, your livelihood, and your rebirth in a future existence?

"I do not say 'I say this'" does not occur to him. [The Blessed One said:] "Māgaṇḍiya, there is no firm grasping after deciding among doctrines. But seeing [the danger] in views, without grasping, searching for internal peace, I have seen [Nibbāna]."

"I do not say 'I say this'" does not occur to him means: "I say this view, I say that view, I say this much of a view, I say to this extent, I say this speculative view—such as 'The world is eternal'... or 'The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.'" Such does not occur to me. "I say to this extent" does not occur to him. Thus, "I do not say 'I say this'" does not occur to him.

"Māgaṇḍiya": The Blessed One addresses that Brahmin by name. "Bhagavā" is a term of respect... it is a designation based on realization. Thus, "Māgaṇḍiya," the Blessed One [called].

"Deciding among doctrines and firmly grasping": "Among doctrines" refers to the sixty-two speculative views. "Deciding" means having decided, having judged, having searched, having investigated, having weighed, having scrutinized, having clarified, and having made distinct. Firmly grasping by way of limited grasping, collective grasping, grasping the best, grasping by parts, grasping by accumulation, or grasping by total collection—thinking "This alone is the truth, real, factual, actual, certain, and not otherwise"—this refers to what is grasped, handled, and adhered to.
142:
Having decided among things, having specifically decided, having sought, having specifically sought the manner, having weighed and investigated, having made distinct, having made manifest, grasping by way of limitation, grasping by way of collection, grasping as superior, grasping by way of parts, grasping by way of accumulation, grasping by way of specifically combining—this view which is clung to and delighted in as 'this is true, it is not otherwise, it is real, it is not false'—such a view does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtainable; it is abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, burnt by the fire of knowledge. This is the meaning of the phrase 'dhammaesu niccheyya samuggahītaṃ'.

'Passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' means: one who sees the danger in views does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to views. Alternatively, they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be entered into. In this way also, the meaning of 'passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' should be understood.

Alternatively, the view 'The world is eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile'—this is a thicket of views among the sixty-two views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views. It is accompanied by suffering, by vexation, by despair, and by fever. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna. Seeing the danger in views in this way, one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to views. Alternatively, they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be entered into. In this way also, the meaning of 'passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' should be understood.

Alternatively, the view 'The world is eternal; only this is true, anything else is futile. The world is not eternal. The world is finite. The world is infinite. The soul and the body are the same. The soul is one thing, the body is another. The Tathāgata exists after death. The Tathāgata does not exist after death. The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death. The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. Only this is true, anything else is futile'—this is a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views. It is accompanied by suffering, by vexation, by despair, and by fever. It does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, or to Nibbāna. Seeing the danger in views in this way, one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to views. Alternatively, they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be entered into. In this way also, the meaning of 'passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' should be understood.

Alternatively, 'These sixty-two views, if grasped in this way and misapprehended in this way, will have such a destination and such a future state.' Seeing the danger in views in this way, one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to views. Alternatively, they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be entered into. In this way also, the meaning of 'passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' should be understood.

Alternatively, 'These sixty-two views lead to hell, lead to the animal realm, lead to the realm of hungry ghosts (petas).' Seeing the danger in views in this way, one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to views. Alternatively, they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be entered into. In this way also, the meaning of 'passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' should be understood.

Alternatively, 'These views are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation.' Seeing the danger in views in this way, one does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to views. Alternatively, they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be entered into. In this way also, the meaning of 'passañca diṭṭhīsu anuggahāya' should be understood.

'Ajjhattasanti' (Inner Peace) refers to Nibbāna, which is the stilling of passion (rāga), the stilling of hatred (dosa), the stilling of delusion (moha); the stilling of anger, of enmity, of disparaging, of rivalry, of envy, of stinginess, of deceit, of treachery, of stubbornness, of impetuosity, of conceit, of arrogance, of intoxication, of negligence; the stilling of all defilements, of all misconduct, of all anxieties, of all fevers, of all distresses, and of all unwholesome volitional formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra).
143:
I do not grasp (views), I do not misapprehend them, and I do not settle into them. Alternatively, I see that they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be settled into. Seeing in this way is for the sake of not grasping onto views.

Alternatively, one who sees the danger in these views—that they are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation—does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not settle into views. Alternatively, I see that they should not be grasped, should not be misapprehended, and should not be settled into. Seeing in this way is for the sake of not grasping onto views.

'Ajjhattasantiṃ pacinaṃ adassaṃ' refers to the peace of Nibbāna, which is the calming of lust, the calming of hatred, the calming of delusion, anger, malice, hypocrisy, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, treachery, stubbornness, impetuosity, pride, arrogance, intoxication, and negligence; the calming of all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all burning, and all unwholesome formations; it is the tranquility, the complete calming, the cessation, and the subsiding. 'Pacinam' means investigating, cultivating the truths, searching, weighing, discerning, developing, and making manifest. It is investigating, cultivating the truths, searching, weighing, discerning, developing, and making manifest that 'all conditioned things are impermanent.' It is investigating... that 'all conditioned things are suffering'... that 'all phenomena are not non-self'... It is investigating, cultivating the truths, searching, weighing, discerning, developing, and making manifest that 'whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' 'Adassaṃ' means seeing, realizing, perceiving with wisdom, and penetrating with knowledge. Thus, one has investigated and seen the internal peace within oneself.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'I do not say "I speak this [view]", O Māgandiya,
There is no view grasped and settled upon among the teachings;
But seeing [the danger] in views, for the sake of not grasping,
I have investigated and seen the internal peace.'

Māgandiya said:
'Regarding those decisions that have been fashioned,
Which the Sage says are for the sake of not grasping,
This matter called "internal peace",
How is that proclaimed by the wise?'

'Vinicchayā yāni pakappitāni' means the decisions which are the sixty-two types of views. 'Pakappitāni' means they are called 'pakappita' because they are fashioned, specially fashioned, highly constructed, and well-established. Alternatively, they are called 'pakappita' because they are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. In the phrase 'iti Māgandiyo', 'iti' is used for connecting words, combining words, completing words, joining syllables, the euphony of consonants, and the sequence of words. 'Māgandiya' is the name, designation, and appellation of that brahmin.
144:
They are called 'pakappita' (fashioned) because they are specially constructed, or alternatively, because they are impermanent, conditioned by causes, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to decay, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to change. Thus, these views that are grasped through decision are called 'pakappita'.

In the phrase 'iti Māgandiyo', 'iti' refers to the connection of words, the combination of words, the completion of words, the joining of syllables, the euphony of consonants, and the sequence of words. 'Māgandiya' is the name, the mark, the designation, the appellation, and the conventional term for that brahmin.

In the phrase 'te ve munī brūsi anuggahāya, ajjhattasantīti yametamatthaṃ', 'te ve' refers to the sixty-two views. 'Munī' refers to wisdom... one who has transcended the net of craving and views is called a Sage (muni). 'Anuggahāya' means saying 'I do not grasp, do not misapprehend, and do not settle into views' because of seeing the danger in them. 'Ajjhattasanti' means the peace within oneself (Nibbāna). 'Yametamatthaṃ' refers to that supreme goal of Nibbāna.

In the phrase 'kathaṃ nu dhīrehi paveditam taṃ', 'kathaṃ nu' is a term for asking out of doubt, asking out of uncertainty, asking with a divided mind, or asking because of not knowing for certain. It is asking, 'Is it so or not? How is it? By what means is it?' 'Dhīrehi' refers to the wise, the learned, those possessed of wisdom, those who see benefit and harm, and those who destroy defilements. 'Paveditam' refers to what is known, specially known, heard, taught, designated, made manifest, opened, analyzed, clarified, and shown.

Therefore, that Māgandiya brahmin addressed the Buddha thus:
'Regarding those decisions that have been fashioned,
Which you, Venerable Sir, do not grasp,
And which you proclaim as internal peace (Nibbāna),
How is that supreme benefit known by the wise?'

The Blessed One addressed him as 'Māgandiya' and said:
'I do not say there is purification by view (diṭṭhi), I do not say there is purification by hearing (suti), I do not say there is purification by knowledge (ñāṇa), nor do I say there is purification by virtue and vows (sīlabbata).
I do not say there is purification apart from view, apart from hearing, apart from knowledge, or apart from virtue and vows.
Having relinquished these (views, etc.) and not grasping them further,
The peaceful one, not depending on anything, would not long for a new existence.'
145:
Not by view, not by hearing, nor by knowledge (do I say one is purified). I do not say, preach, speak, show, or declare that there is purity, supreme purity, or ultimate purity, nor liberation, total liberation, or complete liberation in the animal kingdom, in the deva world, or in the Brahma world, nor liberation after passing through eighty-four thousand eons, nor liberation without danger, nor liberation in every aspect by means of view. I do not say, preach, speak, show, or declare that there is purity... or complete liberation by means of hearing. I do not say, preach, speak, show, or declare that there is purity... or complete liberation by means of both view and hearing. I do not say, preach, speak, show, or declare that there is purity... or complete liberation by means of knowledge. This is the meaning of the words: 'Not by view, not by hearing, nor by knowledge (do I say one is purified).'

'Māgaṇḍiya,' thus the Blessed One addressed that Brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' is a title of respect... The name 'Bhagavā' is a designation realized by the Blessed Ones at the end of the fruit of Arahantship. It is a designation realized along with Omniscience. This is the meaning of the words: 'Māgaṇḍiya, (said) the Blessed One.'

Nor do I say one is purified by virtue and vows. I do not say, preach, speak, show, or declare that there is purity... or complete liberation in the animal kingdom, in the deva world, or in the Brahma world, nor liberation after passing through eighty-four thousand eons, nor liberation without danger, nor liberation in every aspect by means of virtue. I do not say... by means of vows. I do not say... by means of both virtue and vows. This is the meaning of the words: 'Nor do I say one is purified by virtue and vows.'

Not by lack of view, lack of hearing, lack of knowledge, lack of virtue, or lack of vows (do I say one is purified). Right view (Sammādiṭṭhi) is also to be desired. The ten-fold Right View is: there is what is given, there is sacrifice, there is offering, there is the fruit and result of good and bad deeds, there is this world, there is the next world, there is mother, there is father, there are spontaneously born beings, there are in the world recluses and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who having realized this world and the next by their own higher knowledge, make them known. Hearing is also to be desired: hearing from others, Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. Knowledge is also to be desired: knowledge of ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-ñāṇa), knowledge in conformity with the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa), higher knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa), and attainment knowledge (samāpatti-ñāṇa). Virtue is also to be desired: the restraint of the Pātimokkha. Vows are also to be desired: the eight ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). They are: the forest dweller's practice, the alms-food eater's practice, the refuse-rag wearer's practice, the triple-robe wearer's practice, the house-to-house seeker's practice, the one-session eater's practice, the sitter's practice, and the any-bed user's practice.
146:
Not by mere right view, nor by mere hearing, nor by mere knowledge, nor by mere virtue, nor by mere vows does one reach inner peace (Nibbāna); nor does one reach inner peace without these qualities. Rather, these qualities are the supporting factors (sambhāra) for reaching, attaining, touching, and realizing inner peace. Therefore, it is said: 'Not by lack of view, lack of hearing, lack of knowledge, lack of virtue, or lack of vows.'

'Relinquishing these without grasping' means the desire to abandon unwholesome qualities by uprooting them. Detachment (atammayatā) from wholesome qualities in the three realms is also desired. When unwholesome qualities are abandoned by the path of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), they are uprooted like a palm-tree stump and become non-existent, not liable to arise in the future; and when there is detachment from wholesome qualities in the three realms, to this extent, one does not take, grasp, or cling to them. Alternatively, it means those qualities should not be taken, grasped, or clung to. Thus should the meaning of 'Relinquishing these without grasping' be understood. When craving, views, and conceit are uprooted like a palm-tree stump and become non-existent, not liable to arise in the future; to this extent, one does not take, grasp, or cling to them. This is also the meaning of 'Relinquishing these without grasping.'

When meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) are uprooted like a palm-tree stump and become non-existent, not liable to arise in the future; to this extent, one does not take, grasp, or cling to them. Thus should the meaning of 'Relinquishing these without grasping' be understood.

In the phrase 'The peaceful one, not depending, does not long for existence,' 'the peaceful one' (santo) refers to one whose heart is peaceful due to the stilling of lust, one whose heart is peaceful due to the stilling of hatred, and one whose heart is peaceful due to the stilling of delusion. One is called 'santo'—tranquil, calmed, stilled, quenched, and at peace—because of the stilling, calming, complete subsiding, quenching, and cessation of anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), denigration (makkha), domineering (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), and negligence (pamāda); all defilements, all misconduct, all distress, all fever, all anguish, and all unwholesome formations.
147:
"Not depending" (anissāya) means there are two kinds of dependence: dependence through craving (taṇhā-nissaya) and dependence through views (diṭṭhi-nissaya). ... This is called dependence through craving. ... This is called dependence through views. Having abandoned dependence through craving and relinquished dependence through views, one does not depend on the eye-sensitivity, the ear-sensitivity, the nose-sensitivity, the tongue-sensitivity, the body-sensitivity, or the mind. One does not depend on, take up, grasp, or misapprehend visible forms, sounds, odors, flavors, tangibles; nor family, group, monastery, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, or medicinal requisites for the sick; nor the sensual realm, the fine-material realm, the immaterial realm; nor sensual existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, five-constituent existence; nor the past, future, or present; nor things seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. This is the meaning of "the peaceful one, not depending."

"Does not long for existence" means one should not long for sensual existence, fine-material existence, or immaterial existence; one should not repeatedly long for or excessively long for them. This is the meaning of "the peaceful one, not depending, does not long for existence."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Māgaṇḍiya, I do not say that purity is by view, by hearing, or by knowledge;
Nor do I say that purity is by virtue and vows.
Nor is it by the absence of view, the absence of hearing, the absence of knowledge, the absence of virtue, or the absence of vows.
Having relinquished these without grasping, the peaceful one, not depending, would not long for existence."

If indeed you do not say that purity is by view, by hearing, by knowledge, or by virtue and vows;
And if it is not by the absence of view, the absence of hearing, the absence of knowledge, the absence of virtue, or the absence of vows,
Then I consider this teaching to be utterly confused. Some believe that purity is only by view.

"If indeed you do not say that purity is by view, by hearing, or by knowledge" means: I do not say, speak, declare, point out, or designate purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or complete liberation by means of view.
