Nor do I say purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or complete liberation by means of hearing... nor by means of what is seen and heard... nor by means of knowledge.
148:
"You do not speak, point out, or designate" refers to: "If indeed you do not say that purity is by view, by hearing, or by knowledge."

In the phrase "iti Māgaṇḍiyo", "iti" is a particle used for connecting words... "Māgaṇḍiya" is the name of that brahmin... thus "iti Māgaṇḍiyo."

"Nor do I say that purity is by virtue and vows" means: I do not say, speak, declare, point out, or designate purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or complete liberation by means of virtue, or by means of vows, or by means of virtue and vows.

"Nor is it by the absence of view, the absence of hearing, the absence of knowledge, the absence of virtue, or the absence of vows" means: You say that view is to be desired, you say that hearing is to be desired, you say that knowledge is to be desired. You are unable to definitely affirm, nor are you able to definitely reject. This is the meaning.

"I consider this teaching to be utterly confused" means: I know, perceive, understand, fully understand, and penetrate that this is your foolish nature, confused nature, ignorant nature, and a nature as distorted as the doctrine of equivocation (amarāvikkhepa).

"Some believe that purity is by view" means: Some recluses and brahmins arrive at purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or complete liberation through purity of view. Some recluses and brahmins arrive at purity through the view: "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, everything else is false." Some recluses and brahmins arrive at purity and liberation through the view: "The world is not eternal... a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, everything else is false."

Therefore, that brahmin Māgaṇḍiya addressed the Blessed One thus:

"If indeed you do not say that purity is by view, by hearing, or by knowledge, (Māgaṇḍiya said)
Nor do you say that purity is by virtue and vows,
Nor is it by the absence of view, hearing, knowledge, virtue, and vows,
Then I consider this teaching to be utterly confused; some believe that purity is only by view."
149:
Māgandiya, when you ask repeatedly relying on views, you fall into confusion regarding the views you have firmly grasped. You do not see even a slight perception from this (Nirvana, practice, or teaching); therefore, you view (this Dhamma) only with confusion.

'Diṭṭhiñca nissāyanupucchamāno' means the brahmin named Māgandiya asks about views relying on views, asks about attachment relying on attachment (to views), asks about bonds relying on bonds, and asks about impediments relying on impediments. 'Anupucchamāno' means asking repeatedly.

'Māgandiyāti bhagavā' means the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by name. 'Bhagavā' is a term of respect... it is a realized designation (paññatti) for the Blessed Ones who are endowed with glory, coinciding with their attainment of omniscience at the root of the Bodhi tree.

'Samuggahītesu pamohamāgā' means that regarding the view you have taken, misapprehended, established, entered into, and become obsessed with—by that very view, you are bewildered, utterly bewildered, completely bewildered; you have arrived at confusion, arrived at great confusion, arrived at total confusion, and have plunged into deep darkness.

'Ito ca nāddakkhi aṇumpi saññaṃ' means that from this internal peace (Nirvana), or from the practice, or from the teaching of the Dhamma, one does not obtain the appropriate perception, the attained perception, the perception of characteristics, the perception of causes, or the perception of grounds; how then could one obtain knowledge? Thus, 'from this, you did not see even a slight perception.' Alternatively, one does not obtain [the perception of] impermanence or the insight knowledge in accordance with the perception of impermanence; suffering or the insight knowledge in accordance with the perception of suffering; non-self or the insight knowledge in accordance with the perception of non-self; or even the mere arising of perception or mere cognizing; how then could one obtain the path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa)? Thus also, 'from this, you did not see even a slight perception.'

'Tasmā tuvaṃ momuhato dahāsi' means for that reason, because of that cause, due to that condition, on account of that basis, you regard, see, behold, look upon, contemplate, and examine (this Dhamma) through the nature of utter confusion, through the nature of foolishness, through the nature of bewilderment, through the nature of ignorance, and through a nature as distorted as the 'eel-wriggling' (amarāvikkhepa).

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
150:
The Blessed One said:
“Māgandiya, when you ask relying on your own views, you fall into confusion (regarding the Dhamma I have taught). You do not see even a slight perception from this (Dispensation); therefore, you view (Me) as one who is utterly confused.”

“Whoever conceives 'I am equal (to him),' or 'superior,' or 'inferior,' would dispute because of that (conceit). For one who is unwavering in the three modes (of conceit), the conception 'I am equal' or 'superior' does not exist.”

“Whoever conceives 'I am equal, superior, or inferior,' would dispute because of that (conceit)” means: whoever conceives “I am equal,” or “I am better,” or “I am worse,” that person, because of that conceit, because of that view, or with that person, would engage in quarrel, dispute, strife, verbal battle, and contention. (Saying:) “You do not understand this Doctrine and Discipline (Dhamma-Vinaya); I understand this Doctrine and Discipline. How could you understand this Doctrine and Discipline? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. My words are beneficial; yours are not. You said last what should have been said first, and said first what should have been said last. Your long-practiced habit is reversed. Your view is refuted. You are defeated. Go and seek to release yourself from your views, or explain yourself if you are able!” (Thus one disputes). “Whoever conceives 'I am equal, superior, or inferior,' would dispute because of that (conceit).”

“For one who is unwavering in the three modes (of conceit), the conception 'I am equal or superior' does not exist” means: for whom these three modes of conceit have been abandoned, cut off at the root, stilled, calmed, made impossible to arise again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge—that person does not waver, does not tremble in the three modes of conceit. For such an unwavering person, the conception “I am equal,” “I am better,” or “I am worse” does not exist. It means “it does not occur to me.” For one who is unwavering in the three modes, the conception “I am equal or superior” does not exist.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Whoever conceives 'I am equal, superior, or inferior,' would dispute because of that (conceit);
For one who is unwavering in the three modes (of conceit), the conception 'I am equal or superior' does not exist.”
151:
What would that Brāhmaṇa say as "truth", or with what would he dispute as "falsehood"? In whom there is no "equal" or "unequal", with what would he engage in a dispute?

"Saccanti so brāhmaṇo kiṃ vadeyya" means: He is called a Brāhmaṇa because he has discarded the seven evil qualities. ... He who is not dependent on craving and views, and is endowed with the quality of tādi, is called a Brahma. How would that Brāhmaṇa say, how would he preach, how would he recite, how would he demonstrate, or how would he proclaim: "The world is eternal, this alone is the truth, all else is vain"? How would that Brāhmaṇa say, how would he preach, how would he recite, how would he demonstrate, or how would he proclaim: "The world is not eternal ... the being neither exists nor does not exist after death, this alone is the truth, all else is vain"? Thus, it means "Saccanti so brāhmaṇo kiṃ vadeyya".

"Musāti vā so vivadetha kena" means: With what conceit, with what view, or with what person would that Brāhmaṇa (Arahant) engage in dispute, quarrel, contention, or debate, saying "Only my view is true, your view is false"? How would he dispute, saying "You do not know this Dhamma-Vinaya ... if you are able, resolve the fault I have presented"?

"Yasmiṃ samaṃ visamaṃ vāpi natthi" means: In that Arahant whose taints are exhausted, the conceit "I am equal", the conceit "I am superior", and the conceit "I am inferior" do not exist and are not found. Those conceits have been burnt by the fire of knowledge, abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, and extinguished so that they cannot arise again.

"Sa kena vādaṃ paṭisaṃyujeyya" means: With what conceit, with what view, or with what person would that Arahant engage in a doctrine, or engage in dispute, quarrel, contention, or debate? How would he act, saying "You do not know this Dhamma-Vinaya ... if you are able, resolve it"?

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "What would that Brāhmaṇa say as 'truth', or with what would he dispute as 'falsehood'? In whom there is no 'equal' or 'unequal', with what would he engage in a dispute?"
152:
Having abandoned the abode (the abode of consciousness) and wandering homeless, not making intimacy in the village, the sage (muni), being empty of sensual pleasures and not looking forward to the future, how would he not engage in dispute with people? Then, the householder Hāliddukāni approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna, and after paying homage to the Venerable Mahākaccāna, sat at a respectful distance. Sitting there, the householder Hāliddukāni said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: "Venerable Kaccāna, this was said by the Blessed One in the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta of the Aṭṭhakavagga: 'Having abandoned the abode and wandering homeless, not making intimacy in the village, the sage, empty of sensual pleasures and not looking forward to the future, how would he not engage in dispute with people?' Venerable Kaccāna, how should the meaning of this which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One be understood in detail?"

"Householder, the element of form (rūpadhātu) is the abode (home) of consciousness. One whose consciousness is bound by lust to the element of form is called 'one who dwells in an abode' (okasārī). Householder, the element of feeling... the element of perception... the element of mental formations is the abode of consciousness. One whose consciousness is bound by lust to the element of mental formations is called 'one who dwells in an abode'. Householder, in this way, one is a dweller in an abode.

And how, householder, is one 'not dwelling in an abode' (anokasārī)? Householder, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever four attachments, and whatever underlying tendencies (anusaya) of mental adherence and bias exist in the element of form—those the Tathāgata has abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, and made such that they are not liable to arise in the future. Therefore, the Tathāgata is called 'one who does not dwell in an abode'. Householder, in the element of feeling... in the element of perception... in the element of mental formations... in the element of consciousness, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving, whatever four attachments, and whatever underlying tendencies of mental adherence and bias..."
153:
The Blessed One has abandoned those unwholesome states such as desire, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, the Blessed One is called 'Anokasārī' (one who does not roam in a home). Thus, householder, is one an Anokasārī.

How, householder, is one a 'Niketasārī' (one who roams in a home)? One is called a Niketasārī because of being bound by the roaming in the signs of forms. One is called a Niketasārī because of being bound by the roaming in the signs of sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles... mental objects. Thus, householder, is one a Niketasārī.

How, householder, is one an 'Aniketasārī' (one who does not roam in a home)? Householder, the Blessed One has abandoned the roaming and the constant attachment to the signs of forms, which are the causes of defilements; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, the Blessed One is called an Aniketasārī. The Blessed One has abandoned the roaming and the constant binding to the signs of sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, the Blessed One is called an Aniketasārī. Thus, householder, is one an Aniketasārī.

How, householder, is one intimate with people in the village? Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu lives in association with laypeople; he rejoices with them and grieves with them; he is happy when they are happy and sad when they are sad; when duties and affairs arise, he personally exerts himself in those matters. Thus, householder, is one intimate with people in the village.

How, householder, is one not intimate with people in the village? Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu lives without associating with laypeople; he does not rejoice with them nor grieve with them; he is not happy when they are happy nor sad when they are sad; when duties and affairs arise, he does not personally involve himself in those matters. Thus, householder, is one not intimate with people in the village.

How, householder, is one not empty of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu is not free from lust, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, and not free from craving regarding sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, is one not empty of sensual pleasures.
154:
“How, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, a certain bhikkhu is free from lust, free from desire, free from affection, free from thirst, free from fever, and free from craving regarding sensual pleasures. Thus, householder, is one empty of sensual pleasures.

“How, householder, does one look forward (to the cycle of rebirth)? Here, householder, it occurs to a certain bhikkhu: ‘May I have such a form in the future,’ and he delights in that form. It occurs to him: ‘May I have such a feeling... such a perception... such volitional formations... such a consciousness in the future,’ and he delights in those (feeling, perception, volitional formations, consciousness). Thus, householder, does one look forward.

“How, householder, does one not look forward? Here, householder, even though it might occur to a certain bhikkhu: ‘May I have such a form in the future,’ he does not delight in that form. Even though it might occur to him: ‘May I have such a feeling... such a perception... such volitional formations... such a consciousness in the future,’ he does not delight in those. Thus, householder, does one not look forward.

“How, householder, is one who engages in disputatious speech with people? Here, householder, a certain person speaks such words as: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya, I understand this Dhamma-Vinaya; how could you understand this Dhamma-Vinaya? You have fallen into wrong practice, I have practiced rightly. My words are consistent, yours are inconsistent. What should have been said first, you said last; what should have been said last, you said first. Your long-practiced view is overturned. I have refuted your thesis; you are defeated. Go and learn how to escape your thesis, or explain it away if you can.’ Thus, householder, is one who engages in disputatious speech with people.

“How, householder, is one who does not engage in disputatious speech with people? Here, householder, a certain person does not speak such words as: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya... (pe) ... explain it away if you can.’ Thus, householder, is one who does not engage in disputatious speech with people. Thus, householder, this was said by the Blessed One in the Questions of Māgaṇḍiya in the Aṭṭhakavagga:

“Having abandoned the home, roaming without a home,
A sage does not form intimacies in the village;
Empty of sensual pleasures, not looking forward,
Why would he engage in disputatious speech with people?”
155:
## 
"Householder, the meaning of this sutta spoken in brief by the Blessed One should be understood in detail in this way."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Having abandoned the home, wandering without a fixed abode, the sage does not form intimacies in the village; empty of sensual desires, without preference, how could he not engage in disputes with people?"

"Detached from those (views) he should wander in the world; the Nāga (Arahant) should not speak by grasping those (views). Just as a lotus born in water with a rough stalk is unsmeared by water and mud, so the sage, a speaker of peace, ungreedy, is unsmeared by sensual desires and the world."

Regarding the phrase "Detached from those (views) he should wander in the world": "Those" refers to those views (diṭṭhigata). "Detached" means being empty of, detached from, and especially secluded from bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct... mental misconduct... lust... (p)... being empty of, detached from, and especially secluded from all unwholesome formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra). "He should wander" means he should wander, dwell, move, proceed, maintain, subsist, and carry on. "In the world" means in the world of humans. This is the meaning of "Detached from those (views) he should wander in the world."

Regarding the phrase "The Nāga should not speak by grasping those (views)": He is called a "Nāga" because he does not commit faults (āguṃ na karoti); he is called a "Nāga" because he does not go (na gacchati) [to the paths of bias]; he is called a "Nāga" because he does not come back (nāgacchati) [to abandoned defilements]. How is he a "Nāga" because he does not commit faults? Evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death are called "āgū" (faults).

The Blessed One said this to Sabhiya:
"Sabhiya, he who commits no fault (āguṃ na karoti) in the world, having relinquished all bonds and cut the fetters, unattached in all places (postures), being liberated—such a one, being firm, is called a 'Nāga' because of his suchness."
In this way, he is called a "Nāga" because he does not commit faults.

He is called a "Nāga" because he does not go (na gacchati): he does not follow the path of bias through desire (chandāgati), bias through hatred (dosāgati), bias through delusion (mohāgati), or bias through fear (bhayāgati); he does not go by the power of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, views, restlessness, doubt, or underlying tendencies; he is not led by sectarian phenomena, not carried toward sense objects, and does not grasp them. In this way, he is called a "Nāga" because he does not go.

He is called a "Nāga" because he does not come back (nāgacchati): he does not return, does not resort to, and does not come back to the defilements already abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). He does not return, does not resort to, and does not come back to the defilements already abandoned by the path of once-returning, the path of non-returning, and the path of Arahantship. In this way, he is called a "Nāga" because he does not come back.

Regarding the phrase "The Nāga should not speak by grasping those (views)":
156:
## 
How is he a "Nāga" because he does not go? He does not go to the path of bias through desire, he does not go to the path of bias through hatred, he does not go to the path of bias through delusion, he does not go to the path of bias through fear; he does not go by the power of lust, he does not go by the power of hatred, he does not go by the power of delusion, he does not go by the power of pride, he does not go by the power of views, he does not go by the power of restlessness, he does not go by the power of doubt, he does not go by the power of underlying tendencies; he is not moved, led, carried away, or drawn by sectarian phenomena. In this way, he is called a "Nāga" because he does not go.

How is he a "Nāga" because he does not come back? He does not return, does not resort to, and does not come back to the defilements already abandoned by the path of stream-entry. He does not return, does not resort to, and does not come back to the defilements already abandoned by the path of once-returning... the path of non-returning... the path of Arahantship. In this way, he is called a "Nāga" because he does not come back.

Regarding the phrase "The Nāga should not speak by grasping those views": The one called a Nāga does not speak, preach, recite, show, or express by holding, grasping, seizing, misinterpreting, or adhering to those views. He does not speak, preach, recite, show, or express such views as: "The world is eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is false." This is the meaning of "The Nāga should not speak by grasping those views."

Regarding the phrase "Just as a lotus born in water with a rough stalk is unsmeared by water and mud": "Ela" means water; "Ambuja" means the paduma lotus; "Kaṇḍaka" means the rough stalk; "Vāri" means water; "Vārija" means the paduma lotus born in water; "Jala" means water; "Paṅka" means mud. Just as the paduma lotus born in water is not smeared, not stained, and not tainted by water and mud, so it is.

Regarding the phrase "So the sage, a speaker of peace, ungreedy, is unsmeared by sensual desires and the world": "So" completes the simile. "Sage" (Muni): "Mona" means knowledge (wisdom). One who stands having crossed the net of attachment (craving and views) is called a sage. "Speaker of peace" (Santivāda) means the sage who has the view of and habitually speaks of Nibbāna, which is the state of safety, the shelter, the refuge, the state free from passing away, and the deathless. "Ungreedy" (Agiddha): "Gedha" means craving. There is the unwholesome root of lust, intense lust, covetousness, and greed. For whom this craving is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called "ungreedy." He is not greedy for sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes...
157:
In almsfood... in lodgings... in medicinal requisites for the sick... in the sensual realm... in the form realm... in the formless realm... in sensual existence... in form existence... in formless existence... in existence with perception... in existence without perception... in existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception... in one-constituent existence... in four-constituent existence... in five-constituent existence... in the past... in the future... in the present... he is not greedy, not attached, not infatuated, and not obsessed with things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. He has greed removed, greed gone, greed relinquished, greed vomited, greed released, greed abandoned, and greed forsaken. He has lust removed, lust gone, lust relinquished, lust vomited, lust released, lust abandoned, and lust forsaken. He is without hunger, quenched, cooled, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime. Thus, the sage who speaks of peace is one who is not greedy.

Regarding "unsullied in sensual pleasures and in the world": Sensual pleasures (kāma) are twofold by way of collection—objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma). ... These are called objective sensuality. ... These are called subjective sensuality. The world (loka) refers to the world of misery, the human world, the celestial world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases. Sulliedness (lepa) is twofold—the sulliedness of craving (taṇhā-lepa) and the sulliedness of views (diṭṭhi-lepa). ... This is the sulliedness of craving. ... This is the sulliedness of views. The sage, having abandoned the sulliedness of craving and having relinquished the sulliedness of views, is not sullied, not smeared, and not tainted in sensual pleasures and in the world. He is unsullied, un-smeared, untainted, departed, escaped, liberated, dissociated, and dwells with a mind that has abolished boundaries. Thus, the sage who speaks of peace is one who is not greedy and is unsullied in sensual pleasures and in the world.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One should wander in the world secluded from those things; the noble sage should not speak by grasping them.
Just as a lotus born in the water is not sullied by water or mud,
Even so, the sage who speaks of peace is not greedy and is unsullied in sensual pleasures and in the world."

The Vedagū (one who has reached the end of knowledge) is not led by views or by what is sensed; he does not come to conceit, for he is not made of that.
He is not to be led by action (kamma) nor by what is heard; he is not led into any dwellings (of craving and views).
158:
In the phrase "Na vedagū diṭṭhiyā na mutiyā, sa mānameti," the word "na" denotes negation. "Vedagū": Knowledge (Veda) refers to the knowledge in the four paths, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, inquiry, insight, and right view. Through these knowledges (Vedas), he has reached the end of birth, aging, and death by the Path, and arrived at the end by the Fruit; he has reached the limit by the Path, and arrived at the limit by the Fruit; he has reached the boundary by the Path, and arrived at the boundary by the Fruit; he has reached the conclusion by the Path, and arrived at the conclusion by the Fruit; he has reached the shelter by the Path, and arrived at the shelter by the Fruit; he has reached the cave by the Path, and arrived at the cave by the Fruit; he has reached the refuge by the Path, and arrived at the refuge by the Fruit; he has reached fearlessness by the Path, and arrived at fearlessness by the Fruit; he has reached the unshakable Nibbāna by the Path, and arrived at the unshakable Nibbāna by the Fruit; he has reached the deathless Nibbāna by the Path, and arrived at the deathless Nibbāna by the Fruit; he has reached Nibbāna by the Path, and arrived at Nibbāna by the Fruit. Thus he is a Vedagū. Or he is a Vedagū because he has reached the end of the Vedas. Or he is a Vedagū because he has reached the end through the Vedas. Or he is a Vedagū because seven things are known by him. (Those seven are:) personality view is known, doubt is known, adherence to rules and observances is known, lust is known, hatred is known, delusion is known, and conceit is known. Evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, productive of renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death are known by him.

(The Blessed One said this to Sabhiya:)
"Having distinguished all knowledges (Vedas),
Whatever there are of recluses and brahmins in this world,
Being free from lust for all sensations,
Having transcended all knowledge (Veda), he is a Vedagū."

"Na diṭṭhiyā": For him, the sixty-two views are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. He does not go, is not led, is not carried away, and is not brought near by views. He does not rely on those views as having essence, nor does he return to them. This is the meaning of "Na vedagū diṭṭhiyā." "Na mutiyā": He does not come to conceit, does not approach, does not go near, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not settle into things sensed (muta), or the reports of others, or the consensus of the public. This is the meaning of "Na vedagū diṭṭhiyā na mutiyā sa mānameti."

"Na hi tammayo so": He is not "made of that" (tammayo) through the power of craving or the power of views; he does not hold them as supreme (tapparamo) or as his final resort (tapparāyano). Because craving, views, and conceit are abandoned by him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, abolished, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. By this much, he is not made of that, does not hold them as supreme, and does not have them as his final resort. This is the meaning of "Sa mānameti na hi tammayo so."
159:
"Not by action, nor by learning is he to be led" (na kammunā nopi sutena neyyo): "Not by action" (na kammunā) means he is not moved, not led, not carried away, not brought along by formations of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra), formations of demerit (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), or formations of the imperturbable (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra). "Nor by learning is he to be led" (nopi sutena neyyo) means he is not moved, not led, not carried away, not brought along by purity of learning, or by the voice of another (paratoghosa), or by the convention of the masses. Therefore, it is said, "Not by action, nor by learning is he to be led."

"He is not led into dwellings" (anūpanīto sa nivesanesu): There are two kinds of attachments (upaya): the attachment of craving (taṇhūpaya) and the attachment of views (diṭṭhūpaya). This is the attachment of craving... this is the attachment of views. For that person, the attachment of craving has been abandoned and the attachment of views has been relinquished. Because the attachment of craving is abandoned and the attachment of views is relinquished, he is not led into, not smeared by, not attached to, not entering, not leaning towards those dwellings (nivesana) of craving and views. He has emerged, escaped, is liberated, dissociated, and dwells with a mind that has made no boundaries. Therefore, it is said, "He is not led into dwellings."

Therefore, the Blessed One said—

"The Knower (vedagū) does not reach [Nibbāna] by views or by perception; he does not approach conceit, for he is not made of that. Not by action, nor by learning is he to be led; he is not led into dwellings."

For one detached from perception, there are no ties (gantha); for one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions (moha). Those who have grasped perception and views wander the world clashing.

"For one detached from perception, there are no ties" (saññāvirattassa na santi ganthā) means: Whoever develops the Noble Path preceded by serenity (samatha), for him, starting from the beginning, the ties are suppressed. Upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, for the Arahant, ties, delusions, hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and perceptions of sensuality, ill-will, cruelty, and views are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, and are of a nature not to arise in the future. This is the meaning of "For one detached from perception, there are no ties."

"For one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions" (paññāvimuttassa na santi mohā) means: Whoever develops the Noble Path preceded by insight (vipassanā), for him, starting from the beginning, delusions are suppressed.
160:
Upon reaching Arahantship, for the Arahant, delusion, ties, and hindrances, along with the perceptions of sensual desire, ill-will, cruelty, and views, are abandoned. Because these states are cut off at the root and made like a palm stump, they are of a nature not to arise again in the future. Therefore, it is said: "For one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions."

"Those who have grasped perception and view wander the world clashing and striking against one another" means: those who grasp at perceptions—the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill-will, and the perception of cruelty—clash and strike against one another by the power of perception. Kings dispute with kings, kshatriyas with kshatriyas, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders. A mother disputes with her son, a son with his mother, a father with his son, a son with his father. Brothers and sisters dispute with each other, and friends dispute with friends. In those quarrels, brawls, and disputes, they attack one another with hands, with clods of earth, with sticks, and with weapons. There, they meet death or deadly suffering.

Those who grasp at views, such as "The world is eternal" or "The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death," clash and strike against one another by the power of views. They clash teacher against teacher, teaching against teaching, group against group, view against view, practice against practice, and path against path.

Alternatively, they dispute, quarrel, engage in strife, brawls, and conflicts, saying: "You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya... explain your own view if you can." Because their volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are not yet abandoned, they meet with oppression in various destinations (gati), such as hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the human world, and the deva world. They wander, dwell, and live, being repeatedly oppressed from destination to destination, from rebirth to rebirth, from conception to conception, from existence to existence, through saṃsāra, and through the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). "The world" refers to the world of misery, the world of the sense bases, and so on. This is the meaning of "Those who have grasped perception and view wander the world clashing."

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "For one liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions. Those who have grasped perception and view wander the world clashing."

What kind of vision does he have? What kind of virtue? Who is called one at peace (upasanta)? O Gotama, please tell me of that supreme person who, being asked, is called one at peace. "What kind of vision does he have?" (kathaṃdassī) means: with what kind of nature of vision, what form, what variety, and what similar vision is he endowed?
161:
“For one who is detached from perception, there are no bonds; for one who is liberated by wisdom, there are no delusions. Only those who have grasped at perception and views wander about in the world, clashing with others.”

## The Exposition of the Māgandiya Sutta, the ninth, is finished.

## 10. Purābheda Sutta Niddesa

Next, I shall preach the exposition of the Purābheda Sutta—

“With what kind of vision, with what kind of virtue, is one called ‘calmed’ (upasanta)? O Gotama, being asked about the supreme man, please tell me that.”

In the words “With what kind of vision, with what kind of virtue, is one called calmed?”, “With what kind of vision” (kathamdassī) means: endowed with what kind of vision, of what nature, of what manner, of what form? “With what kind of virtue” (kathamsīlo) means: endowed with what kind of virtue, of what nature, of what manner, of what form? “Is called calmed” (upasanta) means: one who is peaceful, calmed, particularly calmed, extinguished, and tranquil; thus he is called, described, spoken of, recited, shown, and designated. By asking “With what kind of vision”, one asks about higher wisdom (adhipaññā); by asking “With what kind of virtue”, one asks about higher virtue (adhisīla); by asking “calmed”, one asks about the higher mind (adhicitta).

In the words “O Gotama, please tell me that”, “that” (taṃ) means what I ask, request, urge, or respectfully state. “Gotama” is how the created Buddha addresses the Blessed One by his lineage. “Please tell” (pabrūhi) means speak, tell, preach, designate, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and show.

In the words “asked about the supreme man”, “asked” (pucchito) means questioned, requested, urged, or respectfully stated. “Supreme man” (uttamaṃ naraṃ) means the foremost, best, distinguished, prominent, supreme, and excellent human being.

Therefore, that created Buddha said:
“With what kind of vision, with what kind of virtue, is one called calmed?
O Gotama, being asked about the supreme man, please tell me that.”
162:
Even before the breaking up of the body, he is one whose craving is gone.
He does not depend on the past.
He is not to be reckoned in the middle (present).
For him, there is no “preferring” (the future). (Thus the Blessed One said.)

“Even before the breaking up of the body, he is one whose craving is gone” means: before the breaking up of the body, before the breaking up of the self-identity (attabhāva), before laying down the carcass, before the cutting off of the life-faculty, he is one whose craving is gone, craving has departed, craving is abandoned, craving is vomited, craving is released, craving is relinquished; one whose lust is gone, lust has departed, lust is abandoned, lust is vomited, lust is released, lust is relinquished; one without craving, whose defilements are calmed, who is cooled, who habitually experiences happiness, and who dwells with a self that has become sublime (brahmabhūta).

“Bhagavā” is a name used out of respect. Alternatively, he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed lust; he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed hatred; he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed delusion; he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed conceit; he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed wrong views; he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed craving; he is called “Bhagavā” because he has destroyed defilements. He is called “Bhagavā” because he associated with, analyzed, and classified the Jewel of Dhamma. He is called “Bhagavā” because he made an end of existences. He is called “Bhagavā” because he has a developed body, virtue, mind, and wisdom. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he resorts to remote forest dwellings and lodgings that are quiet, free from noise, secluded, and suitable for solitary retreat. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicines. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the taste of meaning, the taste of Dhamma, the taste of liberation, higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the eight liberations, the eight bases of transcendence, and the nine successive dwellings. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the ten developments of wisdom, the ten kasiṇa attainments, mindfulness of breathing, and foulness attainments. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Or, he is called “Bhagavā” because he is a possessor of the ten Tathāgata powers, the four intrepidities, the four analytical insights, the six higher powers, and the six Buddha-dhammas.

This name “Bhagavā” was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by his friends and ministers, nor by his relatives...
163:
The name 'Bhagavā' was not made by ascetics or brahmins, nor was it made by deities. This name 'Bhagavā' is the name of the Blessed Buddhas occurring at the end of the Fruition of Arahantship. It is a designation realized together with the attainment of Omniscience at the root of the Bodhi tree. He is called 'Bhagavā' because he is one whose craving is gone even before the breaking up of the body.

'One who does not lean on the past' means: The past is called 'pubbanta'. Craving based on the past has been abandoned; views have been relinquished. Because craving is abandoned and views are relinquished, he is called 'one who does not lean on the past.' Alternatively, he does not continue to produce craving and delight in the past, thinking, 'I had such a form in the past.' He does not continue to produce craving and delight in that consciousness, thinking, 'I had such a feeling... such a perception... such mental formations... such a consciousness.' In this way also, he is called 'one who does not lean on the past.' Alternatively, thinking, 'In the past, I had such an eye, such forms,' the consciousness is not bound by desire and lust for that eye and those forms. Because the consciousness is not associated with desire and lust, he does not delight in that object; and because he does not delight in it, he is called 'one who does not lean on the past.' Thinking, 'In the past, I had such an ear, such sounds,' 'I had such a nose, such smells,' 'I had such a tongue, such tastes,' 'I had such a body, such tangibles,' 'I had such a mind, such mental objects,' the consciousness is not bound by desire and lust for those sense bases. Because the consciousness is not associated with desire and lust, he does not delight in that object; and because he does not delight in it, he is called 'one who does not lean on the past.' Alternatively, he does not enjoy, desire, or find pleasure in the laughing, talking, and playing with women in the past. In this way also, he is called 'one who does not lean on the past.'

'One who is not to be reckoned in the middle' means: The middle refers to the present time. Craving based on the present has been abandoned; views have been relinquished. Because craving and views are abandoned, he is not to be reckoned as 'one with lust,' 'one with hatred,' 'one with delusion,' 'one who is fettered,' 'one who misapprehends,' 'one who is distracted,' 'one who is indecisive,' or 'one who is obsessed.' Since those volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) have been abandoned, he is not to be reckoned by way of destination as 'a denizen of hell,' 'an animal,' 'a peta,' 'a human'...
164:
...or 'a deva,' or 'one with form,' or 'one without form,' or 'one with perception,' or 'one without perception,' or 'one with neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' The cause, the condition, the reason by which he might be reckoned does not exist. Thus, he is not to be reckoned in the middle.

'Tassa natthi purakkhatam' (For him there is no looking forward) means: 'Tassa' refers to the Arahat whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). There are two kinds of 'looking forward' (purakkharā): looking forward with craving and looking forward with views. ...pe... This is called looking forward with craving. ...pe... This is called looking forward with views. For that person, looking forward with craving has been abandoned, and looking forward with views has been relinquished. Because looking forward with craving is abandoned and looking forward with views is relinquished, he does not live placing craving or views in front. He has no banner of craving, no standard of craving, no predominance of craving. He has no banner of views, no standard of views, no predominance of views. He does not live surrounded by craving or views. In this way also, for him there is no looking forward.

Alternatively, he does not continue to produce delight in the future, thinking, 'May I have such a form in the future.' He does not continue to produce delight in that consciousness, thinking, 'May I have such a feeling... such a perception... such mental formations... such a consciousness.' In this way also, for him there is no looking forward.

Alternatively, he does not direct his mind with longing to obtain what has not yet been obtained, thinking, 'In the future, may my eye be like this, may forms be like this.' Due to the non-longing of the mind, he does not delight in that object; and because he does not delight in it, (he does not remain). In this way also, for him there is no looking forward. Thinking, 'In the future, may my ear be like this, may sounds be like this,' 'may my nose be like this, may smells be like this,' 'may my tongue be like this, may tastes be like this,' 'may my body be like this, may tangibles be like this,' 'may my mind be like this, may mental objects be like this,' he does not direct his mind with longing to obtain what has not yet been obtained. Due to the non-longing of the mind, he does not delight in that object; and because he does not delight in it, (he does not remain). In this way also, for him there is no looking forward.

Alternatively, he does not direct his mind with longing to obtain a result not yet obtained, thinking, 'By this virtue, or this vow, or this austerity, or this holy life, I shall become a deva or one among the devas.' Due to the non-longing of the mind, he does not delight in that state of being a deva; and because he does not delight in it, (he does not remain). In this way also, for him there is no looking forward.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'One whose craving is gone even before the breaking up of the body,
Who does not lean on the past, the first extreme,
Who is not to be reckoned in the middle (by lust, etc.),
For him, there is no looking forward (craving and views).'
165:
One who is free from anger, free from trembling, free from boasting, free from remorse, one who speaks with wisdom, not restless—he is indeed a sage restrained in speech.

"Akkodhana asantāsī" means: The word "akkodhana" is explained. Alternatively, anger (kodha) is spoken of. Anger arises in ten ways: "He has done me harm," thus anger arises; "He is doing me harm," thus anger arises; "He will do me harm," thus anger arises; "He has done harm... is doing harm... will do harm to one dear and pleasing to me," thus anger arises; "He has done good... is doing good... will do good to one not dear and pleasing to me," thus anger arises; or anger arises groundlessly. Such malice of mind, resentment, counter-resentment, hostility, irritation, intense irritation, extreme irritation, hatred, intense hatred, extreme hatred, mental perversity, mental corruption, anger, being angry, the state of being angry, hatred, hating, the state of being hated, perversity, being perverse, the state of being perverse, opposition, counter-opposition, ferocity, speaking bad words, displeasure of mind—this is called anger.

Furthermore, the intensity and weakness of anger should be known. At some times, anger is merely mental agitation, but does not yet cause facial distortion or frowning. At some times, anger is merely facial distortion or frowning, but does not yet cause trembling of the jaw. At some times, anger is merely trembling of the jaw, but does not yet cause the uttering of harsh speech. At some times, anger is merely the uttering of harsh speech, but does not yet cause looking around in all directions. At some times, anger is merely looking around in all directions, but does not yet cause the seizing of sticks or weapons. At some times, anger is merely the seizing of sticks or weapons, but does not yet cause the threatening with sticks or weapons. At some times, anger is merely the threatening with sticks or weapons, but does not yet cause the actual striking with sticks or weapons. At some times...
166:
Anger is merely the act of striking with sticks or weapons, but does not yet cause cutting into pieces. At some times, anger is merely cutting into pieces, but does not yet cause crushing or pulverizing. At some times, anger is merely crushing or pulverizing, but does not yet cause the mutilation of limbs. At some times, anger is merely the mutilation of limbs, but does not yet cause the taking of life. At some times, anger is merely the taking of life, but does not yet reach the point of total sacrifice (taking one's own life as well). When anger causes one to kill another person and then kill oneself, at that point, anger has reached its peak and its maximum expansion. He for whom that anger is abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, is called "one free from anger" (akkodhana). He is akkodhana because anger is abandoned, because the objects of anger are fully understood, and because the causes of anger are cut off.

"Asantāsī" means: In this world, some people are fearful, terrified, and anxious. They tremble, are terrified, and fall into fear. They fear: "I might not get a family, a group, a monastery, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicinal requisites for the sick, or an attendant for the sick; I am unknown," and thus they tremble, are terrified, and fall into fear.

In this Dispensation, a monk is free from trembling, not terrified, and not anxious. He does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not fall into fear. He does not fear: "I might not get a family, a group, a monastery, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicinal requisites for the sick, or an attendant for the sick; I am unknown," and thus he does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not fall into fear. This is what is meant by "one free from anger, free from trembling" (akkodhana asantāsī).

"Avikatthī akukkucco" means: In this world, some people are boastful, given to boasting about their own virtues. They boast: "I am accomplished in virtue," or "I am accomplished in practices," or "I am accomplished in virtue and practices," or by birth, or by lineage, or by status as a gentleman...
167:
By means of beauty, or wealth, or study, or occupation, or craft, or science, or learning, or eloquence, or any other object, one praises oneself. Or saying, 'I am one who went forth from a high family,' or 'I am one who went forth from a great family,' or 'I am one who went forth from a wealthy family,' or 'I am one who went forth from a family of noble wealth.' Or saying, 'I am well-known and famous among householders and those who have gone forth,' or 'I am a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.' Or saying, 'I am a Suttantika (expert in the Suttas),' or 'a Vinayadhara (expert in the Vinaya),' or 'a Dhammakathika (Dhamma preacher).'

Or saying, 'I am an observer of the forest-dweller’s practice (āraññika),' or 'the alms-food eater’s practice (piṇḍapātika),' or 'the rag-robe wearer’s practice (paṃsukūlika),' or 'the triple-robe wearer’s practice (tecīvarika),' or 'the practice of uninterrupted alms-round (sapadānacārika),' or 'the practice of refusing later food (khalupacchābhattika),' or 'the sitter’s practice (nesajjika),' or 'the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered (yathāsanthatika).'

Or saying, 'I am a gainer of the first jhāna,' or 'the second jhāna,' or 'the third jhāna,' or 'the fourth jhāna.' Or saying, 'I am a gainer of the attainment of the base of infinite space... the base of infinite consciousness... the base of nothingness... the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,' one boasts and vaunts. One who does not boast or vaunt in this way, who is far from, abstains from, and refrains from boasting and vaunting, who has emerged, is released, and is liberated from them, and who dwells with a mind that has removed boundaries—such a person is called 'one who does not boast' (avikatthī).

'Akukkuco' (without remorse) means: Kukkucca (remorse) is the fidgeting of the hands, the fidgeting of the feet, or the fidgeting of both hands and feet. It is perceiving the unallowable as allowable, or the allowable as unallowable; perceiving the wrong time as the right time, or the right time as the wrong time; perceiving a fault where there is none, or perceiving no fault where there is one. Such remorse, the act of being remorseful, the state of being remorseful, regret of the mind, and mental irritation—this is called kukkucca.

Furthermore, kukkucca, regret of the mind, and mental irritation arise from two causes: because of what has been done and because of what has not been done. How do kukkucca, regret of the mind, and mental irritation arise from what has been done and what has not been done? (Thinking,) 'I have committed bodily misconduct, I have not performed bodily good conduct,' kukkucca, regret of the mind, and mental irritation arise. (Thinking,) 'I have committed verbal misconduct, I have not performed verbal good conduct... I have committed mental misconduct, I have not performed mental good conduct,' kukkucca, regret of the mind, and mental irritation arise. (Thinking,) 'I have committed the taking of life, I have not performed the abstinence from taking life,' kukkucca, regret of the mind, and mental irritation arise.
168:
Remorse (kukkucca) is the subsequent regret of the mind, the scratching (irritation) of the mind. Remorse, the subsequent regret of the mind, the scratching of the mind, arises thinking: "I have taken what was not given; I have not practiced restraint from taking what was not given." Remorse, the subsequent regret of the mind, the scratching of the mind, arises thinking: "I have committed sexual misconduct; I have not practiced restraint from sexual misconduct." Remorse... arises thinking: "I have spoken falsely; I have not practiced restraint from speaking falsely." ... "I have spoken slanderous speech; I have not practiced restraint from slanderous speech." ... "I have spoken harsh speech; I have not practiced restraint from speaking harsh speech." ... "I have spoken frivolous talk; I have not practiced restraint from speaking frivolous talk." ... "I have committed covetousness (abhijjhā); I have not practiced non-covetousness." ... "I have committed ill-will (byāpāda); I have not practiced non-ill-will." ... "I have held wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi); I have not practiced right view (sammādiṭṭhi)." Remorse, the subsequent regret of the mind, the scratching of the mind, arises in this way because of what has been done and what has not been done.

Alternatively, remorse, the subsequent regret of the mind, the scratching of the mind, arises thinking: "I have not fulfilled the practice of the virtues (sīla)." ... "I have been one with unguarded doors in the sense faculties." ... "I have been one who does not know moderation in eating." ... "I have been one who does not apply himself to wakefulness." ... "I have not been endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña)." ... "I have not developed the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)." ... "I have not developed the four right efforts (sammappadhāna)." ... "I have not developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda)." ... "I have not developed the five faculties (indriya)." ... "I have not developed the five powers (bala)." ... "I have not developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga)." ... "I have not developed the Noble Eightfold Path (ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga)." ... "I have not fully understood suffering (dukkha)." ... "I have not abandoned the origin (samudaya)." ... "I have not developed the path (magga)." ... "I have not realized the cessation (nirodha)." For whom this remorse is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called "one without remorse" (akukkucca). This is the meaning of "one who does not boast and is without remorse" (avikatthee akukkucco).

In the phrase "one who speaks with wisdom and is not restless" (mantabhāṇī anuddhato), "wisdom" (mantā) refers to understanding. That wisdom, the act of knowing... (detailed) ... non-delusion, investigation of states (dhammavicaya), right view (sammādiṭṭhi). Having repeatedly grasped and reflected with wisdom, one speaks, even when saying much, even when teaching much, even when explaining much, even when using many terms. One who does not speak speech that is poorly said, poorly spoken, poorly uttered, or poorly expressed is called "one who speaks with wisdom" (mantabhāṇī). "Not restless" (anuddhato) means—among those states, what is restlessness (uddhacca)? It is the [restlessness] of the mind...
169:
Restlessness of mind, agitation of mind, and distraction of mind are called restlessness (uddhacca). For whom this restlessness is abandoned, cut off at the root by the Path of Arahantship, calmed, tranquilized, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge—he is called 'one free from restlessness' (anuddhata). Therefore, one who speaks with wise reflection is one free from restlessness.

'He is indeed a sage restrained in speech' means: In this Dispensation, a bhikkhu, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech. He speaks the truth, is bound to truth, is firm, trustworthy, and not a deceiver of the world. Having abandoned slanderous speech, he abstains from slanderous speech. He does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here in order to divide these people from those, nor does he repeat to these people what he has heard elsewhere in order to divide those people from these. Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and an encourager of those who are united. He rejoices in harmony, delights in harmony, loves harmony, and speaks words that create harmony. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are blameless, pleasant to the ear, lovely, reaching the heart, polite, desired by many, and agreeable to many. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter. He speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya. At the proper time, he speaks words that are worth treasuring, accompanied by reasons, defined, and connected with the goal. Endowed with the four types of right verbal conduct, he speaks words free from the four faults of verbal misconduct. He keeps far away from, abstains from, and is specially withdrawn from the thirty-two types of lowly talk (tiracchānakathā, talk that is an obstacle to heaven and Nibbāna); he has emerged from them, is detached from them, is liberated from them, is dissociated from them, and dwells with a mind that is unbounded.

He speaks on the ten subjects of discourse. These are: talk on wanting little, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-entanglement, talk on arousing energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation. He also speaks on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the bases of power (iddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), the path (magga), the fruit (phala), and Nibbāna. 'Restrained in speech' (vācāyato) means one whose speech is controlled, thoroughly restrained, guarded, protected, and calmed. 'Sage' (muni): knowledge is called 'mona'. That wisdom, discerning [...] non-delusion, investigation of states, right view [...] he who has transcended the net of attachment is called a sage. Therefore, it is said: 'He is indeed a sage restrained in speech.'

## Therefore, the Blessed One said:
## "Free from anger, free from trembling, not boastful, free from remorse,
## Speaking with wisdom, not restless—he is indeed a sage restrained in speech."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One who is free from anger, free from trembling, who does not boast of his own virtues, who is free from remorse,
Who speaks with wise reflection, who is free from restlessness—he is indeed a sage restrained in speech."
170:
He is free from craving for the future, does not grieve over the past, sees seclusion in contacts, and is not led by views.

'Free from craving for the future' means: attachment is called craving. Whatever lust, intense passion... covetousness, greed, unwholesome root there is. For whom this clinging craving is abandoned, completely cut off by the Noble Path, especially calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge. In this way, too, he is free from craving for the future.

Alternatively, he does not continue to delight in the thought, 'May I have such a form in the future.' He does not continue to delight in the thought, 'May I have such a feeling, perception, formation, or consciousness in the future.' In this way, too, he is free from craving for the future.

Alternatively, he does not direct his mind to obtain what has not yet been obtained, thinking, 'May I have such an eye and such forms in the future.' Because of the non-direction of the mind, he does not delight in it; because of not delighting, he is free from craving for the future. 'May I have such an ear, sound... mind, mental objects in the future'—he does not direct his mind to obtain what has not yet been obtained. Because of the non-direction of the mind, he does not delight in it; because of not delighting, he is free from craving for the future.

Alternatively, he does not direct his mind to obtain what has not yet been obtained, thinking, 'By this virtue, vow, austerity, or holy life, may I become a god or one among the gods.' Because of the non-direction of the mind, he does not delight in that state of being a god; because of not delighting, he is free from craving for the future.

'Does not grieve over the past' means: he does not grieve over an object that has changed, nor does he grieve in a changed object. He does not grieve, thinking, 'My eye has changed.' He does not grieve, thinking, 'My ear, nose, tongue, body, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robe, alms-food, lodging, medicinal requisites, mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister, relative, or kinsman has changed.' He does not become weary, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, and does not fall into great confusion. This is 'not grieving over the past.'
171:
'One who sees seclusion in contacts' (vivekadassī phassesu) refers to: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, mind-contact; designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa), resistance-contact (paṭighasamphassa) occurring at the five doors; contact that results in pleasant feeling, contact that results in painful feeling, contact that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; wholesome contact, unwholesome contact, indeterminate contact; sense-sphere contact, fine-material-sphere contact, immaterial-sphere contact; empty contact, signless contact, undirected contact; mundane contact, supramundane contact; past contact, future contact, and present contact. Such a nature of touching, the manner of touching, the state of being well-touched—this is called contact (phassa).

'One who sees seclusion in contacts' means: he sees eye-contact as secluded (vivitta) from a self (attā), or from what belongs to a self (attaniya), or from what is permanent (nicca), or stable (dhuva), or eternal (sassata), or not subject to change (avipariṇāmadhamma). He sees ear-contact as secluded... nose-contact as secluded... tongue-contact as secluded... body-contact as secluded... mind-contact as secluded. He sees designation-contact as secluded. He sees resistance-contact occurring at the five doors as secluded. He sees contact that results in pleasant feeling, contact that results in painful feeling, contact that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, wholesome contact, unwholesome contact, indeterminate contact, sense-sphere contact, fine-material-sphere contact, and immaterial-sphere contact as secluded. He sees mundane contact as secluded from a self, or from what belongs to a self, or from what is permanent, or stable, or eternal, or not subject to change.

Alternatively, he sees past contact as secluded from future and present contacts; he sees future contact as secluded from past and present contacts; he sees present contact as secluded from past and future contacts. Alternatively, there are those contacts that are noble, free from taints (anāsava), supramundane, and associated with emptiness (suññata); he sees those contacts as secluded from greed, hatred, delusion, anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), hypocrisy (makkha), malice (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), craftiness (sāṭheyya), obstinacy (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), pride (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), all defilements, all misconduct, all distress (daratha), all fever (pariḷāha), all burning (santāpa), and all unwholesome volitional formations. This is the meaning of 'one who sees seclusion in contacts'.

'And is not led by views' (diṭṭhīsu ca na nīyati) means: for that person, the sixty-two types of wrong views (diṭṭhi) have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, tranquilized, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. That person, by means of view...
172:
(That person) does not go, is not led, is not carried away, and is not gathered. He does not believe in that wrong view as having essence, nor does he return to it. Thus, he is not led by views.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"One who is without longing for the future, does not grieve for the past,
Who sees seclusion in contacts, and is not led by views."

Withdrawn, not deceitful, not longing, not stingy,
Not impudent, not loathsome, and not engaged in backbiting.

'Patilīno akuhako' means: 'Patilīno' refers to one who is withdrawn because of the abandoning of lust, withdrawn because of the abandoning of hatred, withdrawn because of the abandoning of delusion, anger... malice... hypocrisy... spite... envy... stinginess... because of the abandoning of all unwholesome formations (akusala-abhisaṅkhāra). The Blessed One said this: "And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu withdrawn (patilīno)? Here, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna) is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to future arising. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is withdrawn." This is the meaning of the term 'patilīno'.

'Akuhako' means there are three grounds for deceit (kuhana). They are: deceit regarding the use of requisites, deceit regarding postures (iriyāpatha), and deceit regarding indirect talk (sāmantajappana).

What is deceit regarding the use of requisites? Here, householders invite a bhikkhu with robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. That bhikkhu, having evil desires, overwhelmed by evil desires, although actually wanting the robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicine, rejects them because he wants more. He says: "What use has a monk for expensive robes? It is proper for a monk to collect rags from a cemetery, a rubbish heap, or a shop, make them into an outer robe (saṅghāṭi), and wear it. What use has a monk for expensive alms-food? It is proper for a monk to sustain his life with scraps of food obtained by wandering for alms. What use has a monk for expensive lodging? It is proper for a monk to be a tree-root dweller, a cemetery dweller, or an open-air dweller. What use has a monk for expensive medicinal requisites? It is proper for a monk to make medicine with fermented cow urine or pieces of yellow myrobalan." Based on that desire for more, he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse alms-food, and uses coarse lodging.
173:
He uses coarse medicinal requisites for the sick. Householders know him thus: "This monk has few desires, is contented, secluded, not associated (with laypeople), energetic, and speaks of ascetic practices (dhutavādo)." They invite him more and more with robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He says: "Because of the presence of three things, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit. Because of the presence of faith, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit; because of the presence of the gift, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit; because of the presence of the recipients, a faithful son of a good family generates much merit. You have this faith, the gift is available, and I am the recipient. If I do not accept, you will be deprived of merit. I have no need for this gift, but I accept it only out of compassion for you." From that day on, he accepts many robes, many alms-foods, and many medicinal requisites for the sick. Such frowning, grimacing, deceit, act of deceiving, and state of being deceitful—this is called deceit regarding the use of requisites.

What is deceit regarding postures (iriyāpatha)? Here, someone has evil desires, is overwhelmed by evil desires, and wants to be esteemed. Thinking, "In this way, people will esteem me," he regulates his walking, regulates his standing, regulates his sitting, and regulates his lying down. He walks, stands, sits, and lies down with premeditated grace. He walks as if composed, stands as if composed, sits as if composed, and lies down as if composed. He shows a calm state as if he were pure to those who see him. Such firm maintenance of posture, the manner of maintaining it, making oneself look inspiring, frowning, the state of one who frowns, deceit, the act of deceiving, and the state of being deceitful—this is called deceit regarding postures.

What is deceit regarding indirect talk (sāmantajappana)? Here, someone has evil desires, is overwhelmed by evil desires, and wants to be esteemed. Thinking, "In this way, people will esteem me," he speaks words based on the Dhamma of the Noble Ones. He says, "The one who wears such a robe is a monk of great power." He says, "The one who carries such an alms-bowl... carries a bronze bowl... carries a water-strainer (dhammakaraṇa)... carries a filter... carries a key... carries sandals... carries a waist-band... carries a meditation strap (āyoga), that monk is of great power."
174:
He says, 'That monk is one of great influence.' He says, 'One who has such a preceptor is a monk of great influence.' He says, 'One who has such a teacher... such fellow preceptors... such fellow teachers... such friends... such acquaintances... such intimates... such companions is a monk of great influence.' He says, 'One who dwells in such a monastery is a monk of great influence.' He says, 'One who dwells in such a lean-to hut... dwells in a mansion... dwells in a flat-roofed mansion... dwells in a cave... dwells in a mountain cleft... dwells in a hut with a peaked roof... dwells in a gabled house... dwells in a shed... dwells in a shed... dwells in a walled building... dwells in an assembly hall... dwells in a pavilion... dwells at the foot of a tree is a monk of great influence.'

Furthermore, one who is very shifty-eyed, habitually knitting the brows, very deceitful, very fawning, and accomplished in facial expressions, speaks such deep, hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane talk connected with emptiness, saying, 'This monk is an attainer of such peaceful attainments of the dwellings.' Such knitting of the brows, the state of knitting the brows, deception, the act of deceiving, the state of being deceptive—all this is the ground for deception known as indirect talk. For whom these three grounds for deception are abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'non-deceitful' (akuhaka)—one who is withdrawn and non-deceitful.

'Not longing, not stingy' (api hālu amaccharī): Craving is called 'longing' (pihā). Whatever passion, intense lust... covetousness, greed, unwholesome root there is. For whom this 'longing' called craving is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'not longing' (api hālu). He does not long for forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles. He does not long for, desire, enjoy, yearn for, or crave after family, group, dwelling, gain, fame, praise, happiness, robes, alms-food, lodging, medicinal requisites for the sick, the sense element, the fine-material element, the immaterial element, sense existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, five-constituent existence, the past, the future, the present, or things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. This is 'not longing'. 'Not stingy' (amaccharī) refers to the five types of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding status, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. Such stinginess, the act of being stingy, the state of being stingy, the various desires for 'let it be for me only', the state of always desiring...
175:
...the state of mental contraction, the state of holding on tightly is called stinginess (macchariya). Furthermore, stinginess regarding the aggregates, stinginess regarding the elements, stinginess regarding the bases, and grasping—this is called stinginess. For whom this stinginess is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'not stingy' (amaccharī). (This is) one who is not longing and not stingy.

'Not impudent, not loathsome' (appagabbha ajeguccha): Regarding impudence (pāgabbhiya), there are three types: bodily impudence, verbal impudence, and mental impudence. What is bodily impudence? In this Dispensation, someone shows bodily impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, in the dining hall, in the sweat-house, at the watering place, while entering the village, and while inside the village.

How does one show bodily impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha? In this Dispensation, someone in the midst of the Saṅgha, acting without respect, stands brushing against elder monks, sits brushing against them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing, and speaks while waving his arms. Thus one shows bodily impudence in the midst of the Saṅgha.

How does one show bodily impudence in the midst of a group? In this Dispensation, someone in the midst of a group, acting without respect, walks on the cloister path wearing sandals near elder monks who are walking without sandals; walks on a higher cloister path near those walking on a lower one; walks on the cloister path near those walking on the ground; stands brushing against them, sits brushing against them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing, and speaks while waving his arms. Thus one shows bodily impudence in the midst of a group.

How does one show bodily impudence in the dining hall? In this Dispensation, someone in the dining hall, acting without respect, sits crowding the elder monks, prevents new monks from having a seat, stands brushing against them, sits brushing against them, stands in front of them, sits in front of them, sits on a high seat, sits with his head covered, speaks while standing...
176:
He also speaks while swinging his arms. In this way, he displays bodily impudence in the refectory.

How does he display bodily impudence in the fire-house? Here, a certain monk, without showing respect, stands while jostling the elder monks; he sits while jostling them; he stands in front of them; he sits in front of them; he sits on a high seat; without asking permission or being invited, he throws wood [into the fire]; he closes the door; and he speaks while swinging his arms. In this way, he displays bodily impudence in the fire-house.

How does he display bodily impudence at the water-landing? Here, a certain monk, without showing respect, enters the water while jostling the elder monks; he enters the water in front of them; he bathes while jostling them; he bathes in front of them; he bathes upstream from them; he emerges from the water while jostling them; he emerges in front of them; he emerges upstream from them. In this way, he displays bodily impudence at the water-landing.

How does he display bodily impudence while entering the village? Here, a certain monk, while entering the village, without showing respect, walks while jostling the elder monks; he walks in front of them; and leaving the path, he walks ahead of the elder monks. In this way, he displays bodily impudence while entering the village.

How does he display bodily impudence when he has entered the village? Here, a certain monk, when he has entered the village, enters even though he is told, "Venerable sir, do not enter"; he stands even though he is told, "Venerable sir, do not stand"; he sits even though he is told, "Venerable sir, do not sit"; he enters an inappropriate place; he stands in an inappropriate place; he sits in an inappropriate place. There are those private, secluded, and screened rooms of families where the women, maidens, daughters-in-law, and young girls of the family sit; he enters there abruptly and even strokes the head of a child. In this way, he displays bodily impudence when he has entered the village—this is the display of bodily impudence.

What kind of verbal impudence does he display? Here, a certain monk displays verbal impudence while in the midst of the Saṅgha, while in the midst of a group, and when he has entered the village.
177:
How does a monk in the midst of the Saṅgha display verbal impudence? Here, a certain monk, while in the midst of the Saṅgha, without showing respect and without asking permission or being invited, preaches the Dhamma, answers questions, or recites the Pātimokkha to the monks who have come to the monastery. He speaks while standing and speaks while swinging his arms. In this way, a monk in the midst of the Saṅgha displays verbal impudence.

How does a monk in the midst of a group display verbal impudence? Here, a certain monk, while in the midst of a group, without showing respect and without asking permission or being invited, preaches the Dhamma or answers questions to the monks who have come to the monastery. He speaks while standing and speaks while swinging his arms. He also preaches the Dhamma or answers questions to the nuns, laymen, and laywomen who have come to the monastery. He speaks while standing and speaks while swinging his arms. In this way, a monk in the midst of a group displays verbal impudence.

How does a monk who has entered the village display verbal impudence? Here, a certain monk, when he has entered the village, speaks to a woman or a young girl in this way: "You of such-and-such a name and such-and-such a clan, what is there? Is there gruel? Is there rice? Is there food? What shall we drink? What shall we eat? What shall we chew? What else is there? What will you give me?" Thus he prattles repeatedly. Speaking such words, prattling, talking in such a manner, and the state of being a prattler constitute verbal impudence. In this way, a monk who has entered the village displays verbal impudence. This is verbal impudence (vācasika pāgabbhiya).

What is mental impudence (cetasika pāgabbhiya)? Here, a certain monk, though he is one who has gone forth from a high-born family, does not mentally regard himself as equal to one who has gone forth from a high-born family. Though he is one who has gone forth from a noble family, he does not mentally regard himself as equal to one who has gone forth from a noble family. Though he is one who has gone forth from a wealthy family, he does not mentally regard himself as equal to one who has gone forth from a wealthy family. Though he is one who has gone forth from a family of great wealth... though he is a reciter of the Suttas, he does not mentally regard himself as equal to a reciter of the Suttas.
