Though he is a master of the Vinaya... though he is a preacher of the Dhamma... though he is a forest-dweller... though he is an alms-food eater... though he is a rag-robe wearer... though he is a three-robe wearer... though he is a consecutive-house-to-house alms-goer... though he is one who refuses later food... though he is a sitter-up... though he is one who uses whatever seat is assigned... though he is an attainer of the first jhāna, he does not mentally regard himself as equal to an attainer of the first jhāna. ...pe... though he is an attainer of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...
178:
Being one who has attained the meditative attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he considers himself equal in mind to another who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is impudence of the mind (cetasika pāgabbhiya). For whom these three types of impudence have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'not impudent' (appagabbha).

'One who is not loathsome' (ajeguccho) means—there is the loathsome person and there is the person who is not loathsome. And what kind of person is loathsome? Here, a certain person is immoral, of evil nature, of impure and suspicious conduct, of concealed actions; not a recluse but claiming to be one, not a celibate but claiming to be one; rotten within, oozing with lust, and like a heap of refuse. This person is called loathsome.

Alternatively, he is irritable and full of turbulence; even when spoken to slightly, he becomes annoyed, angry, resentful, and stubborn, and displays anger, hatred, and discontent. This person is called loathsome.

Alternatively, he is angry and resentful; he is a disparager and one who dominates; he is envious and stingy; he is deceitful and crafty; he is stubborn and extremely arrogant; he has evil desires and wrong view; he is one who tenaciously clings to his own views and finds it difficult to let go. This person is called loathsome.

And what kind of person is not loathsome? Here, in this Dispensation, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and having undertaken the rules of training, he trains in them. This person is called not loathsome.

Alternatively, he is not angry and not full of turbulence; even when spoken to much, he does not become annoyed, angry, resentful, or stubborn, and does not display anger, hatred, or discontent. This person is called not loathsome.

Alternatively, he is not angry and not resentful; he is not a disparager and not one who dominates; he is not envious and not stingy; he is not deceitful and not crafty; he is not stubborn and not extremely arrogant; he does not have evil desires or wrong view; he is not one who tenaciously clings to his own views and he lets go easily. This person is called not loathsome. All foolish worldlings are loathsome. Starting from the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), the eight noble persons (ariya-puggala) are not loathsome. This is the meaning of 'not impudent and not loathsome'.

'Not engaged in slander' means—slander (pesuñña) is when a certain person in this world is a slanderer; having heard something here, he tells it there to divide these people; or having heard something there...
179:
...having heard from those people, he tells it to these people to divide them. Thus, he is a divider of those who are united, or an encourager of those who are divided; he is one who delights in discord, rejoices in discord, finds pleasure in discord, and speaks words that create discord. This is called slander.

Furthermore, one conveys slander for two reasons: either through the desire to be loved or with the intent to divide. How does one convey slander through the desire to be loved? Thinking, 'I will be dear to this person, I will be pleasing, I will be an intimate, I will be an insider, I will be a close friend.' Thus, one conveys slander through the desire to be loved. How does one convey slander with the intent to divide? Thinking, 'How may they be separated, be alienated, be divided into groups, be split in two, be made into two factions, be broken apart, not be united, and dwell in suffering and discomfort?' Thus, one conveys slander with the intent to divide. For whom this slander has been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is not engaged, not attached, not devoted, and not fully committed to slander. Therefore, it is said, 'not engaged in slander'.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Withdrawn, not deceitful, not covetous, not stingy,
Not impudent, not loathsome, and not engaged in slander.'

'No oozing of craving in pleasant things, not engaged in extreme arrogance,
Gentle and possessing ready wit, not a blind believer, and not dispassionate.'

'No oozing of craving in pleasant things' means—the five cords of sensual pleasure are called 'pleasant things' (sātiya). For what reason are the five cords of sensual pleasure called pleasant things? Generally, devas and humans desire, enjoy, long for, wish for, and are attached to the five cords of sensual pleasure. For that reason, the five cords of sensual pleasure are called pleasant things. For those who have not abandoned this craving for pleasant things, craving for forms flows from the eye, it oozes, it streams, it proceeds. Craving for sounds from the ear... craving for smells from the nose... craving for tastes from the tongue... craving for tangibles from the body... craving for mental objects from the mind flows, oozes, streams, and proceeds. For those who have abandoned this craving for pleasant things, cut it off at the root, calmed it, stilled it, made it incapable of arising again, and burnt it with the fire of knowledge, craving for forms does not flow from the eye, does not ooze, does not stream...
180:
...flows. Craving having sounds as objects from the ear-door... [pe]... craving having mental phenomena as objects from the mind-door does not occur, does not leak, does not flow, does not repeatedly occur. Because of this, he is called 'one who does not flow in cravings for agreeable things' (sātiyesu anassāvī).

'Atimāne ca no yuto' means: what is over-conceit (atimāna)? Here, someone despises another by birth, or by lineage... [pe]... or by some other basis. Such conceit, conceiving, the state of conceiving, haughtiness, the act of haughtiness, lifting up like a banner, exaltation, the desire of the mind for a banner—this is called over-conceit. For whom this over-conceit is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, burned by the fire of knowledge, he is not joined with, not attached to, not well-joined with over-conceit. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Atimāne ca no yuto'.

'Saṇho ca paṭibhānavā' means: 'Saṇho' is called gentle because he is endowed with gentle bodily action. He is called gentle because he is endowed with gentle verbal action. He is called gentle because he is endowed with gentle mental action. He is called gentle because he is endowed with gentle foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). He is called gentle because he is endowed with gentle right efforts (sammappadhāna), with gentle bases of power (iddhipāda), with gentle faculties (indriya), with gentle powers (bala), and with gentle factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). He is called gentle because he is endowed with the gentle Noble Eightfold Path.

'Paṭibhānavā' means: there are three kinds of those possessing analytical insight—one possessing analytical insight through learning (pariyatti), one possessing analytical insight through inquiry (paripucchā), and one possessing analytical insight through attainment (adhigama). What is one possessing analytical insight through learning? Here, someone has naturally learned the Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla; based on that learning, insight arises. This person is called pariyatti-paṭibhānavā. What is one possessing analytical insight through inquiry? Here, someone is an inquirer into his own welfare, into the meaning of the cause, into characteristics, into causes, and into what is a cause and what is not a cause. Based on that inquiry, insight arises. This person is called paripucchā-paṭibhānavā. What is one possessing analytical insight through attainment? Here, someone has attained the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the Noble Eightfold Path, the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and the six direct knowledges (abhiññā). To him, the meaning (attha) is known, the Dhamma is known, the language (nirutti) is known. When the meaning is known, insight into the meaning arises; when the Dhamma is known, insight into the Dhamma arises; when the language is known, insight into the language arises. Insight that occurs within these knowledges is called the analytical insight of perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). One who is endowed with, well-endowed with, approached by, well-approached by, possessed of, well-possessed of, and complete with this analytical insight of perspicacity is called paṭibhānavā. For whom there is no learning, no inquiry, and no attainment, from where will insight arise for him? This is the meaning of the phrase 'Saṇho ca paṭibhānavā'.

In the passage 'Na saddho na virajjati', 'na saddho' means he does not believe the Dhamma—which he has known by himself through higher knowledge and realized by himself—because of the words of anyone else. He does not believe because of the words of another recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā.
181:
The knowledge that occurs within these three knowledges—meaning (attha), Dhamma, and language (nirutti)—is called the analytical insight of perspicacity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). One who is endowed with, well-endowed with, approached by, well-approached by, possessed of, well-possessed of, and complete with this analytical insight of perspicacity is called paṭibhānavā (one possessing analytical insight). For whom there is no learning, no inquiry, and no attainment (adhigama), from where will insight arise for him? This is the meaning of the phrase "Saṇho ca paṭibhānavā".

In the passage "Na saddho na virajjati", "na saddho" means he does not believe the Dhamma—which he has known by himself through higher knowledge and realized by himself—because of the words of another recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā. He has known by himself through higher knowledge: "All conditioned things are impermanent," ... "All conditioned things are suffering," "All phenomena are non-self," "With ignorance as condition, formations arise," ... "With birth as condition, aging and death arise," "With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease," ... "With the cessation of birth, aging and death cease," "This is suffering," ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," "These are the taints (āsava)," ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints," "These dhammas should be known through higher knowledge," ... "These dhammas should be realized." He has known by himself through higher knowledge the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact; the arising, etc., of the five aggregates of clinging; the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the four great elements. He has known by himself through higher knowledge and realized by himself the Dhamma that "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease"; he does not believe it because of the words of another recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā.

For this was said by the Blessed One: "Sāriputta, do you believe that the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and has the Deathless as its final goal? Do you believe that the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunge into the Deathless, have the Deathless as their destination, and have the Deathless as their final goal?"

"Venerable Sir, in this matter I do not go merely by faith in the Blessed One's words (I speak from direct knowledge). The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunge into the Deathless, have the Deathless as their destination, and have the Deathless as their final goal. Venerable Sir, those for whom this Dhamma is not yet known, not seen, not understood, not realized, and not touched by wisdom, they would go by faith in others in this matter, believing that the faculty of faith, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and has the Deathless as its final goal. The faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness..."
182:
...the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless (Nibbāna), has the Deathless as its destination, and has the Deathless as its final goal. Venerable Sir, for those by whom this Dhamma has been known, seen, understood, realized, and experienced through wisdom, they have no doubt or perplexity in it. The faculty of faith... the faculty of energy... the faculty of mindfulness... the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and has the Deathless as its final goal. Venerable Sir, for me also, this Dhamma has been known, seen, understood, realized, and experienced through wisdom; I have no doubt or perplexity in it. The faculty of faith... the faculty of energy... the faculty of mindfulness... the faculty of concentration... the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and has the Deathless as its final goal.

“Well said, Sāriputta! Well said! Sāriputta, those for whom this Dhamma has not yet been known, seen, understood, realized, or experienced through wisdom, they would go by the faith of others in this matter. The faculty of faith... the faculty of wisdom, when developed and cultivated, plunges into the Deathless, has the Deathless as its destination, and has the Deathless as its final goal.

The man who is not credulous (without blind faith),
Who knows the Uncreated (Nibbāna),
Who has severed the connection (to saṃsāra),
Who has destroyed the occasion (for rebirth),
Who has vomited out all desires,
He is indeed the supreme man.

Regarding the phrase “not having faith, not being attached”: All foolish worldlings (puthujjanas) are attached; starting from the noble worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana), the seven types of trainees (sekhas) are free from attachment. The Arahant is neither attached nor especially detached (as he is already free). That Arahant is detached due to the destruction of lust, because of the state of being free from lust; he is free from hatred due to the destruction of hatred, because of the state of being free from hatred; he is free from delusion due to the destruction of delusion, because of the state of being free from delusion. That Arahant has lived the holy life, has practiced the conduct... there is no more wandering in the cycle of birth and death; for that Arahant, there is no more renewed existence. This is the meaning of the phrase “not having faith, not being attached.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Not craving for pleasant sensual pleasures,
Not joined with excessive conceit,
Gentle and possessing ready wit,
He is not credulous and not attached.”

He does not train (in the precepts) out of desire for gain, nor is he angry when not receiving gain; he is not in conflict with craving, and does not greedily lust after tastes.

Regarding “He does not train out of desire for gain, nor is he angry when not receiving gain”: How does one train out of desire for gain? Here, monks, a monk sees another monk who receives the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The thought occurs to him: “By what means does this venerable one receive these four requisites?” This hearing (or thought) occurs to him: “This venerable one learns the Suttas; therefore, he is rich in these requisites.” For the sake of gain, because of gain...
183:
“Does this venerable one receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick?” (such a thought occurs). The thought occurs to that monk: “This venerable one is a Suttantika (one who learns the Suttas); therefore, this venerable one receives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites.” For the sake of gain, because of gain, by reason of gain, for the production of gain, and for the ripening of gain, he learns the Suttas. In this way, he trains out of desire for gain. 

Or again, a monk sees another monk who receives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. The thought occurs to him: “By what means does this venerable one receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites?” The thought occurs to him: “This venerable one is a Vinayadhara (expert in Vinaya)... a Dhammakathika (Dhamma speaker)... an Ābhidhammika (expert in Abhidhamma); therefore, this venerable one receives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites.” For the sake of gain, because of gain, by reason of gain, for the production of gain, and for the ripening of gain, he learns the Abhidhamma. In this way, he trains out of desire for gain.

Or again, a monk sees another monk who receives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites. The thought occurs to him: “By what means does this venerable one receive robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites?” The thought occurs to him: “This venerable one is an āraññika (forest dweller) who observes the dhutaṅga... a piṇḍapātika (alms-food eater)... a paṃsukūlika (rag-robe wearer)... a tecīvarika (triple-robe wearer)... a sapadānacārika (uninterrupted alms-goer)... a khalupacchābhattika (refuser of later food)... a nesajjika (sitter's practice)... a yathāsanthatika (any-bed user); therefore, this venerable one receives robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites.” For the sake of gain, because of gain, by reason of gain, for the production of gain, and for the ripening of gain, he becomes an āraññika... he becomes a yathāsanthatika. In this way, he trains out of desire for gain.

How does one train without desire for gain? Here, a monk trains not for the sake of gain, not because of gain, not by reason of gain, not for the production of gain, and not for the ripening of gain, but only for the purpose of taming himself, for the purpose of calming himself, and for the purpose of his own final cooling (Nibbāna), he learns the Suttas, he learns the Vinaya, and he learns the Abhidhamma. In this way, he trains without desire for gain.
184: Alternatively, a monk does not train in the training rules for the sake of gain, because of gain, by reason of gain, for the production of gain, or by ripening gain. Relying only on fewness of wishes, relying only on contentment, relying only on effacement, relying only on seclusion, and relying only on the fact that this is beneficial, he becomes a forest dweller (āraññika), an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika), a refuse-rag wearer (paṃsukūlika), a three-robe wearer (tecīvarika), a house-to-house alms seeker (sapadānacārika), a one-session eater (khalupacchābhattika), a sitter-up (nesajjika), and one who uses whatever seat is assigned (yathāsanthatika). Thus, the meaning of the phrase 'He does not train out of desire for gain' (Lābhakamyā na sikkhati) should be understood.## 'And he does not get angry at the lack of gain' (Alābhe ca na kuppati)How does one get angry at the lack of gain? Here, some person gets angry, is hostile, and is resentful, thinking: 'I do not get a family as supporters, I do not get a group, I do not get a monastery, I do not get gain, I do not get fame, I do not get praise, I do not get happiness, I do not get robes, I do not get alms-food, I do not get a lodging, I do not get medicines and provisions for the sick, I do not get an attendant for the sick, I am obscure.' He manifests anger, hatred, and discontent. Thus, one gets angry at the lack of gain.How does one not get angry at the lack of gain? Here, a monk does not get angry, is not hostile, and is not resentful, thinking: 'I do not get a family... (and so on) ... I am obscure.' He does not manifest anger, hatred, and discontent. Thus, the meaning of the phrase 'He does not train out of desire for gain and does not get angry at the lack of gain' (Lābhakamyā na sikkhati alābhe ca na kuppati) should be understood.## 'Not opposed to craving, he is not greedy for tastes' (Aviruddho ca taṇhāya, rasesu nānu-gijjhati)In this phrase, 'opposition' (virodha) means: annoyance of mind, repeated annoyance, striking, opposition, anger, being angry, being very angry, hatred, being hateful, being very hateful, abnormality of mind, mental ill-will, wrath, the act of being wrathful, the state of being wrathful, hatred, the act of hating, the state of being hateful, abnormality, the act of being abnormal, the state of being abnormal, opposition, repeated opposition, ferocity, bad speech, and the state of the mind's displeasure. This is called 'opposition'. For whom this opposition is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising again, and consumed by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'unopposed' (aviruddho). 'Craving' (taṇhā) means: craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental objects. 'Taste' (rasa) means: taste of roots, taste of stems, taste of bark, taste of leaves, taste of flowers, and taste of fruits.
185: There are sour tastes, sweet tastes, bitter tastes, pungent tastes, salty tastes, alkaline tastes, jujube-like tastes, astringent tastes, good tastes, bad tastes, cold tastes, and hot tastes. In this world, there are some recluses and brahmins who are greedy for tastes. They wander about seeking various excellent tastes with the tip of their tongue. When they get a sour taste, they seek a non-sour taste; when they get a non-sour taste, they seek a sour taste. When they get a sweet taste, they seek a non-sweet taste; when they get a non-sweet taste, they seek a sweet taste. When they get a bitter taste, they seek a non-bitter taste; when they get a non-bitter taste, they seek a bitter taste. When they get a pungent taste, they seek a non-pungent taste; when they get a non-pungent taste, they seek a pungent taste. When they get a salty taste, they seek a non-salty taste; when they get a non-salty taste, they seek a salty taste. When they get an alkaline taste, they seek a non-alkaline taste; when they get a non-alkaline taste, they seek an alkaline taste. When they get a jujube-like taste, they seek an astringent taste; when they get an astringent taste, they seek a jujube-like taste. When they get a good taste, they seek a bad taste; when they get a bad taste, they seek a good taste. When they get a cold taste, they seek a hot taste; when they get a hot taste, they seek a cold taste. Whatever object they get, they are not content with it and seek here and there repeatedly. They are attached to, greedy for, intensely greedy for, infatuated with, absorbed in, stuck to, fastened to, and obstructed by tastes that increase the heart's delight. For whom this craving for tastes is abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, reached the state of non-arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he consumes food reflecting wisely: 'Not for fun, not for intoxication, not for ornament, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and endurance of this body, for ending the suffering of hunger, and for assisting the holy life. Thus, I shall eliminate old feelings and not produce new feelings, and I shall have maintenance, blamelessness, and living in comfort.' Thus he consumes, reflecting.Just as one might set fire to a forest only for the purpose of planting, or just as one might grease an axle only for the purpose of carrying a load, or just as one might eat the flesh of one's son only for the purpose of crossing a desert; even so, a monk consumes food reflecting wisely: 'Not for fun... (and so on) ... living in comfort.' He abandons craving for tastes, dispels it, makes an end of it, and brings it to non-existence. He is remote from craving for tastes, abstains from it, refrains from it, has emerged from it, is released from it, is detached from it, and dwells with a mind that has no boundaries. This is what is meant by 'Not opposed to craving, he is not greedy for tastes.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:
186:
"He does not practice out of desire for gain, nor is he angry when gain is not obtained; he is not in conflict with craving, and he does not greedily hanker after tastes."

"Always mindful and equanimous, he does not conceive himself as equal, superior, or inferior in the world; for him, there are no protuberances (ussada) of defilements such as lust."

'Always mindful and equanimous' means he is endowed with the six-factored equanimity (chaሷaᅅgupekkhā). Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having seen a form with the eye, he does not hanker after a pleasant object, does not rejoice in it, and does not give rise to lust; his body remains steady, and his mind is well-established within, well-settled, and well-liberated. Furthermore, having seen a form with the eye, he is not dejected by an unpleasant object, his mind is not established in anger, his mind is not shrinking, and his heart is free from ill-will; his body remains steady, and his mind is well-established within, well-settled, and well-liberated. Having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having felt a touch with the body... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not hanker after a pleasant object, does not rejoice in it, and does not give rise to lust; his body remains steady, and his mind is well-established within, well-settled, and well-liberated. Furthermore, having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not dejected by an unpleasant object, his mind is not established in anger, his mind is not shrinking, and his heart is free from ill-will; his body remains steady, and his mind is well-established within, well-settled, and well-liberated.

Having seen a form with the eye, in the face of both pleasant and unpleasant forms, his body remains steady, and his mind is well-established within, well-settled, and well-liberated. Having heard a sound with the ear... having cognized a mental object with the mind, in the face of both pleasant and unpleasant mental objects, his body remains steady, and his mind is well-established within, well-settled, and well-liberated.

Having seen a form with the eye, he is not lustful toward what is lust-inducing, he is not hateful toward what is hate-inducing, he is not deluded by what is delusion-inducing, he is not angry at what is anger-inducing, he is not intoxicated by what is intoxicating, and he is not defiled by what is defiling. Having heard a sound with the ear... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not lustful toward what is lust-inducing, he is not hateful toward what is hate-inducing, he is not deluded by what is delusion-inducing, he is not angry at what is anger-inducing, he is not intoxicated by what is intoxicating, and he is not defiled by what is defiling.
187:
In the seen, there is only the seen; in the heard, there is only the heard; in the sensed, there is only the sensed; in the cognized, there is only the cognized. He is not smeared by the seen, he is not smeared by the heard, he is not smeared by the sensed, he is not smeared by the cognized. He is not attached to the seen, being detached, not depending on craving or views, without bonds, well-liberated, dissociated, and he dwells with a boundless mind. In the heard, in the sensed, and in the cognized, he is also not attached, being detached, not depending on craving or views, without bonds, well-liberated, dissociated, and he dwells with a boundless mind.

An Arahant possesses the eye-faculty; the Arahant sees a form with the eye. Desire and lust (chandarāga) are absent in the Arahant; the Arahant has a well-liberated mind. An Arahant possesses the ear-faculty; the Arahant hears a sound with the ear. Desire and lust are absent in the Arahant; the Arahant has a well-liberated mind. An Arahant possesses the nose-faculty; the Arahant smells an odor with the nose. Desire and lust are absent in the Arahant; the Arahant has a well-liberated mind. An Arahant possesses the tongue-faculty; the Arahant tastes a flavor with the tongue... An Arahant possesses the body-faculty; the Arahant feels a touch with the body... An Arahant possesses the mind-faculty; the Arahant cognizes a mental object with the mind. Desire and lust are absent in the Arahant; the Arahant has a well-liberated mind.

The eye delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and is satisfied with forms. For the Arahant, that eye is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained; and he teaches the Dhamma for the restraint of that eye-faculty. The ear delights in sounds... The nose delights in odors... The tongue delights in flavors, rejoices in flavors, and is satisfied with flavors. For the Arahant, that tongue is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained; and he teaches the Dhamma for the restraint of that tongue-faculty. The body delights in touches... The mind delights in mental objects, rejoices in mental objects, and is satisfied with mental objects. For the Arahant, that mind is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained; and he teaches the Dhamma for the restraint of that mind-faculty.

"They lead the tamed (elephant or horse) to the assembly; the king mounts the tamed. Among humans, the tamed one who endures harsh words is the best."

"Tamed mules are excellent, as are thoroughbred horses and Sindhu horses, and great noble elephants (mahānāga); but more excellent than these is one who has tamed himself."

"For not by these vehicles could one go to the unreached land (Nibbāna), as a tamed person goes by means of his own well-tamed self."
188:
They do not tremble in the modes (of conceit: superior, equal, or inferior); they are well-released from repeated existence. Having reached the state of the tamed, the fruit of Arahantship, they are victors in the world.

For whom the faculties are developed within oneself, externally, and in the whole world; having penetrated this world and the other world, with a developed mind that has completed its task, that tamed one awaits the time (of death).

'Always equanimous' means: at all times, for all time, constantly... until the final stage of the aggregates. 'Mindful' means: being mindful through four reasons. Being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body in the body; being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of feelings... the mind... phenomena in phenomena. He is called 'mindful'—thus, 'always equanimous and mindful.'

'Does not think of oneself as equal in the world' means: he does not produce conceit (māna) such as 'I am equal' by way of birth, lineage... or any other basis. Thus, 'does not think of oneself as equal in the world.'

'Not superior, not inferior' means: he does not produce over-conceit (atimāna) such as 'I am superior' by way of birth, lineage... or any other basis. He does not produce low-conceit (omāna) such as 'I am inferior' by way of birth, lineage... or any other basis. Thus, 'not superior, not inferior.'

'For him there are no protuberances (ussada)' means: 'tassa' refers to the Arahant whose taints are exhausted. 'Ussada' refers to the seven protuberances (sattussada)—the protuberance of lust, the protuberance of hatred, the protuberance of delusion, the protuberance of conceit, the protuberance of views, the protuberance of defilements, and the protuberance of kamma. For that Arahant, these protuberances do not exist, are not present, are not found, are not obtained; they are abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge. Thus, 'for him there are no protuberances.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'The one who is always equanimous and mindful does not think of himself as equal in the world; he is not superior nor inferior; for him there are no protuberances.'
189:
For whom there is no state of dependence, having known the Dhamma, he is independent; for whom craving for existence or non-existence does not exist.

'For whom there is no state of dependence' (yassa nissayatā natthi) means: 'yassa' refers to the Arahant who is worthy of special offerings. 'Nissaya' (dependence) are of two kinds: dependence on craving (taṇhā-nissaya) and dependence on views (diṭṭhi-nissaya). ... This is the dependence on craving. ... This is the dependence on views. For that Arahant, the dependence on craving is abandoned, and the dependence on views is relinquished. Because the dependence on craving is abandoned and the dependence on views is relinquished, for him there is no state of dependence; they do not exist, are not present, are not found, are not obtained; they are abandoned, cut off by the path of Arahantship, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge. Thus, 'for whom there is no state of dependence.'

'Having known the Dhamma, he is independent' (ñatvā dhammaṃ anissito) means: 'ñatvā' means having known, having seen the qualities, having weighed, having investigated, having expanded, and having made clear by analysis. Having known, seen, weighed, investigated, expanded, and made clear that 'All conditioned things are impermanent'; ... 'All conditioned things are suffering'; ... 'All phenomena are non-self'; ... 'Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.' 'Anissito' (independent) means the dependencies are of two kinds: dependence on craving and dependence on views. ... This is the dependence on craving. ... This is the dependence on views. Having abandoned the dependence on craving and relinquished the dependence on views, he does not depend on the eye, does not depend on the ear, does not depend on the nose, does not depend on the tongue, does not depend on the body, does not depend on the mind; he does not depend on visible forms... sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles... family... group... dwelling... or on things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized; he is not attached, not clinging, not adhering, not misinterpreting; having emerged, being released, being liberated, being dissociated, he dwells with a mind that has no boundaries. Thus, 'having known the Dhamma, he is independent.'

'For whom craving for existence or non-existence does not exist' (bhavāya vibhavāya vā, taṇhā yassa na vijjati) means: 'taṇhā' (craving) refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental objects. 'Yassa' refers to the Arahant who is worthy of special offerings. 'Bhavāya' means in the view of existence; 'vibhavāya' means in the view of non-existence. Alternatively, 'bhavāya' means in the eternalist view; 'vibhavāya' means in the annihilationist view. Alternatively, 'bhavāya' means in repeated existence, in repeated destinations, in repeated rebirth, in repeated conception, in the manifestation of repeated selfhood. For that Arahant, craving does not exist, is not present, is not found, is not obtained; it is abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge. This is the meaning of the phrase 'for whom craving for existence or non-existence does not exist.'
190:
For that Arahant, craving for becoming in a new life, for becoming repeatedly in a destination, for becoming repeatedly in rebirth, for becoming repeatedly in conception, for becoming repeatedly in a manifest personality—does not exist, is not found, is not obtained; it has been abandoned, cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. This is the meaning of the phrase 'For whom there is no craving for existence or non-existence' (bhavāya vibhavāya vā taṇhā yassa na vijjati).

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
'For whom there is no dependence [on craving and views], having known the Dhamma, he is independent. For whom there is no craving for eternalism or annihilationism, I call him one who is calmed from the defilements.'

I call him peaceful, who is indifferent to sensual pleasures; for him, the four knots do not exist; he has crossed over the entangler (craving).

'Taṃ brūmi upasanto' means: I call him calmed, especially calmed, peaceful, stilled; I say, I speak, I recite, I show, I declare—thus 'I call him peaceful'.

'Kāmesu anapekkhiṇaṃ' means: Sensual pleasures (kāma) are twofold in brief: objective sensual pleasures (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensual pleasures (kilesa-kāma). ... These are called objective sensual pleasures. ... These are called subjective sensual pleasures. Having fully understood objective sensual pleasures, and having abandoned, given up, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the subjective sensual pleasures, he is indifferent to sensual pleasures, free from sensual pleasures, has relinquished sensual pleasures, has vomited sensual pleasures, is released from sensual pleasures, has abandoned sensual pleasures, has discarded sensual pleasures. He is free from lust in sensual pleasures, has gone beyond lust, has relinquished lust, has vomited lust, is released from lust, has abandoned lust, has discarded lust. He is without hunger, cooled, stilled, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime (brahma-bhūta). This is the meaning of 'indifferent to sensual pleasures'.

'Ganthā tassa na vijjanti' means: There are four knots (gantha): the bodily knot of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha), the bodily knot of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha), the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbata-parāmāsa-kāyagantha), and the bodily knot of dogmatic attachment to truth (idaṃsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha). Lust for one's own view is the bodily knot of covetousness. Malice or resentment toward the doctrines of others is the bodily knot of ill-will. Over-estimation of one's own virtue (abstinence from sexual intercourse), or practice (cow-practice, etc.), or both virtue and practice as 'purifying' is the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances. Firmly taking to heart one's own view as 'this alone is the truth' is the bodily knot of dogmatic attachment to truth. 'Tassa' refers to the Arahant, the one whose taints are destroyed. For that Arahant, the knots do not exist, do not exist, do not exist, are not obtained; they have been abandoned, cut off completely by the path of Arahantship, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising, and burnt by the fire of knowledge. This is the meaning of 'the knots do not exist for him'.

'Atarī so visattikaṃ' means: Craving is called 'visattikā' (the entangler). Whatever attachment, great desire, longing, greed, or unwholesome root exists. For what reason is it called 'visattikā'?
191:
Why is it called 'visattikā'? It is called visattikā because it spreads (visata); because it is wide (visāla); because it is extensive (visata); because it is uneven (visama); because it moves toward objects (visakkati); because it brings suffering (visam-harati); because it is deceptive (visamvādikā); because it has poison as its root (visa-mūla); because it has poison as its fruit (visa-phala); because its enjoyment is like poison (visa-paribhoga). Alternatively, that craving is spread and extended (visata, vitthata) among forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, families, groups, dwellings... and among things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized. Thus it is called visattikā. 'He has crossed over the entangler' means that Arahant has crossed over, transcended, gone beyond this clinging craving.

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
'I call him peaceful, who is indifferent to sensual pleasures; for him, the four knots—the bodily knot of covetousness, the bodily knot of ill-will, the bodily knot of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily knot of dogmatic attachment to truth—do not exist. He has crossed over the entangler (craving).'

For that Arahant, there are no sons, nor livestock, nor fields, nor property. In that Arahant, 'self' (attā) or 'not-self' (nirattā) cannot be found.

'For him, there are no sons, nor livestock, nor fields, nor property': Here, 'na' is a negation. 'Tassa' refers to the Arahant, the one worthy of offerings, whose taints are destroyed. 'Sons' (putta) are of four kinds: sons born of oneself, sons born of the field, adopted sons, and pupil-sons. 'Livestock' (pasavo) refers to goats, sheep, poultry, pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. 'Fields' (khetta) refers to fields of hill-paddy, rice, beans, kidney beans, barley, wheat, and sesame. 'Property/Site' (vatthu) refers to house-sites, granary-sites, front-sites, back-sites, garden-sites, and monastery-sites. For that Arahant, the acquisition of sons, livestock, fields, or property does not exist, is not obtained; they have been burnt by the fire of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship and are incapable of arising again.

'Self or not-self cannot be found in him': Here, 'attā' refers to the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) that 'there is a self'; 'nirattā' refers to the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) that 'it is cut off'. Alternatively, 'attā' is that which is to be grasped, and 'nirattā' is that which is to be relinquished. When there is nothing to be grasped, there is nothing to be relinquished. The Arahant is one who has transcended grasping and relinquishing, and has gone beyond growth and decline. He has completed his stay [in the holy life], has practiced the conduct... the round of birth and death no longer exists for him, and there is no further becoming.

Therefore, the Blessed One said—
192:
For that Arahant, there are no sons, nor cattle, nor field, nor property. In that Arahant, neither the grasping of a self (eternalism) nor the grasping of no-self (annihilationism) is to be found. By whatever [fault such as lust] worldlings or recluses and brahmins might speak of that Arahant, that [fault] is not placed before him; therefore, he does not tremble in the face of censures.

'Worldlings or recluses and brahmins' means: They are called worldlings (puthujjana) because they produce many (puthu) defilements. They are called worldlings because they have not yet abandoned the many forms of self-identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). They are called worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers. They are called worldlings because they have not yet emerged from all destinations (gati). They are called worldlings because they construct many various formations (abhisaṅkhāra). They are called worldlings because they are carried away by many various floods (ogha). They are called worldlings because they are tormented by many various torments (santāpa). They are called worldlings because they are burned by many various fevers (pariḷāha). They are called worldlings because they are attached, greedy, tied, infatuated, deeply absorbed, clinging, and perpetually obstructed by the five cords of sensual pleasure. They are called worldlings because they are covered, hindered, obstructed, closed off, concealed, and overturned by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa).

'Recluses' (samaṇa) refers to any who have gone forth and entered the wandering life outside of this Dispensation. 'Brahmins' (brāhmaṇa) refers to any who are 'Bho'-sayers (bhovādī).

Worldlings might speak of that Arahant by way of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, view, restlessness, doubt, or underlying tendencies, saying: 'one who is lustful, corrupt, deluded, bound, misapprehending, distracted, undecided, or one who has reached the strength [of defilements].' Since those formations (abhisaṅkhāra) have been abandoned, and because they are abandoned, there is no reason, no condition, no cause for them to speak, tell, say, show, or designate him by way of destination as: 'a denizen of hell, an animal, a ghost, a human, a deva, one with form, one without form, percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.'

'Taṃ tassa apurakkhatam' means: For that Arahant, the one who has destroyed the taints, there are two kinds of precedence (purekkhāra)—the precedence of craving and the precedence of view... (pe)...
193:
This preoccupation with craving... (pe)... this preoccupation with views. For that Arahant, preoccupation with craving is abandoned, and preoccupation with views is relinquished. Because preoccupation with craving is abandoned and preoccupation with views is relinquished, he does not wander about putting craving or views in the forefront. He has no craving as a banner, no craving as a flag, no craving as a dominant influence; no view as a banner, no view as a flag, no view as a dominant influence. He does not wander about surrounded by craving or views—this is his 'not putting in front' (apurekkhatam).

Regarding the phrase 'Therefore, he is unshaken in disputes'—'Therefore' means for that reason, because of that support, because of that cause, or because of that origin, he is unshaken, does not move, does not stir, does not tremble, does not shake, and is not perturbed by accusations, blame, reproach, ill-fame, or the bringing of discredit. Thus, 'Therefore, he is unshaken in disputes.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'By whatever fault worldlings might blame him, or likewise recluses and brahmins, he does not put that in front; therefore, he is unshaken in disputes.'

Free from greed, not stingy, the sage does not speak of himself among the superior, nor among the equal, nor among the inferior; being without mental constructions (kappa), he does not enter into mental constructions.

Regarding 'Free from greed, not stingy'—greed (gedha) is called craving. Whatever lust, intense passion... (pe)... covetousness, greed, or unwholesome root exists. For the person by whom this greed is abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'free from greed.' That person is not greedy for forms... (pe)... he is not greedy, not attached, not infatuated, and not absorbed in things seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. He is free from greed, gone beyond greed, has relinquished greed, vomited greed, is liberated from greed, has abandoned greed, has cast away greed, is without the hunger of craving... (pe)... and because he dwells with a sublime mind, he is called 'free from greed.' Regarding 'not stingy'—stinginess (macchariya) consists of five types: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding status, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma. Such... (pe)... grasping is called stinginess. For the person by whom this stinginess is abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt by the fire of knowledge, he is called 'not stingy.' Thus, 'free from greed, not stingy.'

Regarding 'The sage does not speak of himself among the superior, nor among the equal, nor among the inferior'—a sage (muni) is one who possesses the knowledge called mona... (pe)... he who has transcended the web of attachment is a sage. He does not say, speak, utter, manifest, or declare 'I am superior,' or 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.' Thus, 'The sage does not speak of himself among the superior, nor among the equal, nor among the inferior.'
194:
"One who is without attachment does not go to attachment" means: There are two types of attachment (kappa)—attachment through craving (taṇhā-kappa) and attachment through views (diṭṭhi-kappa). That Arahant has abandoned attachment through craving and has relinquished attachment through views. Because attachment through craving has been abandoned and attachment through views has been relinquished, he does not go to, does not approach, does not reach, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to attachment through craving or attachment through views. Therefore, it is said that he "does not go to attachment." "One who is without attachment" means: There are two types of attachment—attachment through craving and attachment through views. That Arahant has abandoned attachment through craving and has relinquished attachment through views. Because he has abandoned that attachment through craving and relinquished that attachment through views, he does not conceptualize, does not produce, does not generate, and does not bring into existence attachment through craving or attachment through views. Therefore, it is said that "one who is without attachment does not go to attachment."

For that reason, the Blessed One said:

"Free from greed, not stingy, the Sage does not speak of himself among the superior, nor among the equal, nor among the inferior; being without attachment, he does not go to attachment."

He for whom there is nothing of his own in the world, and who does not grieve because of what is non-existent, and does not go (by way of craving, etc.) among things—he is truly called "at peace."

"He for whom there is nothing of his own in the world" means: For the Arahant whose taints are destroyed, there is nothing in the world that is "mine." For that Arahant, there is no grasping, misapprehending, dogmatizing, entering into, or leaning towards any form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, thinking "this is mine" or "this is others'." It has been burnt by the fire of knowledge. Therefore, it is said that "there is nothing of his own in the world." "He does not grieve because of what is non-existent" means: He does not grieve over a thing that has changed, nor does he grieve when a thing is changing. He does not grieve, thinking "My eye has changed." He does not grieve, thinking "My ear, my nose, my tongue, my body, my mind, my forms, my sounds, my smells, my tastes, my touches, my family, my group, my dwelling, my gain, my fame, my praise, my happiness, my robe, my alms-food, my lodging, my medicinal requisites, my mother, my father, my brother, my sister, my son, my daughter, my friend, my colleague, my relative, my blood-relation has changed." He does not worry, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, and does not fall into confusion. Thus, it is said that "he does not grieve because of what is non-existent."

Alternatively, when touched, oppressed, encountered, or affected by painful feeling which is non-existent (as a permanent self), he does not grieve, does not worry, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, and does not fall into confusion. Even when touched and oppressed by eye-disease, he does not grieve, does not worry, does not lament, does not weep beating his breast, and does not fall into confusion. Ear-disease, nose-disease, tongue-disease, body-disease, headache, earache, mouth-disease, toothache, cough, asthma, catarrh, internal burning, fever, stomach-ache, fainting, dysentery, piercing pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, nail-disease, foot and hand disease, hemorrhage, diabetes, rough skin disease, abscess, fistula, illnesses arising from bile, illnesses arising from phlegm, illnesses arising from wind, illnesses arising from the conflict of humors (sannipāta), illnesses produced by change of season, illnesses produced by improper care, illnesses produced by external agency...
195:
He does not lament by beating his breast with his hands, nor does he fall into great confusion. Though touched, oppressed, encountered, and endowed with eye disease, he does not sorrow, is not weary, does not cry, does not lament by beating his breast, and does not fall into confusion. [The same applies to] ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-lobe disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, internal burning, fever, stomach ache, fainting, dysentery, sharp pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, nail/toe disease, palm/sole disease, vomiting blood or passing blood, diabetes, skin roughness, abscesses, fistula, diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from a conflict of humors, diseases arising from change of season, diseases arising from improper posture, diseases arising from the efforts of others, diseases arising from the result of Kamma, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and though touched, oppressed, and reached by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, snakes, scorpions, and lice, he does not sorrow, is not weary, does not cry, does not lament by beating his breast, and does not fall into great confusion. Thus it is said, 'he does not sorrow for what is non-existent'.

Alternatively, regarding a non-existent, unavailable object, he does not sorrow, is not weary, does not cry, does not lament by beating his breast, and does not fall into great confusion, thinking: "Alas, I do not have that object; if only I had that object, it would be good; indeed, I do not obtain that object." Thus it is said, 'he does not sorrow for what is non-existent'. 'He does not go to prejudices in things' means he does not go to the path one should not go through favoritism, he does not go to the path one should not go through anger, he does not go to the path one should not go through delusion, he does not go to the path one should not go through fear; he does not go by the power of lust, he does not go by the power of anger, he does not go by the power of delusion, he does not go by the power of conceit, he does not go by the power of views, he does not go by the power of restlessness, he does not go by the power of doubt, he does not go by the power of underlying tendencies; he is not led, carried, swept away, or brought near by things that form factions—this is 'he does not go to prejudices in things'.

'He is truly called calmed' means that Arahant is called, proclaimed, spoken of, said, illustrated, and designated as one whose defilements like lust are calmed, closely calmed, especially calmed, extinguished, and subsided—this is 'he is truly called calmed'.

Therefore, the Blessed One preached: "For that Arahant who has no sense of possession in the world, and does not sorrow because of non-existence, and does not go to the path of favoritism etc. in things—such a person is truly called one who is calmed from defilements like lust." The explanation of the tenth, the Purābheda Sutta, is finished.

11. Explanation of the Kalahavivāda Sutta. Following the Purābheda Sutta, the explanation of the Kalahavivāda Sutta will be preached in sequence. Why do disputes occur? Why do quarrels, lamentations, and sorrows occur, along with states associated with stinginess? Why do conceit and arrogance occur, along with states associated with slander? Why do these eight defilements occur?
196:
“For the Arahant who has no sense of possession in the world, and who does not grieve because of what is not present, and who does not go astray among things (dhammas), he is truly called 'one at peace'."

## The Exposition of the Purābheda Sutta, the tenth, is finished.

## 11. Kalahavivāda Sutta Niddesa

Immediately following the Purābheda Sutta, the exposition of the Kalahavivāda Sutta will be taught in sequence:

From where do quarrels, disputes, lamentations, and sorrows arise, along with stinginess? From where do conceit and arrogance arise, along with slander? From where do these things arise? Please tell me that.

"Kuto pahūtā kalahā vivādā" means: Kalaha (quarrel) is a dispute in one sense, and vivāda (dispute) is the same. That which is a quarrel is a dispute; that which is a dispute is a quarrel. Alternatively, vivāda is said to be the precursor to kalaha. Kings dispute with kings, nobles (khattiyas) dispute with nobles, brahmins dispute with brahmins, householders dispute with householders, a mother disputes with her son, a son disputes with his mother, a father disputes with his son, a son disputes with his father, a brother disputes with his brother, a brother disputes with his sister, a sister disputes with her brother, and a friend disputes with a friend. This is called vivāda.

What is kalaha? Laypeople, taking up sticks and weapons, engage in quarreling by body or by speech. Monks, having committed offenses (āpatti), engage in quarreling by body or by speech. This is called kalaha.

"Kuto pahūtā kalahā vivādā" means: From where do quarrels and disputes arise, from where are they born, from where are they produced, from where are they generated, from where do they come into being, from where do they manifest? What is their origin, what is their source, what is their birth, what is their cause? It is an inquiry into the root, cause (hetu), origin (nidāna), source (sambhava), beginning (pabhava), rising (samuṭṭhāna), nutriment (āhāra), object (ārammaṇa), condition (paccaya), and cause (samudaya) of quarrels and disputes.
197:
Regarding the phrase "From where do quarrels and disputes arise?", he asks in detail, requests, urges, and inspires. From where do quarrels arise? From where do disputes arise? For what reason do they arise? How do they come into being? How do they manifest? What is their source? What is their origin? What is their lineage? What is their beginning? Thus, he asks about the cause of quarrels and disputes, their source, their origin, their beginning, their starting point, their nutriment, their object, their condition, and their cause. This is the meaning of the phrase "Kutopahūtā kalahā vivādā."

Regarding the phrase "Lamentation and sorrow, along with stinginess":

Parideva (Lamentation) refers to the wailing of one afflicted by the loss of relatives, the loss of wealth, the loss of health, the loss of virtue, or the loss of right view, or of one endowed with any other kind of loss, or of one afflicted by any other kind of painful state. It is the crying out "my son, my wife," the mourning of various qualities, the act of lamenting, the manner of lamenting, the state of being one who laments, the state of being one who repeatedly laments, the speech of lamentation, idle talk, distorted lamentation, repeated talk, and the state of being one who repeatedly talks.

Soka (Sorrow) refers to the sorrow of one afflicted by the loss of relatives, wealth, health, virtue, or right view, or of one endowed with any other kind of loss, or of one afflicted by any other kind of painful state. It is sorrow, the act of sorrowing, the state of sorrowing, inner sorrow, inner parching, inner burning, inner inflammation, the state of mental burning, unhappiness, and the dart of sorrow that constantly pierces.

Macchariya (Stinginess) refers to the five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya), stinginess regarding families (kula-macchariya), stinginess regarding gains (lābha-macchariya), stinginess regarding beauty or reputation (vaṇṇa-macchariya), and stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya). Such stinginess, the act of being stingy, the state of being stingy, the desire "let it be for me alone, not for others," the state of one who desires because of the arrival of wealth, the state of an ignoble person, the state of one whose hand shrinks upon seeing those who receive alms, and the lack of cheerfulness of the mind—all this is called stinginess. Furthermore, stinginess regarding the aggregates (khandha), stinginess regarding the elements (dhātu), and stinginess regarding the sense bases (āyatana), and the grasping through decision, is also called stinginess. This is the meaning of the phrase "Paridevasokā sahamaccharā ca."

Regarding the phrase "Conceit and overbearing conceit, along with slander":

Māna (Conceit) means that in this world, someone generates conceit based on birth, lineage, being a gentleman, beauty of complexion, wealth, study, occupation, craft, field of knowledge, learning, eloquence, or any other ground. Atimāna (Overbearing conceit) means that in this world, someone despises others based on birth, lineage... or any other ground. Pesuñña (Slander) means that in this world, someone is a slanderer. Having heard something from these people, he tells it to those people to divide them; or having heard something from those people, he tells it to these people to divide them. Thus, he divides those who are united and encourages those who are divided. He delights in discord, enjoys discord, rejoices in discord, and speaks words that create discord. All this is called slander.

Furthermore, one conveys slander for two reasons: out of a desire to be loved or with the intention to divide. How does one convey slander out of a desire to be loved? Thinking, "I will be loved by this person, I will be one who pleases his heart, I will be an intimate, I will be an insider, I will be one with a good heart," he speaks slanderous words out of a desire to be loved. How does one convey slander with the intention to divide? Thinking, "How may these people be divided from each other?" (he speaks).
198:
"I shall be one who is dear, I shall be one who is pleasing, I shall be an intimate, I shall be an insider, I shall be one with a good heart"—thus, out of a desire to be loved, one brings about slander. How does one bring about slander with the intention of causing division? "How might these people be separated, be divided, be in groups, be in two parts, be in two ways, be in two factions, be split, not meet, and live in suffering and discomfort?"—thus, with the intention of causing division, one brings about slander. This is conceit and arrogance along with slander.

"Where do these things arise from? Please tell me that cause." (He asks). These eight defilements—quarrel, dispute, lamentation, sorrow, avarice, conceit, arrogance, and slander—why do they occur? Where do they arise from? Where are they specifically born? Where do they originate? Where are they exceedingly produced? Why do they become manifest? What is their source? What is their origin? What is their birth? What is their beginning? Thus he asks the root of these eight defilements, he asks the cause, he asks the source, he asks the production, he asks the beginning, he asks the origination, he asks the nutriment, he asks the object, he asks the condition, he asks the origin, he asks in detail, he requests, he urges, and he clarifies. "Where do these things arise from? Please tell me that cause." (This is the meaning). "Ingha brūhi" means: I urge you, please speak, tell, show, make known, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and manifest. "Where do these things arise from? Please tell me that cause." (This is the meaning).

Therefore, that created Buddha said—
"Where do quarrels and disputes arise from?
Where do lamentation and sorrow along with avarice arise?
Where do conceit and arrogance along with slander arise?
Where do these things arise from? Please tell me that cause."

Quarrels and disputes, lamentation and sorrow along with avarice, and conceit and arrogance along with slander arise from dear things. Quarrels and disputes are connected with avarice. When disputes arise, slanders occur.

In the verse, "Quarrels, disputes, lamentation, and sorrow along with avarice arise from dear things," "dear" (piya) refers to two: beings or formations. Which beings are dear? In this world...
199: ...those who wish for one's benefit, welfare, comfort, and security (from the four yokes)—be it mother, father, brother, sister, son, daughter, friend, minister or intimate, relative, or blood relation. These beings are dear. Which formations are dear? Pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. These formations are dear. They quarrel even when suspecting that a dear object will be snatched away; they quarrel while it is being snatched away; they quarrel after it has been snatched away. They quarrel even when suspecting that a dear object will change and perish; they quarrel while it is changing; they quarrel after it has changed. They dispute even when suspecting that a dear object will be snatched away; they dispute while it is being snatched away; they dispute after it has been snatched away. They dispute even when suspecting that a dear object will change and perish; they dispute while it is changing; they dispute after it has changed. They lament even when suspecting that a dear object will be snatched away; they lament while it is being snatched away; they lament after it has been snatched away. They lament even when suspecting that a dear object will change and perish; they lament while it is changing; they lament after it has changed. They sorrow even when suspecting that a dear object will be snatched away; they sorrow while it is being snatched away; they sorrow after it has been snatched away. They sorrow even when suspecting that a dear object will change and perish; they sorrow while it is changing; they sorrow after it has changed. They protect, guard, keep, cherish as "mine," and are stingy over the dear object. Conceit and arrogance occur along with slander. Based on a dear object, they produce conceit; based on a dear object, they produce arrogance. How do they produce conceit based on a dear object? "We are the gainers of pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches"—thus they produce conceit based on a dear object. How do they produce arrogance based on a dear object? "We are the gainers of pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches; but these others are not gainers of pleasant sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches"—thus they produce arrogance based on a dear object. Slander means: in this world, a certain person is a slanderer; having heard from this person, he tells those people to divide them... (pe)... thus with the intention of causing division, he brings about slander. ... (pe) ... Conceit and arrogance occur along with slander. Quarrels and disputes are joined with avarice. These seven defilements—quarrel, dispute, lamentation, sorrow, conceit, arrogance, and slander—are joined with avarice, joined in detail, joined, and well joined. Therefore, it is said: "Quarrels and disputes are joined with avarice."
200:
## And Slander among those where Disputes have arisen

'Vivādajātesu ca pesuṇāni' means that when disputes and quarrels have arisen, have well arisen, have been produced, have been fully produced, or have manifested, people carry slander. Having heard from this person, they tell those people in order to divide them; or having heard from those people, they tell these people in order to divide them. Thus, they are dividers of those who are united, or they are those who further establish those who are already divided (in their division). Delighting in discord, devoted to discord, rejoicing in discord, they speak words that create discord. This is called slander (pesuṇya).

Furthermore, they carry slander for two reasons: either out of a desire for affection or with the intention to divide. How do they carry slander out of a desire for affection? Thinking, "We shall be dear to this person, we shall be pleasing, we shall be confidants, we shall be intimates, we shall be well-wishers," they thus carry slander out of a desire for affection.

How do they carry slander with the intention to divide? Thinking, "How may these people become separate, become detached, become divided in group, become split in two, become two-faced, become two factions, be divided and not meet, and live in suffering and discomfort?"—thus they carry slander with the intention to divide. Therefore, it is said, "And slander among those where disputes have arisen."

For that reason, the Blessed One said:
"Quarrels and disputes arise in abundance from dear things,
Lamentation and sorrow, along with stinginess, also arise.
Pride and conceit, along with slander, also arise;
Quarrels and disputes are joined with stinginess,
And when disputes have arisen, slanders also occur."

From what cause do dear things in the world originate?
And from what cause do those who wander with greed in the world originate?
From what cause do aspirations and fulfillment, which lead a man to the next life, originate?

"From what cause do dear things in the world originate?" means: What is the cause of dear things? From where are they born? From where are they well-produced? From where do they come into existence? From where do they fully arise? From where do they manifest? What is their origin? What is their source? What is their birth? What is their provenance? Thus, he asks about the root of dear things... (pe)... he asks about the source, he asks in detail, he requests, he entreats, he seeks clarification. This is the meaning of the phrase "Piyā su lokasmiṃ kuto nidānā."

In the phrase "And those who wander with greed in the world," the words "ye cāpi" refer to nobles, brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, monastics, devas, and humans. "Lobha" (greed) refers to whatever greed, the act of greed, the state of being greedy, lust, the act of lusting, the state of being lustful, covetousness (abhijjhā), longing, which is a root of unwholesome action. "Vicarantī" means they wander, they dwell, they move their postures, they maintain their postures, they protect, they sustain. "Loka" (world) refers to the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates (khandha), the world of elements (dhātu), and the world of sense bases (āyatana).
201:
And humans (wander). "Lobha" (greed) refers to whatever greed, the act of greed, the state of being greedy, lust, the act of lusting, the state of being lustful, covetousness (abhijjhā), longing, which is a root of unwholesome action. "Vicarantī" means they wander, they dwell, they move their postures, they dwell by moving their postures, they protect, they sustain, they dwell by sustaining. "In the world" refers to those occurring in the world of misery, the human world, the deva world, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases—whatever greeds wander in the world.

From what cause do aspirations and the fulfillment of aspirations originate? From where are they born? From where are they well-produced? From where do they come into existence? From where do they fully arise? From where do they manifest? What is their origin? What is their source? What is their birth? What is their provenance? Thus, he asks about the root of aspirations and the fulfillment of aspirations, he asks about the source, he asks in detail, he requests, he entreats, he seeks clarification. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Āsā ca niṭṭhā ca kuto nidānā'. Those (aspirations and fulfillments) which become the destination, the support, the protection, the shelter, the refuge, the end, and the destination for humans. This is the meaning of the phrase 'Ye samparāyāya narassa honti'.

Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said this:
"From what cause do dear things in the world originate? And whatever greeds wander in the world?
From what cause do aspirations and the fulfillment of aspirations originate? Those which lead to the benefit of a man's next life?" (Thus he asked).

Dear beings in the world have desire (chanda) as their cause. In the world, those (nobles, etc.) also wander having greed as their cause.
Aspirations and fulfillments have this desire (chanda) as their cause. Those which lead to the benefit of a man's next life.

In the Pali 'Chandanidānāni piyāni loke', "chanda" refers to whatever sensual desire (kāmacchanda), sensual lust (kāmarāga), delight in sensual pleasures, attachment to sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, fever of sensual pleasures, infatuation with sensual pleasures, immersion in sensual pleasures, the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, grasping through craving and views, and the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) which obstructs wholesome states. Furthermore, there are five types of desire (chanda): the desire for seeking (pariyesana-chanda), the desire for obtaining (paṭilābha-chanda), the desire for consuming (paribhoga-chanda), the desire for storing (sannidhi-chanda), and the desire for relinquishing (visajjana-chanda). What is the desire for seeking? Here, someone who is deeply immersed, who has a need, who has a desire that has arisen, seeks after forms (rūpa), seeks after sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible objects.
202: This is the desire for seeking (pariyesanacchanda). What is the desire for acquisition (paṭilābhacchanda)? Here, a certain person, being truly absorbed, being one who has a need, being one in whom desire has arisen, acquires forms, acquires sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles. This is the desire for acquisition. What is the desire for enjoyment (paribhogacchanda)? Here, a certain person, being truly absorbed, being one who has a need, being one in whom desire has arisen, enjoys forms, enjoys sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles. This is the desire for enjoyment. What is the desire for hoarding (sannidhicchanda)? Here, a certain person, being truly absorbed, being one who has a need, being one in whom desire has arisen, hoards wealth, thinking, 'It will be for times of danger.' This is the desire for hoarding. What is the desire for spending (visajjanacchanda)? Here, a certain person, being truly absorbed, being one who has a need, being one in whom desire has arisen, spends wealth on elephant riders, horse riders, charioteers, archers, and infantry, thinking, 'These will protect me, guard me, and surround me.' This is the desire for spending. 'Piyāni' refers to two kinds of dear things: either beings or formations... These beings are dear... These formations are dear. 'In the world, dear things have desire as their source.' Dear things have desire as their source, desire as their origin, desire as their birth, desire as their cause. This is the meaning of the phrase 'In the world, dear things have desire as their source.'## And whatever greeds move about in the world. 'Ye cāpi' refers to Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, householders, renunciants, devas, and humans. 'Greed' (lobha) refers to whatever longing, the state of longing, the state of being longed for, intense passion, the state of intense passion, the state of being intensely passionate, covetousness, and the unwholesome root of greed. 'Vicaranti' means they move about, dwell, maintain their postures, proceed, protect, subsist, and are made to subsist. 'Loke' refers to the world of suffering... the world of the sense bases. This is the meaning of the phrase 'And whatever greeds move about in the world.'## Expectation (āsā) and completion (niṭṭhā) have this (desire) as their source. Craving is called 'expectation.' Whatever passion, intense passion... covetousness, the unwholesome root of greed. 'Completion' (niṭṭhā) means here, a certain person seeking forms acquires forms; he has completion in forms. [Seeking] sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles... family... group... dwelling... gain... fame... praise... happiness... robes... alms-food... lodging... medicinal requisites for the sick... Sutta... Vinaya... Abhidhamma... the forest-dweller's practice... the alms-food-eater's practice... the refuse-rag-wearer's practice... the triple-robe-wearer's practice... the house-to-house alms-seeker's practice... the one-session-eater's practice... the sitter's practice... the any-bed-user's practice... the first jhāna... the second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna... the attainment of the base of infinite space... the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness...
203: ...from the attainment of the base of nothingness to the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one who seeks the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception acquires it; he is one who has completion in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. 'With hope (expectation), the field is ploughed; with hope, the seed is sown. Merchants seeking wealth go to the ocean with hope. By whatever hope I stand, may that hope of mine be fulfilled.' The fulfillment of hope is called 'completion' (niṭṭhā). 'Expectation' and 'completion' have this (desire) as their root cause. Expectation and completion have this desire as their source, desire as their origin, desire as their birth, desire as their cause. Therefore, it is said, 'Expectation and completion have this as their source.' 'Ye samparāyāya narassa honti' means: those things which are a man's destination, island, shelter, cave, refuge, completion, and destination. Therefore, it is said, 'Those which are for a man's future state.' Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'In the world, dear things have desire as their source, and greeds also move about in the world. Expectation and completion have this (desire) as their source; these are for a man's future state.'## From what source does desire arise in the world? From where do judgments (vinicchaya) originate? Anger (kodha), falsehood (mosavajja), and doubt (kathaṃkathā), and those states spoken of by the Ascetic (the Buddha)—how do they come to be? 'From what source does desire arise in the world?' means: What is the source of desire? From where is it born? From where is it produced? From where is it generated? From where is it specifically generated? From where does it manifest? What is its source? What is its origin? What is its nature? What is its cause? Thus he asks about the root of desire... he asks about the origin, he inquires, he requests, he invites, he seeks clarification. Therefore, it is said, 'From what source does desire arise in the world?' 'From where do judgments originate?' means: Why do judgments arise? From where are they born? From where are they produced? From where are they generated? From where are they specifically generated? From where do they manifest?
204:
"From where do they manifest? What is their cause? What is their origin? What is their nature? What is their source?" He asks about the root of decisions. ... He asks about the cause, asks repeatedly, requests, entreats, and expresses appreciation. Therefore, it is said: "From where do decisions also arise?"

Anger, lying, and doubt.
