Anger (kodha) is such resentment of the mind, hostility, striking, opposition, destruction, special destruction, extreme destruction, ruin, special ruin, extreme ruin, making the mind into a different state, destroying the mind, anger, the act of being angry, the state of being angry, hatred, the act of hating, the state of hating, malice, the act of being malicious, the state of being malicious, opposition, counter-opposition, ferocity, abruptness, and dissatisfaction of the mind. Lying is called mosavajja. Doubt is called kathaṃkathā. These are anger, lying, and doubt.

"And those states spoken of by the Recluse." "And those" refers to those states that are associated with, born together with, conjoined with, and concomitant with anger, lying, and doubt—having the same arising, the same cessation, the same physical basis, and the same object. These are called "and those states." Alternatively, those defilements of a different class or a different nature—these are called "and those states." "Spoken of by the Recluse" means spoken of, proclaimed, declared, taught, laid down, established, opened up, analyzed, made plain, and manifested by the Buddha, who is the Recluse because he has calmed evil, the Brahmin because he has barred evil states, the Bhikkhu because he has broken the root of defilements and is liberated from the bond of all unwholesome roots.

Therefore, that created Buddha said:
"Where does desire in the world have its origin? From where do decisions also arise?
Anger, lying, and doubt, and those states spoken of by the Buddha (from where do they arise)?"

"Desire arises depending on what they call pleasant and unpleasant in the world.
Having seen the passing away and arising of forms, a person in the world makes a decision."

In the phrase "what they call pleasant and unpleasant in the world": "Pleasant" (sāta) is pleasant feeling and a desirable object. "Unpleasant" (asāta) is painful feeling and an undesirable object. "What they call" means—
205:
"In the world" means what they say, what they speak, what they utter, what they point out, what they designate. Thus, "what they call pleasant and unpleasant in the world" is said. 

"Desire arises depending on that" means depending on the pleasant and unpleasant, depending on pleasure and pain, depending on joy and grief, depending on the desirable and undesirable, depending on attraction and repulsion, desire arises, originates, is born, is produced, is generated, is manifested. Thus, "desire arises depending on that" is said. 

"Having seen the passing away and arising of forms" means: "Forms" (rūpa) are the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. What is the arising (bhava) of forms? That which is the arising, birth, production, generation, and manifestation of forms—this is the arising of forms. What is the passing away (vibhava) of forms? That which is the exhaustion, passing away, breaking up, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance of forms—this is the passing away of forms. "Having seen the passing away and arising of forms" means having seen, having observed, having weighed, having investigated, having developed, and having made clear the arising and passing away in forms. 

"A person in the world makes a decision" means there are two kinds of decisions: decision through craving (taṇhā-vinicchaya) and decision through views (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya). 

How does one make a decision through craving? Here, for a certain person, unarisen wealth does not arise, and arisen wealth goes to destruction. To him, it occurs: "By what means does my unarisen wealth not arise, and my arisen wealth go to destruction?" Then it occurs to him: "Because I am devoted to the practice of taking fermented and distilled liquors which cause negligence, my unarisen wealth does not arise and my arisen wealth goes to destruction. Because I am devoted to the practice of wandering the streets at improper times... because I am devoted to the practice of frequenting fairs... because I am devoted to the practice of gambling which causes negligence... because I am devoted to the practice of associating with evil friends... because I am devoted to the practice of laziness, my unarisen wealth does not arise and my arisen wealth goes to destruction." Having thus understood with wisdom, he does not frequent the six causes of ruin (apāyamukha) for wealth, and he frequents the sources of income (āyamukha) for wealth. In this way, he makes a decision through craving.
206: Alternatively, one makes a living through plowing, trading, cattle herding, archery, royal service, or some other craft. In this way also, one makes a determination of craving. How does one make a determination of view? When the eye-sensitivity arises, one knows: 'My self has arisen.' When the eye-sensitivity disappears, one knows: 'My self has disappeared, my self has vanished.' In this way also, one makes a determination of view. Regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches... when a touch arises, one knows: 'My self has arisen.' When a touch disappears, one knows: 'My self has disappeared, my self has vanished.' In this way also, one makes a determination of view; one produces it, brings it into being, generates it, fully generates it. 'Jantu' means a being, a person, a youth... a human. 'In the world' means in the world of suffering... in the world of the sense bases. Thus, a being makes a determination in the world. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'What they call pleasant and unpleasant in the world, based on that pleasure and displeasure, desire arises. Having seen decay and growth in forms, a being makes a determination in the world.' Anger, lying, and doubt—these states also exist as long as the duality [of pleasant and unpleasant] exists. One who is doubtful should train for the path of knowledge, having known the states proclaimed by the Ascetic. Anger, lying, and doubt: Anger (kodha) is such resentment of the mind, hostility... Lying (mosavajja) means false speech (musāvāda). Doubt (kathaṃkathā) means uncertainty (vicikicchā). Anger arises based on a pleasant object, and anger also arises based on an unpleasant object. Lying arises based on a pleasant object, and lying also arises based on an unpleasant object. Doubt arises based on a pleasant object, and doubt also arises based on an unpleasant object. How does anger arise based on an unpleasant object? Anger arises based on an object that is naturally unpleasant. Anger arises thinking, 'He has done me harm,' anger arises thinking, 'He is doing me harm,' anger arises thinking, 'He [will do] my...'
207: ...will do harm,' thus anger arises. Anger arises thinking, 'He has done harm, is doing harm, or will do harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me.' Anger arises thinking, 'He has done a benefit, is doing a benefit, or will do a benefit to one who is not dear and not pleasing to me.' In this way, anger arises based on an unpleasant object. How does anger arise based on a pleasant object? Anger arises in those who suspect that a pleasant object will be stolen by thieves, or while it is being stolen, or after it has been stolen. Anger arises in those who suspect that a pleasant object will change, or while it is changing, or after it has changed. In this way, anger arises based on a pleasant object. How does lying arise based on an unpleasant object? Here, a certain person is bound by the bond of shackles; for the sake of release from that bond, he deliberately speaks a lie. Or he is bound by a rope, by iron chains, by canes, by creepers, by a moat, by a wall, by a village, a town, a city, a country, or by the bond of a province; for the sake of release from that bond, he deliberately speaks a lie. In this way, lying arises based on an unpleasant object. How does lying arise based on a pleasant object? Here, a certain person deliberately speaks a lie for the sake of pleasant forms. He deliberately speaks a lie for the sake of pleasant sounds, smells, tastes, or touches; or for the sake of robes, alms-food, lodgings, or medicinal requisites for the sick. In this way, lying arises based on a pleasant object. How does doubt arise based on an unpleasant object? Doubt arises thinking, 'Will I be released from this eye disease, or will I not be released?' or 'Will I be released from ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear disease, mouth disease, or tooth disease, or will I not be released?' In this way, doubt arises based on an unpleasant object.
208:
How does doubt arise based on a desirable object? "Will I obtain delightful visual forms, or will I not obtain delightful visual forms? Will I obtain delightful sounds... smells... tastes... tangibles... family... group... dwelling... gain... fame... praise... happiness... robes... alms-food... lodging... medicinal requisites for the sick?" Thus, based on a desirable object, doubt arises. Anger, lying, and doubt also (arise in this way).

"These states also exist only when there is a duality" means that when there is the pleasant and the unpleasant, happiness and suffering, joy and grief, the desirable and the undesirable, attraction and repulsion—when these are present, existing, and found—then these states also exist only when there is a duality.

"One who has doubt should train for the path of knowledge" means that knowledge itself is called the path of knowledge (ñāṇapatha), the object of knowledge is also called the path of knowledge, and the states associated with knowledge are also called the path of knowledge. Just as the path of the Noble Ones is called the Ariyapatha, the path to the deva realm the Devapatha, and the path to the brahma realm the Brahmapatha; in the same way, knowledge itself is the path of knowledge, the object of knowledge is the path of knowledge, and the states associated with knowledge are the path of knowledge.

"Should train" refers to the three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). What is the training in higher virtue? Here, a monk is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and undertaking the rules of training, he trains in them. From the small aggregate of virtue to the great aggregate of virtue, virtue is the foundation, the beginning, the conduct, the restraint, the protection, and the gateway for the attainment of wholesome states. This is the training in higher virtue. What is the training in higher mind? Here, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures... (and so on)... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This is the training in higher mind. What is the training in higher wisdom? Here, a monk is wise, possessed of wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering. He understands as it really is, "This is suffering"... (and so on)... He understands as it really is, "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering." He understands as it really is, "These are the taints (āsavas)"... (and so on)... He understands as it really is, "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints." This is the training in higher wisdom.
209:
How does a person who has doubt train for the path of knowledge? A person who has doubt, who is full of uncertainty, who is double-minded, and who is indecisive, should train in higher virtue, train in higher mind, and train in higher wisdom for the sake of attaining knowledge, for the sake of touching knowledge, and for the sake of realizing knowledge. He should train while reflecting on these three trainings, train while knowing, train while seeing, train while investigating with wisdom, train while resolving the mind, train while being convinced through faith, train while exerting energy, train while establishing mindfulness, train while concentrating the mind, train while understanding with wisdom, train while fully knowing what should be fully known (abhiññeyya), train while comprehending what should be comprehended (pariññeyya), train while abandoning what should be abandoned (pahātabba), train while developing what should be developed (bhāvetabba), and train while realizing what should be realized (sacchikātabba). He should practice, perform well, and undertake the practice—this is what is meant by "One who has doubt should train for the path of knowledge."

"The Dhamma has been taught by the Ascetic (Samaṇa) having known it" means: "Having known" implies having known, having understood, having weighed, having investigated, having removed the inferior parts of the object and developed it, and having made it distinct. It has been spoken, taught, declared, pointed out, established, opened, analyzed, made clear, and manifested. Having known, understood, weighed, investigated, developed, and made distinct that "All formations (saṅkhāra) are impermanent," it has been spoken, taught, declared, pointed out, established, opened, analyzed, made clear, and manifested. (Similarly) "All formations are suffering"... "All things (dhamma) are non-self"... "With ignorance as condition, formations arise"... (and so on)... "With birth as condition, aging and death arise"... "With the cessation of ignorance, formations cease"... (and so on)... "With the cessation of birth, aging and death cease"... "This is suffering"... (and so on)... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"... "These are the taints"... (and so on)... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints"... "These states should be fully known"... "These states should be comprehended"... "These states should be abandoned"... "These states should be developed"... "These states should be realized." Having known, understood, weighed, investigated, developed, and made distinct the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact... the five aggregates of clinging... the four great elements... and that "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease," it has been spoken, taught, declared, pointed out, established, opened, analyzed, made clear, and manifested.
210:
The Blessed One said this: “Monks, I teach the Dhamma having known it with direct knowledge, not without direct knowledge. Monks, I teach the Dhamma with a cause, not without a cause. Monks, I teach the Dhamma with marvels, not without marvels. Monks, since I teach the Dhamma with direct knowledge and not without direct knowledge, with a cause and not without a cause, with marvels and not without marvels, my advice should be followed, and my instruction should be followed. Monks, it is fitting for you to be satisfied, to be joyful, and to be glad that the Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the Saṅgha has practiced well.” While this exposition was being spoken, the ten-thousandfold world system shook. Having known this, the Ascetic (the Buddha) taught these states.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Anger, falsehood, and doubt—these states also exist when there is a duality. One who is doubtful should train for the path of knowledge. Having known them, the Ascetic taught these states.”

“From what cause do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise? When what is absent do these not occur? Tell me this meaning of non-existence and existence, and from what cause they arise.”

“From what cause do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?” means: What is the cause of the pleasant and the unpleasant? From where are they born? From where are they produced? From where do they arise? From where do they specifically arise? From where do they manifest? What is their root? What is their origin? What is their lineage? From where do they begin? Thus, it refers to asking about the root of the pleasant and the unpleasant... (pe)... asking about the origin, repeatedly asking, requesting, inviting, and seeking clarification.

“When what is absent do these not occur?” means: When what is absent, not existing, not present, or not found, do the pleasant and the unpleasant not occur, not arise, not be born, not be produced, not be generated, or not be specifically generated?

“This meaning of non-existence and existence” means: What is the existence (bhava) of the pleasant and the unpleasant? Whatever is the existence, origin, birth, production, generation, specific generation, or manifestation of the pleasant and the unpleasant—this is called the existence (bhava) of the pleasant and the unpleasant. What is the non-existence (vibhava) of the pleasant and the unpleasant? Whatever is the exhaustion, fall, breaking, dissolution...
211:
Impermanence and disappearance are called the non-existence (vibhava) of the pleasant and the unpleasant. “This matter” (yametam-atthaṃ) refers to the ultimate meaning. It means asking about this ultimate meaning of non-existence and existence.

In the phrase “Tell me from what cause this arises,” “this” (etaṃ) refers to what I am asking, requesting, urging, and seeking clarification on. “Tell me” (pabrūhi) means speak, say, point out, teach, designate, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and manifest. “From what cause” (yato-nidānaṃ) means what is the cause, what is the origin, what is the birth, and what is the root.

Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said:
“From what cause do the pleasant and the unpleasant arise?
When what is absent do these not occur?
Tell me this ultimate meaning of non-existence and existence,
And from what cause they arise.”

(The Blessed One replied thus:)
“The pleasant and the unpleasant have contact as their cause;
When contact is absent, these do not occur.
This ultimate meaning of non-existence and existence,
I tell you, has this contact as its cause.”

“The pleasant and the unpleasant have contact as their cause” means: Dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant, pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling born of contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and is stilled. Dependent on contact to be experienced as painful, painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding feeling—the painful feeling born of contact to be experienced as painful—ceases and is stilled. Dependent on contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) arises. With the cessation of that contact which causes neutral feeling, the corresponding feeling—the neutral feeling born of that contact—ceases and is stilled. The pleasant and the unpleasant have contact as their cause, contact as their origin, contact as their birth, and contact as their root.

“When contact is absent, these do not occur” means: When contact is absent, not existing, or not found, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not occur, do not arise, do not manifest, do not come to be, do not reach completion, do not reach full completion, and do not appear.

“This ultimate meaning of non-existence and existence” means: The view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi) also has contact as its cause; the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) also has contact as its cause. “Yametam-atthaṃ” refers to the ultimate meaning.

In the phrase “I tell you, has this contact as its cause,” “this” (etaṃ) refers to the matter asked. “I tell you” (pabrūmi) means I will teach, speak, point out, make known in detail, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and manifest. This means it has contact as its cause, contact as its origin, contact as its birth, and contact as its root.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: “The pleasant and the unpleasant have contact as their cause; when contact is absent, these do not occur. This ultimate meaning of non-existence and existence, I tell you, has this contact as its cause.”

From what cause does contact arise in the world? Does it arise because of possession (pariggaha)? When what state is absent does possessiveness (mamatta) not exist?
212:
In the phrase "vibhavaṃ bhavañcāpi yametamattham," the view of non-existence (vibhava-diṭṭhi) has contact as its cause, and the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi) also has contact as its cause. "yametamattham" refers to that which is the supreme goal.

In the phrase "etaṃ te pabrumi itonidānaṃ," "etaṃ" refers to the meaning that you ask about, request, urge, and express devotion for. "pabrumi" means I tell, declare, teach, point out, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and manifest. "itonidānaṃ" means having this contact as its cause, having contact as its origin, having contact as its birth, and having contact as its source.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"The pleasant (sāta) and the unpleasant (asāta) have contact as their cause; when contact is absent, these do not exist. The view of non-existence, the view of existence, and that which is the supreme goal—I declare to you that these have this contact as their cause."

Where does contact in the world have its cause? From where do possessions (pariggaha) arise?
When what is absent does the sense of 'mine' (mamatta) not exist? When what has disappeared do contacts not touch?

"phasso nu lokasmiṃ kutonidāno" means: where does contact have its cause, from where is it born, from where is it produced, from where does it arise, from where is it specifically produced, from where does it manifest, what is its cause, what is its origin, what is its nature, what is its beginning? Thus, he asks about the root of contact, asks about its cause... asks about its origin, asks specifically, requests, urges, and expresses devotion.

"pariggahā cāpi kutopahūtā" means: from what cause do possessions arise, from where are they born, from where are they produced, from where do they arise, from where are they specifically produced, from where do they manifest, what is their cause, what is their origin, what is their nature, what is their beginning? Thus, he asks about the root of possessions, asks about their cause... asks about their origin, asks specifically, requests, urges, and expresses devotion.
213:
When what is absent, not present, not found, does the sense of 'mine' (the grasping of 'this is mine') not exist, is not present, is not found, is abandoned, completely cut off, calmed, stilled, incapable of arising, burnt by the fire of knowledge—when what is absent does the sense of 'mine' not exist? When what is vanished, specifically vanished, surpassed, well-transcended, far-transcended, do contacts not touch—when what has disappeared do contacts not touch? Therefore, that created person (nimmita) asked: 'Where does contact in the world have its cause? From where do possessions (pariggaha) arise? When what is absent does the sense of 'mine' not exist? When what has disappeared do contacts not touch?'

(The Buddha replied:) 'Dependent on mentality (nāma) and materiality (rūpa), contact arises. Possessions (pariggaha) have desire (icchā) as their cause. When desire is absent, the sense of 'mine' does not exist. When materiality has disappeared, contacts do not touch.'

'Dependent on mentality and materiality, contact arises' means: dependent on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and visible objects (rūpārammaṇa), eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is called contact. The eye-sensitivity and visible objects are included in materiality (rūpa). The associated states, excluding eye-contact, are included in mentality (nāma). Thus, dependent on mentality and materiality, contact arises.

Dependent on the ear-sensitivity and sound objects, ear-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is called contact. The ear-sensitivity and sound objects are included in materiality (rūpa). The associated states, excluding ear-contact, are included in mentality (nāma). Thus, dependent on mentality and materiality, contact arises.

Dependent on the nose-sensitivity and odor objects, nose-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is called contact. The nose-sensitivity and odor objects are included in materiality (rūpa). The associated states, excluding nose-contact, are included in mentality (nāma). Thus, dependent on mentality and materiality, contact arises.

Dependent on the tongue-sensitivity and taste objects, tongue-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is called contact. The tongue-sensitivity and taste objects are included in materiality (rūpa). The associated states, excluding tongue-contact, are included in mentality (nāma). Thus, dependent on mentality and materiality, contact arises.

Dependent on the body-sensitivity and tangible objects, body-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is called contact. The body-sensitivity and tangible objects are included in materiality (rūpa). The associated states, excluding body-contact, are included in mentality (nāma). Thus, dependent on mentality and materiality, contact arises.

Dependent on the mind-sensitivity and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of these three is called contact. The heart-base materiality and mental objects are included in materiality (rūpa). The associated states, excluding mind-contact, are included in mentality (nāma). Thus, dependent on mentality and materiality, that contact arises.

'Possessions (pariggaha) have desire (icchā) as their cause' means: craving (taṇhā) is called 'desire (icchā)'. That which is lust, intense lust, preoccupation, the unwholesome root of greed (is desire). 'Possessions (pariggaha)' are of two kinds: grasping through craving and grasping through views. This is grasping through craving. This is grasping through views. 'Possessions have desire as their cause' means: possessions have desire as their source (nidāna), desire as their cause (hetu), desire as their condition (paccaya), desire as their reason (kāraṇa).
214:
The physical base (vatthu-rūpa) exists in form; the mental objects (dhammā) exist in those things that have form. Excluding mind-contact (manosamphassa), the associated states (sampayutta-dhammā) exist in name (nāma). Thus, contact (phassa) arises dependent on name and form.

"Possessions (pariggaha) have desire (icchā) as their source" means: Desire is called craving (taṇhā). That which is lust, intense passion ... covetousness, greed, is the unwholesome root. Possession is of two kinds: possession through craving (taṇhā-pariggaha) and possession through views (diṭṭhi-pariggaha). ... This is possession through craving, ... this is possession through views. "Possessions have desire as their source" means possessions have desire as their source, desire as their cause (hetu), desire as their condition (paccaya), desire as their reason, desire as their origin. Thus, "possessions have desire as their source."

"When there is no desire, there is no sense of 'mine' (mamatta)" means: Desire is called craving. That which is lust, intense passion ... covetousness, greed, is the unwholesome root. The sense of "mine" is of two kinds: the sense of "mine" through craving (taṇhā-mamatta) and the sense of "mine" through views (diṭṭhi-mamatta). ... This is the sense of "mine" through craving, ... this is the sense of "mine" through views. "When there is no desire, there is no sense of 'mine'" means when desire (craving) is absent, when it does not exist, when it is not found, the senses of "mine" do not exist, they are not present, they are not found; they have been abandoned, cut off at the root, calmed, stilled, made incapable of arising again, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge. Thus, "when there is no desire, there is no sense of 'mine'."

"When form has disappeared (vibhūta), contacts do not touch" means: Form refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements (upādāya-rūpa). "When form has disappeared" means form disappears through four causes. These are: disappearance through knowing (ñāta-vibhūta), disappearance through investigation (tīraṇa-vibhūta), disappearance through abandoning (pahāna-vibhūta), and disappearance through transcending (samatikkama-vibhūta). How does form disappear through knowing? One knows form—one knows and sees that "whatever form there is, all form is just the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements." In this way, form disappears through knowing.

How does form disappear through investigation? Having known it in this way, one investigates form as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as a plague, as a disaster, as a terror, as a menace, as fickle, as perishable, as non-enduring, as no protection, as no shelter, as no refuge, as empty, as vain, as void, as not-self, as a danger, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of calamity.
215:
One investigates form as a murderer, as non-existence, as accompanied by taints (sāsava), as conditioned (saṅkhata), as Mara's bait, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to illness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, as a state that defiles, as the cause of arising, as the cause of passing away, as gratification, as danger, and as the escape. In this way, through the transcendence that is investigation, form is transcended (disappeared).

How does form disappear through the transcendence that is abandoning? Having investigated in this way, one abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence the desire and lust (chandarāga) for form. For this was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, whatever desire and lust there is for form, abandon it. When it is thus abandoned, that form will be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, and made such that it is no longer subject to future arising." In this way, through the transcendence that is abandoning, form is transcended.

How does form disappear through the transcendence that is complete transcending? For one who has attained the four formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti), forms are transcended, disappeared, surpassed, completely transcended, and gone beyond. In this way, through the transcendence that is complete transcending, form is transcended. Through these four causes, form is transcended.

When form is transcended, contacts do not touch. When form is transcended, disappeared, surpassed, completely transcended, and gone beyond, the five contacts—eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact—do not touch. Therefore, it is said: "When form is transcended, contacts do not touch."

For that reason, the Blessed One said:
"Contact arises dependent on name and form; possessions have desire as their source.
When there is no desire, there is no sense of 'mine'; when form is transcended, contacts do not touch."

In what state of practice does form disappear for a person? How do pleasure and pain also disappear?
Tell me this, how they disappear; it was my thought that we should know this.

In the phrase "In what state of practice does form disappear for a person?", the words "In what state of practice" mean: for one practicing in what way, for one fulfilling the practice in what way, for one conducting the postures in what way, for one proceeding with the postures in what way, for one guarding in what way, for one maintaining life in what way, does form disappear, vanish, be surpassed, be completely transcended, and be gone beyond?
216:
How is it surpassed, how is it well surpassed, how is it far surpassed? — In what way does form disappear for one who is practicing?

How do pleasure and pain also disappear? — In what way do pleasure and pain disappear? Especially, how are they surpassed, how are they surpassed, how are they well surpassed, how are they far surpassed? — How do pleasure and pain also disappear?

Tell me the manner in which it disappears — That which I ask, that which I request, that which I urge, that which I express devotion for—tell me that, explain it, point it out, establish it, open it, analyze it, make it clear, and reveal it. Tell me the manner in which it disappears. Especially, how is it surpassed, how is it surpassed, how is it well surpassed, how is it far surpassed? — Tell me the manner in which it disappears.

The thought occurred to me: "Let us know that" — That we may know, that we may fully know, that we may specifically know, that we may know by depending on various teachings, that we may penetrate and know. The thought occurred to me: "Let us know that." Thus my mind occurred, thus my thought occurred, thus my intention occurred, thus my consciousness occurred — The thought occurred to me: "Let us know that."

Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said:
“How does form disappear for one thus attained? How do pleasure and pain also disappear? Tell me the manner in which it disappears; the thought occurred to me: ‘Let us know that.’”

Neither with normal perception, nor with abnormal perception,
Neither without perception, nor with perception vanished.
For one thus attained, form disappears;
For the conceptual proliferations have perception as their cause.

Neither with normal perception, nor with abnormal perception — Those who abide in normal perception are called “percipient” (saññasaññī); he does not abide in normal perception. Those who are mad or deranged are called “abnormally percipient” (visaññasaññī); he is neither mad nor deranged — Neither with normal perception, nor with abnormal perception.
217:
“Neither without perception, nor with perception vanished” — Those who have entered the attainment of cessation and non-percipient beings are called “non-percipient” (asaññī); he is neither one who has entered the attainment of cessation nor a non-percipient being. Those who have attained the four formless attainments are called “those with perception vanished” (vibhūtasaññī); he is not one who has attained the four formless attainments. Therefore, it is said, “Neither without perception, nor with perception vanished.”

“For one thus attained, form disappears” — Here, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. With the mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the attainment of the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana). For one thus attained, thus practicing, thus behaving, thus conducting himself, thus guarding, thus maintaining, thus sustaining himself, form disappears, is surpassed, well surpassed, far surpassed. Therefore, it is said, “For one thus attained, form disappears.”

“For the conceptual proliferations have perception as their cause” — The conceptual proliferations (papañcasaṅkhā) are the proliferations of craving (taṇhā), views (diṭṭhi), and conceit (māna). They have perception as their cause, perception as their origin, perception as their birth, perception as their source. Therefore, it is said, “For the conceptual proliferations have perception as their cause.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Neither with normal perception, nor with abnormal perception, neither without perception, nor with perception vanished. For one thus attained, form disappears; for the conceptual proliferations have perception as their cause.”

What we asked, you have explained to us; we ask another thing, please tell us that. Do some wise men here say that this is the highest purity of the being (yakkha), or do they say there is something else besides this?

“What we asked, you have explained to us” — What we asked, requested, urged, and expressed devotion for. “Explained to us” means: it has been told, explained in detail, pointed out, established, opened, analyzed, and clearly revealed.

“We ask another thing, please tell us that” — We ask another question, request, urge, express devotion, and ask further. “Please tell us that” means: I request, please tell, explain, point out, establish, open, analyze, make clear, and reveal.
218:
Venerable Sir, please speak, point out, designate, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and make it manifest. We ask you another question; please answer that question. Do some who claim to be wise in this world say that this extent of formless attainments (arūpa-samāpatti) is the highest purity of a being? Some recluses and brahmins speak of these formless attainments as the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the principal, the highest, and the most excellent; they utter, speak, show, and designate them. 'Yakkhassa' means of a being, a man, a youth, a creature, a person, a soul, a jāgu, a living being, an indagu, or a human. 'Suddhiṃ' means purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and total liberation. 'Idha paṇဍitāse' refers to those who are usually called wise in this world according to their own views, those who speak firmly, those who speak methodically, those who speak with reason, those who speak with characteristics, those who speak with causes, and those who speak with opportunity. Do they say that this extent is the highest purity of a being? Or do they say there is something else other than these formless attainments? Or do some recluses and brahmins, having surpassed, transcended, and gone beyond these formless attainments, speak of another superior purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and total liberation of a being? 

Therefore, that created being (nimmita) asked this: 
'You have explained to us what we asked; we will ask another question, please answer that too. Do some who claim to be wise in this world say that this extent is the highest purity of a being? Or do they say there is something else other than this?' 

[The Buddha replied:] 
'Some who claim to be wise in this world say that this extent is the highest purity of a being. Among them, some, claiming to be skilled, speak of a doctrine regarding the state without remainder (anupādisesa). Some who claim to be wise in this world say that this extent is the highest purity of a being.' 

There are some recluses and brahmins who hold the view of eternalism (sassatavāda); they speak of these formless attainments as the foremost, the best, the distinguished, the principal, the highest, and the most excellent; they utter, speak, show, and designate them. 'Yakkhassa' means of a being, a man, a youth, a creature, a person, a soul, a jāgu, a living being, an indagu, or a human. 'Suddhiṃ' means purity, supreme purity, complete purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and total liberation. 'Idha paṇဍitāse' refers to those who are usually called wise in this world, those who speak firmly, those who speak methodically...
219:
...because of speaking with reason, speaking with characteristics, speaking with causes, and speaking with opportunity according to their own views, some who claim to be wise in this world say that this extent is the purity of a being. 

Among those recluses and brahmins, some hold the view of annihilationism (ucchedavāda); being threatened by existence, they delight in non-existence (vibhava). Those annihilationists speak of the calming, the stilling, the complete stilling, the cessation, and the subsiding of a being. They say, 'Friends, does this self get cut off due to the breaking up of the body, does it perish, does it not exist after death? To this extent, it is the Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna).' Because of claiming to be skilled, claiming to be wise, speaking firmly, speaking appropriately, speaking with reason, speaking with characteristics, speaking with causes, and speaking with opportunity according to their own views, some among them speak of a doctrine regarding the Nibbāna without remainder. 

Therefore, the Blessed One said: 
'Some who claim to be wise in this world say that this extent is the purity of a being. 
Among them, some, claiming to be skilled, speak of a doctrine regarding the Nibbāna without remainder.' 

That investigating sage (muni), knowing these people as 'those who resort to eternalism,' 'those who resort to annihilationism,' or 'those who resort to both eternalism and annihilationism,' having weighed, investigated, and developed the knowledge of their lack of benefit, and having made each clear, understands the views they depend on. 

A 'Muni' is so called because knowledge is called 'mona.' ... One who has transcended the net of craving and views is called a Muni. That Muni, knowing that they are resorting to eternalism, annihilationism, or both eternalism and annihilationism, having weighed, investigated, and developed the knowledge of their lack of benefit, makes each clear. That Muni, who is an investigating wise one, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious, knows the views they depend on and is liberated. Having known and been liberated, that Muni does not enter into disputes; that wise Muni does not go to repeated existence (bhavābhava). 

'Knowing and being liberated' means knowing the lack of benefit, weighing, investigating, developing, and making each clear, thus being liberated from suffering, liberated from danger, and liberated from all aspects. Without clinging through defilements and views, and through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga), one knows that 'all formations (saṅkhāra) are impermanent,' 'all formations are suffering,' and 'all phenomena (dhamma) are non-self (anatta),' and thus is liberated. Knowing that whatever is of the nature to arise is of the nature to cease, one is liberated from suffering.
220:
‘Vimutto’ (liberated) means one who is liberated, freed, released, and well-liberated through the ultimate liberation of non-clinging. Having known, understood, weighed, investigated, developed, and made clear that ‘All formations are impermanent,’ one is liberated, freed, released, and well-liberated through the ultimate liberation of non-clinging. Having known... that ‘All formations are suffering’... that ‘All things are non-self’... [Pe]... having known, understood, weighed, investigated, developed, and made clear that ‘Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease,’ one is liberated, freed, released, and well-liberated through the ultimate liberation of non-clinging; thus, one is liberated through knowledge.

‘Na vivādameti’ (does not enter into dispute) means he does not quarrel, does not engage in strife, does not contend, does not dispute, and does not engage in verbal conflict. For this was said by the Blessed One: ‘Aggivessana, a monk whose mind is thus liberated does not agree with anyone, does not dispute with anyone, and uses the expressions current in the world without clinging to them.’ Thus, one who is liberated through knowledge does not enter into dispute.

‘Bhavābhavāya na sameti dhīro’ (the wise one does not agree with various states of existence) means he does not agree with, does not go towards, does not grasp, does not misapprehend, and does not adhere to existence, to karmic existence, to renewed existence, to karmic existence and renewed existence in the sensual realm, to karmic existence and renewed existence in the fine-material realm, to karmic existence and renewed existence in the immaterial realm, to repeated existence, to repeated destinations, to repeated rebirths, to repeated relinking, to repeated individual existence, and to repeated production. ‘Dhīro’ (the wise one) means the wise, the learned, the one possessing wisdom, the intelligent, the sagacious, the discerning, and the mindful. The wise one is one who is steadfast in wisdom, knows the benefit, accumulates the benefit of both the present and the future, is unshakable in the welfare of oneself and others, always enters into the profound meaning and benefit, possesses clear wisdom, and possesses wisdom like a true scale. Therefore, the wise one does not agree with various states of existence.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
‘Having known these views that are resorted to, and having known the dependencies, that investigating sage, being liberated through knowledge, does not enter into dispute; the wise one does not agree with various states of existence.’

## The Exposition of the Kalahavivāda Sutta, the Eleventh, is finished.

## 12. Cūḷaviyūha Sutta Niddesa

Now, the Exposition of the Cūḷaviyūha Sutta will be stated:

Abiding firmly in their respective views, disputing with one another, they speak as experts: ‘Whoever knows thus, he knows the Dhamma.’ He who thus disparages others is not one who is complete in knowledge.
221:
“They abide constantly in their own respective views” means: There are some ascetics and brahmins who hold views. Among the sixty-two types of views, they accept one or another view, particularly grasping it, firmly holding it, touching it, and adhering to it; they live, dwell together, reside, and abide solely within their own views. Just as householders live in houses, or as those with offenses live in their offenses, or as those with defilements live in their defilements, even so, some ascetics and brahmins who hold views accept one or another of the sixty-two views, particularly grasping it, firmly holding it, touching it, and adhering to it; they live, dwell together, reside, and abide solely within their own views. This is the meaning of “They abide constantly in their own respective views.”

“Disputing, they each say they are experts” means: Having accepted, particularly grasped, firmly held, touched, and adhered to (their own views), they speak differently, speak in various ways, speak against one another, and speak much. They do not speak of a single view, but they speak, recite, show, and express (diverse views). “Experts” means: those who, based on their own doctrine, call themselves experts, call themselves wise ones, call themselves firm ones, call themselves logical ones, call themselves reasoners, call themselves those who possess the characteristics, call themselves those who have the grounds, and call themselves those who have the opportunity. This is the meaning of “Disputing, they each say they are experts.”

“He who knows thus, he knows the Dhamma” means: Whoever knows this Dhamma, this view, this practice, this path. That person has known, has understood, has seen, and has penetrated the Dhamma. This is the meaning of “He who knows thus, he knows the Dhamma.”

“He who rejects this is incomplete” means: Whoever rejects this Dhamma, this view, this practice, this path. That person is incomplete, unfinished, unfulfilled, inferior, very inferior, low, base, insignificant, and meager. This is the meaning of “He who rejects this is incomplete.”

Therefore, the created one said:
“Abiding constantly in their own respective views, disputing, they each say they are experts. ‘He who knows thus, he knows the Dhamma; he who rejects this is incomplete,’ they say.”

In this way, they dispute and argue, and they also say, “The other is a fool and unskilled.” Which of their doctrines is true? For all of them say they are experts.
222:
“In this way, they dispute and argue” means: Having thus accepted, learned, grasped, touched, and adhered (to their views), they argue, create quarrels, create strife, create disputes, and create contention—saying, “You do not understand this Dhamma and Vinaya... [etc.]... explain it if you can.” In this way, they dispute and argue.

“They also say, ‘The other is a fool and unskilled’” means: They say the other is a fool, inferior, very inferior, lacking in effort, lacking in reason, lacking in refuge, lacking in power, unskilled, ignorant, fallen into ignorance, unknowing, unable to distinguish, and of little wisdom. Thus they say, thus they speak, thus they recite, thus they show, and thus they express: “The other is a fool and unskilled.”

“Which of their doctrines is true?” means: Among the doctrines of these ascetics and brahmins, which doctrine is true, real, actual, factual, authentic, and unerring? This is the meaning of “Which of their doctrines is true?”

“For all of them say they are experts” means: All these ascetics and brahmins hold the view that they are skilled in their own doctrine, that they are wise, that they are firm, that they are proper, that they have reasons, that they have signs, that they have causes, and that they have a basis. This is the meaning of “For all of them say they are experts.”

Therefore, that created Buddha said:
“In this way, they dispute and argue, and they also say, ‘The other is a fool and unskilled.’ Which of their doctrines is true? For all of them say they are experts.”

If one who does not approve of another’s practice is a great fool and of very inferior wisdom, then all of them are fools and of very inferior wisdom, for all of them abide particularly in their own views.

“One who does not approve of another’s practice” means: One who does not know, does not see, does not attend to, does not reflect upon, and does not rejoice in another’s Dhamma, view, practice, or conduct. This is the meaning of “One who does not approve of another’s practice.”
223:
"Bālomako hoti nihīnapañño" means: Another is a fool, low, very low, inferior, insignificant, wretched, or of little account. One is of low wisdom, very low wisdom, inferior wisdom, insignificant wisdom, wretched wisdom, or of little wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "Bālomako hoti nihīnapañño."

"Sabbeva bālā sunihīnapaññā" means: All these ascetics and brahmins are fools, low, very low, inferior, insignificant, wretched, or of little account. All of them are of low wisdom, very low wisdom, inferior wisdom, insignificant wisdom, wretched wisdom, or of little wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "Sabbeva bālā sunihīnapaññā."

"Sabbevime diṭṭhiparibbasānā" means: All these ascetics and brahmins are those who dwell in views. Among the sixty-two views, they take up, grasp firmly, seize, misapprehend, and adhere to one or another view, and they live, cohabit, reside, and dwell within their own respective views. Just as householders live in houses, or as those with offenses live in offenses, or as those with defilements live in defilements; in the same way, all these ascetics and brahmins are those who dwell in views... and dwell within them. Therefore, it is said, "Sabbevime diṭṭhiparibbasānā."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"If one does not acknowledge another's Dhamma (view), one is a fool and of inferior wisdom.
All these are fools of very inferior wisdom, all these are established in their views."

"If they are not purified by their own view, (yet they claim to be) those of pure wisdom, skillful and sagacious.
None among them is of deficient wisdom, for their views are likewise perfected (in their own eyes)."

"Sandiṭṭhiyā ceva navīvadātā" means: They are not purified, not cleansed, not fully whitened by their own view, their own preference, their own liking, or their own doctrine; they are defiled and possess defiling qualities. Therefore, it is said, "Sandiṭṭhiyā ceva navīvadātā."

"Saṃsuddhapaññā kusalā mutīmā" means: One with pure wisdom, very pure wisdom, extremely pure wisdom, bright wisdom, or fully cleansed wisdom. Alternatively, one with pure vision, very pure vision...
224:
...extremely pure vision, bright vision, or fully cleansed vision—this is "pure wisdom." "Kusalā" means those who are skillful, wise, endowed with wisdom, powerful, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. Thus, one with pure wisdom is "skillful." "Mutīmā" means those who are sagacious, wise, endowed with wisdom, powerful, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious. Thus, one with pure wisdom is "skillful and sagacious."

"None among them is of deficient wisdom" means: Among those ascetics and brahmins, there is no one who is of low wisdom, very low wisdom, inferior wisdom, insignificant wisdom, wretched wisdom, or of little wisdom. All of them possess only excellent wisdom, distinguished wisdom, foremost wisdom, supreme wisdom, or pre-eminent wisdom. Therefore, it is said, "None among them is of deficient wisdom."

"For their views are likewise perfected" means: The views of those ascetics and brahmins are perfected just like those of the wise; they are well-undertaken, grasped, misapprehended, attended to, firmly adhered to, and resolved upon. Therefore, it is said, "For their views are likewise perfected."

For that reason, the Blessed One said:
"Not being purified by their own view, they (claim to be) those of pure wisdom, skillful and sagacious.
None among them is of deficient wisdom, for their views are likewise perfected (so they say)."

"I do not say this is true, which fools say to one another; they have made their own views the truth, therefore they regard others as fools."

In the phrase "I do not say this is true," "Na" is a negation. "Etam" refers to the sixty-two views. I do not say, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, or manifest that this view is true, not vain, evident, factual, or unerring. Therefore, it is said, "I do not say this is true."

In the phrase "which fools say to one another," "Mithu" refers to two people who engage in disputes, quarrels, strife, many words, various arguments, legal questions, retorts, and talk. They say to one another, speak, utter, show, and call each other a fool, a low person, one of inferior application, one of inferior energy, one of inferior cause, one of inferior disposition, or one of inferior mindfulness.
225:
Fools say this to one another; they speak thus, they declare thus, they recite thus, they manifest thus, they designate thus. They establish their own respective views as the truth.

"The world is eternal; only this is the truth, anything else is futile"—thus they establish their own view as the truth. "The world is not eternal; only this is the truth, anything else is futile" ... "A Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; only this is the truth, anything else is futile"—thus they establish their own view as the truth.

Therefore, for that reason, because of that cause, on account of that condition, on that basis, they regard others as "fools, low, inferior, insignificant, wretched, of little worth, and trifling." They see, behold, look at, contemplate, and examine them as such.

Therefore, the Blessed One said this:
"I do not say that what the fools say to one another is true. They establish their own respective views as the truth; therefore, they regard others as fools."

Some say that what they hold is the truth, the reality; others say that very same thing is empty and false. Thus, taking different views, they argue. Why do ascetics not speak one [and the same] thing?

Some ascetics and brahmins say of a certain teaching, view, practice, or path: "This is the truth, real, factual, actual, authentic, and unerring." Thus they say, speak, recite, manifest, and designate.

Other ascetics and brahmins say of that very same teaching, view, practice, or path: "This teaching is empty, this teaching is false, this teaching is unreal, this teaching is a lie, this teaching is not authentic." Thus they say, speak, recite, manifest, and designate.
226:
“Thus disputing and speaking differently” means: having taken up, grasped, seized, misapprehended, and adhered [to a view], they speak differently. They engage in quarrels, they engage in strife, they engage in disputes, they speak differently, they engage in verbal contention. “You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya... if you are able, resolve the original [point].” Thus disputing, they speak differently.

In the phrase “Why do ascetics not speak one word?”: “Why” (kasmā) means for what reason, because of what cause, on account of what condition, by what indication, from what origin, of what nature, from what source do they not speak one [thing] but speak variously, speak differently, speak diversely, speak against one another, speak many [things], preach, recite, manifest, and designate? Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) said this:

“Some say that what they hold is the truth, the reality; others say that very same truth is empty and false.
Thus disputing, they speak differently. Why do ascetics not speak one [and the same] thing?”

“Truth is indeed one, there is no second, knowing which a person would not dispute.
They themselves praise various truths; therefore, ascetics do not speak one [and the same] thing.”

“Truth is indeed one, there is no second” means: Nibbāna, which is the cessation of suffering, is called the one truth. That which is the stilling of all formations (saṅkhāra), the relinquishing of all acquisitions (upadhi), the destruction of craving (taṇhā), dispassion (virāga), cessation (nirodha), Nibbāna. Alternatively, the Truth of the Path (maggasacca), the truth of leading out, the practice leading to the cessation of suffering, the Noble Eightfold Path, is called the one truth. Namely: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration. Thus, truth is indeed one, there is no second.

In the phrase “Knowing which beings would not dispute”: “In which” (yasmiṃ) means in which truth. “Beings” (pajā) is a designation for living beings. Those who know, understand, comprehend, fully realize, and penetrate that truth would not engage in quarrels, would not engage in strife, would not engage in disputes, would not speak differently, would not engage in verbal contention. They would abandon, dispel, destroy, and bring to non-existence quarrels, strife, disputes, different speaking, and verbal contention. Thus, it means “Knowing which beings would not dispute.”
227:
'nānā te saccāni sayaṃ thunantīti' means they themselves proclaim, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express various truths. They themselves proclaim, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is eternal; this alone is true, any other is false.' They themselves proclaim, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, any other is false.' Thus, it is said: 'They themselves proclaim various truths.'

'tasmā na ekaṃ samaṇā vadantīti': In this passage, 'tasmā' means for that reason, because of that cause, depending on that condition, originating from that cause, [recluses] do not speak of one view; they speak of various [views], they speak of diverse [views], they speak differently from one another, they speak of many, they teach, recite, demonstrate, and express. Thus, it is said: 'Therefore, recluses do not speak of one [truth].'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Truth is indeed one, there is no second,
Knowing which, the people do not dispute.
They themselves proclaim various truths,
Therefore, recluses do not speak of one [truth].'

'Why then do they speak of various truths, those who proclaim themselves as skilled? Have many various truths been heard, or do they follow their own reasoning?'

'kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānāti': In this passage, 'kasmā' means for what reason, because of what cause, depending on what condition, originating from what cause do they speak of various truths, do they speak of diverse ones, do they speak of individual ones, do they speak of many, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express? Thus, it is said: 'Why then do they speak of various truths?'

'pavādiyāse kusalāvadānāti': In this passage, 'pavādiyāse' means they are called 'proclaimers' because they speak specifically. Alternatively, they speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express their own respective views. They speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is eternal; this alone is true, any other is false.' They speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, any other is false.'
228:
'kusalāvadānā' refers to those who hold views, claiming to be skilled by their own view, wise, firm, reasonable, causal, having signs, having immediate causes, and having a basis.

'saccāni sutāni bahūni nānā' means it is said that many, various, diverse, and individual truths have been heard.

'udāhu te takkamanussarantī' means: Or do they arrive by thought, by right thought? Are they led, carried away, or well-conveyed? Thus, do they follow after reasoning? Alternatively, it means they speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express their own intuition, which is driven by reasoning, followed by investigation, and appears to themselves. Thus also, do they follow after reasoning?

Therefore, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) asked:
'Why then do they speak of various truths,
Those who proclaim themselves as skilled?
Have many various truths been heard,
Or do they follow their own reasoning?'

'Apart from the views held as permanent in the world,
There are not indeed many various truths;
Having speculated on reasoning regarding views,
They speak of the dual dharma: "True" and "False".'

'na heva saccāni bahūni nānā' means there are not indeed many, various, diverse, and individual truths.

'aññatra saññāya niccāni loke' means that apart from the firm grasping of permanence through one's own perception, only one truth is spoken of, recited, demonstrated, and expressed in the world: Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering. That Nibbāna is the calming of all conditioned things, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and the escape from craving. Alternatively, the Truth of the Path (Magga-sacca), which leads to the escape from suffering, is called the one truth. The practice leading to Nibbāna is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: Right View... up to Right Concentration.

'takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā, saccaṃ musāti dvayadhammamāhū' means having reasoned, speculated, and thought, they generate views, cause them to increase, make them manifest, and make them very manifest. Having generated views, they speak, teach, recite, demonstrate, and express: 'My view is true, your view is false.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'There are not indeed many various truths... they speak of the dual dharma.' One who is well-dependent on these views in what is seen, heard, practiced as virtue, or sensed, and who does not see clearly, remains in the determined view and is like the many...
229:
They produce, they bring into existence, they bring forth fully. Having produced, brought into existence, and brought forth fully the views, they say: "My truth is real, yours is false." Thus they speak, thus they preach, thus they recite, thus they explain, thus they express. Having speculated on thoughts and views, they speak of the dual phenomena of "truth and falsehood."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Indeed, there are not many and various truths, eternal in the world, apart from perception. Having speculated on thoughts and views, they speak of the dual phenomena of 'truth and falsehood'."

One who does not see clearly, relying on these things—on what is seen, heard, virtue and vows, or what is sensed—stands on their decision and, laughing, says: "The other is a fool, unskilled."

Regarding the phrase "One who does not see clearly, relying on these things—on what is seen, heard, virtue and vows, or what is sensed": this means living by relying on, depending on, grasping, misapprehending, and being obsessed with a view or the purity of a view, what is heard or the purity of what is heard, a habit or the purity of a habit, a practice or the purity of a practice, or what is sensed or the purity of what is sensed. "Vimānadassī" (one who does not see clearly/disparages) means not showing respect. Alternatively, causing displeasure is also called "vimānadassī."

Regarding the phrase "stands on their decision and, laughing": the sixty-two types of views are called "decisions" (vinicchaya). Standing, being firmly established, grasping, misapprehending, and being obsessed with that decision of views is called "standing on decision" (vinicchaye ṭhatvā). "Pahassamāno" (laughing) means being pleased, joyful, very joyful, delighted, and having fulfilled intentions. Alternatively, laughing while showing one's teeth is also called "pahassamāno."

Regarding the phrase "says the other is a fool, unskilled": this means they speak, preach, recite, explain, and express thus: "The other is a fool, low, very low, inferior, base, of poor disposition, insignificant, unskilled, ignorant, fallen into ignorance, unknowing, unable to distinguish, of little wisdom, or witless."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
230:
“Whether in what is seen, heard, virtue, or what is sensed (muta), one who, relying on these, looks down upon others, and standing by their own judgment, laughs and says, 'The other is a fool, an unskilled person.' By whatever reason one regards another as a fool, by that same reason one calls oneself skilled. Being one who considers oneself skilled, he looks down on others and says that very thing,” (so said the Blessed One).

“By whatever reason one regards another as a fool” means: by whatever cause, by whatever condition, by whatever reason, by whatever origin one regards, sees, views, looks at, gazes at, or examines another as a fool, as inferior, as low, as base, as wretched, as one of low disposition, or as one of little power. This is the meaning of the phrase “By whatever reason one regards another as a fool.”

“By that same reason one calls oneself skilled” means: the self is called “ātumāna.” That person, by that same cause, by that same condition, by that same reason, by that same origin, says of himself, “I am skilled, I am wise, I am a person of wisdom, I am intelligent, I am possessed of knowledge, I am discerning, I am a sage who knows correctly.” This is the meaning of the phrase “By that same reason one calls oneself skilled.”

“Being one who considers oneself skilled” means: one who, by his own view, considers only himself as skilled, as wise, as firm, as proper, as logical, as consistent with characteristics, as having a reason, or as having a foundation. This is the meaning of the phrase “Being one who considers oneself skilled.”

“He looks down on others and says that very thing” means: “looking down on others” refers to not showing respect to others or causing them displeasure. “Says that very thing” means saying of that very view, “This person is one of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), one of perverted vision.” This is the meaning of the phrase “He looks down on others and says that very thing.”

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“By whatever reason one regards another as a fool, by that same reason one calls oneself skilled; being one who considers oneself skilled, he looks down on others and says that very thing.”
231:
That person is complete with an overreaching view; intoxicated with pride, he considers himself perfect. He has anointed himself (as wise) with his own mind; for that view of his is thus fully grasped.

"Atisāradiṭṭhiyā so samatto" means: Overreaching views refer to the sixty-two views. Why are the sixty-two views called overreaching views? Because all those views transcend reason, transcend characteristics, and transcend proper grounds; for that reason, the sixty-two views are called overreaching views. All views are also overreaching views. Why are all views called overreaching views? Because those [holders of views] surpass, exceed, and go beyond one another to generate, produce, bring into being, and specifically manifest views; for that reason, all views are called overreaching views. "Atisāradiṭṭhiyā so samatto" means he is complete with that overreaching view, fully possessed of it, and not deficient in it.

"Mānena matto paripuṇṇamānī" means: He is intoxicated by his own view and by the pride associated with that view; he is heedless, crazed, and excessively intoxicated; thus, "intoxicated with pride." "Paripuṇṇamānī" means one who considers himself perfect, one who considers himself fully complete, one who considers himself not deficient; thus, "intoxicated with pride, imagining himself perfect."

"Sayameva sāmaṃ manasābhisitto" means: He anoints himself with his own mind, thinking, "I am skilled, a pundit, wise, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious"; thus, "he has anointed himself with his own mind."

"Diṭṭhī hi sā tassa tathā samattā" means: That view of his is thus fully accepted, taken up, grasped, adhered to, entered into, and resolved upon; thus, "for that view of his is thus completed."

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"That person is complete with an overreaching view; intoxicated with pride, he considers himself perfect. He has anointed himself with his own mind; for that view of his is thus fully grasped."

If one were inferior because of another's word, then he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other]. If one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge, then there would be no fool among the recluses.

"Parassa ce hi vacasā nihīno" means: By another's word, by speech, because of blame, because of contempt, or because of accusation, another is a fool, inferior, very inferior, low, base, of mean disposition, or of mean courage.

"Tumo sahā hoti nihīnapañño" means: He too, along with that speech, is one of inferior wisdom, one of inferior wisdom, one of deficient effort in wisdom, one of low wisdom, one of base wisdom, one of mean doubt in wisdom, or one of mean courage in wisdom. If he himself...
232:
Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'That person is complete with an overreaching view; intoxicated with pride, he considers himself perfect. He has anointed himself (as wise) with his own mind; for that view of his is thus fully grasped. If one were inferior because of another's word, then he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other]. If one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge, then there would be no fool among the recluses.'

'Parassa ce hi vacasā nihīno' means: By another's word, by speech, because of blame, because of contempt, or because of accusation, another is a fool, inferior, very inferior, of inferior effort, of inferior cause, of mean disposition, or of mean courage; thus, 'if one were inferior because of another's word.'

'Tumo sahā hoti nihīnapañño' means: He too, along with that speech, is one of inferior wisdom, one of deficient effort in wisdom, one of inferior effort in wisdom, one of inferior cause in wisdom, one of mean doubt in wisdom, or one of mean courage in wisdom; thus, 'he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other].'

'Atha ce sayaṃ vedagū hoti dhီro' means: Furthermore, if he himself is one who has reached the end of knowledge, a wise man, a pundit, one who knows distinctly, one of great wisdom, one who possesses knowledge, one who can analyze, or one whose wisdom is like a true scale; thus, 'if one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge.'

'Na koci bālo samaṇesu atthi' means: Among recluses, there is no fool, no inferior person, no person of deficient effort, no person of inferior effort, no person of inferior cause, no person of mean disposition, or no person of mean courage. All of them possess praised wisdom, specially praised wisdom, chief wisdom, distinguished wisdom, supreme wisdom, or excellent wisdom; thus, 'there would be no fool among the recluses.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'If one were inferior because of another's word, then he would be a person of inferior wisdom along with [the other]. If one were himself a wise man who has reached the end of knowledge, then there would be no fool among the recluses.'

Those who proclaim a doctrine other than this Right View have fallen away from purity and are incomplete. Thus do the many sectarians speak, for they are enamored with their own views.

'Aññaṃ ito yābhivadanti dhammaṃ, aparaddhā suddhimakevalီ te' means: Those who proclaim a doctrine, view, practice, or cause other than this Right View have fallen away from the stainless path, the faultless path, the well-purified path, the bright path, or the completely bright path. They have missed it, erred, declined, fallen from the cause, or failed through ignorance...
233:
They have failed [in purity], they are not complete, not perfect, they are low, base, inferior, mean, of poor intent, and of poor capability. Those who speak of a doctrine (view, practice, cause) other than this Sammādiṭṭhi have failed and fallen away from the pure path and the white path; they are not complete.

"Thus sectarians speak of many views" means: A view is called a "tittha." Those who hold views are called "titthiyas." Many sectarians speak, teach, recite, show, and express many views.

"They are deeply attached to their own views through the passion for views" means: They are attached and deeply devoted to their own views through the passion for views.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"Those who speak of a doctrine other than this [Sammādiṭṭhi] have failed in purity and are not complete. Thus sectarians speak of many views; they are deeply attached to their own views through the passion for views."

"They say purity is only in this [view], they do not say there is purity in other doctrines. Thus many sectarians are established, each speaking firmly of their own path."

"They say purity is only in this [view]" means: They speak, teach, recite, show, and express that in their own view alone there is purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation. "The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, any other is false"—thus they speak, teach, recite, show, and express that in this view alone there is purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, and absolute liberation. "The world is not eternal... the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, any other is false"—thus they speak, teach, recite, show, and express that in this view alone there is purity (suddhi), visuddhi, parisuddhi, mutti, vimutti, and parimutti.

"They do not say there is purity in other doctrines" means: Setting aside their own teacher, teaching, group, view, practice, and path, they cast away, reject, and discard all other doctrines. They say, "That teacher is not all-knowing, the doctrine is not well-expounded, the group is not well-practiced, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path does not lead out [of suffering]. There is no purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or absolute liberation here. In this [other] view, they are not purified, not supremely purified, not absolutely purified, not liberated, not supremely liberated, or absolutely liberated." Thus they speak, teach, recite, show, and express.
234:
"They are low, poor in effort, poor in intent, poor in cause, poor in disposition, and poor in capability"—thus they say, teach, recite, show, and express. Setting aside their own teacher, teaching, group, view, practice, and cause, they reject all other doctrines and say there is no purity in other doctrines. "That teacher is not all-knowing, the doctrine is not well-expounded, the group is not well-practiced, the view is not good, the practice is not well-prescribed, the path does not lead out [of suffering]. There is no purity, supreme purity, absolute purity, liberation, supreme liberation, or absolute liberation here. In this [other] view, they are not purified, not supremely purified, not absolutely purified, not liberated, not supremely liberated, or absolutely liberated."

"Thus many sectarians are established, each in their own way" means: A view is called a "tittha." Those who hold views are called "titthiyas." Many sectarians are well-established, fixed, attached, resorted to, deeply involved in, and convinced of many views.

"They speak firmly of their own views" means: The doctrine, the view, the practice, and the path are called one's own path (sakāyana). In their own path, they are firm-speakers, steady-speakers, strong-speakers, and established-speakers.

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
"They say purity is only in this Dispensation; they say there is no purity in other doctrines. Thus many sectarians are established, each speaking firmly of their own view."

One who speaks firmly of his own path, saying "Only this view is correct," whom among others would he regard as a "fool" based on that? He himself would bring about quarrels, calling another a fool and one of impure doctrine.

"One who speaks firmly of his own path" means: The doctrine, view, practice, and path are called one's own path. One who speaks firmly in his own path, saying "Only this view is correct," is one who has a determined view, a strong view, and is an established-speaker.

"Whom among others would he regard as a fool?" means: In one's own view, one's own preference, one's own liking, and one's own doctrine, whom would he regard as a fool, as low, as base, as inferior, as mean, as of poor cause, as of poor intent, or as of poor capability? Whom would he see, whom would he look upon, whom would he observe, whom would he contemplate, or whom would he investigate [as such]?
235:
He who says that another is a fool and of impure nature brings about disputes by himself. One who says that another is a fool, low, very low, extremely low, of low cause, of low disposition, of low power, of impure nature, of especially impure nature, of completely impure nature, or not of pure nature—such a person, speaking thus, talking thus, reciting thus, showing thus, and calling thus, brings about, well-brings about, carries, well-carries, pulls, well-pulls, takes up, grasps, and adheres to quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, and verbal conflicts by himself. Therefore, it is said: 'He who says that another is a fool and of impure nature brings about disputes by himself.'

Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'One who speaks while standing firmly in one's own view, whom could he regard as a fool in this matter?
He who says that another is a fool and of impure nature brings about disputes by himself.'

Standing in judgment (views) and measuring by oneself, one enters into great disputes in the world.
Having abandoned all judgments (views), a being does not engage in verbal conflict in the world.

'Vinicchaye ṭhatvā sayaṃ pamāya' means: 'Judgments' refers to the sixty-two types of wrong views. Standing, being established, grasping, adhering to, and being obsessed with those judgments (views) is called 'standing in judgment'. 'Measuring by oneself' means comparing and measuring by oneself. Thinking, 'This teacher is the Omniscient Buddha,' 'This Dhamma is well-expounded,' 'This Saṅgha is well-practiced,' 'This view is good,' 'This practice is well-prescribed,' 'This path leads out of suffering'—measuring and comparing in this way is called 'standing in judgment and measuring by oneself'.

'Uddhaṃsa lokasmiṃ vivādameti' means: 'Uddhaṃsa' refers to the future. Placing one's own view above, one enters, approaches, arrives at, grasps, adheres to, and becomes obsessed with quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, and verbal conflicts by oneself. Thus it is said, 'one enters into disputes in the world regarding the future.' Alternatively, one engages in quarrels, strife, contention, disputes, and verbal conflicts with another superior view, saying, 'You do not understand this Dhamma-Vinaya... and so on... explain it if you can.' This also is 'entering into disputes in the world regarding the future'.
236:
'Having abandoned all judgments (views)' means: The sixty-two types of views are called judgments (vinicchaya).
